Title: Flaw in Linux NFS file sharing exposes servers to remote takeover
Context: Researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s NFS file-sharing server that lets unauthenticated attackers obtain a root shell on affected systems
Full Text:
Researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s NFS file-sharing server that lets unauthenticated attackers obtain a root shell on affected systems. The flaw remained undetected in the kernel for 12 years, until two researchers, one using an AI agent, discovered it independently.

NFS is typically used inside local networks, including in container networks in Kubernetes clusters and on build servers in development environments. However, it is also enabled on many embedded devices and in network-attached storage (NAS) devices which might be running older kernel versions and can only be patched with firmware updates.

Tracked as CVE-2026-99362 and dubbed NFS2ROOT, the flaw affects systems running the NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 versions of the Network File System protocol, the default in many Linux distributions. The vulnerability allows anyone who can reach a server’s port 2049 to corrupt the memory of the nfsd process, the kernel component that serves NFS requests. It is rated 9.8 in severity.

A researcher with French security agency ANSSI, Jérémy Jean, found the bug in August, and his fix was merged into the mainline kernel on September 14.

According to security firm OpenSec Intelligence, which also discovered the heap overflow vulnerability and published technical details about it this week, the flaw can be exploited to gain a shell with root privileges. OpenSec found the bug using its AI-powered security testing harness and submitted its own patch to the Linux kernel maintainers on September 22.

However, since it takes time for all supported kernel branches to backport fixes, the bug wasn’t disclosed, nor was a CVE ID assigned, until November 19.

The flaw was introduced in Linux 3.16 in 2014 and is now patched in eight stable kernel branches: 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1.

On systems that can’t be immediately patched, administrators are advised to use firewall rules that block access to port 2049 from untrusted systems. Another option is to turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2 in the nfsd config and then restart the service, but this will turn off pNFS and some features.

Title: pCloud confirms password manager hack after suspicious login alerts
Context: The pCloud Pass password manager suffered a cyberattack, with users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts even with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled
Full Text:
The pCloud Pass password manager suffered a cyberattack, with users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts even with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled.

The incident was first reported by numerous pCloud customers who began receiving email notifications informing them that a new device had connected to their pCloud Pass accounts.

In two Reddit threads, customers worldwide reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named "pd" connected to their account from the IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg, which users say belongs to pCloud's own infrastructure.

Several customers reported receiving the alerts despite having two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled on their accounts. However, when customers checked their accounts for connected devices, some found no unfamiliar devices listed.

Other pCloud customers reported receiving the same notifications despite never having used the company's password manager, including one who said the notification was sent to an email address associated with a pCloud storage account they had requested be deleted almost a year ago.

In response to the reports, pCloud confirmed its password manager had suffered a cyberattack, which the company says was quickly contained.

"A cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred, which was promptly contained by the pCloud team," reads pCloud's statement.

"Unfortunately, a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made. Our system sends a notification automatically to each of these addresses."

pCloud says the attack was isolated to its password manager and that its cloud storage services were not affected.

The company says that passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass have not been compromised, explaining that the data is encrypted on customers' devices and can only be decrypted using their master passwords.

However, pCloud did not disclose whether any encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack.

This matters because threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults could try to crack them offline without being subject to the service's login rate limits or two-factor authentication protections.

This was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults.

Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak or reused master passwords to access stored cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.

A reader who contacted BleepingComputer also noted that the "Open settings" link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, which appears to be a quality assurance (QA) environment rather than the password manager's production website.

BleepingComputer confirmed that the link pointed to the same hostname in a copy of the notification shared with us.

In its statement, pCloud also discussed how advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, but did not specifically state that this was an AI-powered attack.

The company is also warning customers to watch for phishing attacks, stating that it will never ask for their master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat.

The pCloud Pass incident is the latest in a series of cyberattacks impacting password managers this month.

Earlier in November, mSeven Software warned mSecure customers to change stored passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys after a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database.

On Wednesday, 1Password disclosed a data breach after a threat actor compromised an employee's GitHub account and deployed malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

However, 1Password said customers' password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised.

Title: New Boston Scientific data breach exposes personal, medical info
Context: However, the investigators found no evidence that the attackers compromised cloud applications
Full Text:
Medical technology company Boston Scientific is sending data breach notices to individuals affected by a cyberattack on the firm.

According to a notification sample Boston Scientific shared with U.S. authorities, the hacker used social engineering in a voice phishing (vishing) attack to gain access to the company's cloud infrastructure.

The attack exposed cloud-based applications and cloud-hosted data between May 7 and 1.

The company became aware of the unauthorized access on May 12, and the investigation determined that a data breach occurred on November 5.

Individuals in multiple U.S. states have been impacted, exposing personal details and medical information. According to the Texas Attorney General breach portal, the incident exposed information from 117,789 people, which included:

Full name

Physical address

Social Security Number (SSN)

Government-issued ID number (e.g., passport, state ID card)

Medical information

Health insurance information

Date of birth

The letter sent to impacted individuals specifies that patient medical records and data from remote monitoring systems, connected medical devices, and clinical case management or workflow applications were not exposed.

Boston Scientific is a Massachusetts-based medical device maker whose products include stents, catheters, pacemakers, defibrillators, and endoscopes.

It is one of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers, with more than 59,000 employees, 13 manufacturing facilities, and a presence in 127 countries. In 2025, Boston Scientific reported more than $20 billion in revenue.

The company said there was no disruption to manufacturing, ordering, distribution, or service to patients and healthcare providers as a result of this incident.

It also said the incident had no impact on operations, performance, remote monitoring, or the safety of its products and medical devices.

Boston Scientific says it contained the incident, investigated with outside cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement. The notification does not offer free credit monitoring to impacted individuals but recommends using free credit reports and considering placing fraud alerts and credit freezes.

Second breach in 2026

The breach is the second cybersecurity incident this year. On August 25, Boston Scientific disclosed a cyberattack that caused network outages and a global operational disruption for the company, including to order processing and shipping.

CrowdStrike’s investigation determined that the attacker breached an internet-facing network device and pivoted to a limited part of the on-premises IT environment. However, the investigators found no evidence that the attackers compromised cloud applications.

BleepingComputer contacted Boston Scientific to learn more about the most recent incident, and a spokesperson confirmed that it is unrelated to the August 2026 intrusion.

The spokesperson declined to share additional details.

Title: Unpatched Cacti zero-day with public PoC gives remote code execution
Context: A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute...
Full Text:
A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers.

The exploit, dubbed "4HTTP2SHELL" (previously 4HTTP2ROOT), was published on Thanksgiving Day by a cybersecurity researcher known as ek0ms savi0r from the Church of Malware, who demonstrated how the vulnerability can be exploited using just four HTTP requests.

Cacti is an open-source network monitoring and graphing tool used to monitor the performance of servers, routers, switches, firewalls, and other network infrastructure.

Because the software can store credentials and SNMP passphrases used to access or read data from monitored devices, compromising a Cacti server could potentially give attackers access to other systems on a corporate network.

The researcher published a technical write-up, a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, and a video demonstrating the attack in a GitHub repository named "Sad Girls 0day Club."

"I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests. No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface," explains the researcher.

The vulnerability stems from weak input validation that allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject SQL statements into the application's database and modify commands executed by Cacti's real-time poller.

The attack requires the Cacti guest account to be enabled but does not require attackers to possess valid credentials.

While the researcher demonstrated the exploit providing root access to a vulnerable server, cybersecurity firm watchTowr explains that the privileges gained through exploitation depend on the account running the Cacti web server and poller processes.

In many deployments, this could be a low-privileged web server account rather than root.

Cybersecurity firm RavenAI explains that the attack abuses weak validation of guest users' graph display settings, resulting in a stored SQL injection vulnerability.

The attack involves an attacker saving malicious SQL statements in a guest user's graph display preferences, which are stored in Cacti's database.

When Cacti processes these saved preferences, it executes the SQL statements, allowing the attacker to modify the poller's configuration and cause it to run malicious operating system commands.

The researcher tested the exploit against Cacti Core 1.2.31, but it is unclear whether earlier versions are also vulnerable.

In a separate post on the GitHub repository, ek0ms savi0r expressed frustration with how companies handle vulnerability disclosures, describing years of security reports being dismissed or closed as duplicates, expected behavior, or issues that could not be reproduced.

"Security researchers are not the bad guys. We're the ones trying to help. We're the ones who read the docs, wrote the repro, and sent the packet capture," wrote the researcher.

"We get cracked because we get gaslit for years by billion dollar companies that treat disclosure like a PR problem."

In an Instagram post announcing the Cacti exploit, the researcher shared a video demonstration of the PoC and said that the vulnerability was not reported to Cacti before being released.

Until a patch is released, administrators are advised to deactivate the Cacti guest account and restrict access to the application's web interface to trusted networks.

Administrators should also review poller configurations for unexpected commands and examine application logs for warnings involving non-numeric values in graph display settings, which could indicate attempted exploitation.

As of November 27, there have been no reports of the vulnerability being exploited in attacks.

Title: Suspected Vietnam-Linked Hackers Target Southeast Asia in South China Sea Espionage Campaign
Context: The attackers deployed a lightweight Python C2 server to automate post-exploitation and targeted a third-party document management system (DMS) by launching password spraying...
Full Text:
A Vietnam-sponsored hacking group has been attributed to attacks targeting Southeast Asian military, government, and legislative organizations with an aim to gather intelligence on South China Sea defense and military agreements.

The previously undocumented incursion set, detailed by SOCRadar, has been codenamed WeaveLotus. The activity is assessed to have comprised five intrusions in Thailand and the Philippines and reconnaissance efforts against Indonesian government organizations.

"Initial access was achieved primarily by exploiting web application vulnerabilities and default credentials in open-source software, including GeoServer, JasperReports, osTicket, and exposed Laravel debug mode configurations," SOCRadar said in an analysis published Thursday.

"The threat actor established persistent internal network access using reverse SSH tunnels and moved laterally into downstream networks and applications."

The links to Vietnam are based on the presence of native Vietnamese-language code comments, operational activity aligning with UTC+07:00 working hours, regional strategic targeting, and custom scripting. The sustained campaign, codenamed RedOps, was observed between August and September 2026.

The threat actor has also been observed conducting open-source intelligence (OSINT), setting up automated Bing search scripts that scraped news and documents on military agreements involving the Philippines, China, and the U.S., with a particular emphasis on the South China Sea, a region of strategic and geopolitical importance.

Earlier this August, Hunt.io disclosed details of another cyber espionage operation undertaken by a suspected Chinese threat actor targeting a nuclear research organization and a marine engineering and shipbuilding company to steal sensitive documents after gaining access through known security vulnerabilities.

"Following the OSINT phase, the operators enumerated government, military, and legislative entities across the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, compromising targets in Thailand and the Philippines across five confirmed intrusions," SOCRadar said. "Activity against Indonesian targets did not progress beyond reconnaissance."

"The core objective of RedOps appears to be the exfiltration of internal records and documents from Southeast Asian governments in support of Vietnam's foreign policy and military intelligence priorities."

A brief overview of the intrusion activity is as follows -

Thai military organization, which likely involved the exploitation of a critical GeoServer flaw (CVE-2024-36401, CVSS score: 9.8) to deploy a SOCKS5 proxy and open a reverse SSH tunnel, followed by hands-on reconnaissance, persistence, and unauthenticated access to Directus CMS API's file collection and asset download endpoints to enumerate records and download a subset of those records. The threat actor also ran Optical Character Recognition (OCR) on the collected data to extract English and Thai text from PNG images, and unsuccessfully attempted to gain access to surveillance video feeds hosted on Wowza to possibly gain real-time visibility into military operations.

Thai legislative organization, which involved the attacker leveraging an exposed JasperReports server with default administrative credentials (jasperadmin:jasperadmin) to upload a malicious report that ultimately executed SQL scripts on the backend Microsoft SQL Server and then deleted the report to cover up the tracks. The SQL commands, in turn, employed xp_cmdshell to launch a reverse SSH SOCKS proxy tunnel over port 443 to WeaveLotus infrastructure ("172.235.245[.]49"). The attackers deployed a lightweight Python C2 server to automate post-exploitation and targeted a third-party document management system (DMS) by launching password spraying attacks using real employee names paired with National ID numbers as passwords. Once authenticated, the attackers collected the entire system configuration, the complete application user directory comprising 1,502 records), along with system audit logs and 5,000 ZIP archives containing sensitive data.

Thai government organization, which involved the attacker gaining root SSH access to a server running Keycloak 3.4 and dumping its credential database, following cracking the PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes offline with wordlists built around Thai Buddhist Era years and then validating them in real-time against the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) token endpoint. The working accounts belonged to users from various Thai ministries and agencies, with two of them granting the attackers administrative privileges. The valid credentials were then used to pull 349,782 records from a downstream application that contained national strategy alignment, reform directives, masterplan targets, sustainable development goals, and five-year fiscal plans, among others.

Philippine government organization A, which involved the exploitation of an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in osTicket (CVE-2021-42235, CVSS score: 9.8) to extract database schemas and dump usernames, email addresses, and bcrypt password hashes for registered staff accounts.

Philippine government organization B, which probed a web application built on the Laravel framework to obtain server paths and fragments of application source code, ultimately revealing directories tied to an internal project-management and budgeting system.

"WeaveLotus conducted broad reconnaissance against Indonesian government agencies [between August and September 2026]," SOCRadar said.

"The operators began with passive reconnaissance, harvesting Certificate Transparency (CT) logs via CertSpotter and crt.sh, before progressing to active Nmap port scans, VPN service fingerprinting (targeting Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Secure, Cisco ASA, and Fortinet FortiGate), and IMAP/POP3 banner grabbing across more than 30 organizations."

The RedOps campaign is notable for the fact that it has only singled out government, military, and legislative institutions in the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, with no evidence that private-sector entities were targeted. This indicates that the activity is consistent with state-directed intelligence collection.

"The RedOps campaign illustrates how a suspected Vietnam-linked espionage operation leveraged exposed applications, weak authentication controls, and persistent network tunnels to conduct intelligence collection across Southeast Asian government and military environments," SOCRadar said.

"The recovered tooling and operational artifacts provide valuable insight into the actor's methods, while the available evidence supports tracking WeaveLotus as a distinct activity cluster without conclusively establishing state sponsorship."

Title: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly hacked in latest federal breach
Context: According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive...
Full Text:
Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department.

According to Reuters, the intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates.

Launched in 2017, Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform managed by the US Air Force that allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance.

According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information.

US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown.

The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, telling Reuters that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities.

The reported Air Force breach follows other cybersecurity incidents disclosed over the past week targeting US federal agencies.

On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies.

The database contains information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records.

The intrusion came two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov.

Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA).

Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems.

It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected.

AI-powered hacking tools fuel cyberattacks

The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform, which the FBI recently warned was being used to automate cyberattacks worldwide.

In an advisory, the FBI said multiple threat actors had used ARTEX since at least August 2026 in attacks targeting government, defense, healthcare, financial, and technology organizations.

ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data.

The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention.

According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

The platform was used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940 in an October attack targeting ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service. Cybersecurity firm Huntress identified at least 162 compromised Microsoft 365 customer tenants during the campaign.

Other attacks linked to ARTEX include:

Attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information of approximately 67,000 people.

A South Korean hacking campaign targeting more than 90 organizations, resulting in the theft of approximately 8.2 million data records and the arrest of seven suspects.

A cyberespionage campaign attributed by CrowdStrike to a Chinese hacking group tracked as Vapor Panda, which targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries and compromised at least nine.

As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX management consoles, with the number believed to be much higher.

It remains unknown whether ARTEX or other AI-powered hacking tools were used in the attacks against the Air Force, FBI, or FinCEN.

Title: Your Firewall Isn't Enough: The Hidden Risk of Unmanaged VMs
Context: Incidents often begin not with the exploitation of a vulnerability or bypassing protection systems, but with shortcomings in basic infrastructure management
Full Text:
When discussing IT infrastructure security, the focus is usually on firewalls, EDR, backup, vulnerability management, and network segmentation. However, all of them are effective only under one condition — if the infrastructure itself is under control.

Incidents often begin not with the exploitation of a vulnerability or bypassing protection systems, but with shortcomings in basic infrastructure management. Every virtual machine, server, access, and IP address must have an owner, a lifetime, and a controlled path for creation and deletion.

When management processes are opaque, the infrastructure itself becomes a source of information security risks, and security tools have to operate over an unknown environment and merely contain the consequences.

This principle is equally critical for enterprise companies and service providers — regardless of whether the platform serves internal services, development teams, or external customers, a loss of control over administration can lead to the compromise of the entire environment.

Why Security Grows Out of Manageability

In modern IT infrastructure, hundreds of systems run on the same resources, and the environment itself is constantly changing — dozens of services are created, scaled, and deleted daily.

In such conditions, provisioning comes to the fore. Deploying a new virtual machine without a regulation and recording the owner leaves "forgotten" VMs in the environment. They do not receive updates, fall out of monitoring, and become an easy entry point for an attacker.

Centralized access management is no less critical. The platform must delineate the rights of users and administrators and record all operations; otherwise, excessive rights accumulate, allowing attackers to move laterally across the network.

We should not forget about the isolation of environments — the resources of different customers at a hosting provider, or internal systems, external services, and development environments in corporate IT infrastructure. If isolation is violated, an incident in the test environment can affect business-critical services.

All this is impossible without lifecycle control — linking capacity allocation to billing, quotas, and timely deletion of resources, so that outdated accounts and "abandoned" IP addresses do not remain in the network.

Finally, manageability is impossible without accurate accounting of the physical layer: the appearance, decommissioning, and movement of servers between racks and sites. Inaccurate accounting generates unaccounted servers and loss of control over security configurations.

Therefore, the foundation of information security is the transparency of resource management throughout their entire lifecycle.

Migration from VMware and the Change in the Management Model

Broadcom's change in licensing policy forced companies to reconsider their infrastructure strategies and look for alternatives to VMware — for example, considering Proxmox VE, OpenStack, and other open-source solutions. However, migrating to a new platform requires more than just the correct transfer of virtual machines.

Over the years of working with VMware, many have become accustomed to perceiving it as a single whole — virtualization, resource management, access, automation, and accounting.

When migrating to another stack, it quickly becomes clear that virtualization is not equal to infrastructure management: the hypervisor is just one element, and the remaining functions have to be assembled from several independent solutions.

Proxmox and OpenStack solve virtualization tasks on their own, but without additional software, they do not cover operational processes and control over the other layers of the environment. As a result, organizations have to independently integrate equipment management systems, resource accounting, access control, and inventory.

The more individual components in the infrastructure, the harder it is to maintain unified security policies — risks arise of losing a unified RBAC, end-to-end inventory, action auditing, and automation.

Therefore, it is important to view migration from VMware not just as a change of hypervisor, but as a revision of the entire infrastructure management model: if centralized control, automation, and lifecycle management are postponed for later, over time they become a source of new risks.

Which Processes a Management Platform Must Cover

After abandoning VMware, companies face the main question — how to rebuild infrastructure management.

When choosing a replacement, it is important to look not only at the capabilities of the hypervisor itself but also at what operational and security processes the chosen solution can cover and what additional integrations will be required.

At the foundation, there should be centralized management of the entire environment from a single interface and role-based access control (RBAC).

Equally important are the isolation of environments or customers, transparent resource accounting, and control of the entire lifecycle — from the creation of a virtual machine to its deletion and the revocation of access.

Also, the platform must manage the physical layer of servers and automate routine operations.

Such an architecture can be built in different ways: assembled from separate open-source tools and independently solving the issue of their integration, or by choosing a ready-made comprehensive solution.

Regardless of the approach, it is precisely the coverage of these processes that returns the infrastructure to the transparency and manageability that the VMware ecosystem previously provided.

How to Build a Unified Management Environment

To avoid assembling infrastructure management from disparate systems, all these processes can be combined within a single ISPsystem product stack.

In this architecture, VMmanager is responsible for virtualization, DCImanager for the physical level of the infrastructure, and BILLmanager acts as the end-to-end layer for resource provisioning, quotas, accounting, and FinOps.

VMmanager automates the lifecycle of virtual machines, including deployment with a preinstalled software stack, and scales up to 60,000 VMs and 700 nodes in a single environment.

Network isolation based on VxLAN supports more than 16 million isolated segments between geographically distributed sites, and a self-service portal is provided for users.

In parallel, DCImanager provides centralized management and full inventory of the physical layer in multi-vendor environments — from servers to switches and UPSs. The platform checks equipment health and disk S.M.A.R.T. data, configures BMC, performs secure drive wiping, automatically installs the OS, monitors hardware status, and controls warranty periods.

All three products integrate seamlessly with each other and work as a single environment, and if necessary, can interact with external solutions — for example, with OpenStack. BILLmanager acts as the end-to-end layer here: it links the provisioning of IT resources with authorization and accounting, allows assembling combined services, and implements showback and chargeback mechanisms.

The built-in BI module with customizable dashboards for analyzing resource utilization deserves special attention. In a corporate environment, it helps to find "abandoned" capacity in time, which development teams forget to delete after completing tasks — such servers do not sit idle without updates and control, and the company reduces hardware and license costs.

How Implementing a Unified Management Environment Affects IT Infrastructure Security

When the processes of managing virtualization, physical equipment, and the resource lifecycle are linked into a single environment, security ceases to be just a set of protective tools and becomes the result of systemic manageability.

Information security and operations teams get a transparent picture of the entire environment — from the physical server to the virtual machine, its owner, and the history of changes, which directly reduces the number of "blind spots."

Automation of provisioning, delineation of rights, and control over resource lifetimes reduce the risk of errors in issuing access, the appearance of unaccounted servers, and the retention of "forgotten" virtual machines. This also simplifies the migration from VMware itself: companies do not just replace the hypervisor, but build a transparent and manageable operating model.

In this article

A hijacked website can expose your personal data or serve phishing pages and malicious downloads

Attackers are exploiting two critical Drupal flaws to take over websites

Drupal site owners should install the latest security update and check for signs of a break-in

Attackers are exploiting a second critical flaw in Drupal, the content management system (CMS) behind many government, university, corporate, and media websites. Site owners are responsible for applying the fix. For visitors, a hijacked site can put personal data and devices at risk.

On November 18, Drupal released a patch for a remote code execution (RCE) flaw, CVE-2026-132165. The flaw could let attackers take over a site by abusing Drupal’s installer file, install.php. Drupal’s security team received a report of attacks on live sites as early as November 19.

On November 25, Drupal released a second advisory for CVE-2026-136716. Some sites in “unusual or incomplete install states” remained vulnerable to takeover after the first fix, including live sites. Drupal says the new flaw is also being exploited in the wild.

These flaws is a serious problem for website owners, because:

No login is needed. Anonymous attackers can exploit the first flaw. They can attempt to reinstall Drupal and gain control of the site or run code on the server.

Hard to spot. Drupal says the user interface doesn’t show whether a site is in the vulnerable state. Already-compromised sites may no longer show as vulnerable.

Already exploited. CISA added the first flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until November 27 to fix it.

Drupal has a history of abuse. CISA has flagged six Drupal flaws as exploited since November 2021. Two of them were used in ransomware attacks.

How to stay safe

A hijacked site could expose data stored there, such as account details, email addresses, and form submissions. Attackers could also serve phishing pages or malicious downloads from a trusted domain or deface the site.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

If you’re a visitor or customer:

Be wary of unexpected login prompts, “verify your account” pop-ups, or surprise downloads on sites you normally trust.

Use unique passwords and a password manager. If a site you use reports a breach, change that password and anywhere you reused it.

Turn on multi-factor authentication where it’s offered.

Keep your operating system, browser, and security software up to date.

Treat emails that cite a “security incident” with caution. Go to the site directly instead of clicking links.

If you run a Drupal site:

Update to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14, then run update.php. Drupal says an update hook must run to fix existing production sites.

Block access to /core/install.php in your web server configuration or .htaccess file if you can’t upgrade right away.

Check your logs for unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account (the first account created when a site is installed). Make sure you control the email address on that account, and consider resetting its password.

If you suspect a break-in, follow Drupal’s guide to responding to a hacked site.

Drupal 10.5 and earlier 10.x releases, and Drupal 11.2 and earlier 11.x releases, have reached end of life. Move to a supported release to receive security fixes.

Sites protected by the paid Drupal Steward service are covered against known attack vectors, but Drupal still recommends upgrading.

Patching alone may not be enough. A compromised site can still look normal after patching, so site owners should update Drupal and check for signs of a break-in.

Cybercriminals broke into FIFA’s systems and gained access to “a limited set of personal and business information,” world football’s governing body confirmed on Thursday.

“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the Zurich-based football governing body told The Associated Press, without saying when the attack happened or what kind of information the intruders took.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. The confirmation came a week after a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) posted a screenshot on X of what it said were FIFA files.

According to the group, the data was exported from FIFA’s Microsoft environment, and the haul contains “a full export from their internal governance systems, as well as some other assorted documents and screenshots from various services.”

The post lists identity documents, immigration records, executive information, financial data and legal documents among the stolen material.

HBHC is a relatively new cybercrime group that listed its first victim on its data leak site on November 19.

“We would like to clarify that we are purely financially motivated. We are not interested in the country of origin,” the gang wrote, before signing off with a promise of “more leaks soon.“

The attack couldn’t have come at a worse time for FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who is under scrutiny after a scrapped plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

FIFA is the second football organization to disclose a cyberattack this week. On Monday, Spain’s LaLiga confirmed that a cybercriminal broke into one of its fan services platforms and stole personal data of people registered with the league’s digital services and those of some clubs.

In this article

Remus malware installs a Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets

The extension can resume stealing unread Gmail messages when you sign back in on the infected device

If you suspect an infection, check your Chrome extensions and secure your Google Account from a clean device

In our earlier post about Remus, we covered the claim that the infostealer could read your Gmail even after you changed your password. New research from Gen Threat Labs traced the supposed Gmail “zero-day” to a Chrome extension that masquerades as Google Sheets. The malicious extension stays installed after a password change and can start reading your mail again when you sign back in on the infected device.

On November 8, the developers of the Remus infostealer began advertising a Gmail “zero-day.” They said it gave access to a victim’s mailbox even after they changed their password and signed out of all sessions.

Gen Threat Labs published its findings on November 24. The researchers found no email-stealing code in the main stealer. That lives in a separate module that Remus downloads from the attackers’ server when the malware runs. The developers advertised the feature as exclusive to their $1,000-a-month Enterprise tier.

The module is a native DLL whose only job is to install a malicious extension in Google Chrome, the only browser it targets. It edits the victim’s Chrome profile files to register the extension and recalculates the integrity checks that protect those files. It also turns on Developer mode, which Chrome requires to run unpacked extensions.

The extension calls itself “Google Sheets” and copies the description of the Google Docs Offline extension. It requests access to all websites. Every minute, it checks Gmail for unread messages, retrieves the contents, and then sends the subject, body, sender, and your email address to the attackers.

So, the password change claim is true?

Only partly. When you sign out or end your Gmail session, the extension stops reading your mail. But it stays installed in Chrome. As soon as you sign back in on the infected device with your new password, it can start reading your mail again.

You might never notice it. The visible clues are a new extension card and the Developer mode switch turned on. But it’s still a persistence trick and a marketing pitch, not a Google vulnerability. Malware able to install an extension silently could just as easily steal your session cookies directly. Which doesn’t make it any less dangerous. Especially when your inbox holds password-reset links and verification codes for your other accounts.

What to do

If you think your device may be infected with an infostealer:

Clean the device. The extension can start reading your mail again if you sign back in on the infected computer. Scan with an up-to-date anti-malware solution, and use a separate, clean device to change your Google password.

Check your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in your address bar. Look for extensions you don’t recognize or no longer use. The fake “Google Sheets” extension is marked as unpacked, meaning it was loaded from local files. Google’s real Docs Offline extension is only available from the Chrome Web Store. Remove anything suspicious.

Check Developer Mode. On the same page, look for the Developer mode toggle in the top-right corner. If it’s on (and buttons like Load unpacked appear) and you didn’t turn it on, treat that as a red flag.

Secure your Google account. When you’re sure your device is clean, change your password, sign out of all devices, and review your recovery options, connected apps, and Gmail forwarding rules and filters.

Review accounts tied to that inbox. Look for unexpected changes, starting with accounts that use your Gmail address for sign-in or recovery. Where available, enable multi-factor authentication or set up a passkey.

To stay safe in the future, only download software from trusted sources. Cracked software and fake installers are common ways infostealers reach your device.

Title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
Context: People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy
Full Text:
This essay originally appeared in The Guardian. It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For.”

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

Title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Microsoft Store App Found Delivering Vinci RAT Capable of Remote System Control
Context: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber attack in which a threat actor leveraged a Microsoft Store application to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) called...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber attack in which a threat actor leveraged a Microsoft Store application to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) called Vinci RAT.

The intrusion, according to eSentire, begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool ("snipp.codes-team[.]com"), from where a Microsoft-signed installer called "Snipping-Tool.exe" is downloaded. Executing the binary leads to the installation of Setup Assistant, an Electron-based application published on the Microsoft Store by ETPS Ltd.

"The application was heavily obfuscated, maintained communication with C2 [command-and-control] infrastructure, monitored the victim's Downloads folder, and supported execution of C2-supplied PowerShell and JavaScript," eSentire said.

"This access was used to launch a malicious PowerShell stager, establish persistence through a scheduled task, and retrieve a previously undocumented PowerShell-based RAT."

Once installed, Setup Assistant acts as a backdoor and is designed to run obfuscated JavaScript that allows it to contact the C2 server at "setup-assistant[.]com" and retrieve arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript code, ultimately resulting in the deployment of the RAT by means of a stager.

Vinci RAT, as the malware is called, is equipped to fingerprint the host, enumerate installed security tools, facilitate remote and reverse shell access, deliver files, and execute shellcode, DLL, EXE, and PowerShell payloads.

Interestingly, the arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript execution is triggered by means of two methods -

Monitor for file names in the victim's Downloads directory by matching them against a predefined list specified in a C2-retrieved configuration ("MSTeamsSetup.exe" and "Reader_install.exe"). If a match is found, it sends an HTTP POST request to the C2 server and executes the response.

The C2 server initiates an update action via the URL setup-assistant[.]com/api/update-status?device=<victim_id>"

The Vinci RAT stager is responsible for running a PowerShell command that disables the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI), generates a unique victim identifier, establishes communication with a C2 server ("monkeysholder[.]info/api.php"), set up persistence via a scheduled task that runs every 10 minutes, and downloads the RAT payload.

Further analysis of the root domain "codes-team[.]com" has identified additional sub-domains that suggest that the threat actors are spoofing software download pages for legitimate applications like Microsoft Teams and Roblox -

roblx.codes-team[.]com

teams.codes-team[.]com

teamsmac.codes-team[.]com

teams-bing.codes-team.com

As of writing, Setup Assistant is no longer accessible on Microsoft Software. It was first released on June 1, 2026, while the "codes-team[.]com" domain was registered in late March 2026.

It remains unclear whether the threat actors themselves took down the app in response to the public disclosure or whether Microsoft removed it, as eSentire noted that the tech giant had failed to take action despite reporting the app through its abuse form on November 10, 2026, responding that it was "not a violation of our terms."

"The campaign highlights how attackers are combining search-engine redirection, fake software download pages, obfuscated Electron applications, and trusted software distribution channels to gain persistent access to victim environments," the Canadian cybersecurity company said.

SAP has confirmed a security incident, and most of the details come from the press, not from the company. The global enterprise found suspicious activity in its IT systems. DER SPIEGEL reported that attackers stole company employees’ access tokens and used them to change and copy source code on GitHub.

“According to information obtained by SPIEGEL, the software manufacturer SAP is now dealing with an incident. The perpetrators may have used AI systems for assistance.” reads the report published by DER SPIEGEL.

The German software maker says it took immediate steps to protect customers and secure its services.

SAP says investigators had found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data at that stage. It didn’t answer detailed questions about the incident. An internal memo cited by Spiegel calls the incident active, and SAP is reportedly handling the investigation under the name “Project Granite”.

Sources inside the software giant also told Spiegel that the attackers may have used AI agents. SAP has not confirmed this, and it is still unclear whether AI played any role in the attack. For now, this should be treated as an unconfirmed report.

Employees were reportedly told not to discuss the incident. The report also says SAP management does not believe it needs to inform customers proactively. SAP reportedly told German broadcaster Tagesschau that customer data was not affected.

SAP has not disclosed how the attackers obtained the employees’ tokens. Cybersecurity News recently reported a separate case in which a malicious VS Code extension stole GitHub tokens, but there is no evidence linking that attack to the SAP incident.

SAP publishes source code for its products and open-source projects on GitHub. However, the report does not say which repositories were affected or whether the stolen code was public or private. This information is important to understand the impact of the incident.

GitHub’s audit log guidance explains how organizations can trace recorded actions back to a compromised token, and administrators can revoke credentials by user and token type.

Title: Microsoft removes WSUS server role in Windows Server 2028
Context: "WSUS remains available and supported in earlier Windows Server releases, including Windows Server 2025, for the duration of each release's support lifecycle
Full Text:
Microsoft will remove the WSUS server role from Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system.

Introduced in 2005 as Software Update Services (SUS), WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) lets IT administrators manage and distribute updates for Microsoft products across corporate networks with many Windows devices.

It gives admins centralized control over the updates, rather than having each device download them individually from Microsoft's servers.

Microsoft has officially deprecated WSUS in September 2024, but said that it still plans to maintain functionality and continue publishing updates through the channel. The change affects enterprise environments that rely on WSUS to manage updates delivered to many devices but does not impact home users or those using Microsoft Configuration Manager.

In a recently updated support document, Microsoft went even further and confirmed that Windows Server 2028 removes the WSUS server role altogether.

"WSUS remains available and supported in earlier Windows Server releases, including Windows Server 2025, for the duration of each release's support lifecycle. You can continue to use WSUS on those releases to manage updates for supported Windows client and Windows Server releases, which includes updates to Windows Server 2028," it said.

"Microsoft recognizes the need to manage updates in disconnected and highly controlled environments. We're invested in supporting these scenarios and we'll share more as the work progresses."

Businesses are now encouraged to adopt cloud-based solutions, such as Windows Autopatch, Microsoft Intune, and Azure Update Manager, for keeping endpoints and servers on their network up to date.

"While the WSUS role remains available in Windows Server 2025, we recommend organizations transition to cloud tools, including including Windows Autopatch and Microsoft Intune for client update management and Azure Update Manager for server update management," Microsoft's Nir Froimovici said in September 2024. "Remember: WSUS remains operational but is no longer investing in new features."

Windows Server 2028 also removes VBScript (disabled by default in Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10) and the legacy Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) utility (deprecated in Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10 21H1) to thwart a wide range of malware and attack tactics abusing them.

Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) support, deprecated with the release of Windows Server 2022 in August 2021, is also being removed in the next Windows Server version, as Microsoft announced a year ago.

Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 last week at the Ignite 2026 conference, and it can be tested by registering for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or applying to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access.

Title: UK Welfare and Pension Services Taken Offline Following Cyber Incident
Context: In November, NCSC CEO Richard Horne warned that AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028
Full Text:
The UK government department responsible for welfare and pension payments has been impacted by a cyber incident, resulting in services being taken offline.

The Department of Work and Pensions (DWP) announced the incident on the official gov.uk website on November 27, confirming online services had been taken offline “as a precaution.”

Regular benefit and pension payments have not been affected and will be paid as normal, the short statement noted.

“We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption,” the DWP said.

“If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links,” the department added.

Claimants are currently unable to sign into online accounts for services like universal credit and state pensions.

No information has so far been provided on how the incident occurred or any alleged perpetrators.

Steven Swinford, political editor at The Times newspaper, reported on X on November 27 that the DWP took down all online services at around 21.00 GMT on November 26. He added that the department has said that although regular benefit payments are continuing, people will be unable to make new claims while online services remain offline.

The DWP is one of the UK’s largest government departments, with 96,890 employees as of 2025. It administers the State Pension and a range of working age, disability and ill health benefits to around 20 million claimants and customers.

Incident Follows UK Government Warnings Over Threat Landscape

The incident affecting the DWP follows repeated warnings from the UK government about the potential for cyber-attacks to take crucial services offline.

In October, Secretary of State for Defence, Wes Streeting, told the public to be prepared for cyber incidents that could remove access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.

In November, NCSC CEO Richard Horne warned that AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028.

It was reported in October that a number of UK government websites were taken offline in response to the ‘PHP2Shell’ vulnerabilities being disclosed ahead of planned security patches, to prevent exploitation of such services.

Trevor Dearing, senior director of critical infrastructure at Illumio, said that the public will need to get used to public services being shut down temporarily to mitigate cyber-attacks.

“Public sector networks are huge, interconnected and full of legacy systems, so when you can't be sure how far an attacker has moved, the only safe option is to pull the plug.”

However, Dearing warned that this approach should not be the long-term answer to dealing with cyber-attacks, particularly when it comes to critical services like pensions and welfare, which millions are reliant upon.

Title: Chinese and North Korean state hackers add ARTEX AI framework to their arsenal
Context: The attackers got in by exploiting a vulnerability in a Citrix NetScaler Gateway appliance and were spotted before they could move deeper into the network, Darktrace reported
Full Text:
State-sponsored hacking groups tied to Beijing and Pyongyang have started running the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft Threat Intelligence warned this week.

Published on GitHub in July 2026 by a user going by Autumn-27, ARTEX is an LLM-driven open-source penetration testing framework that runs attacks largely on its own, with the operator setting a goal and AI agents planning and carrying out the steps needed to reach it.

In November, China-based cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX and began selling access to an ARTEX Pro version, though Microsoft does not link the company to the attacks.

“In the past few weeks, we’ve reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation,” researchers wrote. “These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.”

“As of November 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed both state-sponsored and financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling,” Microsoft reported.

Typhoon is the label Microsoft uses for China-based groups, while Sleet marks those tied to North Korea.

The most recognizable group on the list, Salt Typhoon, is linked to a long-running espionage campaign against telecommunications providers.

In December 2024, the White House confirmed that the group had compromised at least eight US telecommunications providers, where it stole subscribers’ call records, intercepted the calls and texts of specific targets in government and politics, and accessed systems used for court-ordered communication interception by law enforcement and intelligence agencies.

Salt Typhoon was also tied to a July 2025 intrusion at a European telecommunications organization. The attackers got in by exploiting a vulnerability in a Citrix NetScaler Gateway appliance and were spotted before they could move deeper into the network, Darktrace reported.

Three hours to privileged access

In one password spraying run against Microsoft 365, Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group, logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 failures per minute. The group went from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.

Another case moved faster, with an AI agent going from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Storm-0940’s ARTEX-assisted campaigns also include a supply chain compromise linked to ConnectWise and the abuse of app credentials.

Noisy by design

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques. ARTEX does sometimes transmit distinctive characteristics associated with its integrated penetration testing tools. However, threat actors using ARTEX can and do vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking,” Microsoft explained.

Behavior is harder to disguise, and by default ARTEX makes no attempt to hide what it does. Its bursts of varied requests, rapid retries and jumps between attack stages at machine speed stand out in logs.

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre came to the same conclusion about agentic attack frameworks in general. In a blog post published on November 24, the agency said such tools “trade stealth for speed,” generating heavy traffic and interacting with almost everything they find, which makes them easier to detect. It also warned that this may change once future frameworks are built with stealth in mind.

Title: In Other News: Tanker Cyberattacks, EU Quantum Act, New VirusTotal Capabilities
Context: This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help...
Full Text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

ChatGPT Sites exposure

Pluto researchers combed web archives, public code repositories, search engines and other sources and found 16,666 sites created with ChatGPT Sites (which builds and hosts web apps for ChatGPT and Codex users), 12,830 of which were accessible to anyone. Manual checks confirmed sensitive data exposure at 27 organizations, including a Fortune 500 company’s sales dashboard, a freight forwarder’s customer quotes, and a vendor’s sales pitch. Sites are visible only to their owners and admins unless shared, but owners can open them to the entire internet.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

RansomwareHelp co-founder accused of profiting from ransom payments

US authorities have charged Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a Colombian national and co-founder of the ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, with three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that instead of using its own decryption technology as advertised, his company purchased decryptors from cybercriminals at prices significantly lower than what it charged customers. In one case involving undercover FBI agents, Palacio allegedly paid a $6,000 ransom and billed the purported victim $13,260 for decrypting their files.

USDA payment systems breach

A system used by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make payments to farmers has been breached, according to NBC News. Two former department officials said the intrusion could let hackers access databases containing sensitive information on food safety and diseases carried by animals.

SolarWinds and Adobe patch vulnerabilities

SolarWinds has patched several critical vulnerabilities in its Serv-U managed file transfer product, including flaws that can lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution. Adobe has addressed critical security holes in Campaign Classic and Experience Manager, including ones that allow arbitrary code execution, and a medium-severity DoS vulnerability in InDesign.

Container Store restores systems after cyberattack

US retailer The Container Store has restored its systems following a cyberattack that prevented customers from placing orders online. There is currently no evidence that customers’ financial information was stolen. The n0n ransomware group listed the company on its leak site earlier this month, but The Container Store has not addressed the claim.

VirusTotal adds new ransomware detection capabilities

VirusTotal has introduced new ransomware detection capabilities that rely on evidence of user files being encrypted during sandbox analysis. The improvements include a new behavior tag and stricter requirements for assigning the MITRE ATT&CK technique associated with data encryption for impact. VirusTotal demonstrated the effectiveness of the changes against ransomware that evaded detection by all 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

$17 billion targeted in US government anti-scam operation

The US Justice Department’s crackdown on fraud has targeted more than 800 defendants across over 400 cases since March. Authorities have also helped disrupt scam centers in more than 10 countries. According to the FBI, its Operation Blackout has led to the seizure or restraint of nearly $17 billion.

McDonald’s Japan hacked

McDonald’s Japan has disclosed a breach involving a database storing information associated with its mobile application. Hackers gained access to customer purchase histories, device location information, internal customer identifiers and IP addresses, but not names, contact details or credit card data. The number of impacted customers has not been disclosed.

Bithumb uncovers wider breach

South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says more individuals and more types of personal information were compromised in an October cyberattack than initially reported. Bithumb also said the hackers had access for more than two weeks, not one hour as initially believed. The hackers stole data from an internal collaboration system, including identity documents, bank account numbers, transaction histories, and crypto wallet addresses. South Korean media reported that the initial victim count exceeded 7,000, including customers and staff.

Artex gains traction among state-sponsored hackers

Microsoft has observed several state-sponsored hacking groups, including China’s Salt Typhoon, as well as cybercriminals using the AI-powered penetration testing framework Artex. Hackers have leveraged the tool to identify exposed secrets in public code repositories, conduct supply chain attacks and find vulnerable systems. Microsoft says the framework can significantly accelerate intrusions, with attackers achieving privileged access and establishing persistence within minutes.

Quantum Act targets Europe’s cryptographic readiness

The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act includes measures to accelerate the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography and prepare the EU for the security risks posed by quantum computers. The legislation is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe’s quantum technology industry, reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and establish global leadership in the field by 2030.

Tanker cyberattacks

Up to 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially dangerous cargo are believed to have been targeted in a wave of cyberattacks, according to The Wall Street Journal. US authorities are investigating whether Iran is responsible for the attacks.

Radware hacked

An internal report obtained by BleepingComputer shows that hackers breached cybersecurity firm Radware through an unprotected Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet. Customer contact information and credentials associated with AWS, Azure and SFTP storage used by some customers may have been compromised. The company has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment.

Title: Drupal warns of new site takeover flaw exploited in attacks
Context: The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites
Full Text:
The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites.

Last week, Drupal patched a remote code execution (RCE) flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165 / Fail2Install) that lets anonymous users take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.

While the security issue wasn't initially flagged as being abused in the wild, an update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting it one day after patches were released.

The new security issue (CVE-2026-136716), patched one week later, addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched and also lets attackers hijack vulnerable Drupal sites.

"However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state," Drupal said on Wednesday.

"This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised."

While it has yet to share further details regarding these attacks, Drupal warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised admins to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, and to consider resetting it.

They should also check site logs for unauthorized access, focusing on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account, and follow this guide if they find evidence the site may have been compromised.

Those who can't immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14 should secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been exploited in ransomware attacks.
