Title: The British Government is Turning Everyone Into a Prepper
Context: For this reason, he, and several other preppers I spoke to, asked to be identified only by their first name
Full Text:
Prepping was flung into the mainstream, and British preppers—a minority in a largely US-dominated scene—have found themselves drawn out of their (metaphorical) bunkers and into the limelight.

For the most part, preppers I spoke to welcomed the government advice, though they unanimously felt it didn't go far enough (“What’s your plan for day four?” Mike Chappell, a Greater Manchester-based prepper, says.) But public reactions, they say, have been mixed.

Dan Goss, who is based in Liverpool and runs the Start Prepping UK website, says traffic to his site “went bananas,” reaching around 50,000 visitors at one point. The news, he says, has “broken people’s normalcy bias,” legitimising the idea of prepping in a way that no amount of bleak climate news can. He’s observed a rise in what he calls the “normal person prepper”—people who aren’t interested in planning for an apocalypse or learning advanced survival skills, but want to build basic household resilience. Glyn Smith, founder of the prepper community UK Survival Network, reports a similar spike in interest. “It’s not lone survivalists; it’s mums, dads, couples, and retirees,” he says. “Normal people who want practical peace of mind.”

Courtesy of Sawyer

Sawyer

Dual-Threaded Mini Water Filtration System

$37

REI

Dan recommends: In terms of hardware or capabilities it’s hard to beat a Sawyer Mini water filter. They’re tiny, lightweight, need no energy source to run, and can filter something like 100,000 liters of water before they need to be replaced.

There’s also been pushback. Every time prepping hits the news, Brian says, some people respond with aggression. When he’s spoken to media before, multiple people have made death threats. “‘I’m not going to waste money on preps, I’ll just buy a shotgun and come to your house,’ yada yada,” he says. For this reason, he, and several other preppers I spoke to, asked to be identified only by their first name. As well as hostility, Goss says, some people complain that they can’t afford to prep, or that the government should provide. A common sentiment, Chappell says, is that “nothing ever happens anyway.” Some accuse preppers of fearmongering.

The general image of the prepping community probably doesn’t help. Think “prepper” and you might imagine a caricature of a man in camo and armed to the teeth, either hunkering down in a nuclear bunker or camping out in the wilderness. But the preppers I speak to present a much more mundane, inclusive, and, well, British approach to prepping. They are keen to distance themselves from the idea of the “doomsday prepper.” Instead, they prep for less extreme but more likely incidents. As the UK anticipates winter weather buffeted by an El Niño climate pattern, they worry about storms, floods, and crop failures. Something as simple as a burst water pipe or power cut could cause localized chaos. Then there’s the threat of cyberattacks: Just this month, supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe were hacked in an attack France believes was conducted by Iran.

Courtesy of LifeSaver

LifeSaver

6,000-Liter Water Filtration Bottle

$220

LifeSaver

Glyn recommends: A Lifesaver bottle or Lifesaver Jerrycan and an EcoFlow power station such as the Delta 3.

Regardless, says Ana, a prepper based in south Wales, the impacts are likely to be the same. “It’s going to be affecting potentially your food supply in the supermarkets, your water, your electricity,” she says. Ana has a food channel on YouTube, but pivoted to prepper content when she realized most people had no idea how to preserve food for long-term storage. She grew up growing food, cooking from scratch, and keeping a full pantry, and has maintained these habits. The Covid-19 pandemic reminded her just how vulnerable the UK supply chain is. She was pregnant at the time and noticed a shortage of baby formula; a supermarket worker told her people had been buying it to put in their coffee and tea.

It’s always a good idea to keep a store of basics like bottled water and long-life food. True preppers often invest in more specialized items. Brian gives me a virtual tour of the shed where he stores his supplies, neatly arranged in floor-to-ceiling shelving units. He points to different types of water filtration kits, including a LifeSaver Jerrycan capable of purifying up to 20,000 liters, and rattles off medical supplies (“Antibiotics, tourniquets, chest seals, splints”). He has a few different cooking setups, such as foldable stoves that use gas canisters, and keeps buckets of freeze-dried food that will last for 25 years. Next door, he tells me, there are 165 gallons of fresh water that he refreshes every six months.

Courtesy of Bluetti

Bluetti

Elite 300

$1,199 $1,099 (8% off)

Bluetti

$1,699 $1,099 (35% off)

Amazon

Brian recommends: A reasonably sized power bank such as a Bluetti Elite 300, which will give you days of backup power for your home. Add in some solar panels and you have a two-to-three-year renewable power source.

Many preppers prepare to go off-grid if the power and internet fail, but Brian has staked his bets on a tech-heavy setup. He has a generator, his house is fitted out with solar panels, and he uses an air source heat pump for heating. He has a backup heater that runs on diesel, and several extremely powerful portable power stations (think a rechargeable power bank, but with enough capacity to keep appliances like a microwave going). He uses Starlink for internet access and runs two different mesh networking systems, with high-frequency radio acting as his ultimate fallback. In his shed, he has plenty of torches, lanterns, candles, radios, walkie-talkies, and a night-vision headset. The way he sees it, you might be able to survive without power, but it wouldn’t be much fun. “We’ve got enough tech these days that life doesn’t have to be uncomfortable,” Brian says.

This is a key difference between the US and UK prepper scenes: While many US preppers plan to “bug out” and live alone off-grid, British preppers mainly plan to stay at home. “We don’t have that vast wilderness to escape to,” says Chappell, who makes content as the UK Urban Prepper and keeps most of his at-home supplies stacked in what used to be the dining room. When we speak, Chappell has a four-week-old daughter, so his stocks include enough formula milk to get her to solid foods. Nappies are too bulky to stockpile en masse, but he has enough for a short-term issue and a fallback of old-fashioned terry towel nappies.

Courtesy of Varuste

Grayl

Geopress Purifier Bottle 24-Ounce

$100

REI

Mike recommends: My number one would be any kind of water filter. I love the Grayl one for simplicity.

While prepping is often depicted as a lone wolf activity, British preppers are, on the whole, more community-minded. The scene in general has a degree of secrecy around it; some preppers keep their preps tightly under wraps out of fears that, if people know what they have, they could become a target.

Goss dismisses fears of people turning on each other in a crisis. He evokes a sense of Blitz spirit: when times get tough, he suggests, people tend to come together rather than pull apart. In any case, he doesn’t really have a choice. Like Chappell, he lives in a terraced house in an urban area—a far shout from a private bunker. “Like it or not, you’re going to wind up working with your neighbors during a big giant blackout event or something,” he says. “And it would be a really good idea for you to kind of plan for that ahead of time.” He suggests gaining trust by setting up a street WhatsApp group and doing small favors for neighbors. In an emergency scenario, pooling resources and knowledge may be more effective than going it alone. And if things did descend into looting and fighting–well, wouldn’t you want your neighbors on side?

Courtesy of Toolvero

Allpowers

R1500 Lite

$389

Allpowers

Ana recommends: A power station like Allpowers’ R1500, an Aferiy 2400w station, or the Ecoworthy PS2400. All have great capacity and multiple charging options.

Others thought this view might be too optimistic. “When you’re bombarded with information 24/7 and you’re deprived of any information in a general power cut, it wouldn’t take long before people get nervous and start to do stupid things because they panic,” Brian says. “You get a fear response. Fear leads to poor choices, potentially fatal ones.” He’s thought about what he’d do if friends really did turn up on his doorstep like they joke about. “It’s a difficult one,” he says. “I don’t have an answer.”

In that kind of scenario, Chappell has a plan to bug out, but just to a family member’s home. His house is surrounded by people he doesn’t know, and he can’t predict how they might react. It’s not that he doesn’t want to help people, he says, but he’s not willing to risk his family’s safety.

Of course, these plans go well beyond a three-day water-and-beans buffer. For many of the people I speak to, prepping is also a hobby. There are meet-ups and workshops. Goss says he enjoys camping and tending his allotment—activities that fit neatly into the prepper skillset (he’s also into archery, just to complete the image). But still, it’s nice to be ready, just in case. “This is not a way of life where I sit in a bunker hoping for the sky to fall. I want nothing ever to happen,” Chappell says. “But it’s insurance, right?”

Title: SAP confirms security incident after suspicious GitHub activity
Context: This warning comes shortly after the national cybersecurity agencies in Switzerland and Italy reported the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting...
Full Text:
SAP has confirmed to BleepingComputer that it took urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment.

The German software giant said its evidence so far does not show downstream compromise of customer systems or data.

Based in Walldorf, Germany, SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software vendors, with 110,000 employees in 157 countries, 300 million subscribers, and over $40 billion in annual revenue.

Der Spiegel reported earlier today, based on an internal SAP memo it saw, that the software firm was hit by a cyberattack it tracks under the code name “Project Granite.”

The software company reportedly asked all employees to keep the project details confidential.

According to the German outlet, sources within the company said the attackers breached SAP’s GitHub environment, possibly with help from AI tools.

Insider sources say that the attacker managed to steal authentication tokens from SAP employees and leveraged them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub.

BleepingComputer has contacted SAP for a statement on the reported breach, and the company acknowledged the incident and said it had taken steps to protect its customers.

“SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services,” a company representative told BleepingComputer.

“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.”

“Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.”

SAP did not specify the environments where the suspicious activity was observed, or whether customers downloading code from its GitHub repositories or performing updates that are directly fetched or indirectly fed by those repositories should take any action.

BleepingComputer has asked SAP about this, but a spokesperson declined to share any further information.

Meanwhile, Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issued a public warning yesterday about agentic AI tools that empower cyberattacks, such as ARTEX, CAIRN, and PentAGI.

BSI cautioned organizations in the country to focus on responding to security incidents and ensure they follow all recommended security-strengthening practices.

This warning comes shortly after the national cybersecurity agencies in Switzerland and Italy reported the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

Title: Flight Centre Travel Group warns of customer data breach involving some passport details
Context: An initial review found that most of the accessed records contain only customer names, some with basic travel information
Full Text:
Travellers who booked accommodation through Flight Centre and several of its leisure brands may have had their names, and in rare cases passport and health details, accessed by unknown persons, Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) disclosed.

In a statement to the Australian Securities Exchange, the Brisbane-based travel company said it is investigating “unusual activity” in a third-party accommodation booking system used by the Flight Centre brand, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents. Flight bookings “are not impacted,” the travel group noted, and corporate travel bookings “are made through other systems and are not affected.”

“While investigations remain ongoing, at this stage FLT believes that a significant number of customer records in the impacted system may have been accessed by unknown persons, although it is not clear at this time how many of those records have actually been extracted from the third-party system,” the statement reads.

An initial review found that most of the accessed records contain only customer names, some with basic travel information.

“A very small percentage is believed to include data such as limited passport details, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, or in rare cases health or mobility information,” according to FLT.

The company says that, to date, it has found no access to customer credit card, payment or bank account details.

To establish the scope of the incident, FLT is working with the vendor and Mandiant, its cyber security incident response partner, “to implement appropriate safeguards and containment actions.”

After learning of the activity, FLT activated its incident response resources and worked with the third party to contain it. The company says it has changed authentication keys and credentials, increased monitoring on the system, and is notifying the relevant authorities.

“FLT values customer privacy and data security. The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologise for any concern this causes,” the company stated.

In the meantime, FLT advises that customers “should be alert to unexpected emails, calls or messages about their bookings, and should not click on links, open attachments or share personal information, passwords or payment details in response.”

FLT is the latest travel company to disclose a breach linked to a booking system. In April, the online travel platform Booking.com warned that hackers may have accessed customer data linked to travel reservations, including names, email addresses, phone numbers and information shared with accommodations.

More recently, accommodation software provider RMS Cloud, whose booking systems are used by more than 6,000 hotels, holiday parks and serviced apartments, acknowledged a breach after guests of several Australian holiday park operators received phishing messages via WhatsApp, SMS and email in late October.

Title: 100,000 Potentially Impacted by Colorado Data Breach
Context: One week after the outage began, OIT said it discovered the incident after the attackers triggered the automated threat detection systems deployed within its Amazon Web Services...
Full Text:
The Colorado Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) has disclosed a data breach impacting data that residents uploaded to the myColorado application.

Colorado’s official mobile application, myColorado is used for digital identification, state services, and document storage. It has approximately 2.1 million users.

OIT took the application offline last week, after identifying unauthorized access to platform data, and immediately initiated incident response and an investigation into the incident.

One week after the outage began, OIT said it discovered the incident after the attackers triggered the automated threat detection systems deployed within its Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment.

The investigation has determined that the attackers accessed documents stored within the ‘myCards and Documents’ section of the application, which includes user-uploaded data, such as PDF files and photos of government IDs, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards.

According to Colorado, approximately 100,000 individuals might have been affected, but no payment information was accessed.

“Staff are working around the clock to match the inappropriately accessed documents to individual users. As that matching continues, OIT will further refine estimates on the number of people whose data was involved,” Colorado said.

The myColorado application remains offline and OIT has not announced a restoration date. The state expects to start sending direct notifications to the affected individuals on November 27.

“Our main goal is to protect the security of users. Additionally, we are prioritizing direct notification of users involved in the incident and getting the app up and running as soon as possible, with security enhancements in place,” said state CIO and OIT executive director Sarah Tuneberg.

Title: Hackers Trojanize Official Q-Dir and DesktopOK Downloads to Deliver Remote Access Malware
Context: Information about identified security programs is transmitted to the C2 server, so as to help the attackers better plan the next stages of the attack or serve payloads that can...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a software supply chain attack that has tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installation files distributed via the official SoftwareOK website.

"Evidence indicates that malicious files were generated not only when users downloaded the programs directly from the official download page but also during the update process of previously installed legitimate programs," South Korean cybersecurity company AhnLab said.

Q-Dir, also called the Quad Directory Explorer, is a free, lightweight file manager for Windows developed by SoftwareOK. According to its website, DesktopOK is a free Windows utility designed to save and restore desktop icon positions.

The unauthorized modifications are designed such that the malicious activity is challenging to detect when running the programs, while simultaneously retrieving and deploying a Python-based remote control malware (RAT) from an external server.

Once installed, the RAT payload is capable of executing shell commands and Python code, transferring files, capturing screenshots, and collecting system metadata based on commands issued by the attacker.

The following product versions have been confirmed to be poisoned, given the discrepancies in the SHA-256 hashes of the installer files and the presence of additional code that triggers additional file downloads and automatic execution -

Q-Dir 12.85.0.0

Q-Dir 12.84.0.0

Q-Dir 12.83.0.0

DesktopOK 12.85.0.0

DesktopOK 12.82.0.0

The exact mechanism that allowed the installation files to be replaced with a trojanized version remains unknown.

"The malicious installer runs the legitimate Q-Dir or DesktopOK to lower the user's suspicion, while simultaneously downloading and installing a Python RAT package from an external server," AhnLab said.

Specifically, this involves downloading two payloads from "mail.c1a2[.]top" -

7zr.exe, the legitimate 7-Zip tool to decompress files

dsv2_py39_agent.7z, a package containing the RAT and Python runtime environment

The attack chain is fairly straightforward in that it uses the 7-Zip tool binary to extract and run the Python RAT. The malware then sets up persistence on the host by means of a scheduled task that impersonates Microsoft Edge to fly under the radar. The task is configured to execute the RAT by launching a Python script named "py_client_dsv2.py."

Upon execution, the RAT establishes communication with its command-and-control (C2) server ("8.210.69[.]51:9876") to receive tasks and run them. It supports the following features -

Shell command execution

Python code execution

File upload and download

Screenshot capture

Operating system and system information

It also gathers a list of running processes and compares it against an internal list of various security products used in South Korea and abroad, including AhnLab, ESTSecurity, Hauri, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Trend Micro, Avast, McAfee, ESET, Symantec, Kaspersky, Bitdefender, Sophos, Fortinet, Elastic, and Malwarebytes.

Information about identified security programs is transmitted to the C2 server, so as to help the attackers better plan the next stages of the attack or serve payloads that can bypass detection.

The activity has not been attributed to any known threat actor. However, AhnLab said it identified Chinese language comments in the source code, suggesting that the malware authors or attackers may have used a Chinese-speaking environment.

"Users who are currently using Q-Dir or DesktopOK, or who have recently installed or updated these programs, should verify the hash values of the downloaded files and check their systems for any traces of RAT installation or execution," AhnLab said.

"However, simply uninstalling and reinstalling the program may not remove a Python RAT that has already been installed. Therefore, you should also check for suspicious Python execution environments, scheduled tasks, related files, and traces of external network communication, update your antivirus engine to the latest version, and then perform a full system scan."

Title: Microsoft pushes emergency hotpatch to fix Windows Server crashes
Context: Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077)
Full Text:
Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077).

According to Microsoft, the KB5138318 out-of-band update should address stop errors with 0x139 codes triggered on affected servers when IPv6 routes expire.

"Microsoft has released a new Windows out-of-band (OOB) update today, November 25, 2026, to address an issue affecting a limited number of Windows Servers with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes," it said in a message center update.

"Affected devices might stop unexpectedly with stop error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE) when a route timer expires. This issue affects some Windows Server 2025 devices after installing the November 2026 Windows security hotpatch update."

This emergency non-security update is now rolling out to affected Windows Server 2025 devices enrolled in hotpatch updates through Windows Update.

KB5138318 will download and install automatically and will take effect without requiring IT administrators or users to restart affected devices.

The November 2026 hotpatch updates are also causing issues for Windows 11 users, who are experiencing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications, as well as printing issues on systems running Forcepoint's DLP Endpoint Agent data loss prevention solution after installing this month's hotpatch on Windows 11 systems.

Windows Autopatch reached public preview in early June after an initial unveil in April 2022 and has been generally available since July 2022.

Microsoft announced earlier this year, in March, that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed.

One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that was causing driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices in the European Union.

Title: CyberStrikeAI Creator Shuts Down Open-Source AI Offensive Framework
Context: On November 26, the firm announced the immediate discontinuation of CyberStrikeAI (Open Source Version), while a closed source enterprise edition with advanced features remains...
Full Text:
Agentic security company ThreatBook has taken the open-source version of CyberStrikeAI offline after its use in multiple cyber malicious campaigns.

On November 26, the firm announced the immediate discontinuation of CyberStrikeAI (Open Source Version), while a closed source enterprise edition with advanced features remains available to its customers.

ThreatBook said it acquired CyberStrikeAI in September.

This open source, AI-driven penetration testing toolset – also known as an agentic offensive framework (AOF) – was published on GitHub in late 2025 and gained more than 7000 stars on the open source platform.

Since the acquisition, the Singapore and Hong Kong-based business had continued maintaining the open source version CyberStrikeAI but also launched a closed source enterprise edition of with advanced features, accessible as part of its RedAgents offering to verified enterprises only.

The CyberStrikeAI platform and related projects have now been permanently removed from open source communities such as GitHub.

Users who wish to install an open source version of CyberStrikeAI are advised to be “vigilant of forks that appear elsewhere” and that could compromise their security.

CyberStrikeAI Takedown Linked to Misuse by Attackers

The firm said the takedown was due to the increased use of AOFs, including CyberStrikeAI, by attackers worldwide to “orchestrate malicious attacks, enabling perpetrators to execute strikes at speeds and scale that were recently unimaginable.”

This comes a month after the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned financial and cryptocurrency organizations that a threat group tracked as ‘Crafty Falcon’ had been targeting them in successive attacks using several AI-powered tools, including CyberStrikeAI.

A November 25 report from the Shadowserver Foundation, a UK government-funded nonprofit, observed more than 4200 servers running identified AOFs as of November 23, up from under 3700 a day earlier. Among them, 6% were linked to CyberStrikeAI, while 87% were identified as ARTEX, another tool linked to several malicious cyber campaigns.

FIFA confirms a cyberattack exposing personal and business data, while the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claims responsibility for the breach.

FIFA confirmed it was the victim of a cyberattack, threat actors gained access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information.” The organization told The Associated Press it’s working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.

FIFA did not disclose technical details about the attack or what kind of information hackers accessed.

A hacking group, which calls itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club, claimed the security incident before FIFA made its announcement. The threat actors shared a screenshot on X showing what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, the group appeared to claim responsibility for the attack in a reply to a post reporting that more than 12 GB of FIFA internal documents had been leaked.

FIFA has confirmed that hackers broke into its systems and accessed personal and business information.A new group calling itself Handsome Boy Hacking Club claims it took more than 12GB from FIFA's Microsoft environment, including identity and immigration documents, and… pic.twitter.com/ZwxJ7LoQez

At this moment, the group’s X account has been suspended, and their Tor leak site is unreachable.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” states the organization. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a sensitive time for FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, who faces criticism over a failed plan to sell World Cup stakes to private investors and his bid to extend his presidency to 2031.

He remains the favorite ahead of the March 18 election, against Kohzo Tashima and Philippe Diallo. The AP report does not link the cyberattack to these issues. FIFA warns that the exposure of personal data could have serious consequences for those affected.

“Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.” concludes the AP.

Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) is a newly emerged ransomware and data-extortion group first observed in November 2026. Threat intelligence platforms recorded its first activity on November 19, when it listed three organizations on its data-leak site: US-based firearms manufacturer Smith & Wesson, healthcare provider UCHealth, and telecommunications company Frontier Communications. On November 20, the group added FIFA to its victim list, bringing the number of publicly recorded claims to four.

The group has provided little information about its operators, origins, or technical capabilities. Its claims involve organizations in the United States and Switzerland, spanning the manufacturing, healthcare, telecommunications, and sports sectors. While FIFA has confirmed a cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to personal and business information, the other listings should be treated as claims that have not necessarily been independently verified.

Title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges
Context: ​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
Full Text:
​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges.

Found by ANSSI's Jérémy Jean (who submitted a fix in August), the flaw has been dubbed NFS2ROOT by cybersecurity firm OpenSec, which shared a full remote-root exploit and a patch with the NFSD maintainers in late September.

The vulnerability has existed since Linux kernel version 3.16 (released in March 2014), and it stems from a heap buffer overflow weakness in the Linux NFS server (nfsd).

NFS2ROOT affects systems with a Linux kernel older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4-rc1 if nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and running and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet.

Successful exploitation lets remote threat actors without privileges corrupt kernel memory and gain root access to vulnerable Linux servers exposed online through low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction.

In NFS2ROOT attacks, the threat actors can exploit this flaw by sending maliciously crafted requests that cause the NFS server to write data beyond an allocated memory buffer. This lets them read kernel memory, bypass KASLR (which protects kernel memory addresses), and place a callback that can execute a command in a released memory area.

When the attacker closes the NFS connection, the kernel executes the embedded command with root privileges, allowing the attacker to gain root control of the unpatched Linux server.

​Although there are no reports of CVE-2026-99362 exploitation in the wild, security teams should apply the latest kernel security updates from their Linux distribution vendor immediately to block potential attacks, then reboot the system to ensure the patched kernel is in use.

Those who can't apply a patch immediately should restrict access to the NFS server over TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or networks. Additionally, if NFS sharing is not required on the system, admins can stop and disable the nfs-server service in /etc/nfs.conf.

"Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in," OpenSec said. "Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host."

While the NFS2ROOT attacks have no network signatures, security teams can still monitor for potential signs of exploitation attempts by checking for kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames, according to OpenSec.

NFS2ROOT is the latest in a long series of Linux privilege escalation security flaws disclosed and patched since the start of the year, including RefluXFS, CIFSwitch, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, PinTheft, Copy Fail, Pack2TheRoot, and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC.

Title: Hex Package Manager Warns of Potential Data Breach
Context: The incident occurred on November 23, when the attackers exploited a vulnerability in hex
Full Text:
Hex, the package manager for Elixir and Erlang, fell victim to a cyberattack involving unauthorized access to its web servers.

The incident occurred on November 23, when the attackers exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm to execute commands. The attack was immediately blocked, and the underlying security defect was addressed within 20 minutes.

Between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC, the attacker sent 69 malicious requests, affecting six web servers. At 18:30, Hex replaced all hex.pm servers with patched versions rejecting the payload, and its firewall rule fully blocked the attacker’s traffic at 18:33.

“We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems,” the package manager explains.

According to Hex, potential access to database contents, such as email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, sessions, second factor authentication secrets, and audit logs, cannot be ruled out.

While all the observed reads of private packages came from Hex servers, any read from a compromised server would appear legitimate, it says. Additionally, database and private documentation reads are not logged, hindering visibility into potential data exposure.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“The attacker’s commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients,” Hex notes.

The package manager has been working on a new registry signing system with key rotation support. Until new Hex client iterations are rolled out, users should avoid fetching packages from third-party mirrors and rely only on repo.hex.pm.

Hex also recommends that all account holders change their hex.pm passwords and reset their two-factor authentication.

“Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm,” the package manager says.

The attackers exploited an unauthenticated deserialization of untrusted data bug (tracked as CVE-2026-129514, CVSS score of 10) that allowed them to execute OS commands via a crafted Erlang external term format request body and gain remote code execution (RCE).

Hex discovered that the Ash Framework was also impacted by the same class of vulnerability. Ash patched the flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-124283) on November 24, warning it could lead to code execution or SQL injection.

Associated security defects were also patched in two other Elixir libraries: namely db_connection (CVE-2026-133555) and flop (CVE-2026-130411).

Enterprise software giant SAP has confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident following reports that threat actors targeted its development infrastructure.

German publication Der Spiegel [paywalled] broke the news on Thursday, citing SAP insiders and an internal notification sent to employees.

“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP told SecurityWeek.

German news agency DPA reviewed internal SAP communications that revealed the suspicious activity had been identified within GitHub.

According to an insider cited by Der Spiegel, the hackers obtained SAP employees’ authentication tokens, enabling them to copy and alter source code stored on GitHub.

SAP publishes developer tools, sample applications, and open source projects on GitHub. It’s unclear whether the threat actor accessed any proprietary code.

Separately, Handelsblatt reported that SAP’s emergency security measures have affected numerous teams. The software giant has reportedly replaced signing keys, limited access to GitHub, and suspended automated development operations.

None of the reports indicate that tampered code was incorporated into software delivered to SAP customers.

Sources cited by Der Spiegel suggested that the attack may have been assisted by AI. While AI involvement has not been confirmed, several major organizations, including the European Commission, have recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattacks.

In late October, the Gentlemen ransomware group listed SAP on its leak website, pointing to the company’s Latin American operations. Title: In 2027, “the agent did it” stops being an excuse
Context: The company’s Horizons of Identity Security 2026–2027 research found that 79% of enterprises have deployed AI agents in production, while just 2% have implemented identity...
Full Text:
Enterprises will come under growing pressure to establish accountability for autonomous AI agents in 2027, with regulators, corporate boards and insurers demanding evidence of how organizations govern automated decisions, manage access privileges and prevent operational disruption, according to SailPoint’s 2027 Identity Security Predictions.

The company’s Horizons of Identity Security 2026–2027 research found that 79% of enterprises have deployed AI agents in production, while just 2% have implemented identity security controls designed for them, creating what SailPoint describes as a 40:1 agent security gap.

Autonomous agents could trigger billion-dollar operational failures

SailPoint predicts that a major public company will experience a multibillion-dollar supply chain disruption caused by misconfigured autonomous agents with excessive access permissions.

The company describes a potential incident called an “Authorized Outage,” in which misconfigured agents delete inventory databases, terminate supplier contracts and redirect shipments. The speed of automated execution could overwhelm intervention procedures, resulting in financial losses, contractual disputes and regulatory investigations.

Such an incident could accelerate the adoption of separation-of-duties requirements for AI systems. SailPoint expects enterprises to establish independent governance environments that prevent agents from modifying their permissions, disabling security monitoring or authorizing privilege escalation.

“While it will be possible to delegate a complex workflow to an autonomous agent, it will never be acceptable to delegate accountability, because agent accountability is enterprise responsibility,” said Mark McClain, CEO of SailPoint.

Legal standards and executive accountability

The company anticipates the emergence of a mandatory US governance standard for autonomous agents, involving the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state attorneys general.

The predicted framework would require businesses to demonstrate that automated activities comply with legal obligations, fiduciary responsibilities and operating procedures.

Identity governance records could play a role in helping enterprises establish accountability and demonstrate regulatory compliance. Organizations would need to document the relationships between agents, their human owners, assigned permissions and the actions performed throughout their operational lifecycles.

Supply chain attacks and machine credentials

Connections between autonomous agents, third-party applications and business partners are expected to expand the attack surface. Protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduce dependencies that could expose downstream organizations through compromised credentials and connectors.

Major enterprises will begin restricting external agents’ access to their APIs unless vendors and business partners can provide cryptographic proof of the agents’ identities, ownership and authorized access scope.

Credential theft is another area of concern. The company expects passkeys to account for more than 45% of human logins in 2027, prompting cybercriminals to increasingly target API keys, OAuth tokens and machine secrets.

Its research found that 67% of enterprises have secured human access, and 24% govern agentic security. Agents represent 22% of non-human accounts, with machine identities outnumbering human identities by 45 to one.

Zero trust moves toward continuous intent verification

Autonomous systems can generate subtasks and modify workflows during execution, creating challenges for role-based access controls built around predefined responsibilities.

SailPoint expects zero trust architectures to incorporate continuous intent assurance, requiring verification of an agent’s identity, associated human owner and business purpose before each API call.

Organizations are expected to adopt just-in-time access mechanisms, granting permissions when required for a task and removing them upon completion. These measures could reduce exposure associated with persistent administrative privileges.

Identity governance becomes a business performance metric

Upcoming post-quantum cryptography requirements and EU AI Act obligations are expected to increase board-level scrutiny of identity management.

Inventories of human, machine and cryptographic identities will influence corporate valuations, credit ratings and eligibility for cyber insurance. Visibility into credentials and their ownership will support compliance assessments and technology migrations.

Investment policies are also expected to undergo changes. CIOs and CFOs could begin requiring measurable returns and documented security controls before approving funding for agent deployments.

The transition could bring thousands of unsanctioned AI agents operating through employee credentials into centralized management, establishing oversight of their permissions, activities and contributions to business operations.

Title: Unpatched Cacti Zero-Day Enables RCE in Just Four HTTP Requests via Guest Access
Context: Details have emerged about a new zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution
Full Text:
Details have emerged about a new zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution.

The proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, which has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier, has been tracked as 4HTTP2SHELL and 4HTTP2ROOT.

"I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests," a security researcher who goes by the online alias "ek0ms savi0r" said. "No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface."

The shortcoming affects Cacti Core 1.2.31, the latest version, when the guest account is enabled. It's worth noting that the guest account is disabled by default starting with Cacti version 0.8.7.

At a high level, the vulnerability allows an attacker to abuse the guest access to write an unvalidated value (i.e., non-numeric text) into a setting called "preview_graphs_per_page" via "auth_profile.php?action=update_data." The configuration parameter controls how many graphs are displayed per page when viewing graphs in Preview Mode.

The crafted value takes the form of arbitrary SQL strings that can be turned into a second-order SQL injection by taking advantage of the fact that Cacti does not validate that the user-provided input is actually an integer value. This, in turn, opens the door for arbitrary SQL query execution when the graph preview page ("graph_view.php") is loaded with default filters.

The SQL query demonstrated by "ek0ms savi0r" is an UPDATE statement to modify a record in Cacti's poller table. In the final stage of the attack, the realtime poller endpoint ("graph_realtime.php") is invoked from the same guest session, which causes the modified row from the poller table to be read and passed as input to PHP's popen() function without any allowlist or sanitization checks.

The researcher has pointed out four failures that ultimately make it possible to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution -

The guest can write a numeric setting as an arbitrary string

The stored default bypasses request validation

Cacti's PHP PDO database driver accepts stacked statements through the SQL LIMIT clause

The poller executes a database-stored command string

Successful exploitation of the flaw can allow an attacker to compromise the Cacti server and provide a pivot point to the target network as it exposes sensitive data, or even suppress alerts by modifying the poller table.

"Because Cacti often stores credentials and connection details for routers, switches, servers, and other devices across a network, an attacker who reaches this level of command execution can gain a foothold reaching far beyond the monitoring server itself," watchTowr said in an advisory.

In the absence of a fix, users are advised to disable the guest account and restrict access to the Cacti web interface to mitigate potential risks. It's also essential to review poller configuration entries for unexpected command values and apply the fixes as soon as they become available.

Title: US seizes nearly $17 billion in global war on scam rings
Context: The Department of Justice announced that the effort covers more than 400 cases in 85 federal districts, including new charges, guilty verdicts and sentences, and 30 defendants...
Full Text:
The US government has gone after more than 800 alleged scammers in what it calls its largest-ever crackdown on scams targeting Americans.

The Department of Justice announced that the effort covers more than 400 cases in 85 federal districts, including new charges, guilty verdicts and sentences, and 30 defendants were extradited to the United States.

American prosecutors and agents joined police in more than 10 countries to raid scam call centers and compounds abroad. The push began after Executive Order 14390 was signed on March 6, 2026.

“Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” Attorney General Todd Blanche declared.

Phones behind bars

In one case, gang members in Georgia prisons allegedly used smuggled phones to call strangers, tell them they had missed jury duty and demand a “fine” to keep them out of jail.

Fourteen people tied to the scheme were charged in three indictments in federal and state courts. Prosecutors charged 17 more in state court with smuggling the phones into the state’s prisons. Investigators seized websites used to run the scam, and the US Postal Inspection Service took over three domains and sent their visitors to a seizure banner.

The Federal Communications Commission went after the devices themselves. On November 19, it approved a rule that allows prisons to use jamming technology against contraband phones.

“For years, hundreds of thousands of contraband cellphones have entered our prisons allowing offenders to perpetrate scams on ordinary Americans,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

“By allowing jamming in prisons for the first time, we’re taking an aggressive, but responsible approach to eliminate inmates access to contraband phones,” Carr added.

Elderly Americans’ data sold to scammers

Several cases involved people who trade in the personal information of older Americans. A list broker in Mexico knowingly sold the names and contact details of elderly Americans to dozens of scammers.

In a separate sweepstakes scheme aimed at elderly victims, a dozen defendants were charged, including Jamaican nationals. Other targets included a Peruvian call center that told Spanish-speaking Americans they would be arrested or deported unless they paid for English language-learning products.

A Nigerian national was extradited from the UK for allegedly trying to steal the military pay of US service members.

Scam compounds shut down abroad

Prosecutors made the overseas operations a priority. “We will not allow these scammers to hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad,” vowed A. Tysen Duva, Assistant Attorney General for the Criminal Division.

Under Operation Blackout, the FBI seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, dismantled more than 29 scam compounds and helped bring home over 2,200 trafficked workers. The bureau warned more than 11,000 Americans that they were being targeted and estimates it prevented over $690 million in losses.

“The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you,” FBI Director Kash Patel warned.

The State Department helped freeze over $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts. The Federal Trade Commission returned almost $3 billion to consumers.

David Woodcock, who heads the SEC’s Division of Enforcement, argued that the schemes have changed less than the tools behind them. “The technology may be new, but the frauds are familiar.”

The toll on victims

About 10% of US adults experienced a scam in the past year, either themselves or through someone in their household, Gallup found in research the DOJ cited. Nearly three in four victims said it hurt their mental health or well-being, and Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025.

“Too many Americans have suffered from cyber fraud, particularly from scam operations emanating from Southeast Asia, and expanding across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and the Pacific. But the true cost is not in dollars alone. Behind every statistic is a human story – a family bankrupted, a retiree left destitute, or a young person driven to suicide,” noted Deputy Assistant Secretary of State David Bedard.

Title: AI raises new questions about what penetration testing proves
Context: The study, AI and the Future of Threat-Led Penetration Testing: Capability, Control and Credible Assurance, draws on responses from 26 providers and insights from two industry...
Full Text:
AI is becoming an established part of threat-led penetration testing (TLPT), with 81% of surveyed providers using the technology beyond experimentation, according to research from CREST.

The study, AI and the Future of Threat-Led Penetration Testing: Capability, Control and Credible Assurance, draws on responses from 26 providers and insights from two industry roundtables involving cybersecurity professionals and institutional stakeholders, with a focus on financial services.

AI expands threat emulation capabilities

Over the next 12 months, 65% of respondents expect AI to support 40% or more of their TLPT tasks.

Reporting and assessment is the most common area of live AI use, followed by reconnaissance and threat-informed preparation. The technology can influence engagement planning, intelligence prioritization and the selection of attack scenarios.

Of the providers using AI for threat actor emulation, 86% report improved accuracy and realism. Reported benefits include faster intelligence analysis, more effective mapping of adversary TTPs, and support for the development of tools and adaptive attack paths.

Biases in AI models and training data could introduce generic patterns into threat assessments, making it harder to distinguish between adversaries. Practitioners must evaluate whether generated techniques are relevant to the organization, consistent with the threat actor’s behavior and aligned with the engagement’s objectives.

AI-enabled impersonation raises ethical concerns. Voice cloning, synthetic video and personalized content can be used to test verification procedures and escalation controls. Their use requires justification, authorization and safeguards proportionate to the potential intrusion or harm to individuals targeted during exercises.

Autonomous testing remains limited

None of the 11 regulated TLPT providers that answered questions about execution authority permit AI to perform testing activities autonomously. One commercial provider reported allowing autonomous execution.

Scope and operational control, along with client data and confidentiality, were each ranked among the top three delivery risks by 68% of respondents.

Uses selected as most clearly requiring explicit client approval (Source: CREST)

Network restrictions, access permissions, monitoring and stop conditions can help contain unexpected system behavior. Providers need to maintain records of automated actions, practitioner interventions and decisions affecting the engagement.

Human approval procedures can introduce delays into simulated attacks, potentially affecting the assessment of an organization’s ability to detect and respond to threats. The report recommends documenting changes to testing conditions and considering how they affect conclusions about cyber resilience.

Client data protection drives approval requirements

Some 92% of respondents believe that submitting client information to external or cloud-hosted AI services requires explicit client approval.

Autonomous testing actions were identified as requiring explicit client approval by 62% of respondents. Data governance considerations include processing and storage locations, retention policies, model training practices, subcontractor involvement and access rights.

Organizations commissioning penetration tests need visibility into the systems and integrations surrounding AI models. Changes to technology vendors, permissions or data flows during an engagement may require additional approval.

Technical expertise remains essential

Validation of AI-generated technical output was rated as an essential practitioner skill for the coming year by 92% of providers. Secure data handling, manual exploitation and an understanding of AI limitations and failure modes also rank highly.

“TLPT, particularly in production environments, has always been high risk and in need of the strongest assurance. AI is amplifying this and is already changing how it is delivered,” said Nick Benson, CEO of CREST.

The use of AI to develop offensive tools creates a supervision challenge for cybersecurity teams. Training, peer review and secure development practices are necessary to ensure practitioners have the expertise to assess generated code and anticipate its potential consequences before deployment.

Procurement and disclosure requirements set to increase

Looking ahead, 88% of providers anticipate greater use of AI-generated offensive tooling, with the same percentage expecting increased demand for testers with AI-specific skills.

Some 85% of respondents expect AI-related procurement requirements to increase, while 81% anticipate more client requests for disclosure of AI use over the next year.

Some financial institutions are developing internal testing capabilities, potentially changing demand for external cybersecurity services. Independent assessment, complex scenario design, threat relevance and professional judgment may become more important differentiators for external providers as AI capabilities become more accessible.

Title: Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug
Context: ” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to...
Full Text: India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens. The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants. DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities. India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.” eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem. While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities. Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®

Title: Drupal Warns of New Critical Flaw Exploited in the Wild
Context: Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites
Full Text:
Drupal fixes a critical flaw exploited in the wild that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites.

Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites.

Tracked as CVE-2026-136716, the flaw is related to improper handling of unusual or incomplete installation states. It is connected to CVE-2026-132165, also known as Fail2Install, which Drupal patched on November 18. However, the previous fix did not address every vulnerable installation scenario.

“SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.” Drupal maintainers warned.

The issue affects websites where the Drupal installer (install.php) remains remotely accessible. Drupal stressed that the vulnerability does not affect sites where administrators have already properly secured the installer.

One particularly concerning aspect is that administrators cannot easily identify affected installations through the Drupal interface. Moreover, sites that have already been compromised may no longer appear to be in the vulnerable state.

Drupal confirmed that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and urged administrators to investigate possible compromises.

“This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.” continues the advisory.

Recommended actions include reviewing logs for unauthorized access and unexpected changes involving the main administrative account, known as user 1. Administrators should also verify that its email address is under their control and consider resetting its password.

The vulnerability has been addressed in the following releases:

Drupal 11.4.x: Update to 11.4.14

Drupal 11.3.x: Update to 11.3.23

Drupal 10.6.x: Update to 10.6.23

Drupal 11.0.x through 11.2.x and 10.5.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive security fixes.

After updating, administrators should run update.php to fix affected installation states and ensure that the installer is properly secured on all existing and new websites.

Drupal’s own usage statistics provide further evidence of the exposure. Data published on November 15, 2026, show that thousands of websites still report running Drupal 8.x and tens of thousands use Drupal 9.x, both unsupported branches. Although these figures cover only sites reporting their versions through Drupal’s update system, they highlight the persistence of outdated installations and the need for organizations to migrate to supported releases.

Title: Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
Context: "Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack...
Full Text: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week. ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July. Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours. Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more. The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet. Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX. Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July. Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages. According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present. Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once. As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too. It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free. Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses. "In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. "Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor." Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed. In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale. AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions. Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®

Title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins
Context: The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American...
Full Text:
An ongoing phishing campaign dubbed "GoodGuys" impersonates major brands, including Google, Nvidia, Accenture, and SpaceX, to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars.

The attacks offer recipients up to $600 for a 45-minute interview in an attempt to get them to sign in with their work accounts to participate.

The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American Express, Coca-Cola, Culver's, Google Cloud, Nvidia, SpaceX, and Spotify.

The threat actors abuse legitimate email and event platforms, including HireVue, SendGrid, Mandrill, and Cvent, to distribute phishing links.

In one attack, a phishing email sent through HireVue invited recipients to attend a Google Cloud webinar about deploying AI applications into production.

The threat actors use domains themed around interviews, webinars, and research studies, creating brand-specific subdomains to host the phishing pages, such as:

accenture[.]international-interviews[.]com

nvidia[.]feedback-study[.]com

google[.]webinar-cloud[.]com

spotify[.]interview-experts[.]com

Clicking the phishing links typically takes recipients to a CAPTCHA challenge before displaying a website impersonating the company that supposedly sent the invitation.

Each website features customized branding and lures, with the Nvidia phishing site offering $500 to participate in an AI feedback study and the Accenture site offering $600 for an expert interview.

The sites ultimately prompt visitors to sign in with their Google accounts to validate their invitations, allowing the attackers to steal their credentials. The phishing kit specifically targets corporate accounts and rejects email addresses associated with Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.

Unlike adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that use reverse proxies to relay legitimate login pages, GoodGuys uses fake authentication forms controlled by an attacker-controlled server.

After victims enter their Google credentials, the phishing page can display various multifactor authentication (MFA) challenges, including requests for SMS codes, authenticator codes, and Google sign-in prompts requiring users to select a matching number on their phones.

The kit also includes fake Okta authentication forms and support for Okta Verify push notifications.

Push Security believes the threat actors manually attempt to log in using the stolen credentials, instructing the phishing page to display whatever MFA or security challenges Google or Okta show during authentication.

Similar techniques were used in vishing-based data theft attacks linked to the ShinyHunters extortion gang earlier this year to steal corporate single sign-on (SSO) credentials.

Once the process is completed, the phishing kit redirects victims to another website or displays a message thanking them for their application.

The researchers believe the phishing kit may have been developed using an AI coding assistant, based on hidden accessibility labels found in every analyzed version of the kit.

"The sign-in card in every build carries two hidden labels: "Sign-in simulation" and "GoodGuys sign-in simulation." They sit in accessibility text that only screen readers announce, so a visitor never sees them. We think the label is a leftover from how the kit was first built," explained Push Security.

"Calling the page a sign-in "simulation" for a made-up company is the kind of framing someone would use to get an AI coding assistant past its guardrails when asking it to build a phishing page. The label then stayed in every build we've collected."

The researchers also discovered a potentially related phishing campaign that uses fake Coca-Cola interview invitations and the Evilginx phishing kit to target Google Ads accounts.

While both campaigns used the same abused SendGrid click tracker and identical Coca-Cola branding assets, differences in their code and infrastructure prevented researchers from conclusively linking the attacks to the same threat actor.

Title: FIFA Says It Has Been Victim of a Cyberattack Accessing ‘Personal and Business Information’
Context: FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it...
Full Text:
FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday.

“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.

FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
