In this article

A teen and his mom helped find a girl missing for over 500 days

The teens met in the online game Among Us

Talk to kids about in-game chats and what to do if someone asks for help

Here at Malwarebytes, we’re cautious about kids using in-game chats, where they can strike up conversations with people they don’t know. But in one recent case, a teen who had been abducted and held for 521 days managed to contact rescuers via the online game Among Us.

“Jenny” (an alias) was 15 when she met 38-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel online. He offered her money to help him get to Oregon, according to TechSpot.

When they met in Utah in May 2025, Harmel reportedly stole her phone and threw it into the river. Federal prosecutors allege he then took her to his home in Oregon. Jenny said he held her against her will in the basement, physically abused her, and that she tried unsuccessfully to escape.

Rescue eventually came in the form of the online game Among Us, which Jenny accessed via a phone that Harmel gave her. The phone couldn’t make calls, but it had a Wi-Fi connection, which she used to access the game.

In Among Us, players take part in short games set aboard spaceships and on planetary settlements. The crew has to work out who the imposters are before they kill everyone. It’s an anonymous game—you can play without revealing your real name. While playing, Jenny found 16-year-old Landon Tresp and struck up a friendship with him.

A phone that couldn’t call, but could play

After meeting Jenny in the game in the middle of October this year, Tresp said that they “kind of just clicked,” and according to the BBC, the chat moved to the online forum service Discord. There, Jenny told him that she was being held against her will and shared links to news reports about her disappearance.

Mom goes full detective

After two weeks of chatting with Jenny, the boy told his mother, Khristina, on October 31. She immediately jumped into action.

Jenny knew what town she was being held in, but not her address. So Khristina asked her to find a document in the house with a full name on it. Using that information, Khristina searched tax and property records and found a photo of the home on a real estate site. Jenny confirmed it was where she was being held.

Khristina contacted the law enforcement agency working on Jenny’s case, along with Jenny’s mother, who she found on social media. On November 1, when Jenny confirmed that Harmel was out of the house, she coordinated between the girl and law enforcement to help facilitate the rescue.

Harmel was charged in a federal complaint filed in Utah on November 2 with transporting a minor across state lines with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. He made his initial court appearance in Boise, Idaho, on November 4.

What parents and players can do

We often say “talk to your kids about online safety,” but it can be hard to know where to begin. Talk about who they chat with and which trusted adult they can turn to if a conversation makes them uncomfortable or someone says they’re in danger. The Power Up Pact from Ask About Games offers a good framework for a conversation.

Know which games your kids are playing and review the chat settings together, including who can send them private messages.

Conversations that start in games can move to social media or messaging apps. Read our study on child safety across social media and gaming platforms. Incidentally, we also found Among Us to be on the safer side.

Grooming can start with friendship or gifts and move into private chats. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children has a guide to recognizing and responding to in-game grooming.

For more advice, read our online safety guide for parents.

Title: Home Office Reprimanded After GDPR Failure at the Border
Context: “Our investigation found the Home Office introduced a new system without ensuring staff had a clear, effective process for reporting and correcting inaccurate personal...
Full Text:
A major data integrity failure in a new UK border control system led to people being wrongly detained, the country’s data protection regulator has revealed in a reprimand for the government.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) reprimanded the Home Office after finding infringements of Articles 5(1)(d) and 25(1) of the UK GDPR and sections 38(1) and 56(1) of Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018.

They boil down to a failure to ensure the personal information (PII) it processed remained accurate and up to date.

“Our investigation found the Home Office introduced a new system without ensuring staff had a clear, effective process for reporting and correcting inaccurate personal information,” said ICO investigations manager, Joanne Stones.

“That failure could potentially have resulted in serious consequences, including people being wrongly detained for additional checks or refused entry to the UK.”

Read more on Home Office GDPR failures: UK Home Office Breached Data Protection Law with Migrant Tracking Program, ICO Finds

The issue stemmed from the new Helios border control information platform, introduced on October 2 2024. The Home Office failed to put in place a dedicated mechanism for reporting inaccurate personal information, according to the reprimand.

Under the previous system a dedicated team corrected any issues in real time, but the new regime required inaccuracies to be reported to and corrected by the owner of the source data, the ICO said.

Without a system to do so, many of these inaccuracies were left unchecked. Additionally, staff were told not to include PII when filing reports, which the ICO said made it “virtually impossible” to provide the information needed to correct a record.

Over a year later, on October 25 2025, the Home Office introduced a temporary reporting system for inaccuracies in PII. By March the following year, border force officers had raised 6500 incidents through this system, with around 5000 incorrect records removed, the ICO confirmed.

Psychological Distress for Data Subjects

The ICO claimed that these uncorrected inaccuracies in Home Office records led to individuals being wrongly stopped at the border for additional checks.

It said this was likely to cause the “affected individuals psychological distress and potentially result in them experiencing other adverse impacts.”

None have complained to the Home Office since their ordeal, but this may be because the government department never told them about the real cause of their detention at the border, the ICO said.

“Data protection by design is not just about the technology. It’s about making sure the processes, responsibilities, training and safeguards needed to protect people's information are correct from the start,” continued Stones.

“We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay.”

Article 25(1) of the UK GDPR states that organizations must “implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to effectively implement the data protection principles, specifically the accuracy principle.”

Title: Following the Cryptocurrency Trail Behind Europe’s Illegal Streaming Industry
Context: See How Cyble Tracks Threats Across the Dark Web Illegal IPTV services, fraudulent storefronts, and the cryptocurrency wallets behind them often surface first on underground...
Full Text:
Overview

Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have turned their attention to the financial engine powering Europe's illegal streaming industry. Rather than simply shutting down illegal IPTV services one by one, investigators are now tracing the cryptocurrency payments that keep these operations profitable and the people who ultimately pocket the proceeds.

The effort, coordinated by Europol, brought police together with major cryptocurrency exchanges and a blockchain analytics firm. The goal was to map the money flowing from subscribers to the criminal networks behind digital piracy, and to identify who controls the wallets at the end of that chain.

Five Days in Seville Disrupt 57 Illegal IPTV Services

The operation ran for five days, from 16 to 20 November 2026, in Seville, Spain. During that window, investigators worked alongside the cryptocurrency industry to uncover the financial networks supporting illegal IPTV services.

The results were significant. Authorities disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services and identified 321 websites offering copyrighted content without authorization. Together, those websites drew more than 7.3 million visits a year.

So far, investigators have traced more than EUR 26 million in cryptocurrency transactions linked to the services, and that analysis is still ongoing. The market under scrutiny is worth billions of euros annually, with providers selling unauthorized access to premium TV channels, live sports, and films, frequently collecting subscription fees in cryptocurrency.

The Real Cost of the Illegal Streaming Industry

The appeal of illegal IPTV services is easy to understand. For just a few euros a month, subscribers get thousands of TV channels, live sporting events, and premium content, while rights holders receive nothing. Those low prices, however, mask a highly profitable criminal enterprise.

Figures from the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) put the scale in perspective. Roughly 60 million people across Europe are estimated to use unauthorized IPTV services. Legitimate providers lose an estimated EUR 4.83 billion every year as a result, and governments miss out on another EUR 1.08 billion in uncollected taxes.

That revenue does not vanish. It passes through payment accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, and intermediaries, layers that make it harder for investigators to pinpoint who is really benefiting.

Why Cryptocurrency Didn't Keep Illegal IPTV Operators Hidden

Operators of illegal IPTV services have increasingly turned to cryptocurrency because it allows them to receive and transfer funds across borders quickly. Yet paying in crypto does not make anyone invisible.

Throughout the operation, investigators tracked suspicious transactions across blockchain networks. They searched for links between the illegal services, the cryptocurrency wallets receiving payments, and the individuals controlling them.

This approach reflects a broader shift in how authorities tackle the illegal streaming industry. Taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it, since they can often relaunch under a new name. By tracing payments, identifying beneficiaries, and targeting the financial networks that support these operations, law enforcement aims to make it much harder for criminals to keep profiting from digital piracy.

An International Effort Against Illegal IPTV Services

The operation was hosted at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville and brought together about 40 participants. Around 30 of them were law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain, and the United States.

Europol organized and coordinated the activity through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3). The agency provided analytical support, real-time intelligence cross-checks, and a secure channel for participating authorities to exchange information.

Other participants included the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, the AAPA, the cryptocurrency exchanges Binance and Coinbase, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. The intelligence collected will now feed into national investigations, helping authorities identify suspects, disrupt further illegal services, and trace assets tied to criminal activity.

Exchanges Report USD 28.5 Million in Traced Cryptocurrency

Following Europol's announcement on Tuesday, Binance stated that its investigations unit traced more than USD 28.5 million in cryptocurrency across the 57 illegal IPTV networks, describing the effort as a joint Europol and INTERPOL crackdown. According to Cointribune's report on 25 November 2026, this figure corresponds to the more than EUR 26 million cited by Europol, rounded and converted into US dollars in the exchange's statement and later coverage.

Binance said it worked with INTERPOL, Europol, Chainalysis, and national police forces, and that the operation disrupted the 57 services and mapped the 321 associated websites. Alongside the IPTV announcement, the exchange also published broader figures: in 2025, it said it responded to nearly 71,000 law enforcement requests and confiscated USD 131 million in illicit funds. CryptoBriefing separately reported that Coinbase also assisted Europol in the same crackdown.

For market observers, the more telling detail is not any individual token but the scale of data sharing between exchanges and police. Piracy operators used cryptocurrency rails to collect subscription payments, and the case shows that investigators can now routinely reconstruct those flows across multiple exchanges.

Following the Money Behind the Illegal Streaming Industry

The Seville operation signals a change in strategy against the illegal streaming industry. Takedowns alone have limited impact when operators can quickly resurface, so authorities are shifting their focus to the cryptocurrency payments and financial infrastructure that sustain illegal IPTV services.

With 57 services disrupted, 321 websites identified, and more than EUR 26 million in transactions traced so far, the case shows that blockchain activity leaves a trail investigators can follow. As national investigations build on this intelligence, operators who rely on cryptocurrency to stay out of reach may find that the payment method itself becomes the evidence against them.

Title: Data recovery firm co-founder accused of cashing in on ransomware victims
Context: The co-founder of a Florida data recovery firm has been indicted on charges that he secretly paid ransomware gangs while telling victims his company never did
Full Text:
The co-founder of a Florida data recovery firm has been indicted on charges that he secretly paid ransomware gangs while telling victims his company never did.

Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a 52-year-old Colombian national, was arrested in Las Vegas on October 22 and has been charged by a federal grand jury in the District of Rhode Island with three counts of wire fraud, each carrying a maximum of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

According to the indictment, the company told ransomware victims it had “sophisticated decryption technology” that could recover their data without a ransom being paid.

Prosecutors allege he had no such technology and instead negotiated with the attackers behind his clients’ backs, paying them and then charging his clients a higher amount so he could keep the difference. He is accused of using the proceeds to buy several properties in Florida.

“As alleged, the defendant preyed on ransomware victims by falsely marketing a solution he did not possess, secretly negotiating with cybercriminals, and profiting from the difference,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda for the District of Rhode Island.

The case against Palacio leans on an undercover operation run in June 2026, when FBI agents posed as a company hit by ransomware and as the ransomware actor holding its data.

Palacio allegedly paid the fake attacker about $6,000 in Bitcoin for the decryption key, then charged the undercover company about $13,260, more than twice the amount he handed over.

Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Boston Field Office, described it as a “short-sighted shakedown scheme” in which Palacio is accused of “lying, cheating, and negotiating with cybercriminals to line his own pockets.”

“As alleged, Mr. Palacio Escobar is the proverbial wolf in sheep’s clothing, representing both himself and his company as experts in data recovery, when all the while he was paying the perpetrators of these ransomware attacks, under the guise of helping his clients,” added Docks.

“Anyone who tries to target victims of crime for personal gain should know that justice will eventually find them,” Docks concluded.

Palacio isn’t the first ransomware specialist this year to be prosecuted for turning on the victims who hired him. In July, Angelo Martino, a former ransomware negotiator at incident response firm DigitalMint, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for passing confidential details from his negotiations, including victims’ insurance policy limits, to BlackCat (ALPHV) operators, who used them to push up ransom demands.

Title: UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data
Context: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal...
Full Text: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues. The new method went live on October 25, 2025. By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed. The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed. The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks. It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however. "The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated. A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates. "Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security." Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected. "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay." The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice. Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®

Title: Drupal Installer Patch Left a Gap Attackers Are Already Exploiting
Context: Drupal says last week’s patch for an exploited installer vulnerability did not protect every website, and attackers are now leveraging the gap to hack vulnerable sites
Full Text:
Drupal says last week’s patch for an exploited installer vulnerability did not protect every website, and attackers are now leveraging the gap to hack vulnerable sites.

The new issue, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 with a CMSS score of 21/25, was disclosed on November 25, exactly a week after Drupal announced the original patch in advisory SA-CORE-2026-017. Drupal describes the new flaw as an access bypass issue that can lead to site takeover.

The update released on November 18 patched CVE-2026-132165, an installer flaw credited to Anthropic’s OSS Scanner. The affected installer ships with Drupal core and enables users to set up a new site.

Drupal was informed of in-the-wild exploitation soon after, and CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 24.

The advisory for CVE-2026-136716 explains where the earlier fix fell short.

“SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites,” Drupal said in its advisory.

It added, “It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.”

Drupal warned that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and “any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.”

Websites where the installer had already been secured are not vulnerable to attacks. Patches are included in versions 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23. Affected production sites must run an update hook after upgrading to fully address the vulnerability.

Drupal has not shared any information on the attacks, and it’s unclear who is responsible for the exploitation. Users have been advised to check logs for signs of compromise.

Title: Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers
The Insider You Built with author Camille Stewart Gloster.
Context: And even looking at how our understanding of that incident has evolved over time tells us so much about the leaks in capability from January to the summer. But not attribution in the sense of, you know, what we commonly think about in cybersecurity.
Full Text:
Dave Bittner: Welcome to another special edition of the CyberWire. I'm Dave Bittner. Today I'm joined by Camille Stewart Gloster, former Deputy National Cyber Director at the White House and author of the new book, "The Insider You Built: How Organizations Stay in Control of Autonomous AI Agents". Her book looks at what changes when AI stops simply answering questions and starts taking action on our behalf, and how organizations can delegate authority to those systems without surrendering accountability and control. Here's my conversation with Camille Stewart Gloster. [ Music ] Well, let's start off with just some high-level stuff about the book. What prompted you to take on this topic?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I began working with companies to deploy AI within their organizations after leaving the White House, and remarked at just how many organizations were confused, worried, unsure about the effort that they were undertaking. And wanted to move forward because the technology was something they felt they needed to keep pace with how change was happening across industry, but were not making the necessary investments across security and even just operational resilience to understand how the technology was changing the nature of their organizations. And I was learning so many lessons through my client work that I wanted to capture that for a framework that is, in the book, to help organizations really understand that as they move into agentic AI and deploying more in their organizations, here are the organizational realignment, the security, the risk mitigation. Things you need to do and how your organization needs to come together such that you can realize the value of AI. It's really about maximizing the ROI and less about actually being a security book itself.

Dave Bittner: Well, I think the title itself is pretty provocative. It reminds me that perhaps these autonomous AI agents are almost like highly privileged insiders. Is that where we find ourselves with AI that makes this a useful analogy?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, it's exactly where we find ourselves, particularly as we move towards agentic, much like how we understand our employees to have a task that they are designed to undertake, or a role that they embody, but they can either take malicious action for whatever reason that runs counter to business objectives, or they can either be tricked or stumble their way into an action that misaligns with business goals. Agents are much the same. Between emergent behavior, misalignment, misconfiguration, and a whole host of other reasons, an agent is set on a and an agent is set on a trajectory, but you cannot quite predetermine exactly how it will get towards that destination. And that ambiguity there is why it is akin to insider risk and why organizations have to be intentional about understanding how you kind of control and constrain that behavior in an effort to deliver the value you've promised, whether that's internally or externally.

Dave Bittner: The book puts a lot of emphasis on this notion of delegated authority. What do you mean by authority in this context and how is that different from that traditional cybersecurity concept of access?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Great question. Access is part of it. But authority in this instance is really focused on the ability to act and make decisions on behalf of an organization. And when you think about it in that context, rather than around capability and around access to a system, but really taking an action towards a desire goal, it reframes how you think about an agent's place in your organization, how you bind and constrain that action, how much you enable, whether you let one agent do a lot of tasks and have a series of mandates, or if you keep their scope limited. How you monitor how they collaborate and coordinate, how you think about monitoring it. It kind of changes the trajectory on all of the things that you are going to do to enable an agent to move inside of your organization, much like you do with a person.

Dave Bittner: To that point, I mean, humans have always delegated authority to other humans. What makes delegating authority to software fundamentally different?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Accountability. We do not have a legal framework, an organizational framework, that aligns accountability. And the assumption is that the accountability aligns to the person who empowered the agent. But within an organization, if your marketing team deploys an agent to, you know, do something related to customer success, the IT team provisioned it, your security team had a hand in it. How are you thinking about that accountability? Is it really that the person in the marketing team is responsible for the actions taken by the agent? For sure the organization is responsible. But how do you think about that accountability and the work that needs to be done to keep the behavior aligned to the goals in mind as you leverage these new tools? That's the difference.

Dave Bittner: Is there a particular scenario that captures that risk for you? Like an example of when an agent was behaving exactly as it was designed but produced an outcome that nobody intended?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I mean, we can talk about this OpenAI Hugging Face incident that everybody has been talking about [laughter]. The goal was to beat the cybersecurity benchmark, and we have learned so much about how the agents collaborated, their motivations, the objective, how they decided to do what they were doing, that even hacking into Hugging Face wasn't about getting the answer key. It was about covering their tracks and wanting to understand how the grader would work, because they were afraid that they would get dinged for having circumvented the appropriate process to take the benchmark. I mean, that example is gold, because it demonstrates on so many levels how containment wasn't quite enough, how thinking about the cybersecurity implications isn't enough, how thinking about the safety implications isn't enough. You've got to think really holistically about risk and opportunity and how to operationalize it, and what the objectives are for the tool and how that might manifest itself in agents, or even just one agent for that matter, moving in a direction to get to the desired outcome that you did not anticipate.

Dave Bittner: You know, you mentioned accountability, and I remember right after the Hugging Face incident happened, I saw someone, a cyber security person online kind of snarkily commenting that in the aftermath how nice it was that the organizations responsible for it documented their crimes, right [laughter]?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I mean --

Dave Bittner: But I think there's a point to be made there, that while we are in this mode of exploration and things are happening so quickly, perhaps these things are being interpreted or responded to in a different way than in the future they may be.

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, I mean, this is all going to change very rapidly. And to your point, we are in a learning mode as much as a response and mitigation mode. And even looking at how our understanding of that incident has evolved over time tells us so much about the leaks in capability from January to the summer. And that understanding is exactly why organizations have to lean in to a more fulsome understanding of the authority that they are delegating to a given agent so that they have some opportunity to constrain and contain it and maintain some semblance of control within their organization.

Dave Bittner: In the book, you introduce an approach called authority-centered enforcement, or ACE. What were you trying to solve when you developed that framework?

Camille Stewart Gloster: That framework is an opportunity for an organization to align how it looks at some of the common practices that we use to constrain technology, like detection and enforcement and incident response and, you know, thinking about the learning that happens after, whether that's through a postmortem. But in this case, I advocate for continuous learning and a more agile way to kind of be iterative about how you intake information from an incident or a potential incident. That framework is really designed to help an organization think through how those things evolve, how the organization realigns to support doing those in a way that actually will help constrain agent behavior and operationalize it to create some operational reliability rather than just to mitigate risk. And it's not about attribution in the sense of, attribution is important in terms of articulating who is accountable, which agent did what. But not attribution in the sense of, you know, what we commonly think about in cybersecurity. It's not for consequence, but for, to facilitate learning. And if the program is built around that facilitation of learning, that acquisition of understanding and further aligning the runtime enforcement, the detection and response, all of these things around each tidbit of knowledge. And organization becomes a lot more adaptable to the changes that are ahead, because it's going to continue to change. This framework seeks to be a mechanism by which eight organizations can manage not only agent behavior, but whatever comes next, whether that's world models, simulations, anything that we can imagine to come next.

Dave Bittner: There's also this concept that you described called governed execution, which once the agent is running, you put into play. What kind of constraints or mechanisms should organizations have to execute this idea of governed execution?

Camille Stewart Gloster: Yes, across technical, operational and organizational lines, governance has to be an action. So I want everyone to divorce themselves of this idea that governance is just policy and it is a whole of organization, mobilization of capability around constraining behavior. And so that is runtime enforcement of the behaviors and constraints. And there is a great standard that has come out called ARM, and it's under cloud security alliance that kind of articulates the nuance there. And I know that there are others emerging, but it's really about how do you leverage a risk appetite policy and process constraints, as well as technical constraints on behavior that happen in the moment, to constrain behavior? And so then that operationalized this detection response continued learning loop that we are all very used to in a way that is not natural for most organizations. That is the goal. And so that's that governed execution really thinking about how do you operationalize governance across all three of those dimensions continuously as agents take an action throughout your organization. No matter if it's a agent within your security stack that's very focused on, you know, internal workings, or something that's externally focused, how do you make sure that this cycle is running consistently and continuously?

Dave Bittner: You know, one of the things that I really enjoy about the book is you reached out to folks across the board, folks in technology, cybersecurity, investing, even professional sports. What were some of the meaningful insights you got from some of those people that you talked to?

Camille Stewart Gloster: The thing that I was pleasantly surprised about is this emerging recognition of how important it is to really collaborate across disciplines. The predisposition to really hone in on your area of expertise is important. We need depth of discipline, but everyone that I talk to that has been doing this work in any meaningful way has recognized just how collaborative it has to be to be successful. For example, let's go back to the marketing tool, the marketing agent. Whoever owns that on the marketing team has to be a part of threat modeling for it to be effective. They're the only ones that understand with any nuance how that agent is interacting with the customer, how it leverages that data to then provide value for the organization. And that is extremely important insight that has to be a part of threat modeling. And threat modeling has to be more continuous than it traditionally has been. So, I think that recognition from folks across sectors, across disciplines, has been really heartening because it's kind of the core of what we need to do.

Dave Bittner: What's your advice for organizations that are trying to find that balance between autonomy and control? You know, they don't want to put too many gates around the agent because they still want to enjoy that speed and efficiency. Any words of wisdom there?

Camille Stewart Gloster: There is no easy part to that, but what I will say is the investment in constraint and control, and understanding really how to operationalize your agent is reliability. And, you know, one of the reasons we keep hearing so much about, like, works, AI workslop and AI not yielding the value that organizations thought it would is because they haven't quite figured out how to manifest that operational reliability. And investing in disciplines like cybersecurity in really understanding safety and risk mitigation, and getting the entire organization to collaborate around extracting value is how you do that. And so if you're doing that, it might slow you down just a little bit, but you'll yield so much more. And finding that sweet spot for your organization is kind of an individual journey. It's a risk appetite thing. How much risk can the organization manage? But it should be an intentional decision.

Dave Bittner: How can an organization measure success with this? How can they know that they actually have their AI agents under control, as opposed to only thinking that they have it under control?

Camille Stewart Gloster: That's true. I don't want any organization to think that they have gotten it all sewn up and that they have complete control. As we're learning, back to the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, there could be so much happening in the background that we don't understand. This will give you as much control as you can get in terms of having a handle on what the boundaries are, and doing what you can, just like we do with people. So I don't want anyone to be lulled into a false sense of comfort. But metrics for success are around how much value you're yielding all the way to the absence of incidents and kind of understanding, being able to recreate and understand the steps taken to achieve a goal, understand how the objective has manifested itself. So, creating that transparency and visibility so you can maintain some level of understanding of the work that's being done on your behalf. Those will give you the indicators of whether or not you've continued to maintain control or it's more of an illusion.

Dave Bittner: And what do you hope that the reader comes away with, having read the book? What's your desire there?

Camille Stewart Gloster: I hope that every reader, whether technical or nontechnical, owning the AI program or just deploying an agent within any department, walks away feeling a bit more empowered to ask questions, to understand their piece of making sure that the agent yields value and is working on their behalf in the ways that they have designed and desire. That level of intentionality will then map to how we operate in our personal lives and how we think about this on a societal level. And I think that's where the real value lies. Right now we're making the, we're writing the rules within industry, and connecting the dots on how this technology shows up in our professional lives will help us understand how it shows up more broadly.

Dave Bittner: Our thanks to Camille Stewart Gloster for joining us. The book is "The Insider You Built" How Organizations Stay in Control of Autonomous AI Agents". It's a good read worth your time. Thanks for joining us for this special edition of the CyberWire. I'm Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening. [ Music ]

Title: Drupal Warns of New Highly Critical Site Takeover Vulnerability Under Active Exploitation
Context: Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild
Full Text:
Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix.

CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said. "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites."

"It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state."

Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted.

Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions -

Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account

Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password.

The issue has been remediated in the following versions -

Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.14

Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.23

Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.23

Drupal 11.0.x to 11.2.x - No fix (End-of-life)

Drupal 10.5.x and below - No fix (End-of-life)

After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites.

According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

Title: U.S. CISA adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability...
Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the following HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability

The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score of 7.5), is a path traversal vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration management systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit improper restrictions on file paths to retrieve and read files from the underlying system through the XML interface. Access to sensitive files could provide information useful for further compromising the device. There are no publicly confirmed reports of exploitation in the wild or threat actors associated with this vulnerability. Danfoss addressed the issue in software version 3.3.

The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical improper input validation vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient input validation to execute arbitrary commands on the target system, potentially gaining full control of the affected refrigeration controller. Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability to attacks in the wild or identifying threat actors exploiting it. Danfoss released software version 3.3 to address the issue.

The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score of 8.2), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series systems running software versions prior to 4.2. The authentication bypass allows an attacker to generate web reports without proper authorization, potentially exposing sensitive information such as internal IP addresses, usernames and store names. The vulnerability was identified by researchers at Claroty’s Team82. Although it affects the same family of refrigeration controllers targeted in the European supermarket attacks, there is no public confirmation that attackers exploited this particular CVE during those incidents. Danfoss addressed the vulnerability in software version 4.2.

The fourth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting HPE Juniper Session Smart Conductor. The flaw resides in the AutomatedProvisioner component and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges by supplying a specially crafted Salt minion ID. The vulnerability has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming exploitation in the wild. However, no specific threat actor or ransomware campaign has been publicly attributed to these attacks. Administrators should apply the security updates provided by Juniper, including versions 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 for the affected release branches.

The fifth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability affecting the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. The vulnerability affects MiCollab version 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient file type validation to upload arbitrary files to the target system. Depending on the nature of the uploaded files and the system configuration, this could provide an opportunity for further malicious activity. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified any threat actors associated with this vulnerability. The company released a security patch for affected installations.

The sixth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score of 9.0), is a critical XML injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter validation and leverage malicious content staged in advance to perform XML injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the affected installation. Mitel has not disclosed any confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified threat actors behind attacks exploiting this flaw. A security patch is available for affected MiCollab installations.

The seventh flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score of 5.9), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a specific system-generated random identifier or has access to malicious content staged in advance could exploit the weakness to obtain sensitive information. The vulnerability is limited to the affected functionality and does not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary files elsewhere on the system. No confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been publicly reported. Mitel has released a security patch to address the issue.

The eighth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score of 10.0), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter sanitization to perform blind command injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the affected system. Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity and availability. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or attributed attacks to specific threat actors. A security patch is available to address the vulnerability.

The ninth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. Improper handling of authentication could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass security controls and perform unauthorized actions within the application. Successful exploitation could compromise the security of the affected installation. No publicly confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been reported. Mitel has released a security patch for the affected versions.

The tenth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting Vates Xen Orchestra, a management and backup platform for XCP-ng and XenServer environments. The vulnerability affects versions prior to 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of authentication tokens by supplying a specially crafted cookie containing an empty JSON object. The application may then authenticate the attacker as the owner of an existing, unexpired token. Once authenticated, the attacker could retrieve reusable authentication token identifiers, potentially enabling persistent unauthorized access to the environment. The vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild, although no specific threat actors have been publicly identified. Vates addressed the issue in Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1.

The Danfoss vulnerabilities deserve particular attention because they affect the same family of refrigeration management systems involved in the cyberattacks targeting European supermarkets in October and November 2026.

The first wave of attacks, detected between October 11 and 12, compromised refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail sites in France. Attackers manipulated defrost settings, forcing refrigeration equipment to operate at excessively high temperatures. The incidents resulted in substantial food losses and at least 15 reported fires. A second wave between November 1 and 2 affected retailers across several other European countries.

The French authorities’ investigation attributed the October attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, responsibility for the subsequent November attacks across Europe has not been conclusively established.

The technical evidence points to the exploitation of internet-exposed refrigeration management interfaces, with default credentials and outdated firmware considered likely entry points. However, investigators have not confirmed that CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 or CVE-2025-41450 were specifically exploited during these operations. The incidents instead highlight the risks associated with exposing operational technology (OT) systems directly to the internet without adequate authentication, network segmentation and security updates.

An additional development is worth mentioning: a November 2026 advisory from Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre reported research by Midnight Blue identifying six previously unknown pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, affecting firmware versions up to and including 5.3.2. At the time of the advisory, these flaws had not yet received CVE identifiers and no patches were available. Researchers also warned that attackers could establish persistence surviving factory resets and firmware updates. These findings add another layer of concern to the security of refrigeration infrastructure. ncsc.gov.ie

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA order U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate eight of them by November 28, 2026, and the remaining two by December 9, 2026. The individual deadlines are:

November 28, 2026: CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324 and CVE-2026-133469.

December 9, 2026: CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2026-133311.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

Title: 13 Malicious NuGet Packages Turn Fake .NET Job Assessments Into Malware Delivery Traps
Context: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows .NET developers under the guise of a fake take-home job assessment.

"Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF [Windows Presentation Foundation] button controls," Socket security researcher Kush Pandya said in a technical write-up. "In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL sideloading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable."

All the identified NuGet packages have been deleted from the gallery as of writing. The names of the packages are listed below -

WinUI.Button

VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer

VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls

HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer

HappyOne.WinUI3Controls

Web3TotalButton

RevertButtonIcon

WinUI3IconButton

WindowsAccentColorName

SetButtonColor

InitializeCustomButton

StyledAppButton

StyledComponent

The first NuGet package, WinUI3IconButton, was uploaded to the registry on July 23, 2026, indicating that the campaign has been ongoing for quite some time without attracting attention. The last two uploads, HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls, occurred on November 4, 2026, after both VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls were removed by NuGet on November 2, 2026.

The starting point is a GitHub repository ("stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment") created on November 3, 2026. It features a set of assessment tasks revolving around enhancing a FileButton control and exception handling that candidates must implement within a span of three to four hours. It's unclear how targets are led to these decoy projects.

The README file also permits the test participants to use artificial intelligence (AI) development assistants like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude, but discourages them from copying and pasting the entire project into the tool and generating the solution without "understanding it."

Present within the assessment repository is a "WinUI3_Home_Assessment.csproj" file that references VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer version 1.2.7 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls version 1.0.7.

"VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL ['MSBuildAnalyzer.dll'] after every build," Pandya said. "In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it."

The VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package then launches the copied binary via the FileButton control that "routes clicks to Windows files and folders," triggering the execution of the DLL via a known technique called DLL sideloading.

In a similar vein, creating a WUIButton control from the WinUI.Button package starts a background routine in "lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll" that downloads "avast.exe" from the "Carol-White-Super/cloud" repository via the GitHub API using an embedded access token, saves it as "%TEMP%\Launcher.exe," and runs it.

RevertButtonIcon and SetButtonColor "download a Windows executable to the user's temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops," Socket explained.

"Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to."

Socket also said it identified two bogus repositories impersonating the axios JavaScript library -

jason-code-super/axios

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (the same GitHub account hosting the assessment)

Both repositories have been flagged as copies of a malicious Node.js library named "axios-test-one" that impersonates the Axios HTTP client but contains functionality that enables code execution and shell access. The repositories serve a Windows executable named "lib/env/axios.csproj."

An analysis of their commit history has revealed several binaries between the two repositories, including -

A loader ("updater.exe" and "msedgewebview2.exe") that uses a GitHub repository ("James-White-Super/React_prj") as a two-way command and control (C2)

A PyInstaller program that functions as a Google Chrome profile stealer and uploads the information to GitHub ("gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository"), and

A "WeapF" payload that reports the computer name, user name, time zone, and CPU model to an attacker-controlled Telegram bot

What's more, the GitHub account named "gabsantosbus-star" (aka Gabriel) has been found to have made the first commit in the two aforementioned fake Axios repositories, along with "figma-share/axios-http," a third bogus Axios repository.

"On November 13, 2026, gabsantosbus-star [...] published a GitHub release of 'Crypto Wallet Analyzer,' a single-file .NET app," Socket said. "The README presents the app as a first-stage client deliverable that inventories eight crypto wallet extensions in Chrome profiles and makes no network requests."

"The visible app does only that, but its decompiled MainWindow constructor also loads a native DLL bundled in the executable. The DLL starts a background thread when loaded, and closing the window only hides it, so the process keeps running."

The DLL in question is a new version of the loader that uses a different repository ("Best-Seller-Dev/dexTrader") for C2. The GitHub account is no longer accessible as of writing.

Further investigation has uncovered that the lure was advertised on a Web3 freelance marketplace called LaborX on November 7, 2026, under the same persona, with the threat actor posing as a "detail-oriented client looking to work with skilled freelancers on various projects."

The $8,500-10,000 job listing, which is still accessible, claims that they are looking for a C# WPF developer to work on their lightweight Windows .NET desktop application that "inventories crypto wallet software installed on a local PC, including browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications."

On their X profile, they describe themselves as a "blockchain and DeFi specialist" and a "cryptocurrency expert" based out of Miami, Florida. But a check of their "About this account" reveals that the profile is actually based in Korea. The account was created in July 2026.

The web of connections doesn't end there, for evidence indicates that the "axios-test-one" npm library was part of a broader collection of six packages that were published between July 14 and 23, 2026, by three npm accounts gsanbus, jasonsuperstar, and jasonsayman -

axios-test-one

telemetry-metrics

telemetry-axios

axios-native

fs-extra-core

vitest-axios

The use of the name "jasonsayman" is particularly significant as it clearly points to an attempt to pass off as "jasonsaayman," the legitimate GitHub account belonging to the developer and maintainer of Axios.

"Telemetry-metrics and telemetry-axios download a Windows executable from ThoSuperstarDev/axios-http and run it, fs-extra-core downloads one from jason-code-super/axios and saves it as msedgewebview2.exe, and the axios clones pull those packages in," Socket said.

What's notable here is that "ThoSuperstarDev" is the former GitHub account name of "figma-share," which, as it happens, also hosts a ClickFix-style page that shows a fake reCAPTCHA verification prompt and guides the visitor to copy and paste a security token into the Windows Run dialog to address a purported "Security Handshake Error."

The fraudulent job campaign has not been attributed to any named threat actor or group. However, Socket noted that the tradecraft shares similarities with other recruitment-themed campaigns orchestrated by North Korea and Iran.

"We found no indicator or code shared with any published Contagious Interview or other North Korean campaign, none of the malware families publicly tied to Contagious Interview (such as BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, and OtterCookie) in the stages we recovered, and no publicly documented family that matches the loader," Pandya said.

Title: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC
Context: Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations
Full Text:
As your organization plans upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), you should also think about cryptographic agility to more easily update algorithms used to protect your data. Changes to cryptography and related protocols aren’t new, but PQC is accelerating the pace at which organizations must add new algorithms and remove old ones to keep up with changing regulations and evolving business risk. AWS believes our key to success is standardizing on one cryptographic library that embodies three key properties: compatibility, assurance, and performance. In this blog post, you’ll learn how we think of the cost and friction of ongoing cryptographic updates in terms of these properties. You’ll learn how AWS built AWS-LC to embody these properties, thus making cryptographic upgrades straightforward and low-impact for ourselves and our customers. For custom applications where you can’t yet use AWS services and must operate your own stacks, this post also shares why you might consider using AWS-LC as your standardized library.

Every cryptographic algorithm used to protect your data today has an expiration date, even if no regulator has set one yet. Algorithms that were once the standard, such as MD5 and SHA-1, have been retired. Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations. The move to post-quantum cryptography is the current wave of changes, with dates set by governments and regulators to complete the transition. PQC itself will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post-quantum algorithms and then deprecate traditional cryptography. Each change reaches your systems as a software library update, so the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version of your cryptographic library, and what each rollout costs. At AWS, we think of this cost in terms of three properties. Compatibility means an update doesn’t require application changes. Assurance means new code can be trusted when it ships, without a long bake period. Performance means a new algorithm doesn’t add so much computational overhead or latency that it gives teams a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own.

AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. If you’ve called an AWS API, AWS-LC was used on the server side. Through s2n-tls, it provides hybrid post-quantum key exchange on AWS service endpoints and in services like Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer. It’s also the cryptography under aws-lc-rs for Rust, the default provider for rustls, and under the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider for Java. Because so much of AWS depends on one library, we built it to be updated often. AWS-LC keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without a rewrite. It uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct. It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce the latency and compute costs that new algorithms add. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes.

Hand off what you can, standardize what you keep

Each piece of cryptography you own is one more thing to change at every transition. By owning as little of your cryptographic stack as your constraints or requirements allow, and using AWS services to manage the rest, you can minimize your ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

If your workload relies solely on managed services like AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and managed resources like Elastic Load Balancer or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), you’re already reaping the benefits of AWS-LC and the AWS shared responsibility model. You only need to keep your clients and resource configurations updated. Many organizations can rely on AWS to provide the infrastructure and basic automation, but still own and manage the endpoints and applications where most of the work happens. For these components, it’s helpful to standardize on as few cryptographic libraries as possible. With fewer libraries, your team learns each one well: how to configure it, run it, and update it. The library you standardize on also decides how often you can update it. If an update requires application changes, ships new code that no one trusts yet, or adds compute and latency, teams have a reason to wait. In the rest of this post, we show you how AWS-LC removes each of those reasons through compatibility, assurance, and performance.

Compatibility

The best library update is one that doesn’t impact your application and that your users don’t notice. Code changes happen at three points: adopting a library, adding an algorithm, and updating the library. AWS-LC keeps each one small.

Adopting AWS-LC – For TLS, AWS-LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API, so most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes. Applications that call libcrypto directly might need more work, because the AWS-LC libcrypto API differs from OpenSSL’s in places. See the porting guide for where behavior differs.

Adding an algorithm – When new algorithms are added in AWS-LC behind interfaces applications already call, s2n-tls, s2n-quic, aws-lc-rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically. Hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, for example, is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs. For 1Password, that meant a one-line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.

Updating the library – AWS-LC long-term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI). Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild. One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts. The Amazon Linux 2027 preview uses this method to ship AWS-LC as a system library.

We built these properties so AWS services could move to AWS-LC with minimal effort. aws-lc-rs is also used by open source projects; it’s the default cryptography provider for rustls with over 100 million downloads in the past 90 days, CPython tests against AWS-LC in continuous integration, and HAProxy publishes packages built on it. Each new use surfaces problems earlier in the update process, and every fix is recorded in one codebase.

Assurance

Every new algorithm arrives as new code, and new code is where bugs and security vulnerabilities are usually found. If you can’t trust new code when it ships, you wait, and each wait delays the next change. Tests check the inputs you run, and proofs check every input. AWS-LC uses machine-checked proofs for its most critical code, including its post-quantum algorithms and parts of its classical algorithms, such as its 25519 elliptic-curve code.

AWS-LC contributes to and takes its ML-KEM and ML-DSA code from two open source projects: mlkem-native and mldsa-native. The algorithmic implementations in these projects already incorporate formal verification safeguards such as ensuring no out of bound memory access, no integer overflows, constant assembly run time, and functional correctness using tools like CBMC and HOL Light (for more information, see Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon). AWS-LC imports this code from upstream without changing it. The proofs don’t depend on instruction order, so the assembly can be re-optimized without redoing them. That prevents verification from becoming the reason a faster implementation waits. Other cryptographic implementations of the library are verified in s2n-bignum.

We use these proofs alongside testing and FIPS validation. For workloads that require FIPS 140-3, a validated module is required to allow new code to be deployed. AWS-LC FIPS 3.0 was the first cryptographic library to include ML-KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validation. ML-DSA, the NIST post-quantum signature standard (FIPS 204), is in the AWS-LC FIPS 4.0 module, and the FIPS 5.0 module includes the faster, formally verified mldsa-native implementation. Both have been submitted to NIST for validation.

Performance

A new algorithm that costs more to run gives teams a reason to delay, and across many connections a small cost per connection adds up. AWS-LC optimizes each algorithm it adds so that cost doesn’t delay the update. Amazon Science reports 2.0 to 2.4 times more ML-KEM operations per second than the reference implementations across Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance types. Earlier work applied the same approach to 25519 elliptic-curve cryptography. The optimized code is covered by the proofs described in the previous section, so speed doesn’t reduce assurance.

ML-DSA followed the same path. AWS-LC moved from its original implementation to mldsa-native, with optimized assembly for AArch64 and x86_64 platforms, and it now signs and verifies faster on both Graviton and x86 EC2 instance types. As a result, compute is no longer the main cost of post-quantum signatures: in the measurements in the following section, we show that ML-DSA-44 certificates lowered average TLS handshake latency compared with RSA-2048. What remains is size, which the next section measures.

What it costs to move

AWS services handle billions of requests every second, so anything that could affect those requests must be carefully considered. Post-quantum cryptography impacts the performance of every new TLS connection, so before we adopted ML-KEM and ML-DSA, we invested heavily in making them fast. Figure 1 shows the resulting reduction in time for both key exchange and authentication. Today, moving to PQ confidentiality has no net cost for most AWS use-cases, and PQ authentication takes less compute than the RSA certificates we use today.

Figure 1. ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-87 time per handshake, before and after AWS-LC’s native implementations, on AWS Graviton4

ML-KEM-768 key exchange decreased by over 50 percent on both the client and the server (as shown in Figure 1); we described how in Verifying and optimizing post-quantum cryptography at Amazon. In this post, we’re focusing on ML-DSA. In AWS-LC v1.49.1, ML-DSA used the original AWS-LC implementation, adapted from the reference code. In v5.10.0, it runs on mldsa-native, which implements the performance-critical kernels in hand-written Arm64 Neon assembly for AWS Graviton, including: the number-theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse, tuned for Arm cores with the SLOTHY superoptimizer, along with pointwise multiplication, rejection sampling, and the decompose, hint, and norm-check steps of signing and verification. It also expands the public matrix four entries at a time using the AWS-LC four-way parallel SHA-3 (Keccak). These optimizations, as shown in the right half of Figure 1, reduced ML-DSA-87 signing time on the server and verification time on the client, and the same assembly is covered by the formal proofs described earlier. mldsa-native is open source, part of the PQ Code Package in the Linux Foundation’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance (PQCA), and the AWS Cryptography team and Amazon Automated Reasoning Group contribute to it.

Figure 2. TLS 1.3 connection setup time by algorithm, between two AWS Graviton4 hosts in the same Availability Zone

Figure 2 shows total handshake time for various configurations, when the client and server are in the same AWS Region. For a baseline, we used TLS performance when the server prioritized ECDHE with P-256 for key exchange and RSA-2048 certificates for authentication. With the optimizations to ML-KEM, there is negligible overhead from moving to hybrid ML-KEM key exchange (the second bar from left). The hybrid key exchange preferred in AWS systems today pairs X25519 with ML-KEM-768. X25519 is faster than P-256, and that saving covers the remaining ML-KEM work, so a full connection setup takes roughly 12 microseconds more, which doesn’t meaningfully impact throughput or latency. It’s worth noting here that ML-KEM-768 introduces approximately 2.3 KB to the handshake.

PQ authentication carries more risk, because authentication is more of the handshake cost. The server signs once for each handshake, and the client verifies three signatures: the server’s handshake signature, the signature on the leaf, and the signature on the intermediate certificate. RSA-2048 signing is expensive and verification is inexpensive. ML-DSA-87 reverses that balance, shifting some work from the server to the client.

ML-DSA keys and signatures are also much larger, so the server’s handshake messages grow from 4–7 KB to 17–24 KB depending on the chosen certificate parameters. That adds certificate parsing on the client and more data to encrypt and send on the server. Within an Availability Zone, those messages still arrive in one round trip, and we measured no difference in network time between configurations.

Compared to RSA 2048, which is still prevalent today, ECDSA offers faster processing. However, both must be replaced by ML-DSA for post-quantum authentication. With the optimizations in AWS-LC, ML-DSA-44 comes close to ECDSA, and every ML-DSA parameter set is significantly faster than RSA-2048, as shown in Figure 2. As a result, we’re confident in managing the performance impact from migrating to post-quantum certificates.

Another facet of our investments in reducing performance impact is session resumption. Handshake costs apply only to new connections. Session resumption reduces how often that cost is paid. A resumed TLS 1.3 handshake authenticates with a key from the earlier session and sends no certificates or signatures, so the larger ML-DSA keys and signatures apply only to full handshakes. We’ll note here that in psk_dhe_ke mode, the resumed handshake still runs a fresh hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, which preserves forward secrecy. Now, resumption only helps if the client can present its ticket to any server behind the endpoint, so AWS has been extending support for resumption across the hosts behind its service endpoints. AWS SDKs can reuse connections across many requests, and session resumption can skip certificates and signatures entirely, which gives the most performance benefit for workloads using AWS managed services. If you’re using AWS-LC directly in your own custom applications, consider keeping session tickets enabled, prefer TLS 1.3 with psk_dhe_ke, and reuse clients so that they keep their tickets between connections.

Conclusion

Every cryptographic choice has an expiration date, so the goal isn’t to pick the right algorithm once and never replace or update it, but to make each replacement routine. Start by handing off what you can to AWS services and standardizing what you keep on as few libraries as possible. For the cryptography you own, three properties decide how quickly and how often you can implement each update. For compatibility, new algorithms arrive behind the APIs your applications already call, and long-term support releases keep a stable ABI, so adopting one takes a library update and a restart, not a rebuild. For assurance, machine-checked proofs cover a library’s most critical code, ML-KEM is inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module, and ML-DSA is in modules submitted for validation. For performance, optimized implementations keep each new algorithm from adding compute or latency that might give teams a reason to wait. Post-quantum cryptography is the change in front of us now, and it won’t be the last.
