Title: ICYMI: October 2026 @AWS Security
Context: Threat detection and incident response AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security Authors: Alexander Greaves-Tunnell, Neha Rungta | Published: October 5, 2026...
Full Text:
Welcome to this month’s AWS Security news! Organizations need current information about AWS Security developments to maintain their cloud security. This monthly digest covers key AWS Security updates. Each month, we compile new announcements, features, and resources to help you improve your security. Based on AWS Security developments, you’ll find expert perspectives in blogs, announcements of new features and capabilities, ready-to-use code samples, reference architectures, and hands-on workshops and labs to build practical security skills. Not every edition will include all of these categories, but we’ll consistently bring you the most relevant and impactful updates to help you enhance your security and governance posture.

AWS Security Blog posts

October brought 19 AWS Security Blog posts focused on the remediation flow, from a security finding to a tested fix. Learn how AI agents can find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and how to add penetration testing to every deployment. You’ll also find guidance on extending existing access controls to AI agents with trusted identity propagation and preparing your signing workflows for post-quantum cryptography. The PHP2Shell posts show why patch timelines for internet-facing systems are now measured in hours, and how AWS WAF can help reduce risk while you upgrade. Other posts cover identity source changes in AWS IAM Identity Center, workload identity outside AWS, and domain-based filtering in AWS Network Firewall.

Threat detection and incident response

AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security Authors: Alexander Greaves-Tunnell, Neha Rungta | Published: October 5, 2026 AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities achieved an 89.0 percent end-to-end success rate on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. It found, demonstrated, and repaired vulnerabilities in real open source codebases, 23.1 percentage points above the previous public high.

Part 1 – Cybersecurity journeys: I didn’t plan this Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 7, 2026 The first post in a four-part Cybersecurity Awareness Month series shares how 11 AWS security professionals moved into security from unexpected backgrounds, showing there’s no single path into the field.

GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection has added five new indicators to surface attack sequences Authors: Aman Khare, Kyle Koeller | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to use five new indicator types in Amazon GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection: vulnerability, malicious package, reachability, misconfiguration, and sensitive data. They bring signals from Amazon Inspector, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Reachability Analyzer, Amazon Macie, and AWS Security Hub into sequence findings, and the post shows how to add them to your incident response workflow.

Part 2 – Cybersecurity journeys: What even is this job? Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 13, 2026 The second post in the series covers lesser-known security roles. These include measuring risk across a million applications, building detection tools from the customer service side, and securing infrastructure launched into orbit.

Penetration testing every deployment with AWS Continuum Authors: Jigar Bhatt, Benjamin Li | Published: October 14, 2026 Learn to add AWS Continuum for penetration testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) to your continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline as a check after each deployment. It tests only the change you deployed to staging and can stop that change from reaching production when a finding meets a severity threshold you set. The post includes an example for GitHub Actions.

AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum) exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs Authors: Dazhi Zhang, Hamed Soleimani | Published: October 15, 2026 AWS Continuum for penetration testing was tested against a new internal benchmark of 37 recently disclosed CVEs in live, containerized applications. Starting from a low-privilege position, it confirmed 33 of the 37 vulnerabilities end to end through the intended path, an 89.2 percent success rate.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot Author: CJ Moses | Published: October 21, 2026 Amazon Threat Intelligence detected activity targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on its MadPot sensors four days before public disclosure. The post explains what this means for security leaders: patch critical internet-facing systems within hours, and start investigations from the earliest activity seen, not the disclosure date.

Part 3 – Cybersecurity journeys: The work behind the work Author: Shannon Brazil | Published: October 27, 2026 The third post in the series looks at the day-to-day work of AWS security professionals that rarely gets attention. It covers application security reviews that depend on conversations with builders and on sharing hard feedback with empathy.

AI security

Identity-aware AI data agents with AWS Lake Formation and Trusted Identity Propagation Authors: Thiyagarajan Mani, Mihir Borkar, Philippe Duplessis-Guindon, Umang Khambhalikar | Published: October 6, 2026 Learn to pass each user’s identity through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to AWS Lake Formation using trusted identity propagation. Your existing data access policies then apply to AI agent queries without changes to application code, and AWS CloudTrail records the actual user behind each query.

Building your AI vulnerability harness, Part 1 Authors: Nidhi Ramakant, Ievgeniia Ieromenko, Justin Kontny | Published: October 7, 2026 Learn to build a three-layer pipeline that uses AI to reduce raw scanner findings to a small, prioritized set with documented evidence, so engineers can act without repeating the analysis. The architecture works with your own scanners and models.

Configuring your AI vulnerability harness, Part 2: The steering file Authors: Justin Kontny, Ievgeniia Ieromenko, Nidhi Ramakant | Published: October 7, 2026 Learn to configure a steering file that has an AI model confirm the code structure before it reports a finding, score its confidence from that structural evidence, and set priority based on the controls in your infrastructure as code. The result is vulnerability triage that gives the same findings each time it runs.

Identity

Improving SPIRE security and resiliency with AWS managed services Authors: Brendan Paul, Meg Peddada | Published: October 6, 2026 Learn to run SPIRE in production by moving key management, workload identity registration, certificate authority integration, and identity delivery for serverless workloads to AWS managed services. This helps you move from static credentials to short-lived workload identities. A GitHub repository walks you through deploying the reference architecture.

Managing identity source transition for AWS IAM Identity Center Authors: Xiaoxue Xu, Kanwar Bajwa, Laura Reith, Richard Merritt, Taimur Ijlal, Yee Fei Ooi | Published: October 20, 2026 Learn to change the identity source in AWS IAM Identity Center using a step-by-step runbook and sample code. The post covers the new migration from Active Directory to an external identity provider or the Identity Center directory, which keeps your users, groups, memberships, and assignments in place.

Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI Authors: Abhishek Avinash Agawane, Manoj Gupta | Published: October 21, 2026 Learn to apply best practices for connecting your public key infrastructure (PKI) to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere. Workloads running outside AWS can then get temporary credentials using X.509 certificates, each with its own identity and set of permissions.

Data protection

Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 1: Build a software supply chain with ML-DSA Author: Harshvardhan Chunawala | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to build an end-to-end post-quantum signing architecture for binaries, container images, and software bills of materials (SBOMs). It combines ML-DSA keys in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), ML-DSA certificate hierarchies in AWS Private Certificate Authority, and ML-DSA trust anchors in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Quantum-resistant signing on AWS, Part 2: Enforce your ML-DSA algorithm policy with SCPs and IAM Authors: Harshvardhan Chunawala, Blake Roberts | Published: October 12, 2026 Learn to turn your organization’s post-quantum algorithm policy into preventive and detective controls using service control policies (SCPs) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Only approved ML-DSA parameter sets can then be used with AWS KMS across your environment.

Infrastructure security

Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) Authors: Alex Waddell, Eitav Arditti, Lawton Pittenger, Ian Olson | Published: October 21, 2026 Learn to use the AWS WAF PHP application managed rule group to help reduce risk from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities while you upgrade PHP across your fleet. The post also covers guidance for end-of-life PHP versions and a related issue, CVE-2026-115560.

Introducing Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall Authors: Lawton Pittenger, Amish Shah, Amit Gaur, Jesse Lepich, Preetkumar Shah | Published: October 27, 2026 Learn to use Route 53 Resolved IP Validation, available at no additional charge. Amazon Route 53 Resolver shares the IP addresses it returns for each domain name with AWS Network Firewall, which checks new outbound connections against them. You can then filter non-web traffic such as SSH and SFTP by domain name and validate Server Name Indication (SNI) in TLS traffic without turning on TLS inspection.

Governance and compliance

AWS becomes first CSP in Canada to complete the Cloud High profile assessment with 172 services and features in scope Author: Naranjan Goklani | Published: October 27, 2026 AWS completed the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) Cloud High (PBHH) security assessment, with 172 services and features assessed in the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) AWS Regions. This helps public and commercial customers meet security requirements for more sensitive workloads up to the Protected B level. The summary assessment is available in AWS Artifact.

October security bulletins

In October 2026, AWS published 41 security bulletins addressing vulnerabilities across open source SDKs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AI agent frameworks, embedded software, and widely used runtimes. The AI agent tool surface remained the main theme. An authentication bypass in Loom for AWS could allow network clients to gain administrative access to the agent control plane, and the AWS API MCP Server accepted OAuth tokens issued to other applications. Prompt-injected content could turn off secret masking in Strands Agents Tools or trigger command execution through the databases-on-aws agent plugin. The category also included cross-session conversation exposure in the Strands Agents Agent-to-Agent (A2A) server, missing authorization in the Kiro Crew WhatsApp channel, and code injection and server-side request forgery (SSRF) in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Starter Toolkit. Several broad-impact advisories called for customer action, including remote code execution in PHP web runtimes and the native Brotli decoder, a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free issue, and recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA keys in AWS trust bundles.

Other notable issues include OS command injection in the AWS Serverless Application Model Command Line Interface (AWS SAM CLI) Terraform hook and the Amazon SageMaker Distribution startup script, SQL injection in the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) Amazon Redshift alpha constructs, an RSA padding oracle in the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Encryption Client for .NET, and memory-safety issues in FreeRTOS, the AWS Nitro Enclaves SDK for C, and aws-c-mqtt. Credential exposure recurred in client tooling. AWS Tools for PowerShell, the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK, and the Amazon Kinesis Producer Library wrote secrets to logs. The Amazon SageMaker Python SDK and AWS SDK for pandas also used predictably named Amazon S3 buckets without verifying bucket ownership. A common thread: tools trusted inputs they didn’t control, such as content an agent ingests, a token issued to another application, or a bucket in another account. Patches or mitigations are available for every bulletin, so upgrade promptly. For more information, see AWS Security Bulletins.

AWS samples

This month’s eight AWS samples give you deployable code that puts the remediation flow into practice. Learn how to have AI agents investigate an incident together, connect public security events to the affected lines in your code, and hold off risk at the edge until a patch is merged. Other samples show you how to run AI-assisted vulnerability scanning in isolated environments and add security requirements to specs before any code is written. You’ll also find patterns for protecting MCP servers, private VPC workloads, and browser sessions driven by AI agents, plus a dashboard for governing generative AI usage and cost.

Infrastructure security

AWS Lambda Web Functions reference architecture: Amazon CloudFront and private VPC access Learn to run a web application on AWS Lambda Web Functions behind Amazon CloudFront, using Origin Access Control so the function only accepts signed requests. A Lambda network connector lets the function reach private resources in your VPC. The sample uses Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 as the example database, with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication, so no credentials need to be stored.

Architecture patterns for MCP servers behind Amazon CloudFront Learn to run a remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server behind Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF using four AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) patterns, one for each origin type. The origins include Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Each pattern uses the same edge protection and OAuth 2.0 authentication, applies AWS WAF rate limits to each tool and IP address, and only accepts traffic to the origin that comes through Amazon CloudFront.

Mitigating agentic bot threats with Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF Learn to add a human verification step for browser sessions driven by AI agents. AWS WAF Bot Control flags sessions that look automated, and AWS Lambda@Edge sends them to an Amazon Rekognition Face Liveness check, which needs a live person in front of a camera. A daily limit on how often the same face can pass the check helps keep a few people from verifying many agent-controlled sessions.

AI security

Security Scanning with Claude Code on AWS Learn to deploy a separate, isolated Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) environment for each user that runs Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock, so security teams can find, triage, and fix vulnerabilities in code they own. Each environment has no inbound access and is reached through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Prompts, commands, and sessions are recorded in your AWS account for audit.

Specification Hardening Engine – Kiro Power Learn to add security requirements to your Kiro specs before any code is written. The Specification Hardening Engine checks EARS-format requirements against CWE and OWASP weakness categories and proposes security requirements you can trace and test. You review each proposed requirement and confirm it before it’s added to the spec.

Threat detection and incident response

DevOps-orchestrated security investigation Learn to use two managed AWS agents to investigate one incident together. AWS DevOps Agent traces an alarm to a faulty deployment and, using the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, hands the code review to an agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. That agent runs an AWS Security Agent review, and its findings appear in the same investigation timeline, with a human approving every action.

Security Radar Learn to track more than 200 public security sources, including CVE records, CISA advisories, and AWS security bulletins, and match new events to the affected lines in your code. Security Radar then calls AWS Continuum to validate a patch and deliver it as a pull request. Until the patch is merged, temporary rules in AWS WAF and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall help reduce risk.

Governance and compliance

Bedrock Activity Dashboard Learn to deploy a monitoring and governance dashboard for Amazon Bedrock that tracks token use, model use, and cost by user and team. It runs 13 agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime for security, compliance, cost optimization, and usage insights. Usage data comes from Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, and AWS CloudTrail. The dashboard also recommends Amazon Bedrock Guardrails configurations for sensitive data and lets you reconcile chargebacks with AWS Cost Explorer reports.

Conclusion

In October, AI agents took on a larger part of the remediation flow. The posts and samples show agents that find, confirm, and repair vulnerabilities, and pipelines that test each deployment before it reaches production. The PHP2Shell event showed that activity can begin before an advisory is published. Teams can respond by prioritizing findings by evidence, patching internet-facing systems within hours, and keeping edge mitigations in place until patches roll out. The identity guidance applies existing access controls to AI agents and to workloads outside AWS through identity propagation, short-lived credentials, and centrally enforced algorithm policy. In each case, people review and approve the changes that agents propose. To stay current with AWS security updates, subscribe to the AWS Security Blog RSS feed.

Risky Biz Podcast: Eliminating Vulnerabilities Without Upgrading Dependencies

Security teams are often responsible for remediating vulnerabilities in applications that no longer have engineering resources assigned to them. Even a minor dependency upgrade can introduce performance regressions, break production services, or require extensive regression testing. Meanwhile, attackers are exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities faster than organizations can respond.

In a new Risky Business sponsor interview, Socket founder and CEO Feross Aboukhadijeh joins James to discuss Socket's ambition to eliminate every patchable open source vulnerability and how advances in AI are making that possible at scale.

The conversation explores how Socket delivers security fixes for the exact dependency versions organizations already run, without requiring upgrades or introducing breaking API changes.

James presses Feross on some of the harder technical questions behind this approach:

How do you safely backport a security fix across multiple generations of a package?

How can testing the thousands of packages that depend on a vulnerable library help validate a fix?

Can AI make comprehensive CVE remediation economically feasible?

How does Socket prevent the delivery of security fixes from becoming another supply chain attack vector?

Feross also discusses why Socket makes its fixes for critical vulnerabilities freely available to the open source community and what it could take to remediate vulnerabilities in live production applications without redeploying them.

Title: Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks on Local Organisations
Context: Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours
Full Text:
Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours.

Switzerland ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has now seen these attacks firsthand. In recent days, it received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents. The victims include critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent.” reads the report published by NCSC. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

What stands out is the result. In every AI-assisted attack known to the NCSC, the attackers successfully compromised the victims’ IT systems. The agency sees these incidents as more than isolated cases, warning that they mark a shift in the cyber threat landscape.

The attackers used what the NCSC calls “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”. These AI agents can search for vulnerabilities, choose attack tools, assess the results and decide what to do next, all with limited human input. Security teams also use the same software for penetration testing, which makes these tools dual-use.

The targets aren’t exotic. The agents go after standard or easily guessed passwords, known flaws in software, and systems connected to the internet.

“AI agents often require only a fraction of the time a human would need to locate such vulnerable systems and exploit existing vulnerabilities. Furthermore, they can react flexibly to defence mechanisms by switching to other known attack methods. This leaves organisations with significantly less time to detect an attack and respond appropriately.” continues the report.

AI agents can quickly switch tactics when a defence blocks an attack, leaving organisations less time to detect and stop intrusions. The NCSC warns that these tools speed up common attack methods and that internet-accessible agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI have almost doubled since October 2026. This could lead to more frequent, faster and more successful automated attacks against organisations of all types.

ARTEX isn’t a surprise. The FBI recently published a FLASH alert that describes it as open source, with no model of its own, plugged into external language models. The same advisory says some intrusions went from first contact to privileged access in under three hours.

The NCSC expects more successful attacks and urges companies and critical infrastructure operators to strengthen their security and resilience. It monitors the threat landscape, stays in contact with national and international partners, and shares technical indicators for detecting these tools with infrastructure operators. Its recommendations are short, and it wants them applied without delay.

Start by shrinking what’s exposed. Fewer systems facing the internet means a smaller attack surface, and where possible you can restrict access with geo-blocking or an allow list of IP addresses or network segments. Every internal resource reachable from the internet, such as webmail and VPN, should sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys, with no exceptions.

Then limit the damage. Grant the lowest access rights that work, and watch for deviations from normal behaviour and data volumes across identities, applications, workloads and infrastructure. Test your own infrastructure for vulnerabilities on a regular basis, yourself or with an outside specialist.

“Critical security updates for systems accessible via the internet should be installed as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after release.” concludes the report.

Title: Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization
Context: With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users...
Full Text:
AWS Sign-In is introducing support for Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), enabling organizations to securely authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through their existing enterprise identity providers (IdPs), such as Okta. With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users to manage additional long-term credentials or complete separate consent flows.

In our previous blog post, Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server, we introduced OAuth-based authorization, enabling AI agents to securely access AWS MCP Server through interactive sign-in or programmatic authentication using AWS credentials. EMA builds on these capabilities by enabling organizations to authorize AI agents through their existing enterprise IdPs. Because authentication to an AI application doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources, EMA provides a way to authorize access across these separate trust domains while maintaining existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.

In this post, we explain how EMA and ID-JAG work with AWS Sign-In, discuss security best practices, and walk you through configuring Okta to authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server.

How Enterprise-Managed Authorization works with AWS Sign-In

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enables organizations to centrally manage how AI applications access protected resources on behalf of employees. EMA uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), an OAuth-based authorization grant that enables enterprise IdPs to authorize access across different trust domains. Rather than requiring employees to individually authorize each MCP server, administrators can define policies in their existing IdP to control which AI applications can access specific resources.

When an employee signs in to an AI application such as Claude using their enterprise IdP, the authentication establishes their identity within Claude but doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources. When the AI application requests access to an MCP server, the enterprise IdP evaluates its configured access policies and issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion for the intended resource. The AI application then exchanges this assertion with the authorization server configured for the MCP server to obtain an OAuth access token, without requiring the employee to complete an additional interactive authorization flow.

For AWS MCP Server, AWS Sign-In serves as the configured OAuth authorization server. The AI application presents the ID-JAG assertion to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. As part of the authorization process, AWS validates the assertion against the trusted IdP and uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to evaluate the IAM role’s trust policy and establish the authorized role session. AWS Sign-In then issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. IAM policies attached to the role determine which AWS operations the agent can perform, allowing organizations to manage agent authorization through their enterprise IdP while enforcing existing AWS permissions.

Figure 1 illustrates how an AI application, such as Claude, uses EMA with Okta and AWS Sign-In to obtain an OAuth access token and securely access AWS MCP Server using IAM role-based permissions.

Figure 1: Enterprise-Managed Authorization flow using Okta, AWS Sign-In, and AWS MCP Server

The authorization flow consists of the following steps, as illustrated in Figure 1:

Employee authentication: The employee signs in to the AI application, such as Claude, using their enterprise IdP, such as Okta, through single sign-on (SSO).

ID-JAG request: When the AI application needs to access AWS MCP Server, it requests an ID-JAG from Okta for the intended resource.

Enterprise authorization: Okta evaluates the configured access policies to determine whether the employee and AI application are authorized to access AWS MCP Server. If authorized, Okta issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion.

Token exchange with AWS Sign-In: The AI application sends the ID-JAG to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion, including its issuer, signature, audience/tenant, expiration, and intended resource, and verifies the associated IAM role authorization before issuing an OAuth access token.

Access AWS MCP Server: The AI application presents the AWS-issued OAuth access token to AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and access to AWS resources is governed by the permissions associated with the IAM role.

Configure Enterprise-Managed Authorization using Okta and AWS Sign-In

In this section, we walk you through configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) to enable an AI application, such as Claude, to securely access AWS MCP Server using an enterprise identity managed in Okta.

The configuration establishes trust between Okta and AWS, defines IAM permissions for accessing AWS resources, and configures enterprise authorization policies that govern AI application access. This walkthrough uses AWS MCP Server in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region (us-west-2).

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

An AWS account with permissions to configure IAM IdPs, roles, and policies.

An Okta organization with administrative permissions to manage applications and configure Cross-App Access policies.

An AI application, such as Claude, that supports EMA and ID-JAG.

Access to AWS MCP Server with support for OAuth-based Enterprise-Managed Authorization.

The AWS Region where you will configure the integration.

Step 0: Configure the AI application in Okta

Configure an application in Okta so that employees can sign in to the AI application through enterprise single sign-on (SSO). For this walkthrough, we use Claude as the AI application. If your organization already uses Claude with Okta SSO, you can use the existing application. This application is the requesting application when you configure Cross-App Access in Step 3.

Create the Claude SSO application: In the Okta Admin Console, go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example Claude SSO, as shown in Figure 2.

If your agent was imported through an Okta AI Agent Provider, create the OIDC application by going to Directory, AI Agents, then navigating to User access from the selected agent.

Choose the grant types: Select Authorization Code and Refresh Token. Claude uses the refresh token to request new ID-JAG assertions without asking employees to sign in again.

Add the redirect URI: Set Sign-in redirect URIs to Claude’s SSO callback URL.

Assign employees: Under Assignments, select which employees or groups can access the application.

Confirm SSO works: Check that employees can sign in to Claude through Okta before you continue.

Figure 2: Creating the Claude SSO app integration in Okta

Step 1: Configure Okta as an OIDC IdP in IAM

Create an OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP so that AWS trusts the ID-JAG assertions that Okta issues, as shown in Figure 3.

Add the IdP: In the AWS Management Console for IAM, go to Identity providers, choose Add provider, and select OpenID Connect.

Enter the provider URL: For Provider URL, enter your Okta org URL, for example https://integrator-1234567.okta.com. Okta issues ID-JAG assertions from the org authorization server, not from a custom authorization server.

Enter the audience: For Audience, enter the AWS Sign-In authorization server for your Region, for example https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws, and choose Add provider.

Figure 3: Adding Okta as an OpenID Connect identity provider in IAM

Step 2: Create an IAM role and configure permissions

Create an IAM role that defines the AWS permissions granted to the AI application, as shown in Figure 4.

Create the role: In the IAM console, go to Roles, choose Create role, and select Web identity as the trusted entity type. Choose the Okta IdP from Step 1 and its audience. This creates a trust policy that allows access only through assertions from that provider.

Attach the AWS MCP Server permissions: Attach the AWS managed policy AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy. It grants the signin:CreateOAuth2Token permission required for OAuth access to AWS MCP Server.

Attach the AWS permissions the AI application needs: Attach other IAM policies that grant only the AWS permissions required by the AI application. For this walkthrough, we use a read-only role.

Name and create the role: Enter a role name, for example OktaAwsMcpReadOnly, and choose Create role.

Copy the role ARN: You’ll enter the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the Audience/tenant ID in Okta in Step 3.

Figure 4: Reviewing the IAM role and its trust policy

Step 3: Configure Cross-App Access in Okta

In the Okta Admin Console, create a resource application that represents AWS MCP Server, and then connect Claude to it. The Claude SSO App from Step 0 stays the requesting application, so you don’t enable Cross-App Access on it.

Create the AWS MCP resource application: Go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example AWS MCP (us-west-2). Okta doesn’t use this application’s sign-in redirect URI, so you can keep the default value.

Figure 5: Creating the AWS MCP resource application in Okta

Enable Cross-App Access on the resource application: On the Machine Assignments tab, edit the access method and enable Cross-App Access. Set Issuer URL to https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws and set Audience/tenant ID to the IAM role ARN from Step 2.

Figure 6: Enabling Cross-App Access on the AWS MCP resource application

Assign employees: On the Assignments tab, assign the employees or groups who can access AWS MCP Server through Claude.

Register Claude as an AI agent: Go to Directory, AI Agents, and choose Register AI agent. Under User access, choose Select an existing app and pick the Claude SSO App from Step 0.

Skip this step if the agent was already imported via an Okta AI Agent Provider.

Connect the AI agent to AWS MCP Server: On the AI agent page, add a resource connection with the Application resource type. Set Application instance to the AWS MCP resource application. Set the client ID registered in AWS MCP to the client ID that you configure in Claude in Step 4, for example anthropic-claude. Set Resource identifier to https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.

Figure 7: Connecting the Claude AI agent to the AWS MCP resource application

When Claude requests access, Okta checks that the employee is assigned access and issues an ID-JAG for AWS Sign-In that carries the IAM role ARN. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion and issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role.

Step 4: Configure Claude to access AWS MCP Server

Add a custom connector: In Claude, open Admin settings, choose Connectors, and then choose Add, Custom connector. Enter a name and the AWS MCP Server endpoint, for example https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.

Configure OAuth authentication: For Authentication, choose Sign in when needed. For OAuth client, choose Use your own OAuth client, enter the client ID from the resource connection in Step 3 and leave the client secret blank.

Figure 8: Adding AWS MCP Server as a custom connector in Claude

Set up managed authorization: Open the connector, and on the Configuration tab, choose Set up next to Managed authorization.

Figure 9: The connector’s Configuration tab

Configure IdP-managed access: Choose IdP-managed as the identity source and confirm that the connection checks pass. Then choose Continue, select the Claude roles that connect through managed authorization, and choose Save.

Figure 10: Setting up managed authorization with Okta as the identity source

When an employee accesses AWS MCP Server, Claude requests an ID-JAG assertion from Okta. Following successful policy evaluation, Okta issues the assertion, which Claude exchanges at the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint for an OAuth access token associated with the configured IAM role. Claude uses this token to access AWS MCP Server without requiring an additional AWS sign-in.

Step 5: Validate access to AWS MCP Server

To validate the configuration:

Sign in using enterprise SSO: Sign in to the AI application using your Okta identity.

Figure 11: Signing in to Claude with SSO

Connect to AWS MCP Server: Connect the AI application to AWS MCP Server.

Verify OAuth token issuance: Confirm that Claude successfully connects to AWS MCP Server without requiring a separate AWS authorization flow. You can verify successful OAuth token issuance using AWS CloudTrail, as described in Step 6.

Validate authorized access: Perform an AWS operation permitted by the configured IAM role.

Figure 12: Calling AWS MCP Server from Claude Code

Verify access restrictions: Attempt an operation outside the IAM role’s permissions and confirm that access is denied.

You can also validate enterprise authorization policies by attempting access using an employee who is not authorized in Okta and verifying that the ID-JAG request is denied.

Step 6: Verify authorization activity using AWS CloudTrail

AWS Sign-In and AWS MCP Server integrate with AWS CloudTrail to help organizations monitor OAuth authorization activity and API requests made by AI applications. CloudTrail provides visibility into token issuance, the applications requesting access, and operations performed through AWS MCP Server.

After successfully connecting your AI application to AWS MCP Server, you can verify the authorization activity in CloudTrail:

Open the CloudTrail console and navigate to Event history.

Select the AWS Region used for the integration.

Filter events by Event source signin.amazonaws.com or Event name CreateOAuth2Token to locate OAuth token issuance activity.

Review the event details, including the OAuth client identifier, target resource, authorization grant type, and token issuance status, where recorded.

To review subsequent MCP activity, examine events from aws-mcp.amazonaws.com with the same session ARN and verify that the operations performed by the AI application match the permissions configured for the IAM role. Calls to global services such as IAM are recorded in US East (N. Virginia).

Best practices for securing AI agent access with EMA and AWS IAM

When configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA), consider the following security recommendations to help protect AI agent access to AWS resources:

Use short-lived ID-JAG assertions: Configure your enterprise IdP to issue ID-JAG assertions with short expiration periods. This limits the time during which an assertion can be exchanged for an OAuth access token and reduces the risk associated with token exposure.

Use tenant-specific IdP issuers: In multi-tenant environments, configure tenant-specific issuer URLs to establish explicit trust relationships between AWS and the intended enterprise IdP. This helps prevent assertions issued for one tenant from being accepted in another tenant’s authorization context.

Restrict OAuth authorization using IAM condition keys: Use IAM condition keys to limit OAuth token issuance to approved AI applications, authorization flows, and AWS resources. For example, use signin:OAuthClientId to restrict access to approved AI applications, such as arn:aws:signin:::external-client/jwt-bearer/anthropic-claude and signin:OAuthGrantType to restrict the permitted grant type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. Scope these permissions to the AWS MCP Server service principal to prevent unintended access to other AWS services.

Apply least-privilege IAM permissions: Grant the IAM role only the permissions required by the AI application. Use managed policies to control which AWS operations the agent can perform through AWS MCP Server, reducing the impact of unauthorized or unintended actions.

For more information about available IAM condition keys and permissions, see the AWS Sign-In condition keys reference and the AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy documentation.

Conclusion

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) with AWS Sign-In enables organizations to securely connect AI agents to AWS resources using their existing enterprise IdPs. By combining centralized authorization policies with IAM permissions, organizations can control which AI applications access their resources while reducing the need for employees to manage AWS credentials or complete additional authorization flows.

Using ID-JAG, AWS Sign-In exchanges enterprise-issued identity assertions for short-lived OAuth access tokens associated with IAM roles. This approach helps organizations enforce least-privilege access, reduce credential exposure, and simplify how employees securely access AWS resources through AI agents.

To get started, see the Sign-in with OAuth 2.0, Configure EMA for MCP servers, and Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server to learn more about OAuth-based access to AWS resources.

Title: Broadcom issues fixes for 23 new VMware flaws, three critical
Context: Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]
Full Text:
Broadcom on Tuesday reported almost two dozen new security vulnerabilities in VMware, adding to a lengthy list of fixes from this month alone.

The most serious of the flaws in the current advisory is a vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-123903, assigned a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 (Critical). “A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system,” it said.

In a supplemental document accompanying the alert, Broadcom noted that because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing, the advisory comes just two days before the US Thanksgiving holiday, admitting, “this timing is not optimal.”

The company said that the advisory covers a total of 23 issues, seven of which are in vCenter: an authentication bypass and three denial-of-service issues in the VMware Directory Service, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS).

Seven more are in ESX: a heap out-of-bounds write and a use-after-free in the I/O filter service, an out-of-bounds write in the Extensible Host Controller Interface (XHCI) USB controller, a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a security bypass in the host configuration store, a signature verification bypass, and a denial of service in guest RPC.

The remaining flaws affect VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, VMware Tools, and VMware Avi Load Balancer.

However, the company noted that the fixes delivered to address the flaws in last week’s advisory resolve some of the issues highlighted in the current batch.

“If you applied vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009, including on VCF 5.2.x, you do not need to update vCenter again, but vCenter 9.1.x needs the update in this advisory,” Broadcom said.

“ESX was not part of VMSA-2026-0009 and needs the update in this advisory. VMSA-2026-0009 also resolved issues in SDDC Manager, which this advisory does not update. If you have not applied the SDDC Manager update from VMSA-2026-0009, apply it separately. This advisory also includes a VMware Tools update. Updating vCenter and ESX does not update VMware Tools inside virtual machines, so plan that update separately.”

It added, “if you have a question about whether you are affected, it is likely that you are and should take action immediately.”

Difference of opinion on patching urgency

So is this a signal to interrupt the US Thanksgiving holiday to address the flaws? Opinions differ.

Tyler Reguly, Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, argued that although a 9.8 score is about as high as they get, the nature of the holes might not merit extreme scheduling. There are three vulnerabilities rated 9.8 in severity listed in the current batch, affecting VMware vCenter and ESX.

He pointed out, “neither of these [affected] systems should be present on your external interfaces, so the risk would need to be internal. That means we’re talking about an inside threat or a breach that is already underway. These are important vulnerabilities, so there’s no doubt about that, but they are not so important that anyone should interrupt their holiday weekend.”

Reguly suggested a strict interpretation of CISA guidance to support his contention that these patches may not merit emergency response.

“If we take a look at CISA BOD-26-04 as our guidance on this, is the service publicly exposed? It shouldn’t be, so let’s say no. Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]? No. Could it be automated? Unknown, so let’s assume yes for safety’s sake,” he said. “A result of No, No, and Yes translates to line 13 on the BOD-26-04 remediation timelines, which allows for 60 days to fix the issue.”

He observed that the recent onslaught of vulnerabilities has made us “a bit like Pavlov’s dog:” We’ve been conditioned to react every time we see CVSS 9.8.

“This is a dangerous and potentially harmful conditioning that we need to make every effort to break,” he said. “We need to remind ourselves that the severity of a vulnerability does not reflect risk to an organization, just as the bell did not represent food.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, disagreed.

He considered the current advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, to be “a big deal because it hits vCenter and ESX, the two systems that run every virtual machine, with flaws that need no password. Skip the patch, and one attacker can take down or take over every virtual machine you run. You are essentially toast. Patch now.”

Dickson noted that this batch of alerts contains multiple problematic security issues, which include authentication bypass in vCenter; permitting an attacker with network access to run code on the hypervisor itself; and another bug that lets an administrator inside a virtual machine on Workstation or Fusion run code on the host computer. “Let’s face it: AI loves to chain vulnerabilities,” he said.

He is also worried about the large number of VMware patches this month alone, especially those in vCenter. “The frequency of VMware’s vCenter flaws is a concern, as they keep landing in the same place,” he said. “The new flaw is distinct from last week’s. Distinct is not comforting. Three different holes in the same wall is a wall problem.”

He pointed out, “The directory service has become vCenter’s Achilles’ heel. This advisory adds three denial-of-service flaws in the same service for good measure.”

Title: Reduce operational overhead by migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS
Context: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance that most AWS CloudHSM workloads require
Full Text:
AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance that most AWS CloudHSM workloads require. Organizations that migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS have significantly reduced costs while eliminating hardware security module (HSM) provisioning, patching, and high-availability management. For a detailed comparison of both services, see AWS KMS or AWS CloudHSM: Choose the right key management solution. For payment workloads, see AWS Payment Cryptography in the following table.

Is migration right for you?

Most AWS CloudHSM workloads can migrate to AWS KMS. The following requirements might appear to need CloudHSM, but most have a resolution path:

Potential requirement

Resolution

Contractual or compliance mandate requiring single-tenant HSMs

Review your compliance documentation for explicit single-tenant language; many organizations find that it’s assumed, not mandated. Where mandated, a security review of AWS KMS typically confirms that its logical cryptographic isolation architecture satisfies the underlying intent.

Applications that rely on traditional HSM interfaces (PKCS#11, Java Cryptography Extension, OpenSSL Provider, or Key Storage Provider)

These interfaces are a communication pattern, not an architectural constraint. Contact your AWS account team to assess the refactoring effort needed for your workloads to use modern RESTful interfaces to web services.

Deprecated algorithms (TDES, PKCS#1 v1.5 with RSA) or less common operations (AES key wrapping, AES-CTR, AES-CBC)

Evaluate whether you can retire the dependency as part of your security modernization.

Over 1 billion cryptographic operations per month, where higher per-operation AWS KMS costs might favor the per-hour AWS CloudHSM cost model

Per-operation pricing is only one of several factors that affect cost. Also consider saved staff time, patching, and high-availability management. With envelope encryption (Option B in the following section), optional data key caching can further reduce API call volume.

Payment workloads using older or payment-specific cryptography (TDES, AES-CBC)

While AWS KMS embeds cryptographic best practices in a managed service, some payment systems still rely on older cryptography such as TDES. Evaluate Payment Cryptography, which supports payment use cases, including TDES-based algorithms such as CVV2, ARQC, and PIN validation. It also provides low-level algorithms, such as AES-CBC, that third-party systems might require for interoperability.

If you can resolve these requirements, it’s possible to migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. You can use the rest of this post to review the basic steps of migration to AWS KMS.

How migration works

Migration has three parts: updating application code to call KMS APIs, rotating or importing your cryptographic keys, and transitioning existing data. You re-encrypt previously encrypted data under KMS keys, and existing signatures remain verifiable without AWS CloudHSM. You can complete each part gradually, with zero downtime. Application refactoring is the bulk of the effort, though AI-assisted code transformation tools can reduce this work. Because you’re already refactoring application code, this migration is also an opportunity to adopt post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms, discussed in the following section.

Digital signature workloads

During the transition, the AWS CloudHSM private key continues to sign existing workloads. If AWS CloudHSM lets you export (wrap) a copy of your private key, import it directly into AWS KMS to maintain continuity. For details, see How to Migrate Asymmetric Keys from CloudHSM to AWS KMS. If the key is non-exportable, create a new key pair in AWS KMS. A new asymmetric KMS key (or the imported key from CloudHSM) signs new data flowing to AWS KMS. Shift traffic from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS at your own pace. If you created a new key pair, export the CloudHSM public key before decommissioning and use it to verify existing signatures locally with libraries such as AWS-LC or OpenSSL as shown in Figure 1. AWS KMS doesn’t support importing public keys.

Figure 1 – Digital signature migration

Post-quantum readiness: When creating new signing keys in AWS KMS as part of this migration, consider adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC). AWS KMS supports ML-DSA (FIPS 204), so you can begin issuing PQC signatures now rather than as a separate future effort. This matters most for long-lived signatures, such as document signing, code signing, and certificate issuance.

Durability of imported asymmetric keys: Asymmetric key material imported into AWS KMS (using ImportKeyMaterial) doesn’t have the same durability guarantees as keys generated within AWS KMS. In the unlikely event of an AWS Region-wide infrastructure failure, imported key material could become unavailable. To protect against this, create the key as a multi-Region key, then import the same key material into each replica key in other Regions. Also keep secure backups of imported private keys outside of AWS KMS. An AWS CloudHSM cluster backup is a zero-cost option; CloudHSM stores backups in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at no additional charge. For keys created in AWS KMS (not imported), AWS KMS automatically manages durability within a Region, and multi-Region keys replicate the key material for you.

Encryption workloads

For encryption workloads, use the gradual re-encryption pattern: encrypt new data with AWS KMS while a background process re-encrypts existing data created under AWS CloudHSM keys. This achieves a zero-downtime migration. The following are two approaches to gradual re-encryption, depending on your requirements.

Option A: Direct encryption with AWS KMS API (recommended)

Call the AWS KMS Encrypt and Decrypt APIs directly (Figure 2). Your application passes plaintext to kms:Encrypt and receives a self-contained ciphertext blob. To decrypt, pass the blob to kms:Decrypt. There are no data keys to manage, no local cryptography, and no libraries beyond the AWS SDK. When decrypting, AWS KMS identifies the correct key from metadata it embeds in the ciphertext, including the key material identifier. As a result, ciphertext produced by AWS KMS is larger (by about 150 bytes) than AWS CloudHSM would produce for the same plaintext. During transition, your application must handle data encrypted by both systems. On decrypt, call kms:Decrypt first. If the ciphertext was created by kms:Encrypt, it will succeed. If it was created by CloudHSM, kms:Decrypt will return InvalidCiphertextException immediately without attempting decryption. Your application then falls back to the CloudHSM decrypt path and can optionally re-encrypt the plaintext with kms:Encrypt and store the new ciphertext. All new encrypt operations go to AWS KMS immediately; only decrypt needs the fallback until re-encryption is complete.

The following pseudocode illustrates this pattern:

def encrypt_record(record_id, record): response = kms.encrypt(KeyId=kms_key_arn, Plaintext=record) store(record_id, ciphertext=response['CiphertextBlob']) def decrypt_record(record_id): stored = fetch(record_id) try: response = kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=stored.ciphertext) return response['Plaintext'] except kms.exceptions.InvalidCiphertextException: # Not a KMS ciphertext - fall back to CloudHSM return cloudhsm_decrypt(stored.ciphertext)

Figure 2 – Encryption migration with AWS KMS API

More about AWS KMS encryption

AWS KMS direct encryption supports plaintext up to 4 KB per request. For larger payloads, use Option B (AWS Encryption SDK), which handles envelope encryption for you and supports data of any size.

AWS KMS also supports asymmetric encryption with RSA keys for use cases such as encrypting data destined for a specific key pair holder. This post focuses on symmetric encryption because it covers the majority of AWS CloudHSM encryption workloads.

Option B: Envelope encryption with AWS Encryption SDK

For workloads that require envelope encryption, use the AWS Encryption SDK as shown in Figure 3. Your application calls encrypt() on plaintext and decrypt() on ciphertext. The SDK manages data key generation, local 256-bit AES-GCM encryption, and serialization automatically. Its portable ciphertext format works across multiple runtimes of the AWS Encryption SDK. You can also enable data key caching to reduce calls to AWS KMS. Use this approach when you share encrypted data across services, languages, or with third parties outside of AWS.

Figure 3 – Encryption migration with AWS Encryption SDK

Migration results

A financial services company migrated their transaction data encryption from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. Prior to migration, their workload ran 75 million cryptographic operations per month on three HSMs provisioned for high availability and the operational burden was 25 hours per month. After the migration, they no longer had to manage HSMs, which reduced their operational burden to near zero.

Metric

Before (AWS CloudHSM)

After (AWS KMS)

Monthly cost

$3,456 (three HSMs)

Approximately $250 (93% reduction)

Operational burden

25 hours per month (patching, certificates, and monitoring)

Near zero: no HSMs to manage

Compliance

FIPS 140-3 Level 3

Disaster recovery

Multi-Availability Zone (AZ) HSMs that they provisioned, sized, and monitored

Automatic multi-AZ availability. Optional multi-Region replication

Migration duration

–

10 weeks, zero downtime

Recommendations

We recommend the following as you migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS.

Use AI-assisted code transformation tools to accelerate refactoring and reduce manual effort.

Run the complete migration in staging first, including re-encryption of representative data volumes.

Document specific rollback criteria. During gradual re-encryption, you can pause at any point while AWS CloudHSM continues to decrypt data that has not yet moved. Keep KMS keys enabled after a rollback, because data already re-encrypted under AWS KMS still needs them.

Design AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, key policies, grants, and encryption context schemas before migration. Encryption context enables fine-grained audit trails not available in CloudHSM. See the AWS KMS Developer Guide for a list of log entries.

Delete CloudHSM keys only after all data is re-encrypted and verified. Before deleting, create a CloudHSM cluster backup of any keys imported into AWS KMS and export the public key of any signing key you replaced. Maintain an audit trail of the decommissioning.

Next steps

Start by auditing your current AWS CloudHSM usage: document your keys, the applications that use them, your monthly operation volume, and any compliance constraints. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate AWS KMS costs for your workload, then test a proof-of-concept migration with a non-critical application.

Conclusion

Migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS removes the recurring work of provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring HSM clusters, freeing your team to focus on your application rather than the cryptographic infrastructure beneath it. You gain built-in high availability across multiple Availability Zones, with optional multi-Region replication, at a usage-based cost rather than a per-hour commitment for hardware you manage. Because the migration involves refactoring application code, it is also a natural point to adopt post-quantum signing algorithms such as ML-DSA, so you modernize your security posture in the same effort.

For implementation support, contact your AWS account team or AWS Professional Services. For API integration details, see the AWS KMS Developer Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Title: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
Context: The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks
Full Text: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers. According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique: The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22. These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented. Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo. “Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

We're bringing a little bit of Socket's design system to your code editor. Today we're releasing Socket Calm, a free, open source syntax highlighting theme for VS Code, Vim, and Neovim.

The theme borrows from a principle behind Socket's own interface design: use color with intention and reserve stronger visual cues for things that need your attention. The name Calm also captures what we want our products to bring to developers: peace of mind in an increasingly hostile software supply chain.

Socket Calm takes a minimalist approach to syntax highlighting with a six-color palette. Operators, punctuation, and variables retain the default foreground color, while keywords, function calls, strings, keys, and literals are distinguished by color. Additional accents are reserved for diagnostics, Git decorations, diffs, and terminal output.

The theme comes in two variants, featuring the warm plum and sand backgrounds from Socket's design system, with semantic highlighting enabled by default.

Title: Planning for 99.99 percent availability with the Amazon Cognito Plus feature plan
Context: To learn more about the features that Plus adds, see the advanced security features with threat protection
Full Text:
Amazon Cognito handles sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices with managed user directories, social and enterprise federation, and passwordless sign-in with passkeys or one-time passwords.

Sign-in is the front door to your application. If your customer identity and access management (CIAM) layer is unavailable, users can’t sign in or refresh their sessions, and they can’t reach the rest of your application. Your application’s availability directly depends on the availability of your identity layer.

Starting November 1, 2026, the Amazon Cognito Service Level Agreement (SLA) commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of 99.99 percent for user pools on the Plus feature plan, up from 99.9 percent. A user pool is a multi-tenant user directory that stores your users’ profiles and settings. User pools on Essentials and Lite feature plans remain at the 99.9 percent Service Commitment, while user pools already on Plus receive the new Service Commitment automatically.

This post explains why we made the change, how availability is measured, what’s in the updated SLA, how the SLA measures availability, historical availability data, and how to switch a user pool to Plus.

Why we raised the Service Commitment

Many customers use Amazon Cognito for sign-in to applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. We raised the Service Commitment for the Plus feature plan to 99.99 percent so that their identity layer is backed by an SLA that matches their commitments.

The new Service Commitment and Service Credits

For each AWS Region, during each monthly billing cycle, AWS commits to a Monthly Uptime Percentage of at least 99.99 percent for user pools on Plus, and at least 99.9 percent for user pools on Essentials and Lite. If Amazon Cognito doesn’t meet the Service Commitment for your feature plan, you may be eligible for a Service Credit, as shown in Tables 1 and 2. For full terms and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

What 99.99 percent means in practice

The 99.99 percent Service Commitment is a 10-times improvement over 99.9 percent. In a 30-day month, the allowable monthly downtime drops from about 43 minutes to about 4.3 minutes. For teams that set availability targets for their own applications, this gives a stronger baseline to plan against and to share with stakeholders.

How Amazon Cognito measures availability

The SLA measures availability separately for each AWS Region. Amazon Cognito divides each monthly billing cycle into 5-minute intervals and calculates the percentage of requests in each interval that don’t return an HTTP 500 or 503 error. Intervals with no requests count as 100 percent available. The Monthly Uptime Percentage is the average of these interval values over the billing cycle, minus downtime covered by the exclusions in the SLA. For the full definitions and exclusions, see the Amazon Cognito SLA.

Historical availability over the past 12 months

As we introduce the new SLA, we also looked back at the past 12 months to show how Amazon Cognito performed against the new Service Commitment. Table 3 shows monthly availability for Amazon Cognito user pools from November 2025 through October 2026.

Availability was at or above 99.99 percent in 10 of the 12 months. It was below 99.99 percent in January (99.988 percent) and March (99.979 percent), but stayed above the previous 99.9 percent Service Commitment in both months and was at or above 99.99 percent the following month.

Switch to the Plus feature plan

If your user pools use the Plus feature plan, the 99.99 percent Service Commitment applies to them starting November 1, 2026, with no action needed. If your user pools use Essentials or Lite feature plans, you can switch them to Plus in the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito or programmatically. Before you switch, see user pool feature plans and Amazon Cognito pricing to compare features and costs. To learn more about the features that Plus adds, see the advanced security features with threat protection.

To switch a user pool to the Plus feature plan (AWS Management Console):

Sign in to the Amazon Cognito console.

Choose User pools and then choose your user pool.

Choose Settings.

Choose the Feature plans tab.

Choose Switch to Plus.

Review your choice and then choose Confirm.

Figure 1: Amazon Cognito console Feature plans tab with the Switch to Plus button

To switch a user pool to Plus feature plan (AWS CLI):

Important: The Update-user-pool command and the UpdateUserPool API operation reset any parameter that you don’t include in the request to its default value. To avoid unintended changes to your user pool, retrieve your existing configuration first and include it in your update request.

Use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) to retrieve your current user pool configuration with describe-user-pool:

aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool \ --user-pool-id <your-user-pool-id>

Run the update-user-pool command, including your existing configuration parameters and the Plus tier:

aws cognito-idp update-user-pool \ --user-pool-id <your-user-pool-id> \ --user-pool-tier PLUS \ <your existing configuration parameters>

If you use an AWS SDK, set UserPoolTier to PLUS in an UpdateUserPool request, and include your existing settings in the same way.

Conclusion

In this post, we shared the updated Service Commitment for Amazon Cognito user pools on the Plus feature plan, how availability is measured, and 12 months of historical data.
