Title: Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins
Context: The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call...
Full Text: Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing. Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says. The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field." Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported. The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections. The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing." Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated. Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing. The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network." NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on. Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®

Title: US Treasury financial crimes unit becomes latest fed breach victim
Context: FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies...
Full Text: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions. An alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners. In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases. “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.” FinCEN hasn't said which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity. FinCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to update their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them. The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That said, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change. “Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email. Several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI, and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system. While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups, financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies. As the FinCEN breach is still under investigation, the agency hasn’t stated who may be involved and for what purpose. ®

Title: US Anti-Scam Surge Hits 800 Defendants and 29 Scam Compounds
Context: The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced the figures on November 24 as part of what it described as its largest anti-scam crackdown
Full Text:
US prosecutors have pursued more than 400 scam cases involving over 800 defendants across 85 federal districts since March.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced the figures on November 24 as part of what it described as its largest anti-scam crackdown. The effort followed Executive Order 14390, signed by President Donald Trump on March 6, which directed federal agencies to prioritize cybercrime and fraud.

The DOJ said 30 defendants had been extradited to the US, while US prosecutors and agents had supported law enforcement in more than 10 countries during raids on compounds and call centers that targeted Americans.

FBI Targets Scam Compounds

Under Operation Blackout, the FBI said it had helped disrupt or dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across the Middle East, Africa and Asia. The agency said it had restrained nearly $17bn in criminal funds and that more than 50 people allegedly linked to the scams had been federally charged, while partner countries had arrested or detained more than 320 others.

The FBI also reported helping free and return more than 2200 people trafficked into the compounds.

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said the department would not let scammers "hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad."

The FBI credited Operation Level Up with stopping over $143m in losses to victims since March 6 and freezing more than $350m through its Recovery Asset Team.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

Crypto Freezes and BEC Cases

The US Secret Service reported restraining more than $200m and recovering over $119m, while disrupting 1780 domains run by scammers. It also had over 1540 cases of business email compromise (BEC) under investigation.

Its cases included a cryptocurrency investment fraud scheme, allegedly run by scam centers based in Cambodia, that went after at least 174 US victims. In October, the Netherlands extradited a Chinese national over his alleged role, and he was arraigned in federal court in California's Central District.

The State Department said it had funded work by US and Southeast Asian authorities that helped freeze over $1bn of stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fake websites and accounts.

The DOJ cited Gallup research estimating that scams cost Americans $68bn in 2025, with about one in 10 US adults affected either directly or via a household member.

Title: Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments
Your Repository's Risk Doesn't Stop at Intake
Context: That is a critical decision, but it is only one point of many where teams need visibility
Full Text:
Most repository security conversations start with a straightforward request: Should this component enter the development path?

That is a critical decision, but it is only one point of many where teams need visibility. And what about software already stored inside the organization?

Answering that question means looking beyond incoming requests to the repositories where teams publish and store software for reuse. Understanding what hosted repositories contain is the first step to seeing what may still be in circulation.

Hosted Repositories Keep Components in Circulation

A hosted repository is the authoritative location where an organization publishes and stores artifacts for teams to retrieve. Unlike a proxy repository, which fetches and caches content from an external source, a hosted repository stores content published to it.

It can contain:

Internally developed software, such as packages, libraries, container images, and build outputs.

Development versions and releases that teams publish for internal use.

Third-party components that are unavailable from a configured upstream source.

Once published, these artifacts may remain available through established development workflows. An internal library can become a shared dependency across several services. A development version may remain available while a team tests a release. A stored commercial package may be the only version available to a project with a specific requirement.

Over time, a hosted repository can hold multiple versions of a component. Teams may continue to retrieve versions that are no longer the latest release because existing builds or projects still depend on them. That makes the repository a distribution point for software other teams may use well after its initial publication.

Hosted repositories also serve different teams and workflows. The engineer who publishes an artifact may not be the person who maintains a downstream application or decides whether a new finding requires a change. Visibility into hosted contents helps connect those responsibilities: teams can see what remains available, assess the relevant findings, and decide who should follow up.

Risk Can Change After Publication

A component that met an organization's requirements when it was first published or stored may need another look as vulnerability intelligence or organizational policies change. The initial decision still matters, but it cannot provide a complete view of risk over time.

Updated intelligence can also change how an incoming component request is handled. When a request is evaluated against that intelligence and violates a configured policy, controls can block or quarantine the component before it is served through a protected proxy. That protects the intake path, but it does not assess components already stored in hosted repositories. Those require a separate review.

For example, a vulnerability disclosure may identify an affected version of a shared library after several teams have begun using it. The library itself may not have changed, but what teams know about its risk has. If that version remains available in a hosted repository, teams need to determine whether it is still in use and what action is appropriate.

Other developments can also prompt a review:

New vulnerability or component intelligence identifies a concern with a stored version.

A policy change affects whether a component is acceptable for reuse.

A team discovers that an older version is still available and may be retrieved by a build.

This does not mean every hosted component is unsafe, or that the original review was inadequate. It means a one-time decision cannot account for information that becomes available later. The relevant question is whether or not teams can identify which stored components warrant investigation, remediation, or a policy decision.

Repository governance needs to cover both new requests and the components an organization continues to store and share. That means maintaining visibility into existing hosted artifacts as well as evaluating components as they enter through managed paths.

Assess Components After Publication

Hosted repository scanning provides the complementary view: it helps teams identify current findings in selected components already stored in supported hosted repositories.

Teams can select supported repositories for monitoring, define the scan scope, and review component findings. Those results can help identify which components need attention and prioritize follow-up under organizational policies. Continuous monitoring can also surface changes as component intelligence evolves.

Coverage depends on which repositories, formats, and components are included in the scan. Teams should understand that scope so they can interpret the results accurately and know what remains outside the review.

Scanning provides visibility and supports assessment. A scan report does not itself prevent a component from being uploaded or downloaded. Teams need separate controls for those actions. See our hosted repository scanning documentation for more details.

Turn Findings Into Governance

Scanning can show teams where to look. Governance determines what happens next. Organizations should decide which hosted repositories to monitor, who reviews the findings, and how teams prioritize action when a component no longer meets policy.

A practical process can help teams:

Set the monitoring scope, including which hosted repositories are in view.

Assign responsibility for reviewing findings and coordinating follow-up.

Prioritize remediation based on policy and how a component is used.

Reassess components when relevant intelligence or organizational requirements change.

Repository findings also need context. A component's presence in a hosted repository does not establish that it was included in a particular application or release. If a finding could affect shipped software, teams can consult build records or a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine whether that specific component version was used.

That distinction helps teams avoid both overreacting to every stored component and overlooking one because it entered the repository in the past. Repository scanning helps identify and assess hosted components. Build and release records help connect a finding to specific software.

The process also needs an owner. Platform teams may manage the repository configuration, while security teams interpret findings and application teams decide how to update or replace a component in their software. The responsibilities will vary by organization, but documenting them helps ensure that a finding leads to a decision rather than remaining an unresolved report.

Govern What Enters and What Remains

Proxy scanning helps teams assess components as they are requested. Hosted repository scanning helps them review components already stored and available for reuse. Together, these views help teams understand what enters through a managed path and what remains available over time.

The Sonatype Nexus One platform helps teams make trusted component decisions and apply governance into the build process. It connects decisions at intake with policy, remediation, and compliance workflows so teams can manage component risk as information changes. For a broader look at how artifact management supports visibility, governance, and software delivery, see our artifact management solution overview.

Title: Two Newly Disclosed GeoServer Vulnerabilities Under Attack
Context: In August 2026, hackers exploited a vulnerability as a zero-day, and in 2025 it came to light that a US government agency had been breached through the exploitation of a...
Full Text:
Threat actors are targeting two recently disclosed GeoServer vulnerabilities that can be chained with other flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

Cybersecurity firm WatchTowr has observed attempts to exploit two high-severity GeoServer vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243. The activity appears to be aimed at identifying vulnerable servers.

“Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries,” WatchTowr noted.

WatchTowr has not reported any instances of attackers successfully achieving remote code execution. At the time of writing there do not appear to be any other reports of exploitation attempts.

GeoServer is an open source application for publishing and sharing geospatial data. Government agencies widely use it, and utilities also deploy it. Cybersecurity company Eye Security has identified more than 3,000 internet-accessible GeoServer instances.

CVE-2026-120705 is an XML injection vulnerability that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to obtain sensitive files or conduct server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks. CVE-2026-129243 can enable attackers to bypass access controls and perform operations typically reserved for administrators.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The two security holes are part of a five-bug exploit chain discovered by Rapid7 researcher Jonah Burgess, aka CryptoCat, who reported his findings to GeoServer developers in early August.

Burgess also reported CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-129242. He showed how an attacker can gain admin access and execute arbitrary commands with the GeoServer process’s privileges.

The researcher disclosed technical details this week and published PoC exploit code.

Eye Security has independently found some of the vulnerabilities. It demonstrated unauthenticated RCE on Linux and Windows by combining three weaknesses: CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-120704. The security firm said it reported its findings to the vendor in late September.

GeoServer released patches several weeks ago, and it published advisories in recent days. Organizations are advised to upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6, or 2.27.7.

GeoServer vulnerabilities have been targeted in the past. In August 2026, hackers exploited a vulnerability as a zero-day, and in 2025 it came to light that a US government agency had been breached through the exploitation of a GeoServer flaw.

Title: It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It
Palo Alto Fixes Fragnesia Kernel Bug Chained With PHP2Shell in Firewall Attacks
Context: Palo Alto said the only known route to exploiting it on PAN-OS required attackers to first exploit PHP2Shell, the pair of critical PHP flaws disclosed in October
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks has released PAN-OS fixes for Fragnesia, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers chained with PHP2Shell to gain root access to firewalls.

The vendor published advisory PAN-SA-2026-0015 on November 25, saying it had observed CVE-2026-46300 being exploited against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

Palo Alto rated the advisory informational and did not assign a CVSS score.

Exploited Through PHP2Shell

Fragnesia, first disclosed in May, is a kernel bug that lets an attacker with limited access raise their privileges to root. Palo Alto said the only known route to exploiting it on PAN-OS required attackers to first exploit PHP2Shell, the pair of critical PHP flaws disclosed in October.

That first step needed an internet-facing management interface, or a dataplane interface carrying a management profile, the advisory said. Customers already running a PAN-OS build fixed for PHP2Shell were protected against this entry route.

Dream reported in October that a suspected China-nexus actor had chained PHP2Shell and Fragnesia to root 24 Palo Alto firewalls and one internal firewall management server.

Palo Alto's Unit 42 said on October 29 that it had verified the findings and that roughly 0.02% of the company's customer devices worldwide had management interfaces open to the internet and were affected.

Read more on PHP2Shell: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit

Who Needs to Patch Now

Organizations whose management interface could be reached from the internet should install the fix right away and allow access only from trusted internal IP addresses, Palo Alto said. Where access was already limited that way, it said the risk was much lower but still recommended upgrading at the next maintenance window.

Fixed builds covered PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 and 12.2, and the advisory said all later releases were also fixed.

The fixes followed Palo Alto's October advisory for CVE-2026-109618, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws, which rated it critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and reported attacks on management interfaces exposed online. It gave a lower score for setups that restricted access to a jump box, a dedicated machine used to administer other systems.

That advisory said GlobalProtect portals, gateways and Clientless VPN were not affected. The exposure covered the management web interface, including its XML API service.

In this article

AI agents found a new flaw and took over a university server

The agents adapted when attempts failed

Its important to patch public-facing software and limit access where possible

Give an AI agent a target and tell it to break in. According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, that was enough to set an attack in motion that uncovered a previously unknown vulnerability and eventually gave the attacker full control of a university server.

The agents were running through Cairn, an open-source framework designed for legitimate security research and penetration testing. But, like other security tools, it can be turned against the organizations it was intended to help protect.

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence found the attacker’s Cairn server exposed to the internet without authentication. Its accessible records revealed approximately 48 hours of activity targeting universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator supplied IP addresses and variations of a simple instruction: “obtain shell access,” a way to run commands on the target.

Against a server running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the agents discovered a previously unknown file-upload weakness. The application’s maintainers released a fix after Amazon notified them.

Cairn coordinates AI agents. An operator gives it a starting point and an objective. Its agents investigate, run tools, record findings on a shared “blackboard,” and decide what to try next. It can work with different models and delegates tasks to existing coding agents running in containers.

We recently wrote about ARTEX, a similar tool. Both turn plain-language objectives into coordinated actions with limited human supervision. The main distinction is their implementation: Cairn delegates work to existing coding-agent tools, while ARTEX uses an event-driven planner and parallel workers within its own penetration-testing platform.

How to stay safe

Automated hacking is not new. Scanners, password-guessing tools, and exploit scripts existed long before these frameworks. What changes is who, or what, decides the next step. An AI agent can interpret an error, revise its approach, choose another tool, and continue without waiting for a person to make each decision. Scripts were already faster than humans. The bigger change is that AI agents can adapt as they go with less operator involvement.

AI agents can still fail. In Amazon’s investigation, the agents spent roughly 16 hours trying unsuccessfully to take over one target.

The fundamentals still matter:

Reduce unnecessary internet exposure, especially for administrative interfaces and research services.

Patch exposed software and fix authentication and configuration weaknesses.

Limit permissions so one compromised application cannot automatically control everything around it.

Collect and correlate logs and prepare carefully scoped automated responses for high-confidence detections. AI agents can trigger a lot of alerts, so it’s important to recognize the significant ones and respond quickly.

Leaving a weakness exposed gives attackers more opportunities to find it. AI agents can keep trying without an operator supervising every attempt.

Title: Hackers Exploit Two GeoServer Flaws as Researchers Warn of Unauthenticated RCE Chains
Context: 6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS...
Full Text:
Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr.

The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below -

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request.

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules.

Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions -

CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7

CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

"Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today.

Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain -

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below -

Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml").

Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password.

Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer.

According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves -

CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery

CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution

"An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key."

Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026.

"Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said.

"Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands."

In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible.

The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day.

(The story has been updated after publication to include more details of the flaws and emphasize that advisories for the issues were released on November 24, 2026. The patches were originally released in October and early November 2026.)

Title: U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Agency Takes Some Systems Offline After Cyber Intrusion
Context: The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable
Full Text:
The U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has been hit by a cybersecurity incident that resulted in "unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," the bureau said on Tuesday. As a precaution, it has taken some systems offline.

The bureau collects suspicious activity reports and other Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) filings from banks and other financial institutions and analyzes them to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.

The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency has not named the systems it reached or those it took offline.

To support filers affected by the disruption, the bureau is extending some filing deadlines: covered reports originally due between November 18 and December 29 can now be submitted until December 30.

A relief order issued the same day, FIN-2026-R002, applies to three groups:

Financial institutions that used Secure Direct Transfer Mode (SDTM), the channel for sending batches of BSA reports directly from their own servers, as of November 18

Companies required to file a beneficial ownership information report during the covered window

Individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier during the same window

All other Bank Secrecy Act obligations stay in force, including the duty to monitor for suspicious transactions. The service alert says urgent suspicious activity information can still reach law enforcement through the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not affected by the disruption.

The disclosure followed days of filing trouble. Filing providers reported failures in automated batch submissions beginning November 18, and the bureau posted a notice about the disruption to SDTM late last week, according to a filing outages report by the markets news site The Deep Dive.

The bureau has not said whether the intrusion caused those outages. The order grants the relief because of a "service disruption" and does not mention the cybersecurity incident.

Nor has the agency said when the access began, whether any data was viewed or taken, or who was responsible. No group has publicly claimed the intrusion so far. Those answers matter because of what the bureau holds: reports of suspicious financial activity filed by financial institutions nationwide.

The incident is not Treasury's first in recent years: in December 2024, a China-linked group used a compromised BeyondTrust API key in an earlier Treasury breach that reached department systems and documents. No link between the two incidents has been reported.

In this article

About 2 billion login records were exposed, some apparently stolen by malware. Some files were labeled “US”

A separate database held 840 million Chinese ID numbers and 11 million student records

If you suspect malware, use a clean device to change affected passwords and sign out everywhere

Two unsecured databases have exposed billions of records, ranging from passwords and browser cookies to national ID numbers and children’s school details. Researchers discovered the databases separately, and the two appear to be unrelated. Both illustrate how personal information from different sources can end up together in a searchable collection.

Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the larger database, which contained approximately 2 billion login records spread across 8,471 folders. Some files were labeled by country, including the US, though it’s unclear how many US residents were affected. The database required no password to access and stored credentials and account details in plaintext.

Fowler reported that the exposed material included:

Email addresses, usernames, passwords, and associated login URLs.

Browser cookies, session tokens, and other authentication information.

Saved application credentials and browser data.

Device and operating-system information.

Logs that appeared to contain autofill information and cryptocurrency wallet data.

Fowler also identified approximately 400,000 documents that appeared to come from malware capable of creating more detailed collections about individual victims.

That makes this more than a list of passwords. Some of the material could help an attacker connect a person’s accounts, identify their device, and potentially access an account where the person was already signed in.

Fowler could not identify the database’s owner. He notified its hosting provider, and public access was restricted several days later. How long it had been exposed, and whether anyone else accessed it, remain unknown.

In the separate discovery, researcher Greg Pollock identified an Elasticsearch server exposing approximately 259 GB of data on people in mainland China. Anyone who knew its address could search it without a password. Its 99 indices contained almost 1.64 billion records linking names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, student information, and business registrations. These included at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers and about 11 million student enrollment records. Some student records linked a child’s name to their school, class, and a parent’s contact details.

This database brought together information from identity registration, education, telecommunications, payment, and business systems. Based on how the records were organized, UpGuard believes someone combined them to create an illicit identity-lookup service.

Pollock could not identify the operator. During his investigation, the server became inaccessible, apparently following a ransomware or other destructive attack. Other copies of the data may still exist.

How to stay safe

If malware stole your login details, changing affected passwords is a good start. Use a clean device to make those changes, and sign out of existing sessions in case someone also has the cookies that keep you logged in.

Check for infection. Run a scan with a trusted anti-malware product. If you suspect an active infostealer infection, disconnect the affected device and use a separate, clean device for urgent account recovery. Otherwise, malware could capture replacement passwords too.

Secure your most important accounts first. Start with your primary email, followed by banking, payment, work, and other sensitive accounts. Replace exposed or reused passwords with unique ones, using a password manager to generate and store them.

Enable multifactor authentication. An authenticator app or security key adds protection against someone signing in with a stolen password.

Sign out existing sessions. Look in your account’s security settings for an option such as “sign out everywhere,” “log out of all devices,” or “revoke active sessions.” Removing malware and changing passwords do not necessarily stop someone using an already stolen session token.

Watch for financial and identity misuse. Review account activity and credit reports for transactions or accounts you don’t recognize.

Review unsolicited messages with extra care. If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard. It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next.

You can replace a password. Details like the school you attended can stay useful to scammers for years. If an unexpected caller or message mentions something personal, verify who you’re dealing with before sharing information or sending money.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Credential Remediation Is Slow When You Don’t Know What Will Break
Context: GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those...
Full Text:
TL;DR

More than 64% still valid after four years: GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that most valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, because teams stall on what a revoke will break.

Validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets: Prioritize by impact instead, weighing what a credential can access and whether it leaked publicly, and update the risk score as new context arrives.

Revoke last, never first: Issue a replacement, store it in the vault, switch every consumer to the vault call, deploy and monitor, then revoke the original and confirm it no longer authenticates.

Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI connect securely to data, services, and each other. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, but credential remediation is where many secret security programs bog down. This is the second of three articles we are releasing to explain how we help address detection, remediation, and prevention.

The first article in this series, “The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It,” covered detection across every surface where credentials live. Just knowing they exist is not enough. Teams need to take action to remediate those findings. To do that, they need context around every credential they find.

Without the right context, it is impossible to know what risks the secret carries. It is also difficult to understand which systems rely on those secrets and the risk levels that revoking the secret brings. Nobody wants to break production, but we also cannot allow attackers to leverage those secrets.

The resulting decision paralysis leaves many teams struggling to rotate immediately. Sometimes it can take years for the secret to be revoked finally. That is actually all too common, as shown by GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research that found that 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, a full 4 years later.

It would be great if there were a one-size-fits-all solution for remediating every leak; in reality, each one is tied to a specific integration. What we can do is streamline the processes needed to get to the end, making it much easier for organizations of any size. And it does take the whole organization to properly deal with leaked secrets.

Why credential remediation is so hard for so many teams

A team that discovers an exposed credential rarely has all the authority or knowledge needed to fix it without causing further issues. A security engineer can see it’s valid and dangerous, but that security engineer usually cannot immediately tell which services will fail when it is revoked. Breaking production is considered a much higher risk than the possibility of a stolen and abused secret, so they need to go looking for answers, which is a time-consuming process.

The developers who know where and why a key is used and, hopefully, how to rotate it safely are often busy shipping new features and managing existing requests from the business. An alert in their email that shows only a file path and a secret type asks those busy devs to stop their workflow and launch their own investigation. These requests, all too often, sink into the backlog.

At the same time, the larger the organization, the harder it is to find the right person who knows the answer to “what breaks if this key is revoked?” Application security teams monitor code where keys are used, identity and access management (IAM) teams govern identities that were issued keys, and the Platform Engineering team runs the vaults holding the keys. They all have different perspectives and, in most organizations that are early in their secrets security maturity journey, can only tell part of the story.

Endpoint security teams are also watching what happens at the workstation level. They are beginning to track secrets stored there, as software supply chain attacks have increasingly targeted these plaintext credential stores over the last couple of years. A secret leaked here might even be the triggering event for the rotation in case of compromise from an infostealer. The endpoint team is historically not connected to AppSec or Platform teams.

One credential can touch all these teams while each individual, isolated group sees only its own slice of the credential layer. Now, multiply the communication and coordination issue across hundreds or thousands of potential leaks, and the scale of the remediation problem becomes clearer.

Action before investigation invites downtime

The risk of revoking before fully understanding the fallout is fairly high for the business. This is weighed against potential future abuse. Of course, this math changes during an active breach when the clock is ticking and when exfiltration or lateral movement is already occurring. Those emergencies do not get backlogged. Mature organizations understand that addressing leaks before an emergency arises is the better plan overall, but remediation times are still measured in weeks for most teams. How long a remediation process takes really boils down to how fast and accurately responders can gather and communicate information about the issue. Responders need to know a lot of things, starting with whether the credential works, what it can access, and who owns it before they can even ask questions like “where else does it appear?” and “which systems depend on it?”

For example, envision two valid cloud credentials. One grants read-only access to a single storage bucket, and the second one is a root-level key with administrative control over production. While their privileges and dependent workloads determine the appropriate level of urgency, both require the same level of insight and investigation to triage the remediation process and decide whether the response is a rotation next sprint or a revocation this very second.

The ultimate goal is to remove the leaked key rapidly, but in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds. Rotating secrets safely simply requires resources and a coordination plan. If this process is always piecemeal and manual, then mistakes are more likely to happen.

A security team that causes an outage once will face resistance the next time it asks to rotate anything.

Prioritize by impact, not just validity

Validity is the first and clearest signal most responders look at. Alone, this is an incomplete signal. GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those secrets cannot be verified automatically.

While validity still matters, access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency. If the leak happened publicly on the internet, that raises the urgency even further. Any risk scoring needs to explain which factors drove it. It also needs to be a living risk score, adjusting for new information as new context arrives. Scoring it once upon discovery is akin to trusting an initial CVSS score in a CVE disclosure. It is a helpful guide but needs to be updated based on what is really going on in your organization. The organization and its risk tolerance will decide what happens next. Having as much information centrally available as possible is key to a rapid response, as responders reach the boundaries of what systems they can actually touch.

Route the work to the right people who can push the change

Remediation requests should let the developer or platform team act immediately, without requiring the team to repeat the investigation that has already taken place.

Any request to replace a key for a production system should include validity and known exposure locations. It should list dependencies too, and where possible show how it connects to business operations. The more the person picking up the request understands about the issue, the sooner they can act. In an ideal world, all remediation requests would be routed to their named owners. In the messy reality of the enterprise, you will likely need to involve the developer who leaked the secret and gather data from commit attribution or source metadata. We need to establish communication because there is a probability that they will need further instructions or guidance.

Requests should not be ‘thrown over the fence’ and then forgotten about. Follow-up and confirmation about remediation progress should be centrally collected and shared so every department knows where the rotation process is at any given moment. This accountability proves resilience efforts when an auditor shows up.

Engineers need to be enabled with a clean way to communicate once they start the work and once their ticket is ready to close. Routing the work through existing ticketing tools keeps it alongside other engineering work, but those tickets also need to integrate with the responder’s security operational tooling.

Rotate, revoke, and vault: the order matters

Safe rotation means following a specific set of steps, in the right order, so you don’t break anything. Remember: “Availability” is one of the legs of the CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability) security triad.

For mature organizations, this could be as straightforward as rotating the secret in a vault, since the production applications and systems relying on the credential are all already consuming it from the secrets manager. Any plaintext copies are then rendered harmless once the original offending secret is revoked.

For organizations and situations where no existing vaulted copy is in use, this process often starts with issuing a replacement credential. If the responder can do this, they should do so immediately and store it safely in the vault. Then, replace every occurrence of the plaintext secret with that vault call, across every known consumer. The remediation steps from there are to push the changed code or config live and monitor for any issues, ready to roll back if anything breaks. Only when all the new systems are safely consuming the new vaulted credential appropriately can the team revoke the original. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.

GitGuardian’s service account credential rotation checklist covers these steps in detail.

Verify the fix and keep the evidence

Only close the ticket when the key is safely revoked, and the danger is removed. There needs to be an audit trail about what you fixed and how you proved that. You need verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Optionally, and depending on the circumstances, you can show that the old secret was removed from all surfaces.

Any incidents closed while the credential remains valid deserve their own review queue. This common case happens when a team rotates a key in one system while the old key remains active and valid in another. This means a siloed team only accounted for their one occurrence in their tooling that lacks a unified view or relies on manual tracking.

The incident record also serves auditors and security leaders. It shows what was found, who acted, and how long remediation took.

One credential, start to finish with GitGuardian

At GitGuardian, we have helped thousands of developers and organizations streamline their remediation process.

To help visualize how we can help, imagine a Kubernetes application that calls an external service with an API key stored in a secrets manager. During troubleshooting in our imagined scenario, a developer copies the key into a local configuration file and commits it. This is a fairly common scenario we have seen play out many times.

GitGuardian scanning finds the secret as soon as it is committed. The platform generates a new open incident and alerts the assigned team. An automatic validity check confirms the key is still active, and the Secret Analyzer lists its permissions. A presence check confirms the secret is still in the codebase. All these checks can be rerun as remediation progresses.

For customers with full platform integrations, the GitGuardian Exploration Map shows a production workload depending on it, and fingerprint matching ties the committed value to the vaulted copy. The security team can bring that context to the owning developer and operations team.

Once a replacement key is issued, everyone can track the progress of the rotation and see when the PR that accounts for the deployment configuration is pulling from the vault. There is no guessing about whether revoking the original will affect anything critical. GitGuardian then rechecks validity and confirms the committed copy is gone.

The incident might also expose a pattern worth investigating across other teams. Has this same codebase seen similar incidents? Has the same user caused the same issue before? Are vaulted credentials ending up in unmanaged files on developer laptops on a regular basis? These all point to a wider issue that needs to be addressed to prevent further incidents and an increased remediation backlog.

From fixing to preventing

Remediation reduces risk one credential at a time. It also shows where exposures keep coming from.

The third and final article in this series covers prevention, starting on developer machines and in AI coding workflows. Teams that want to see this remediation workflow can take an interactive tour of the GitGuardian platform.

FAQ

What is credential remediation?

Credential remediation is the work of removing the risk from a leaked or exposed credential. The goal is to replace and revoke the leaked key quickly, in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds, and then to confirm the old credential no longer authenticates.

Why does credential remediation take so long?

The team that finds an exposed credential rarely has the authority or the knowledge to fix it alone. A security engineer can see the credential is valid and dangerous, but usually cannot tell which services will fail when it is revoked. The developers, identity, platform, and endpoint teams each see only their own slice of the credential layer, so responders spend their time gathering context instead of fixing the leak.

How do you prioritize which leaked credentials to fix first?

Prioritize by impact, not validity alone. GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that validation-only prioritization misses 46% of critical secrets, because some secrets cannot be verified automatically. Access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency, and a public leak raises it further. The risk score should explain which factors drove it and change as new context arrives.

What is the safe order for rotating a leaked secret?

Issue a replacement credential and store it in the vault. Replace every plaintext copy of the old secret with a call to the vault, across every known consumer. Push the changed code or configuration live and monitor for issues, ready to roll back. Revoke the original only when every system is consuming the new vaulted credential. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.

How do you verify that a leaked credential has been remediated?

Close the ticket only when you have verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Keep an audit trail of what was fixed and how it was proved, including who acted and how long remediation took. Incidents closed while the credential is still valid deserve their own review, since a team may have rotated the key in one system while it stayed active in another.

Title: US Treasury Investigates Cyber Incident Amid Reported Federal Agency Breaches
Context: The US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said on November 25 it is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access...
Full Text:
The US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said on November 25 it is "investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems."

FinCEN, which handles reports about financial crimes including money laundering, trafficking and terrorism financing, said it has taken some services offline as a proactive measure.

However, the agency noted that the Bank Secrecy Act Electronic Filing (BSA E-Filing) System, a secure online system to submit BSA reports electronically, is still operational.

In addition, FinCEN said it has extended deadlines for financial institutions to file required documents.

“If a financial institution needs to expedite the delivery of suspicious activity information to law enforcement, filers can use the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not impacted by this service disruption,” FinCEN added.

This comes as several US federal agencies, including the FBI, the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) have recently started investigating data breaches reportedly targeting criminal records like the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database as well as unclassified intelligence information.

Infosecurity has approached FinCEN for comment.

Title: Drupal Fail2Install Exploit Details Emerge as Critical RCE Flaw Faces Active Exploitation
Context: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core.

"Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site."

As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances.

According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code.

While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources.

As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, and Drupal allows the installation to proceed after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass.

To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use -

EMFILE, which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open

Database connection exhaustion

TCP source-port exhaustion

"We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said.

"Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL."

This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is made possible because the installer doesn't restrict the file name extension.

"By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file."

While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution.

"Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said.

"In Drupal, temporary database failures can produce a FAIL, FAIL, and then SUCCESS sequence that reopens the installer on an existing website and ultimately leads to pre-authentication RCE through an SQLite database containing PHP code."

The issue has been addressed in the following versions -

Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.13

Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.22

Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.22

The addition of CVE-2026-132165 to the KEV catalog follows a report received by the Drupal Security Team that it "was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-132165 is the third Drupal flaw to come under active exploitation this year following CVE-2026-9082 (CVSS score: 6.5) and CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: 6.5).

Title: Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach
Context: The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed
Full Text: London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records. A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited. AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically. Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go. The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected. Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations. The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases." Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated. Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues. Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected. Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual. The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details. Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information. Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded. "The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest. "Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

Title: The ‘True Crime Community’ Is Inspiring Violent Attacks Through TikTok
Context: One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks
Full Text:
“Algorithmically driven engagement has supercharged its spread,” the report’s authors wrote. “Unlike Tumblr, where the fandom is largely isolated, TikTok actively works to expose users to new content through its algorithm, resulting in TCC videos being served to a much larger audience.”

Finkelstein says that while TikTok does remove some of the accounts his team flags to the platform, in general the company is not doing enough to combat the problem.

“[TikTok’s] capacity to manage this is very spotty,” Finkelstein said. “This is an uncontained open wound. Whatever measures they think they're making to manage this are obviously inadequate to deal with the damage that the community is unleashing. If you took TikTok offline for a few weeks, my guess is these attacks would slow down because there's not a permission structure in place that's encouraging vulnerable youth to go out and murder people in order to be famous with their peers because they're so depressed and living in their mom's basement and spending 10 hours a day on social media.”

TikTok, whose US operations are now owned primarily by a group of investors including Oracle, controlled by GOP megadonor and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison, said it had rules in place to proactively remove TCC-linked content.

“We enforce strict rules against content that promotes violence or glorifies perpetrators of mass violence, and we had already banned a large number of the accounts in this report,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED.

WIRED shared the report with several other researchers who closely track TCC activity online, and all broadly concluded that NCRI’s assessment was accurate. One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks.

“When examining perpetrators' social media, I see that they frequently frame threats as a joke, a LARP, or AI-generated,” Terran tells WIRED. “Social media companies should not take these claims at face value, but rather report any credible threats. Without appropriate interventions, TCC-inspired attacks will likely continue to increase.”

Another European-based researcher, who requested anonymity due to fears of retaliation, tells WIRED, “We're panicking here in Europe.” The researcher collaborates with European law enforcement agencies and says they are concerned about the increasing number of attacks taking place globally.

Finkelstein says that US lawmakers and law enforcement need to do more in order to combat this problem. “The FBI seems to want to deal with it by arresting kids. None of this makes any sense,” he says. “We've got to step back and see the scale of this. We should be turning to our law enforcement agencies and our national security apparatus that has the ear of the president and say something's got to be done about this.”

The FBI declined to comment, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security referred WIRED to the FBI.

“The Justice Department remains vigilant against the threat of such violent extremist networks that operate within the United States and around the globe,” Wyn Hornbuckle, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, tells WIRED.

Update: 11/25/2026, 9:02 AM EDT: WIRED has updated a reference to the Network Contagion Research Institute.
