Title: Ransomware Attacks Surge 23% in October Following Record Quarter
Context: Ransomware attacks surged 23% in October compared to September, with 1049 claimed incidents, a new report by NCC Group has found
Full Text:
Ransomware attacks surged 23% in October compared to September, with 1049 claimed incidents, a new report by NCC Group has found.

This rise comes straight after the highest ever quarterly volume of claimed ransomware attacks in Q3 2026, from July to September.

The researchers linked the sharp rise in ransomware to the growing use of AI to rapidly identify vulnerabilities and chained attack paths

“This spike is likely an early indicator of a new cyber environment in which serious vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized more rapidly,” NCC Group wrote.

New Ransomware Groups Increase Activity

The Gentlemen ransomware group claimed the highest number of victims in October at 139, making up 13% of the total.

It was closely followed by N0n, a relatively new actor first observed in September 2026, which claimed 133 victims in the month.

N0n claimed to be responsible for data breaches affecting financial firms JPMorgan, Mastercard and Visa in November.

Qilin, which has been active for a number of years, was in third place, claiming 131 attacks.

A number of other newer groups established in 2026 made up the rest of the top 10 ransomware actors for October. This includes Booba Project with 29 attacks, Emperador with 27 and Wallstreet with 22.

NCC Group researchers noted that the origins of these newer actors remain unknown, and none have been conclusively linked to a specific country or established predecessor.

“These operations should therefore be described as newly observed brands rather than entirely new threat actors, as they may include experienced affiliates, access brokers or developers previously associated with other cybercriminal groups. Their rapid rise also demonstrates the low barrier to creating a new extortion brand within the wider ransomware ecosystem,” they commented.

Industrials Sector Targeted in Third of Attacks

The NCC Group report, published on November 25, found that industrials was the sector most heavily targeted by ransomware in October, making up 31% of claimed attacks. This was followed by consumer discretionary (19%), healthcare (12%) and IT (10%).

Read now: Industrial Control System Vulnerabilities Hit Record Highs

North America was the most targeted region in October, accounting for 46% of attacks. This was followed by Europe at 23%, Asia (15%) and South America (8%).

Title: Ex-OpenAI Employee Accused of Bugging Company Offices Granted $1 Million Bail
Context: A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a...
Full Text:
A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, for allegedly bugging the artificial intelligence (AI) company's offices with the aim of recording sensitive conversations.

Subsequent court filings have pointed out that Alfozan was in touch on WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi royal family, as well as expressed interest in moving back to Saudi Arabia following OpenAI's initial public offering (IPO).

He has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the ChatGPT-maker said at the time.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty to the charges during his appearance in San Francisco federal court earlier this month.

According to CNBC, the decision comes after prosecutors told the court last week that they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

However, they said investigators have found hundreds of audio files on the defendant's personal devices, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that took place at OpenAI throughout September 2026.

Some of these involved meetings with OpenAI customers and contained material protected by attorney-client privilege, prosecutors said, adding he possessed a photograph of what's believed to be a term sheet for a "strategic partnership" between OpenAI and another company.

"What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation," they said.

Under the bail conditions, Alfozan will be required to wear a GPS ankle monitor, observe a curfew from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., stay within the Northern District of California, and avoid airports and train and bus stations. He is expected to be released on Wednesday morning.

"There is no spy story that we're talking about right now," U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said, per The Wall Street Journal. "The government doesn't have that."

Title: NCSC Shares Guidance to Tackle Agentic Threat From ARTEX-Like Tools
Context: However, they’ve been rapidly adopted by threat actors to carry out automated attacks at low cost, often in combination with open models or illegal API resellers
Full Text:
The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has shared new guidance to help organizations avoid being overwhelmed by the “volume, intensity and duration” of attacks from agentic frameworks like ARTEX.

So-called autonomous offensive frameworks (AOFs) like ARTEX – and Cairn, PentAGI, RedAmon, Xalgorix and Darkmoon – began life as legitimate pen-testing tools designed to probe for weaknesses using a collection of agents.

However, they’ve been rapidly adopted by threat actors to carry out automated attacks at low cost, often in combination with open models or illegal API resellers.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm Infrawatch has tracked 10,848 services across 8105 hosts running AOFs.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) responded to the surge in malicious use of AOFs with new advice published on November 24.

The agency argued that the frameworks are not exploiting novel or even known vulnerabilities, but instead low-hanging fruit like API weaknesses, default or leaked credentials, or misconfigurations in infrastructure as code (IAC).

Read more: FBI Highlights Growing Abuse of AI-Driven Pen-testing Framework ARTEX

The NCSC shared an eight-point plan to help security teams develop a holistic approach to the challenge:

Perform rigorous asset management, including regular reviews and probing of externally accessible infrastructure, in order to understand what’s exposed

Lock down as many services currently accessible from the perimeter as possible, so they can only be accessed by staff or partners. Then harden those that can’t be

Learn to recognize agentic attacks through comprehensive logging across a wide variety of endpoints and parameters. Ensure error messages shown to external users give nothing away that the AOF could use to plan its next move

Identify, prioritize and fix vulnerabilities and misconfigurations within internet-facing assets, using pen testing where appropriate

Deploy “bot challenges” to prevent automated tools abusing services across high-priority assets

Protect at the API level by applying rate limits to accounts, API tokens and authenticated sessions, and monitoring for unusual behavior as well as preventing large volumes of requests

Throttle account creation and sign-ups that use disposable email services, and protect accounts with strong authentication and appropriate access controls. This will help minimize abuse by agents

Place honeytokens or tripwires somewhere no legitimate user would go in order to provide early warning of agentic attacks, use up an agent's time and attempt budget, and keep it away from real assets

The NCSC said AI and agentic defense will in time be the best way to deal with these threats, but programs will take time to mature.

In the meantime, foundational cybersecurity and hygiene should be the priority.

That means putting in place the controls recommended by Cyber Essentials, and following zero trust principles such as identify verification, least privilege, and an “assume breach" mentality.

Critical infrastructure providers in particular should consult the NCSC’s Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) to improve resilience, it added.

Title: UK Authorized Push Payment Losses Surge 22% as Fraudsters Steal £660m
Context: The UK’s banks have called for technology and telecommunications firms to be held accountable for fraud originating on their platforms, after revealing total losses increased to...
Full Text:
The UK’s banks have called for technology and telecommunications firms to be held accountable for fraud originating on their platforms, after revealing total losses increased to nearly £660m ($863m) in the first half of 2026.

The figures represent an 8% year-on-year (YoY) increase, according to the UK Finance Half Year Fraud Report 2026 published by UK Finance which represents 300 firms.

Although unauthorized fraud losses dipped slightly (-2%) as banks stopped £811m ($1.06bn) in attempted criminal gains, authorized push payment (APP) scams surged 22% over the year to reach £316m ($472m).

APP fraud refers to incidents where a scammer posing as a trusted entity tricks the victim into transferring money to a bank account under their control.

As well as a surge in losses, APP fraud cases increased 25% to 138,345 in the first half of the year, the banking body said.

Read more on APP fraud: APP Fraud Singled Out as Biggest Financial Crime Threat

The report revealed that 58% of APP fraud originates online, with a further 16% beginning via telecommunications – usually SMS or voice-related scams. Both account for a third (33%) of losses.

That’s why banks are intensifying their calls for tech firms and telcos to share more of the burden in stopping these scams. Specifically, UK Finance called for:

Ofcom to place stronger obligations on high-risk platforms such as social media to stamp out fraudulent advertising, which is where a lot of investment fraud originates

Online marketplaces to verify sellers and use secure payment mechanisms rather than allowing separate bank transfers to take place off platform. This would address purchase fraud, which often starts on marketplace sites, UK Finance claimed

Tech firms and telcos to be required to contribute financially and share expertise, intelligence and capabilities to support proactive fraud prevention

The Biggest APP Offenders

According to the report, investment fraud was responsible for the largest losses in the first half of 2026, accounting for £126m, up 29% from a year earlier. Case numbers surged by 21% over the same period.

In terms of volume, it was purchase scams that dominated, accounting for 69% of all APP cases. These happen when fraudsters trick a victim into paying for something that doesn’t exist. Related losses rose 24% annually to £66m ($86m).

Advance-fee scams, where victims pay an upfront fee or deposit for goods or services that don’t exist, saw losses increase 73% to £34m ($44.5m) and cases more than double.

“Criminals are increasingly exploiting online platforms and telecommunications networks to target and manipulate victims before a payment is ever made,” said Ruth Ray, MD of economic crime at UK Finance.

“The financial services sector cannot tackle this threat alone. We need stronger obligations on technology and telecommunications firms so that every sector exploited by fraudsters is held accountable and plays its part in preventing harm.”

Title: Hackers Exploited CVSS 10.0 Hex.pm RCE Flaw to Compromise 6 Package Registry Servers
Context: The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15...
Full Text:
An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from.

The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request.

Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said.

What Hex Users Should Do Now

Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps:

Change your hex.pm password.

Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes.

Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth.

Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system.

Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm.

API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters.

Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it.

Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it.

The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded.

The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established.

A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account.

The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday.

Load balancer logs recorded 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC on Monday, all from two addresses, the Hex.pm team said in its incident report yesterday. Files created by the exploit appeared on six web servers, in one case just 3 milliseconds after the request. Three of those servers joined mid-attack, when a restart brought up machines still on the vulnerable build.

To check the packages, the team compared every database table against a copy taken two minutes before the first exploit request and traced each difference to normal activity. The 23 releases published during the attack all match the audit log, no older release was changed, and the package and registry files written that evening match the database records.

Database reads, shell commands, environment variables and direct reads from file storage were not logged. For that reason, "we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database," the team wrote. That database holds email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets and session data, and private packages could also have been read without leaving a trace.

The checks found no leftover shells and no new accounts or cloud keys in the audit logs. Who was behind the attack is unknown. Activity from the two addresses going back to late last week suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against, according to the team.

A separate security report describing the same flaw arrived by email at 19:07 UTC on Monday, after the attack had ended. By yesterday morning the team had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key. On Monday night it reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, to CISA in the United States and to ENISA in the European Union.

Related Library Fixes

Alongside the incident, maintainers of three widely used Elixir libraries disclosed flaws of their own involving structs built from untrusted data, and shipped fixed versions yesterday. These are separate disclosures, not further attacks on Hex.pm.

Library

CVE

Affected versions

Fixed versions

ash

CVE-2026-124283

3.31.3 up to, but not including, 3.38.0

3.38.0

db_connection

CVE-2026-133555

1.1.0 up to, but not including, 2.10.3

2.10.3

flop

CVE-2026-130411

From 0.8.0, each branch before its fixed version

0.26.7, 0.27.3, 0.28.1, 0.29.2

Each needs its own conditions to be exploited. The Ash flaw requires keyset pagination with a client-supplied cursor, certain sort field types, and a signing secret left at its unset default, according to the Ash advisory.

The db_connection flaw "is not exploitable in db_connection alone," the DBConnection advisory says, because another component must first decode untrusted data into structs. The Flop flaw has similar conditions around its pagination cursors, according to the Flop advisory.

The exploited flaw sits in the hexpm server code, not in the Hex client, so organizations that run their own copy of the registry are affected until they deploy the patch.

Title: Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
Context: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses...
Full Text:
When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology.

Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment.

And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats.

Has that happened? Well, kind of.

What CISOs are seeing

In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes.

“We asked the same question in Q4 of a similar cohort,” says Laura Koetzle, RSAC’s head of community research. According to preliminary results — the survey isn’t complete yet — nearly 58% now say they’ve seen evidence of AI-powered attack techniques.

As a result, the majority of CISOs are revamping their vulnerability management programs, according to the forthcoming survey. But they’re not upending how they approach cybersecurity, Koetzle adds. “The same foundational principles still apply.”

The main difference today is in speed and quantity, she says.

Lincoln Wallen, CTO at Framestore, an Academy Award–winning visual effects company, isn’t turning a blind eye to what AI could be used for by attackers.

“We take the potential very seriously,” he says. But he’s taking an old-school approach to dealing with this new threat. “We’re putting a lot of emphasis on cleanliness, hygiene, and patching.”

So far, the signs of AI use have been limited to more sophisticated phishing attacks, he says.

“They feel anecdotally more well put-together, more convincing, involving many more disparate elements of data,” he says. “That’s the most concrete thing that we’ve seen.”

To deal with that, the company has updated its anti-phishing training.

Another area that Framestore is investing in is more efficient and prioritized patching and more frequent penetration testing.

Enhanced productivity but familiar threats

The data seems to support Framestore’s approach, even if the headlines don’t.

Last week, headlines quoted Google’s announcement that “the era of autonomous attacks had arrived” — a reference to Google’s original blog post teaser to its latest AI Threat Tracker report.

But in the actual report, John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, seemed to undercut this top line teaser, saying: “For the most part, attackers aren’t using new groundbreaking methods to break into systems — they are still going after known, unfixed issues, just with much greater speed and scale.”

(Google later changed its headline to “Outpace automated cyber threats with security built for nonstop defense.”)

According to Google’s report, the mechanics of intrusion remain the same. Even attackers using new AI-powered attack frameworks are using them to leverage compromised credentials and unpatched systems. It’s the speed and scale at which these frameworks can be used that’s the challenge.

In fact, using LLMs can even hurt the attackers, as the frameworks “trade stealth for velocity,” researchers say. The attacks can be “forensically noisy” and can hallucinate non-existent details or targets. “Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t.”

Or, as Sergej Epp summed up as a takeaway from a recent Cloud Security Alliance CISO huddle call on autonomous attacks, “detecting these attacks is — at least for now — not the hard part. They make a lot of noise, like 1000 interns.”

Austin Berglas, managing director and head of cyber operations at Nardello & Co., a global investigations firm, says he’s not seeing AI-discovered zero days or self-replicating AI agents out in the wild.

“This is one of those examples that is still in the lab environment,” he says.

Most attackers are using AI the way everyone does, he says. “Just like individuals use it for their daily productivity and efficiency, same with the bad actors. They’re able to scale, do it cheaper, do it quicker. And you’re seeing people who typically wouldn’t have the technical chops to do something, who are now able to do it because AI can do the technical side.”

The industry is seeing evidence of faster weaponization of vulnerabilities, confirms Gartner analyst John Watts. “Where it starts to have less evidence is for fully autonomous attacks. What happened with Hugging Face is a fully autonomous attack, and that isn’t that common.”

How CISOs should respond

But if the wave of autonomous attacks and AI-powered malware hasn’t yet fully arrived, what should CISOs do given the reality on the ground?

“The feedback that we get from our client base is that they believe there’s a lot of value in using the controls they already have,” Gartner’s Watts says.

“The wake-up call for the practitioners is to get busy with the patching,” confirms Paul Webber, an analyst at Software Analyst Cyber Research, adding that security by obscurity is no longer an option.

The biggest problem enterprises are facing, he notes, is that they need better automation to handle the increased workload, and the tools aren’t yet where they need to be.

“People need more trust in the security tools so they can move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop towards fully autonomous response,” Webber says. “And that’s going to take some discipline, some standardization, and some proof in the efficacy of the security tools themselves. At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.”

And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog.

“This is a conversation that we’re actively having right now,” says Christina Powers, partner and cybersecurity consulting leader at West Monroe, a management consulting firm.

“We’re working with a mid-sized bank, and they are just completely lost on how to keep up with the number of vulnerabilities that they got,” she says. “They’re sitting on millions of vulnerabilities. They don’t even know where to start. There’s a bit of analysis paralysis that’s happening because there’s so much information coming in.”

The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along.

“If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.

Title: Com-Affiliated Hackers Hijack Cloud Accounts via Vishing for Data Theft and Extortion
Context: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August...
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August 2026 that have led to data theft and extortion attempts.

The attacks have targeted financial services, healthcare, and legal services located in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. Other targets include construction, high-technology, transportation, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, insurance, and real estate sectors.

"The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal, or market consequences," Unit 42 said. "These attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September."

The activity has been attributed to a number of threat clusters, including -

Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters)

CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), first observed in January 2026

CL-CRI-1147 (aka Pink), first observed in May 2026

CL-CRI-1182 (aka Falcon), first observed in mid-2026

CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix and UNC6671), first observed in June 2026

CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex), first observed in September 2026

CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), first observed in September 2026

Intrusions typically commence with voice phishing, with the attackers posing as IT staff to resolve a purported authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page personalized to their organization.

Once the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, abuse cloud utilities and, in a few instances, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

The harvested authentication data is used to authenticate to victim environments, typically by routing such requests through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. The adversaries then seek to establish multi-layered persistence by registering their MFA devices, generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials, authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications; enumerate sensitive data; evade defenses by modifying mailbox rules and clearing security alert events; and harvest data from cloud platforms.

"Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization," Unit 42 said.

"These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices."

CL-CRI-1264 has also been observed enrolling unauthorized MFA devices within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence, often reusing a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. The attack chains involve automated data exfiltration using Python scripts to harvest information from Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint.

Once data is exfiltrated, the threat actor sends Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and instructing them to visit a TOR-hosted ransom negotiation site.

The second new cluster to emerge around the same time is CL-CRI-1274, which has also leaned on vishing for initial access and leveraged the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim's SharePoint and OneDrive environments.

"Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site," Unit 42 said.

The cybersecurity company said it also observed the CL-CRI-1192 attackers using a malicious browser extension named "Google Chrome" that's said to have been sideloaded onto the browser after enabling Developer Mode. The add-on performs a number of malicious actions, such as -

Installing global keyloggers

Stealing local/session storage and authentication cookies for Microsoft and Google accounts

Scanning pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Streaming webcam feeds

Implementing a command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol to capture screenshots, dispatch input events, steal clipboard contents, and allow remote site navigation.

"We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge," Unit 42 said.

"The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this."

One of the defining traits of the threat actors is their use of "apex" domains that impersonate single sign-on (SSO) portals, IT support pages, and passkey configuration services for each of the targeted organizations.

Also shared among the attackers is an AitM phishing kit called Doko's Panel that allows them to steal authenticated sessions and then abuse them to access connected software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms like SharePoint, Salesforce, DocuSign, and Slack to exfiltrate data of interest.

"The same persona behind Doko's Panel has been observed actively recruiting 'experienced callers' via Telegram, specifying requirements including fluent English with no accent, and advertising six-to-seven-figure weekly returns — evidence of the professionalized vishing-as-a-service model that complements the phishing kit ecosystem," Push Security noted in a report published earlier this May.

Microsoft has also revealed cloud-based intrusions in which threat actors have employed passkey and SSO lures to obtain unauthorized access and add their own authentication methods to set up persistence, as well as conduct high-volume Microsoft Graph activity, SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, and mailbox collection through REST APIs.

"Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments," Unit 42 said. "Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives."

Title: WordPress Blocks Six Backdoored WP Connect Plugins Before Malicious Releases Go Live
Context: The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released
Full Text:
WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account.

The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent."

The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below -

Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4)

WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4)

Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3)

Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4)

Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4)

Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2)

These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched.

"Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said.

Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval().

It can also perform the following actions -

Accept queued commands that run shell commands

Read, write, and delete arbitrary files

Query arbitrary database tables

Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes

Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing

Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal.

Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible.

"Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally."

The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors.

The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said. "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding."

Title: This could mess with Thanksgiving, says VMware as it drops third critical patch bundle in a week
Context: The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure...
Full Text: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues. VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

Title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
Context: Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he...
Full Text:
Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries.

In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset.

The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual.

Need to buy time

“For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post. “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.”

But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said.

He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug.

Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out.

“We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said.

Making the infrastructure secure from the start

Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules.

“This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project.

Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed.

All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system.

Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system.

The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post.

Shirudo in the wild

Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024. It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability.

But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code.

“Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post: They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.”

In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors.

Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed.

“This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.”

Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand.

Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said.

Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD.

Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development.

This article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

Title: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall
Context: A rule that names a subnet or VPC applies to each new resource that you launch in it
Full Text:
AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules, which match traffic by the AWS resources that send and receive it instead of by IP address. A rule can name a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, a security group, or a transit gateway attachment. Rules that match on IP addresses have to keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with. A VPC-attached AWS Lambda function can scale out and start sending traffic before an updated IP list reaches the firewall. With context-aware rules, you can filter a function’s traffic by the security group attached to it.

With context-aware rules, you can:

Write rules that follow your workloads – A rule that names a security group applies to each new resource whose network interface has that security group attached. A rule that names a subnet or VPC applies to each new resource that you launch in it. A rule that names a transit gateway attachment applies to traffic that enters through that attachment.

Apply one policy across accounts – One context store tracks the resources in the accounts that attach to a shared transit gateway. A rule can name context from any of those accounts.

See which resources are behind each connection – Your firewall logs record the resources on each side of a flow, along with their IP addresses.

In this post, we explain how context-aware rules work, set them up across accounts, and show what the logs record.

How context-aware rules work

Context-aware rules require transit gateway-attached firewalls, and they combine a control path and a data path (Figure 1). On the control path, a context store tells the firewall which AWS resources exist. On the data path, the transit gateway adds the context of the sender to each packet. The firewall brings the two together and matches that context against your rules.

Figure 1: How context-aware rules work across accounts

A context store tracks your resources. A context store is a catalog of the AWS resources that can send and receive traffic through a transit gateway. You create it in AWS Network Manager and associate it with the transit gateway that your firewall uses. When you share the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), those accounts create transit gateway VPC attachments to it. The context of those attachments, and of the resources behind them, then appears in the same context store. The context store is designed to keep the firewall in sync as you add and remove resources.

The transit gateway tags each packet. When traffic crosses the transit gateway, the transit gateway tags each packet with the context of the resource that sent it. That context is the sender’s VPC, subnet, transit gateway attachment, and the security groups attached to the sender. The firewall gets only the security group IDs, not their rules, so a rule that names any one of those groups matches.

The firewall matches context IDs in your rules. It reads the context on each packet and matches it against your rules. You group context IDs into a context set, a named rule variable that lists resources from the context store associated with the firewall. Then you use the set in the source or destination of a rule, in a Classic or Next Generation firewall policy.

Source context works with every protocol, because each packet carries the context of its sender. Destination context requires TCP-based rules, because the firewall learns the receiving resource from return traffic. For more details, see How context-aware rules work and Matching on destination context. AWS Transit Gateway also shares context with third-party firewalls through Gateway Load Balancer. For that setup, see Introducing resource context for firewall policies with AWS Transit Gateway.

Getting started

In this example, a central networking account owns the transit gateway and the firewall, and shares the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS RAM. You complete steps 1 and 2 once, in the account that owns the transit gateway.

1. Create a context store. In the AWS Network Manager console, select or create a global network and register your transit gateway with it. Then create a context store and associate it with the transit gateway (). Network Firewall discovers the context store on its own, so there’s nothing to configure on the firewall.

Figure 2: A context store associated with a transit gateway

2. Give Network Firewall access to the context store. In the account that owns the context store, create the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role NetworkFirewallContextStoreReadOnly. Use the trust policy and permissions in Onboarding your transit gateway to a context store. You create the role once for each account that owns a context store.

3. Create a context set. In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, create a rule group. On the Rule group variables page, choose Create context set, select your context store, and select the resources for the set. One set can mix context IDs of different resource types, from the accounts in the context store.

Figure 3: Creating a context set from the resources that the context store tracks

4. Check the sync state. Before you write rules, open the firewall’s details page and check the Context store sync state section. It shows the context store that the firewall discovered and its sync state.

Figure 4: The context store sync state on the firewall’s details page

5. Use the context set in your rules. The sample rule from Writing context-aware rules blocks SSH from PROD_RESOURCES to destinations outside your home networks. In a Next Generation firewall rule group, on the Configure rules page, use the Visual rule builder. Choose Drop and TCP. For Sources, choose Match specific criteria, select Context sets, and choose PROD_RESOURCES. For Destinations, choose Match specific criteria, select Destination IP, and enter $EXTERNAL_NET. Set the destination port to 22. Then add the rule group to your firewall policy.

Figure 5: Choosing a context set as a rule’s source in the Next Generation rule builder

The same rule in Suricata-compatible syntax follows. drop:flow is the action and its scope, tcp:all the protocol and connection state, and the rest is the source, destination, and port. In raw rules, you reference a context set with $ and its name; in the console, you pick it from a list.

drop:flow tcp:all $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001;)

Because the rule names resources and not addresses, it covers each new resource that you launch in those VPCs or attach that security group to.

For Classic policies, the same rule looks like this:

drop tcp $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001; rev:1;)

What the logs record

After you associate the transit gateway with a context store, Network Firewall adds a context object to its alert log and flow log records. The following records, shortened, show one outbound TLS connection from an application instance to example.com, through a central egress VPC with a network address translation (NAT) gateway. A rule that references the application’s security group blocks the connection and writes this alert log record. The matched list names the security group that the rule matched.

{ "event": { "event_type": "alert", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "context": { "matched": [ "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ] }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2002, "signature": "Application A: domain not on its allow list" } } }

The flow log record for the same flow_id lists the full context on each side. The src list holds the sender’s context IDs. Flow logs record this context for every flow, even when no rule matches it.

{ "event": { "event_type": "netflow", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "context": { "src": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60011", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60021", "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ], "dst": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60003", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60013", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60023" ] } } }

The dst list shows how destination context works for traffic to the internet. The firewall learns the destination from the response, and the response reaches the firewall from the NAT gateway. So the destination context is the egress VPC, the NAT gateway’s subnet, and the egress VPC’s transit gateway attachment, not the internet host. You can query these fields by context ID in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For example, you can see what an application already connects to before you write its rules. For the fields, see Context in your network firewall logs.

Availability and pricing

Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge. Standard AWS Network Firewall and AWS Transit Gateway charges apply to the resources that you use. For details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing and AWS Transit Gateway pricing. They work in the AWS Regions where both Network Firewall and Transit Gateway context sharing are available.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how you can use context-aware rules in Network Firewall to match traffic on the context of the resources that send and receive traffic. A context store tracks those resources across the accounts that share your transit gateway, and the transit gateway tags each packet with its sender’s context. Your rules and logs then use that context, so your rules can keep up as workloads change. To learn more, see Context-aware rules in AWS Network Firewall.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Title: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy
Context: They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats
Full Text:
When it comes to inspecting network traffic, many security teams want two things from a firewall. They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats. Today, you can do both with AWS Network Firewall, a stateful, managed network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service. In a Classic policy, your access rules and your threat rules run together in one stateful engine and share one rule capacity.

With Next Generation policies, access control and threat protection each get their own engine in the same firewall. A firewall engine allows the traffic you approve and drops the rest. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) engine checks the allowed traffic with AWS managed rule groups or with rules that you write. Each engine has its own rule capacity, so adding access rules doesn’t take capacity away from threat protection.

In this post, we walk through what Next Generation policies are, how they evaluate traffic, and the new concepts they introduce. We use sample records to cover what each engine logs and how to validate a policy with the new monitor mode. To put it all together, we walk through creating an example Next Generation policy.

How a Next Generation policy works

A Next Generation policy inspects traffic with two engines, in sequence. Traffic that the firewall engine allows moves to the IPS engine, and traffic that the firewall engine blocks goes no further. The firewall engine is drop by default, and the IPS engine is pass by default.

If you already write Suricata rules, the two engines will feel familiar. The firewall engine is built on Suricata 8 firewall mode, which follows each connection as it progresses and evaluates rules at each step. The IPS engine uses the Suricata compatible intrusion detection system (IDS) and IPS rules that you already know from the stateful engine in a Classic policy, with one difference: it evaluates rules in action order and doesn’t support Classic options such as strict order.

A Classic policy uses a stateless engine and then a stateful engine that evaluates access rules and threat rules together. In a Next Generation policy, both engines are stateful, so each rule is evaluated with full connection context, which helps keep traffic handling consistent and predictable. The firewall engine works up to the application layer. It follows each connection for its entire flow, from the first packet through the TCP handshake and application layer exchanges such as the TLS client hello, and evaluates your access rules along the way (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Classic and Next Generation policy engines and their rule capacity.

This separation changes how you design a policy. Because each engine has one job, you can plan access control and threat protection on their own, and different teams can work independently. For example, a networking team can manage access rules while a security team handles threat detection, and neither has to rewrite the other’s rules.

The firewall engine controls access

You configure access control by specifying an action for a protocol, along with a source and destination. Rules run in the order that you set. Traffic that no rule allows gets the policy’s firewall default action, which is drop unless you change it. In a Next Generation policy, the drop default action applies from the first packet, so for TCP traffic the firewall can drop the initial SYN. Unlike the drop established default action in a Classic policy, it doesn’t wait for a connection to be established.

A few terms explain how the firewall engine evaluates traffic. Connection states are the protocol states that a connection progresses through, such as the TCP handshake and the TLS client hello. A hook is the point at a connection state where your rules attach, so a rule’s hook sets when the firewall engine evaluates it. Each rule also has an action, such as accept, drop, or reject. Its action scope sets how much of the traffic the action applies to, from one packet or one transaction up to the whole connection, called the flow. For more details, see Firewall engine hooks.

When you build a rule in the console, you choose a protocol and then two settings: Connection state, which sets the rule’s hook, and Action scope. For example, to allow a domain over TLS, you match its server name at the Client Hello connection state with the This flow action scope.

Because the firewall engine is drop by default, a connection advances to the next connection state only while your rules keep accepting it. For example, a connection can pass the TCP handshake and still be dropped at the TLS client hello. That happens when its server name isn’t on your approved list (Figure 2).

Figure 2: A connection is accepted at the TCP handshake hook and dropped at the TLS client hello hook.

In Figure 2, the rule for www.amazon.com accepts the flow when it matches the server name at the TLS client hello hook. No rule accepts example.com at that hook, so the firewall default action drops it.

You don’t have to write every rule in raw Suricata syntax. You can build rules in the console rule builder, or, as in the example later in this post, enter your domains in a domain list rule group, and Network Firewall builds the rules for you.

Action scope also sets where an accepted connection goes next. An accept with the hook scope allows the connection to advance to the next connection state, where the rules at that hook evaluate it. An accept with the flow scope lets the connection skip the remaining hooks and move to the IPS engine (Figure 3). A firewall rule can also bypass the IPS engine for specific traffic when you choose. For the valid combinations of action and scope at each type of hook, see Firewall engine actions and scopes.

Figure 3: An accept with the hook scope compared with an accept with the flow scope.

The IPS engine looks for threats

Traffic that the firewall engine allows then reaches the IPS engine, which inspects it with Suricata compatible rules. The IPS engine is designed to look for specific threats, so it blocks only traffic that matches a threat rule. IPS rules evaluate in action order. Pass rules go first, then drop, reject, and alert rules, regardless of the order in which you define them. For the full path through both engines, see How Network Firewall filters traffic with a Next Generation policy.

We recommend that you start with the AWS managed rule groups. Because the IPS engine is built on the industry standard Suricata engine, you can also run Suricata compatible rule sets from specialized security providers, alongside rules that you write yourself.

Referenced rule groups and embedded rules

Each engine gets its rules from its own section of the policy. You can add rules in two ways and mix both in one section.

Referenced rule groups are separate resources, and they’re the only kind of rule group that Classic policies support. You create a rule group once and add it to as many policies as you need. You can also share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). For details, see Sharing AWS Network Firewall resources. When you update the rule group, each policy that references it picks up the change. You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow.

Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas.

Read what each engine logs

Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration. Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened.

The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list.

To separate access control events from threat events in your queries, filter on the engine field. To find which rule group produced an event, use resource_arn. Embedded rules and the default action show the policy ARN.

Validate in monitor mode, then enforce

Each Next Generation policy has a policy mode, enforce or monitor. In enforce mode, the engines apply their actions. In monitor mode, both engines evaluate your traffic and log what they would do. Your rules and the default action don’t drop or reject traffic.

Monitor mode also turns on alert logging for your rules and the default action, so each firewall rule that would block traffic logs its matches. That makes monitor mode a lower-risk way to stage a rollout of a new policy or a change to an existing one. Monitor logs are close to enforce mode but can differ. When a firewall rule would block a connection, monitor mode lets the connection through but sends it past the IPS engine, just as a blocked connection never reaches the IPS engine in enforce mode. So the monitor logs don’t show IPS alerts for that connection. For the full list of differences, see Policy mode: enforce and monitor.

To validate a policy in monitor mode:

Set Policy mode to Monitor, and confirm that alert logging is on for the firewall. Amazon Route 53 Resolved IP Validation still applies its configured action in monitor mode, so if your policy uses it, set its action to Alert.

Send representative traffic for long enough to cover your normal patterns.

In your alert logs, filter on engine = fw. Check the FirewallDefaultActionApplied metric in Amazon CloudWatch. Traffic that you meant to allow shouldn’t be reaching the default action.

When the results look right, switch Policy mode to Enforce during a maintenance window. Changing the policy mode or the firewall default action restarts stateful inspection on the firewall, which interrupts established connections.

Example policy with a domain allow list and threat protection

The following example puts the engines, logs, and monitor mode together. It allows outbound traffic only to approved domains and checks that allowed traffic for known threats. The firewall engine holds the domain allow list, and the IPS engine runs the AWS active threat defense managed rule group. Figure 4 shows the policy and where each of the earlier log records comes from. Log record 2 comes from the sample embedded rule, which isn’t part of the policy that you create in the following steps.

Figure 4: The example policy, with the sample embedded rule behind log record 2.

To create the domain list rule group:

In the Network Firewall console, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Next Generation as the rule group version, Firewall rule group as the type, and Domain list as the format.

Figure 5: Choosing the rule group version, type, and format for the domain list.

Enter one domain per line, for example .amazon.com and checkip.amazonaws.com, and under Protocols, select HTTPS only. For HTTPS, the firewall matches the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) without decrypting traffic. SNI is the server name that a client sends at the start of a TLS connection. To include a domain and its subdomains, start the name with a dot.

For Capacity sizing, choose Allow room to grow, and then create the rule group.

To create the policy:

Choose Firewall policies, and then choose Create firewall policy. Select Next Generation as the policy version and Drop as the firewall default action, so the firewall blocks traffic that you don’t allow. Set Policy mode to Monitor. We recommend rolling out a new policy in monitor mode first, then switching to enforce after you validate it. Enable Active Threat Defense is selected by default. Active threat defense is optional. Additional charges apply; for details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing.

Figure 6: The policy details page, with Next Generation, Drop, and Monitor selected.

On the Add firewall rule groups step, add the domain list rule group that you created in the previous procedure.

On the Add IPS rule groups step, the active threat defense managed rule group, listed as AttackInfrastructure, is already added. It comes from the Enable Active Threat Defense default that Figure 6 shows. Choose Add rule group to add more AWS managed rule groups, your own rule groups, or embedded rules.

Create the policy, associate it with your firewall, and turn on alert and flow logging.

After you validate the policy, as described in Validate in monitor mode, then enforce, switch Policy mode to Enforce.

For more detail, see Creating a rule group for a Next Generation policy and Generating firewall rules from domain names.

Already using Classic policies?

Classic Network Firewall policies remain supported, and your existing firewalls keep running as they are. Each firewall uses one policy type at a time, either a Classic policy or a Next Generation policy. For new firewalls, we recommend Next Generation policies. We’re working on migration guidance for existing policies, so you can plan a move when it suits you.

To try one now, create a test firewall with a Next Generation policy and start it in monitor mode. To compare the two policy types, see AWS Network Firewall firewall policy versions. Next Generation policies are available at no additional charge. You pay the standard Network Firewall charges for your firewall endpoints and the traffic they process. For Regions and pricing, see AWS Services by Region and AWS Network Firewall pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how a Next Generation policy gives access control and threat protection separate engines, each with its own rule capacity, so you can grow your firewall rules and IPS rules independently. We also showed what each engine logs, how to validate a policy in monitor mode, and how to build a policy that allows only approved domains and checks the allowed traffic for threats. To learn more, see Getting started with a Next Generation policy, and to automate your policies, use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDKs.
