Title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
Context: This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or...
Full Text:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.

We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.

Why migrate?

We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.

Incremental or all at once?

Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)

The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.

As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.

How we verified the migration

General approaches

To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.

Tests

Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).

The tests were coupled to the Python implementation. An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.

The tests were incomplete. The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.

Detecting parity with production

Production data is sometimes “the only true test” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.

The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.

Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.

Common tools for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies can differ for the same input (Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.

With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.

It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the shape of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:

Checkpointing. Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).

Fingerprint. Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.

The result was a shadowing system that produced a small record of each difference between our Rust and Python APIs. Here is an example, with made-up values:

step: build prompt ← where in the code piece: 2 ← where in the prompt first diff: byte 17 ← fingerprint python: 190 bytes ← fingerprint rust: 190 bytes ← fingerprint

We could then pass this record to an agent to fix it.

Verification loops

Each request that differed left a record in our logs. A single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical diff records. Rather than send each to an agent, we ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by which fields differed, then alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new kind of record. This coordinator assigned a worker agent to own each new kind of record. It also created a new thread in a shared Slack channel where human engineers could follow along and steer it when necessary.

To tackle the many bugs, we set up a series of verification loops. A fast inner loop gave agents a sandbox in which they could test ideas and propose fixes. A slower outer loop then validated fixes in production. In addition, a memory loop recorded any mistakes along the way, saving them so that agents could learn over time (Figure 10).

Inner loop

When we first started testing this in April, we gave each agent a record that showed where the Rust and Python versions differed. Agents would guess the root cause from the code and open a pull request. Once the fix was reviewed and merged, they deployed it to staging, a preproduction copy of the Rust API where we ran the same shadow comparison on test traffic. The agents checked whether the difference was eliminated. Since every hypothesis needed a review and a deployment, feedback was taking hours or days.

We needed agents to get a signal from verification much sooner, so we moved them into their own workspace. We redesigned the inner loop so that agents could have a place to test ideas quickly and fail safely. Each agent ran in a cloud sandbox with both codebases and fast, local checks for what happens before and after the model call. The input check took a request, built the prompt that each version would send to the model, and showed what differed. Because this check never actually called the model, comparing the versions took under a second. We later added an output check, which ran both versions against a fake model. The output check passed a scripted reply, such as a tool call, through each version and compared the results.

The main limitation was that agents could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind each record. So an agent would hypothesize what had caused the difference, then write its own request or model reply to try to reproduce the difference. Since each agent was writing these itself, it could read both results in full. If the results matched, its guess was wrong and the agent tried again. If they differed the same way the record described, the agent edited the Rust until the two versions matched, then added a test that failed on the old code and passed on the new (Figure 11).

The seam between the inner and outer loops was a good checkpoint for human review. Inside the sandbox, a wrong guess cost an agent only a few seconds and had no impact on users. Agents could iterate on their own. We allowed a fix to cross into the outer loop only after it had undergone PR review; this allowed engineers to focus their attention on proposed fixes (rather than on guesses) and on the questions the verifiers couldn’t answer, such as whether a difference between the Rust and Python APIs was the result of a bug or a deliberate change.

Agents posted their fixes and evidence to their Slack threads for engineers to review. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences between the Rust and Python APIs came from web search. The production API retrieved the web search tool’s description from an internal service. The Rust API didn’t call this service yet, so the tool description was missing from the prompts. An agent proposed a shortcut to copy the text into files that would be readable by Rust. The prompts then matched, and the fix passed the local verifier. But an engineer turned it down because it didn’t solve the problem: Rust would still need to call the service before launch, at which point the workaround would be thrown out (Figure 12).

But the verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them. A verifier can tell an agent whether the outputs matched, but not whether the fix is good enough to ship. That’s why human review was an important gate.

Outer loop

In the inner loop, agents debugged differences and proposed fixes. At the seam between the inner loop and the outer loop, engineers reviewed the proposed fixes, gave feedback, and approved them to deploy. The outer loop then compared Rust API deployments with and without each fix.

To make that comparison fair, we logged facts about each request we compared, but not its text, including which model and API features it used—for example, prompt caching, tools, or extended thinking. These details let agents compare requests of the same kind (Figure 13) and ask how often the bug’s fingerprint appeared on builds with and without the fix. This way, agents could monitor the new builds for the bug.

We designed the outer loop to catch problems that the inner loop missed. The inner loop simulated production quickly but imperfectly: agents could test a hypothesis in seconds, but only on requests they had written, and with a local verifier that wasn’t always configured exactly like production.

This means that sometimes a fix passed in the sandbox and production still showed the difference. The agent assigned to the bug would either see the difference in the new build’s records, or be alerted by the coordinating agent. It then went back to the inner loop and used that evidence to form a new hypothesis.

Memory loop

The inner and outer loops fixed one difference at a time. The memory loop improved how agents made those fixes. We didn’t want engineers to have to make the same correction twice, so we recorded what came out of reviews and agents’ own work and applied it to every agent that followed.

For example, when an engineer turned down the web search shortcut (Figure 12), the agent saved a note to memory explaining the decision, the reason for it, and the correct fix, which was to have Rust call the service that supplies tool descriptions.

Building that call took our team weeks, and in the meantime the bug kept producing records. Some had new fingerprints, because the missing text fell at other positions in the prompt or belonged to another tool that used the same service. Agents checked the memory note, recognized the known bug, and linked those records to it, instead of writing another workaround (Figure 14).

Other lessons became general rules for porting and writing Rust. After one agent guessed at Python’s behavior, an engineer made it a rule to port exactly what Python did. An agent then compared the existing code with that rule and found seven more places where the port had relied on a guess.

In June, an agent also went through about 60 of the team’s review comments, grouped the recurring problems and proposed rules, which an engineer edited and approved for CLAUDE.md (Figure 14).

The memory loop also encoded some lessons in permanent checks. This included new tests that failed when Rust drifted from Python, lints that banned patterns reviewers kept flagging, and later a merge check that required anyone changing the Python code to make a matching change in Rust or request an exemption.

Looking ahead

It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.

The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.

Lessons learned

Verification is the new bottleneck. Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.

Verification is how you earn confidence. In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or formal verification can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.

Carefully design the verification signal. A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference in the code and fingerprints helped tell one bug from another.

Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal. Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).

Keep the loops simple, so they scale with Claude’s capability. We tried to put human judgment only into what counted as correct; otherwise we left it up to Claude how to get there. Agents chose which hypotheses to test, how to reproduce each bug, and how to fix it. The verifiers judged the result. Simple loops around strong verifiers allowed us to move productively over time (Figure 16).

Move toward outer loops. At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.

Title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
Context: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for...
Full Text:
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”

Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

AWS Network Firewall introduces automated internet firewall mode (Preview)
Context: For outbound-only connectivity, the firewall first inspects the traffic and then performs NAT, so your rules and logs see each workload’s private IP address
Full Text:
AWS Network Firewall now offers automated internet firewall mode (Preview). In this mode, Network Firewall applies your centrally defined rules to traffic at the internet gateway of each of your virtual private clouds (VPCs). It also performs built-in network address translation (NAT) for outbound-only connections. A subnet that reaches the internet needs only one route, directly to the internet gateway. You no longer need to deploy firewall endpoints and NAT gateways in each VPC and configure the routes between them and the subnets. If you’re new to internet traffic inspection, you can start with AWS managed rule groups for Network Firewall. AWS security experts maintain and update these rule groups to help protect your workloads against changing threats. You can deploy these managed rule groups centrally across your environment.

With automated internet firewall mode, you can:

Inspect traffic at the internet gateway – Each VPC gets its own firewall for inbound and outbound IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, with built-in NAT for outbound-only IPv4 connections.

Manage centrally, inspect in each VPC – You define policies in AWS Network Security Manager or start from an AWS managed template. Each VPC’s traffic passes its own firewall, so each VPC you add brings its own inspection capacity. The same central policy also works for VPCs with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ranges.

Extend coverage to new VPCs – You can create a scope that includes all existing and future VPCs, so your policy applies to new VPCs when teams create them.

In this post, we explain how automated internet firewall mode works and how it fits your existing architecture. We also walk through the steps to deploy it across your environment.

How automated internet firewall mode works

In automated internet firewall mode, Network Firewall applies your rules at the internet gateway of each VPC. Before this launch, inspecting a VPC’s internet traffic meant routing each subnet through a firewall endpoint. Resources that needed outbound-only connectivity also went through a NAT gateway. This mode helps simplify that model by moving inspection to each VPC’s internet gateway. Each subnet now has one route to the internet gateway, where the firewall inspects the traffic and performs built-in NAT (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Outbound traffic before and after automated internet firewall

Each VPC gets its own firewall, not a share of one. When you use VPC endpoint associations to protect multiple VPCs with one firewall, those VPCs share that firewall’s capacity in each Availability Zone. In automated internet firewall mode, each VPC’s firewall supports throughput of up to 100 Gbps in each Availability Zone (Service quotas). It also works when VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges, because their traffic doesn’t meet in a shared inspection network where the addresses would conflict.

The firewall inspects inbound and outbound traffic. For outbound-only connectivity, the firewall first inspects the traffic and then performs NAT, so your rules and logs see each workload’s private IP address. Built-in NAT translates outbound IPv4 connections from resources without a public IP address, and IPv6 traffic isn’t translated. If your destinations accept only allowlisted source addresses, an Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) policy lets you choose the NAT addresses that automated internet firewall mode uses (NAT for outbound traffic).

The firewall uses Network Firewall Next Generation firewall policies. You can start from AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline, an AWS managed template that AWS security experts maintain. You can then add AWS managed rule groups and your own rule groups.

Automated internet firewall mode only inspects traffic that crosses the internet gateway. For traffic between VPCs and to on-premises networks over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, we recommend a transit gateway-attached Network Firewall.

Subnet connectivity options

Before this launch, a public subnet had a direct route to the internet gateway, and its resources used public IP addresses, so they could connect out and accept inbound connections. A private subnet had no direct route, and its resources reached the internet through a NAT gateway. With automated internet firewall mode, a subnet that reaches the internet can route 0.0.0.0/0 directly to the internet gateway, so the route table no longer separates public from private. Instead, each subnet’s connectivity type decides how its resources reach the internet. You set it in the Network Security Manager policy, not on the subnet. Table 1 maps each type to the model you know.

Connectivity type

Works like

What happens

Flexible (recommended)

A public and a private subnet in one

A resource with a public IP address, such as an Elastic IP address, gets bidirectional access, as in a public subnet. A resource without one gets outbound-only access through built-in NAT, similar to a private subnet.

Bidirectional

A public subnet

Resources with a public IP address connect out and accept inbound connections. Resources without one can’t reach the internet.

Outbound-only

A private IPv4 subnet behind a NAT gateway, or an IPv6 subnet behind an egress-only internet gateway

Unsolicited inbound connections are dropped. Resources without a public IP address connect out through built-in NAT, and resources with one keep their own address.

Excluded

A subnet without a firewall

Traffic bypasses the firewall and built-in NAT.

The firewall inspects traffic in each type except excluded (Figure 2). Each policy sets one default connectivity type for all subnets in scope. You can override it for specific subnets based on tags or on Amazon Resource Name (ARN). When a subnet matches more than one override, the first one in the list applies.

Figure 2: Flexible, bidirectional, and outbound-only subnets are inspected. Excluded subnets aren’t.

Connectivity types also decide which inbound connections reach your resources. The firewall inspects inbound connections to resources with a public IP address in flexible and bidirectional subnets, such as the Network Load Balancer for a non-HTTP service in Figure 3. Figure 3 also shows the outbound path, where instances without a public IP address connect out through the firewall and then built-in NAT. For web applications and APIs, we still recommend AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer. You can set that load balancer’s subnet to excluded so Network Firewall doesn’t inspect the same request again. Keep in mind that excluded applies in both directions, so any outbound traffic from that subnet also bypasses the firewall.

Figure 3: Inbound and outbound traffic showing inbound, outbound, and excluded connections

Managing automated internet firewall mode

You manage automated internet firewall mode in AWS Network Security Manager. With AWS Organizations, a central security team deploys policies from the Network Security Manager administrator account to the whole organization, to organizational units (OUs), or to specific accounts. Network Security Manager also supports a single-account model, where it applies policies only to that account’s VPCs. You can start from the Network Firewall console or the Network Security Manager console, but the firewall itself is read-only outside Network Security Manager.

Network Security Manager uses three components (Figure 4):

Policy – Combines rules and templates with the connectivity type, enforcement mode, logging, and priority. Rules are the building blocks. A traffic inspection rule decides how the firewall handles traffic, and a firewall configuration rule sets options such as the enforcement mode or logging. A template is an ordered, reusable group of rules, such as AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline, that you can share across policies.

Scope – Selects your organization, OUs, accounts, or VPCs.

Deployment – Binds a policy to a scope. Network Security Manager then creates and manages a firewall in each VPC in scope.

Figure 4: A deployment binds a policy to a scope, and Network Security Manager creates a firewall in each VPC in scope

This model matters most when you manage many VPCs. Because Network Security Manager applies the policy at the internet gateway, the firewall is designed so that VPC owners and subnet owners without the proper privileges can’t bypass inspection by changing routes. Subnets set to excluded and Availability Zones where automated internet firewall mode isn’t supported aren’t inspected.

Many organizations want one security baseline everywhere, while some accounts, organizational units, or applications need rules in addition to the baseline. To do this, you create two policies, each deployed to its own scope. The organization policy holds a baseline template, and the Account A policy holds the same baseline template plus Account A’s rules (Figure 5). The template lets you maintain the baseline rules once and reuse them in both policies. Where policies overlap, the policy with the lower priority number applies in full, and the policies don’t merge. In Account A, the Account A policy (priority 100) wins over the organization policy (priority 1000), so it must include the baseline template. Its enforcement mode, logging, and connectivity type also replace the organization policy’s. To learn more, see How AWS Network Security Manager works.

Figure 5: The Account A policy, priority 100, takes priority in Account A. Other accounts get the organization policy, priority 1000.

Getting started

We recommend starting in monitor mode, especially in VPCs with existing workloads. In monitor mode, the firewall logs what your rules would do but doesn’t drop traffic because of them. After the logs show the results you expect, switch the policy to enforce. In this example, we create a policy in monitor mode in six steps.

Start from the AWS Management Console for Network Firewall. On the Firewalls page, open the Internet firewalls tab and choose Create in AWS Network Security Manager. The Quick create and deploy page opens in the Network Security Manager console. Select Network Firewall automated internet firewall as the firewall type.

Figure 6: Create a new internet firewall

Define protections. Choose Manage templates and add AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline. Under Enforcement mode, select Monitor, and choose destinations for alert logs and flow logs.

Figure 7: Define protections and set destinations for logs

Enter a name for the policy and check its Policy priority. Where policies overlap, the lower number takes priority. The new policy gets a priority that evaluates after your existing policies of the same firewall type, and you can change it later in the policy editor.

Figure 8: Set the policy details

Set the scope. For example, you can set the scope for Accounts and OUs to include the entire organization and the scope for VPCs to include all existing and future VPCs. To learn more about scopes, see How AWS Network Security Manager works.

Figure 9: Set the scope

Choose the Subnet connectivity type. For example, select Flex (recommended).

Figure 10: Choose the subnet connectivity type

Review your settings and choose Create and deploy. Cross-account visibility lets Network Security Manager see resources in the accounts in the scope.

Figure 11: Review and deploy

Network Security Manager then creates a firewall at the internet gateway of each VPC in scope. For the full steps, including the organization baseline with account-specific rules, see Getting started with automated internet firewall.

Migrating existing VPCs to automated internet firewall mode

When you deploy automated internet firewall mode to an existing VPC, you might not need to change routes on day one. With the flexible type, the firewall inspects existing resources and keeps the addresses they already use (Figure 12):

Instance with an Elastic IP address – The firewall inspects its traffic, and the instance keeps its Elastic IP address.

Instance behind a NAT gateway – The firewall inspects the traffic after the NAT gateway translates it and doesn’t translate it again. Your rules and logs see the NAT gateway’s private IP address as the source.

Instance with no public IP address in a subnet that routes to the internet gateway – The firewall inspects its traffic, and built-in NAT gives it outbound-only access, which it didn’t have before. To keep resources without a public IP address isolated from the internet, set the subnet’s connectivity type to bidirectional instead. Resources with a public IP address then keep bidirectional connectivity, and resources without one can’t reach the internet.

Figure 12: Day-one source addresses in an existing VPC with Flexible subnets

Later, at your own pace, you can retire each NAT gateway by routing its subnets directly to the internet gateway. Built-in NAT then takes over. The source address changes to one that automated internet firewall mode assigns or one from your IPAM policy pool, so update allow lists that name the NAT gateway’s address first. Your logs then show each workload’s private IP address. If you inspect inbound or outbound internet traffic today with Network Firewall endpoints, automated internet firewall mode can take over that inspection. After you confirm that your new policy covers the same rules, you can remove the endpoints and routes that you use for internet traffic. For each architecture, see Working with existing architectures.

Availability and pricing

Automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in all AWS commercial Regions. For pricing, see AWS Network Firewall pricing. During the preview, some features and instance types aren’t supported. For the list, see Automated internet firewall. Features, service quotas, and console labels can change during the preview. Your use of the preview is subject to the Betas and Previews section of the AWS Service Terms.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how automated internet firewall mode applies Network Firewall inspection and built-in NAT at the internet gateway of your VPCs. You define and control policies centrally in Network Security Manager. It is designed so that VPC owners without the proper privileges can’t route around it, and your policy applies to new VPCs in scope when teams create them. To learn more, see Automated internet firewall in the Network Firewall Developer Guide.

Title: Delegate user access to AI agents with Amazon Cognito token exchange
Context: 0, the app sends you to the authorization server that your email provider trusts, where you sign in and approve only the access the app requested, such as the contacts
Full Text:
Suppose you use a restaurant review app to check reviews, book tables, and email invitations to your friends. With OAuth 2.0, the app sends you to the authorization server that your email provider trusts, where you sign in and approve only the access the app requested, such as the contacts.read and messages.send scopes. The review app won’t sees your credentials. It only receives a short-lived access token limited to the scopes you approved, which it presents to your email provider’s API to read your contacts and send invitation emails on your behalf.

That works while the app calls the email API directly, but many requests take a second hop to call downstream services. When you book a table, the app calls its reservation service with your token to email details to your friends, which token should the reservation service use to call the email API? Forwarding the access token issued to the review app hides the reservation service because the email API thinks the app sent the request. Using the reservation service’s own token from an OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant loses user identity, because the email API knows which service called, but not for which user. Figure 1 shows this second hop.

Figure 1: The reservation service calling the email API for a signed-in user

OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, defined in RFC 8693, handles this second hop. Instead of forwarding your access token, the reservation service goes back to the authorization server with two things: your access token, which shows what you consented for, and its own credentials, which show who it is. The authorization server returns a new token for the email API, called issued token, which identifies the user, can also name the reservation service, and carries the same scopes or fewer.

AI agents make this second hop more common and more important, for example when the review app adds an AI agent that reserves tables and invites friends for you. The agent picks its tools at run time, such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that sends invitations, and those tools call APIs for you. With token exchange, each hop gets only the scopes it needs, and the email API can see which service acted for you.

In this post, we show you how to use the new OAuth token exchange feature in Amazon Cognito when services and AI agents call your APIs on behalf of users, and Cognito serves as the OAuth 2.0 authorization server. We explain the difference between impersonation and delegation, and show you examples of how the feature works with an MCP server and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

How token exchange works in Amazon Cognito

Every token exchange starts with a subject token that represents the user. In Amazon Cognito, the subject token can be an access token or ID token that your user pool issued to the app where the user signed in. The calling service sends the subject token to Cognito, and Cognito returns a new token for that service to use at the downstream resource server.

Token exchange distinguishes two patterns, impersonation and delegation. The calling service chooses which pattern to use based on whether the downstream API needs to authorize the service that’s acting on behalf of the user:

Impersonation – The calling service doesn’t identify itself as the actor. The issued token represents the user. Its client_id claim identifies the app client that performed the exchange, but it doesn’t have an act (actor) claim to show a service is acting for the user.

Delegation – The calling service identifies itself as the actor by also sending an actor token. Amazon Cognito adds an act claim that names the calling service, so the resource server can see and log who authorized the action and who carried it out.

Impersonation fits when the calling service only relays the user’s request and makes no decisions of its own, such as a backend for frontend (BFF) that forwards requests from a web app to your APIs. It also fits where a downstream API authorizes the user alone and doesn’t need to know which service relayed the call.

For AI agents, delegation is the important pattern. If the agent used a token of its own, the record would show that an agent called the resource server, but not for whom. With impersonation, the record shows the user but not the agent acting for them. You need delegation to see both for proper authorization and audit trails.

Figure 2: Delegated access across two service hops

Figure 2 shows the flow for delegated access between services:

The user signs in to your app through Amazon Cognito.

Cognito issues the user’s access token to the client application.

The client calls the downstream service, such as an MCP server, with the user’s access token.

The service calls the Cognito /oauth2/token endpoint and authenticates with its own app client. It sends the user’s access token as the subject token and names the resource server as the audience. For delegation, it also sends its own token as the actor token.

Cognito validates the request and returns an issued token. The issued token still identifies the user in sub. For delegation, it also identifies the service in the act claim.

The service calls the resource server, such as an email API, with the issued token.

The resource server checks that the token’s aud claim names itself, then authorizes the request for the user and returns the user’s data to the service.

The calling service returns the result to the client.

In addition to requesting a token exchange at the /oauth2/token endpoint on your user pool’s domain, you can call the GetDerivedToken API with an AWS SDK, which doesn’t require a user pool domain. Both accept the same subject token, actor token, audience and scopes, and return an issued token with the same claims.

Here’s an example issued token from a delegation token exchange. The token keeps user’s identity in sub and names the calling service in the act claim.

{ "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE", "sub": "c4b82478-5678-90ab-cdef-EXAMPLE11111", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "version": 2, "token_use": "access", "scope": "email-api/messages.send", "aud": "email-api", "act": { "sub": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE", "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, "exp": 1735689600, "iat": 1735686000 }

The email API authorizes the user identified by sub, and act tells it which service is acting for that user. It can then decide whether it trusts that service, and its logs can show both the user and the service for each request. Accept a delegated token only when act.client_id reflects a service you trust, such as the invitations MCP server, and matches the token’s client_id meaning the trusted service requested the token itself.

Security controls during an exchange

Amazon Cognito checks every exchange before it issues a token. It validates the subject token’s signature and expiry, and refuses a token that has been revoked or that belongs to a disabled user in your user pool. If the request includes an audience, the issued token is bound to that resource server, and every requested scope must belong to it. The issued token carries only scopes that both the subject token and the app client allow, so an exchange can narrow your access but doesn’t add to it. It also doesn’t outlive the subject token, and the exchange doesn’t return a refresh token.

For the full list of checks, see Security model in Exchanging tokens for downstream services in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide. Checks by Cognito don’t replace the resource server’s own: it should still verify the JWT tokens, including signature, issuer, expiry, audience and scopes, and for delegated requests, it should validate the act claim.

Your user pool might have a pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger, which can add or suppress custom claims and scopes in your user pool’s tokens. Amazon Cognito also invokes this trigger during token exchange, with the trigger source TokenGeneration_TokenExchange. However, Cognito doesn’t add any scopes that the trigger returns for an exchange, so the calling service can’t gain more permissions than the user’s token already has. You can still use the trigger to remove scopes from the issued token. For more information, see Customize the exchanged token with a Lambda trigger.

Enable token exchange in your Amazon Cognito user pool

Token exchange is an OAuth 2.0 grant, and you can enable it for each application client as an authentication flow in your Amazon Cognito user pool. Check the prerequisites in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

To enable token exchange for an app client:

Open the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito, and choose your Cognito user pool.

In the navigation pane, under Applications section, choose App clients, and then choose your app client.

In App client information, choose Edit.

Figure 3: Cognito token exchange app client

On the Edit app client information page, under Authentication flows, go to Exchange OAuth 2 token for delegation and impersonation and select the following:

For delegation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION.

For impersonation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_IMPERSONATION.

Figure 4: Amazon Cognito token exchange authentication flows

Choose Save changes.

Example token exchange use cases for agentic workload delegation

Now that you’ve enabled token exchange, we show you two examples of how it works in an agentic workload. Both continue the review app story: its AI agent sends invitations for you by calling the email API, and the email API needs to know who you are and which component acted for you.

The two examples differ in where the exchange happens. Amazon Cognito fills the act claim from the actor token, so act names whichever component sends its own actor token in the exchange. In Example 1, a shared intermediary—such as an MCP server or an AI gateway—performs the exchange for every agent that calls it, so act names the intermediary. In Example 2, the agent requests the exchange itself, so act names the agent.

Example 1: A shared intermediary as the actor

In this example, the intermediary sits in front of the email API. We show it two ways: an MCP server you build that performs the exchange in its own code, and an AI gateway in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway that performs it through configuration.

Using your own MCP server:

The MCP authorization specification doesn’t allow an MCP server to pass along the token it received from the MCP client. To call the email API for you, the invitations MCP server needs a token of its own. It uses its own app client in your user pool to perform a delegation token exchange.

Figure 5 shows how the invitations MCP server sends invites for you.

Figure 5: The invitations MCP server sending invites for a signed-in user

The user signs in to the review app through Amazon Cognito.

The review app’s AI agent calls the send_invites tool on the invitations MCP server with the user’s access token.

{ "sub": "c4b82478-...", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": "<review app client ID>", "scope": "openid invitations-mcp/tools email-api/contacts.read email-api/messages.send", "token_use": "access", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<user-pool-id>" }

The MCP server authorizes the inbound request by checking the token’s client_id and the invitations-mcp/tools scope, then gets its own actor token with its client ID and secret in an OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant flow.

The MCP server sends the user’s token as subject token and its actor token to the Cognito /oauth2/token endpoint in a delegation token exchange. It requests only email-api/messages.send, because sending invites doesn’t require reading your contacts.

curl -X POST "https://<domain>.auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com/oauth2/token" \ -u "$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_ID:$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_SECRET" \ -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \ --data-urlencode "subject_token=$YOUR_TOKEN" \ -d subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \ --data-urlencode "actor_token=$ACTOR_TOKEN" \ -d actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \ -d audience=email-api \ -d scope=email-api/messages.send

Cognito validates both tokens and returns the issued token, while keeping the user in sub claim and adding the MCP server’s app client to act claim.

{ "sub": "c4b82478-...", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": "<MCP server app client ID>", "aud": "email-api", "scope": "email-api/messages.send", "act": { "sub": "<MCP server app client ID>", "client_id": "<MCP server app client ID>", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<user-pool-id>", "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, "token_use": "access" }

The MCP server calls the email API with the issued token. The email API checks aud=email-api and the messages.send scope, and it confirms that act.client_id matches client_id and names an MCP server it trusts. It then sends the invites from your account and records that the invitations MCP server sent them for you.

To set up the MCP server:

In Amazon Cognito user pool, register the email API (email-api) and the MCP server (invitations-mcp) as resource servers in your user pool, with the scopes used.

Create an app client with a client secret for the MCP server in your user pool. Select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION in authentication flows, allow the client credentials grant so the MCP server can get its actor token, and allow the email-api/messages.send scope that it requests in the exchange.

Have the review app request email-api/messages.send when you sign in, along with invitations-mcp/tools. The exchange can remove scopes from your token, but it can’t add any.

Other AI agents can also sign you in through Amazon Cognito and call the invitations MCP server. They can register with your user pool through dynamic client registration (DCR), or identify themselves with a client ID metadata document (CIMD). Token exchange works the same way for these clients. They send your access token to the MCP server, and the MCP server performs the exchange with its own app client, so the issued token names you in sub and the MCP server in act.

Using AgentCore Gateway:

If you don’t want to write the exchange in your MCP server, AgentCore Gateway can perform it for you. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity can perform the same token exchange on behalf of AgentCore Gateway, so the gateway doesn’t store the OAuth client secret or build the request.

Here, AgentCore Gateway replaces the invitations MCP server. It exposes the email API as an MCP tool through an OpenAPI target, and the review app’s AI agent calls that tool with your access token.

Figure 6 shows how AgentCore Gateway sends invites for you.

Figure 6: AgentCore Gateway sending invites through AgentCore Identity

The agent calls the AgentCore Gateway invite tool with user’s access token. The AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against your user pool and accepts only tokens issued to the review app.

AgentCore Gateway passes user’s access token to AgentCore Identity and asks for a token for the email API target.

AgentCore Identity uses the AgentCore Gateway app client in a client credentials grant to get an actor token.

AgentCore Identity sends your token and the actor token in a delegation token exchange, adding the subject_token_type and audience values from the target’s custom parameters.

Amazon Cognito validates the request and returns the issued token, with the user in sub, and the AgentCore Gateway app client in act.

AgentCore Identity passes the issued token to AgentCore Gateway.

AgentCore Gateway calls the email API with the issued token, and the email API applies the same checks as for the preceding MCP server setup.

To set up AgentCore Gateway:

In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for AgentCore Gateway in the same way as for the MCP server.

In AgentCore Identity, create an AgentCore Identity credential provider for the AgentCore Gateway app client. A credential provider stores what AgentCore Identity needs to request tokens from Amazon Cognito: your user pool’s discovery URL and the app client’s ID and secret. Use the CustomOauth2 provider type, and enable delegation in its customOauth2ProviderConfig settings:

{ "oauthDiscovery": { "discoveryUrl": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<user-pool-id>/.well-known/openid-configuration" }, "clientId": "<Gateway app client ID>", "clientSecret": "<client secret>", "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC", "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": { "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE", "tokenExchangeGrantTypeConfig": { "actorTokenContent": "M2M" } } }

In AgentCore Gateway, configure the AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer with your user pool’s discovery URL, and set allowedClients to the review app’s client ID.

In the AgentCore Gateway target’s outbound authorization, reference the credential provider and add subject_token_type and audience as custom parameters. Because your token is an access token, set subject_token_type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token.

{ "providerArn": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:<account-id>:token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/cognito", "scopes": ["email-api/messages.send"], "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE", "customParameters": { "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token", "audience": "email-api" } }

AgentCore Gateway handles the exchange through configuration, so you don’t need to write agent or interceptor code for it. For more information, see Set up outbound authorization for your gateway.

With either your own MCP server or an AI gateway, act names the intermediary rather than the agent that called it. Every agent behind it appears as the same app client. This design still protects the email API. It accepts only tokens with aud=email-api, and your original access token has no such audience, so an agent can’t bypass the intermediary by forwarding your token. Each call that reaches the email API carries a token with only the scope it needs. The agents don’t hold downstream credentials or exchange logic, and the email API trusts one intermediary instead of every agent. If the email API needs to tell agents apart, perform the exchange in the agent, as Example 2 shows.

Example 2: The agent as the actor on AgentCore Runtime

If the review app’s AI agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, the agent can request the exchange itself through AgentCore Identity and call the email API directly. The issued token then names the agent in act, so the email API knows which agent sent the invites.

Figure 7 shows how the agent sends invites for you.

Figure 7: The AI agent on AgentCore Runtime sending invites through AgentCore Identity

The review app invokes the agent on AgentCore Runtime with the user’s access token.

Runtime validates your token with its inbound JWT authorizer, exchanges it for a workload access token from AgentCore Identity, and passes that token to the agent. A workload access token is an opaque token that proves which agent is calling. It carries the user’s access token, which AgentCore Identity uses as the subject token in step 4.

The agent asks AgentCore Identity for a token for the email API by calling GetResourceOauth2Token with the workload access token.

AgentCore Identity gets an actor token with the agent’s app client, then sends user’s token and the actor token to Cognito in a delegation token exchange.

Amazon Cognito returns the issued token, with user in sub and the agent’s app client in act, and AgentCore Identity passes it to the agent.

The agent calls the email API with the issued token. The email API applies the same checks as in Example 1, and confirms that act.client_id names an agent it trusts.

The issued token has the same shape as in Example 1, but client_id and act name the agent’s app client.

To set up the agent:

In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for the agent in your user pool and select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for it. To tell agents apart in act claim, give each agent its own app client and credential provider.

In AgentCore Identity, create a credential provider for the agent’s app client in the same way as for AgentCore Gateway.

In AgentCore Runtime, configure the inbound JWT authorizer on AgentCore Runtime to accept your user pool’s tokens, with allowedClients set to the review app’s client ID.

In the agent’s code, request the issued token with the AgentCore SDK:

from bedrock_agentcore.identity.auth import requires_access_token @requires_access_token( provider_name="<Agent name>", scopes=["email-api/messages.send"], audiences=["email-api"], auth_flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE", custom_parameters={ "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, ) async def send_invites(friends: list[str], *, access_token: str): # Call the email API with access_token ...

The decorator makes the GetResourceOauth2Token call in step 3 of Figure 7 and passes the issued token to your function as access_token.

For more information, see On-behalf-of token exchange with AgentCore Identity.

Conclusion

Think back to the agent at the start of this post. The agent had to book a table and send invitations for you, and forwarding the user’s original access token would have hidden which service acted for you and given it more access than the job needed. With Amazon Cognito token exchange, each hop gets its own scoped-down token, bound to the resource server it calls and limited to the scopes it needs. Each issued token also expires no later than your own token and doesn’t come with a refresh token, so no service can keep access after your token expires.

For AI agents, delegation adds a second identity to the token. The act claim names the service doing the work, so a downstream API can choose which agents it trusts. Your audit records can then show both the person who authorized a request and the agent that made it.

You can try this on a new or existing Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus plan. Enable ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for an app client, register the downstream API as a resource server, and call GetDerivedToken or the token endpoint.

Title: Report: Half of Black Friday-Themed Emails Are Scams
Context: Attackers are also sending delivery-themed scams, which are particularly effective when people are expecting real deliveries
Full Text:
Black Friday scam campaigns began ramping up in late October and continue to target users ahead of the shopping holiday, according to researchers at Bitdefender. Half of Black Friday-themed email campaigns observed by Bitdefender were scams, luring users with phony giveaways or exclusive early deals. Attackers are also sending delivery-themed scams, which are particularly effective when people are expecting real deliveries.

“During the Black Friday pre-ramp period, Bitdefender observed spikes in delivery-themed scam and phishing activity, particularly on October 31 and November 3,” the researchers write. “FedEx was the most frequently impersonated delivery or logistics brand by volume. Amazon activity was nearly as large, although many of those messages used delivery-notification or shipping-status lures rather than classic courier-only scams. EVRI, DHL and DPD were also clearly present. FedEx, Amazon, EVRI, DHL and DPD are not associated with these scam campaigns.”

After Black Friday passes, users should expect to see similar shopping scams throughout the holiday season. Bitdefender outlines the following advice to help users avoid falling for these scams:

“Open the retailer’s official app or type its address into your browser yourself instead of following an email, text, or ad link

Treat dramatic discounts on luxury goods, electronics and gift cards with extra caution

Be skeptical of unexpected prize notifications, reward balances and free-product offers

Check the website address for misspellings, unusual endings or extra words added to a brand name

Never enter payment details on a page you reached through an unsolicited message without verifying the seller first

Keep security protection enabled across your devices to help block phishing pages, fraudulent shops, and malicious links”

Title: Socket Releases Free Patches for 100% of Critical CVEs in RubyGems
Context: Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9
Full Text:
We've completed security patches for 100% of patchable critical-severity CVEs in the RubyGems ecosystem, and we're making those fixes available to everyone for free. Developers can now remediate these vulnerabilities without upgrading their existing dependency versions, even when an upstream fix requires a breaking change.

The milestone follows an intensive engineering sprint focused on expanding RubyGems patch coverage. During the effort, our team also made substantial improvements to the systems used to generate, test, validate, and publish security fixes.

Socket identifies six critical vulnerabilities with available patches in a sample Ruby project.

Fixing Vulnerabilities Without Dependency Upgrades #

Upgrading to a secure upstream version is generally the simplest way to address a vulnerability. But upgrades aren't always straightforward, particularly for applications that depend on older versions of libraries.

Some Ruby applications have been running for a decade or longer and still serve important functions. Their dependencies may have been abandoned, or upgrading to a supported version may require substantial changes to the application itself. In some cases, a compatible upstream fix simply doesn't exist.

Socket Certified Patches provide another option. We develop targeted security fixes for the dependency versions developers already use, often by backporting fixes from newer releases. These changes address the vulnerable code while preserving the package version and minimizing changes to its existing behavior.

For applications that depend on abandoned libraries, this can extend the useful life of software that might otherwise need to be replaced or extensively rewritten. For actively maintained applications, patches allow teams to remediate known vulnerabilities without having to coordinate an immediate dependency upgrade. They can continue upgrading on their own schedule, with time to test compatibility and address breaking changes.

Security patches don't replace the benefits of ongoing dependency maintenance. Upstream releases still provide bug fixes, new features, and compatibility improvements. But a vulnerability doesn't necessarily have to dictate when an application undergoes a larger upgrade, and in some cases, a targeted patch may be the most practical long-term solution.

Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The vulnerability could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files through specially crafted uploads and, under certain configurations, potentially achieve remote code execution.

Our patch gives applications affected by the vulnerability an alternative to immediately upgrading Rails. Developers can apply the security fix to their existing dependency while planning and testing a broader upgrade separately.

The RubyGems coverage milestone extends this approach across the ecosystem's patchable critical vulnerabilities.

New Hosted and Vendored Delivery Options #

We've also expanded the ways developers can install remediated packages. Previously, Socket's patching workflow primarily involved modifying dependency files after installation. Our new hosted and vendored modes integrate directly with existing package management workflows.

Hosted mode lets developers install remediated gems through Bundler. The socket-patch CLI updates the lockfile to reference patched packages served through patch.socket.dev and, when necessary, adds source: settings to the affected gem declarations in Gemfile. The dependency versions remain unchanged, and Bundler installs the patched gems through its normal installation process.

Vendored mode stores the remediated packages directly in the application's repository under .socket/vendor/. Subsequent installations use those local packages without contacting Socket's infrastructure.

Vendored patches are yours to keep. They stay in your repository and go wherever your application goes, even if you stop using Socket.

Neither mode requires an installation hook or the Socket CLI on build machines. Once the dependency changes are committed, developers can continue installing their dependencies normally.

Both options preserve the existing dependency version. They also eliminate the need to run a separate patching step after every dependency installation. Developers can continue using the original in-place patching mode if they prefer that workflow.

These delivery options are particularly useful for organizations that need to control how dependencies enter their build environments or cannot introduce a new step into existing CI/CD pipelines.

We recently expanded support for Ruby gems containing native extensions as well. With socket-patch CLI 5.1.0, native extensions are rebuilt after patching, allowing us to remediate vulnerabilities in packages such as nokogiri, where a source-level change alone would not update the compiled code that applications execute.

Socket's dashboard provides instructions for obtaining a security patch for a critical Nokogiri vulnerability without upgrading the dependency.

Testing Security Fixes Against Existing Package Behavior #

A successful security patch needs to eliminate the vulnerability without introducing regressions elsewhere in the package.

Our validation process includes reproducing the vulnerability against the original dependency and verifying that the same exploit fails after patching. We also run regression tests, differential tests comparing the original and patched versions, compatibility checks against supported runtimes, and performance benchmarks.

We've expanded this testing to include downstream dependents, allowing us to exercise patches against software that actually relies on the affected library. This helps identify compatibility problems that may not be exposed by the package's own test suite.

Developers can inspect individual patches and their verification results on Socket, including test outcomes, exploit validation, performance measurements, and the code changes made.

These checks are especially important when backporting fixes into older library versions. A change that works correctly in the latest upstream release may depend on other changes introduced in the intervening years. Those differences must be accounted for before publishing a patch for an older release.

Some Vulnerabilities Require Different Remediation #

Our 100% critical-CVE coverage applies to vulnerabilities that can be safely patched. We generally consider three types of vulnerabilities unpatchable:

Malicious packages: The correct remediation is to remove the malicious dependency, not attempt to repair it.

Misattributed vulnerabilities: An advisory may identify a package that doesn't contain the vulnerable code because the vulnerability actually exists in another dependency. In those cases, we focus on fixing the package that contains the vulnerability.

Breaking changes: Some vulnerabilities are inherent to a package's design or public interface. Fixing them would require incompatible changes, potentially making dependency replacement or reachability analysis necessary.

We evaluate these cases individually and can make exceptions for particularly serious vulnerabilities where a breaking change may be warranted. Our current assessment is that roughly 95% of RubyGems CVEs are patchable under these criteria.

Free Critical CVE Patches Are Available Now #

All Socket patches for critical-severity CVEs are free, including for developers and organizations without a Socket account or paid subscription.

To get started, install the standalone socket-patch CLI:

curl -fsSL https://install.socket.dev/patch | sh

From a Ruby project's root directory, preview the available fixes without modifying any files:

socket-patch scan --dry-run

To apply patches in the default hosted mode and install the remediated gems:

socket-patch scan bundle install

Alternatively, use vendored mode to store the patched packages in the repository:

socket-patch scan --mode vendored bundle install

The CLI identifies available security fixes for the specific dependency versions in the project and reports which vulnerabilities they address. Patches for high-, medium-, and low-severity vulnerabilities are available through Socket's Enterprise plan.

For more information about patch validation, delivery options, and supported package managers, see our Certified Patches documentation and installation guide.

We're continuing to expand RubyGems coverage across all severity levels while improving our ability to generate, validate, and distribute security fixes. The free critical patches are available now.
