Title: AWS achieves Spain’s national Limited Distribution (Difusión Limitada) and NATO Restricted accreditation in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region
Context: With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe...
Full Text:
Spanish version »

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce that AWS has achieved Spain’s national Limited Distribution (“Difusión Limitada”) and NATO Restricted accreditation for the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation was granted by the Spanish Delegated Authority for the Security of Classified Information, the Secretary of State Director of Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) and the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) are working bodies of the CNI, which audited AWS against the CCN-STIC-004 policy and the applicable ONS requirements.

With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. In Spain, this was a double achievement: AWS first met the national Difusión Limitada requirements and then, in addition to this national methodology, achieved the NATO Restricted accreditation by incorporating the requirements of NATO Directive 32. This demonstrates our continued commitment to helping the public sector, defense, and NATO-affiliated customers run sensitive workloads in the cloud while meeting the highest applicable national and international security requirements.

What this covers

The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation by the CNI confirms that the AWS system in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region meets the procedural and security requirements for handling classified information up to the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted level.

What is Spain’s classified information framework?

Spain’s framework for protecting national classified information is administered by the ONS and the CCN, under the CNI. In 2026, Spain established the framework that enables handling of Difusión Limitada information in the commercial public cloud, under which this accreditation was granted. The accreditation builds on the AWS ENS High certification and the CCN’s IT Product and Service Catalogue (CPSTIC) qualifications. The scope of the accreditation covers the CPSTIC-qualified services and all AWS services certified under ENS High (see the list of AWS services in scope for ENS High). Only the services within this scope that are qualified or certified under the CCN framework (CPSTIC and ENS High) and run in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region can be used for Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted workloads.

What is NATO Restricted?

NATO Directive 32 establishes the security requirements for handling NATO Restricted information in public cloud, and is the directive referenced by Spain’s CCN-STIC-004 policy.

Why this matters to customers

Public sector and defense organizations in Spain can use the AWS Europe (Spain) Region for national Difusión Limitada classified workloads and for NATO Restricted workloads. Under the shared responsibility model, customers that want to process classified information in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region engage the CCN and ONS to accredit their own systems, building on the AWS accreditation.

How to get started

National security and defense customers may build on the AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) to design a cloud architecture for their sensitive workloads. Accreditation documentation is available to eligible customers through AWS Artifact. Customers can also work with their AWS account teams to understand how the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation, and TSE-SE apply to their use cases.

To learn more about AWS compliance in Spain, see the AWS ENS compliance page and the AWS Compliance Programs page.

For more details see AWS NATO Restricted and Difusión Limitada for AWS Europe (Spain) Region web page

Spanish version

AWS obtiene la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted en la Región AWS Europa (España)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido la acreditación nacional de España “Difusión Limitada” y la acreditación NATO Restricted para la Región AWS Europa (España). La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted ha sido concedida por la Autoridad Delegada para la Seguridad de la Información Clasificada de España, la Secretaria de Estado Directora del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). El Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN), y la Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS), son órganos de trabajo del CNI, que auditaron a AWS conforme a la política CCN-STIC-004 y a los requisitos aplicables de la ONS.

Con este hito, AWS se convierte en el primer proveedor cloud acreditado en el nivel NATO Restricted, y en el primero acreditado para Difusión Limitada en la Región AWS Europa (España). En España ha sido un doble logro: AWS cumplió primero los requisitos nacionales de Difusión Limitada y, sobre esta metodología nacional, obtuvo la acreditación NATO Restricted incorporando los requisitos de la Directiva 32 de la OTAN. Esto demuestra nuestro compromiso continuo de ayudar al sector público, a la defensa y a los clientes vinculados a la OTAN a ejecutar cargas de trabajo sensibles en la nube cumpliendo los requisitos de seguridad nacionales e internacionales más exigentes aplicables.

Qué abarca

La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted del CNI confirma que el sistema de AWS en la Región AWS Europa (España) cumple los requisitos procedimentales y de seguridad para tratar información clasificada hasta el nivel Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted.

¿Cuál es el marco español de información clasificada?

El marco español de protección de la información clasificada nacional lo administran la ONS y el CCN, bajo el CNI. En 2026, España estableció el marco que permite tratar información Difusión Limitada en la nube pública comercial, en virtud del cual se ha concedido esta acreditación. La acreditación se basa en la certificación ENS categoría Alta de AWS y en las cualificaciones del Catálogo de Productos y Servicios de Seguridad TIC (CPSTIC) del CCN. El alcance de la acreditación incluye los servicios cualificados en CPSTIC y todos los servicios de AWS certificados en el ENS categoría Alta (consulte la lista de servicios de AWS en el alcance del ENS categoría Alta). Solo pueden utilizarse para cargas de trabajo Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted los servicios de este alcance cualificados o certificados en el marco del CCN (CPSTIC y ENS categoría Alta) que se ejecuten en la Región AWS Europa (España).

¿Qué es NATO Restricted?

La Directiva 32 de la OTAN establece los requisitos de seguridad para tratar información NATO Restricted en la nube pública, y es la directiva a la que hace referencia la política española CCN-STIC-004.

Por qué es importante para los clientes

Las organizaciones del sector público y de defensa en España pueden utilizar la Región AWS Europa (España) para cargas de trabajo clasificadas nacionales Difusión Limitada, así como para cargas de trabajo NATO Restricted. Conforme al modelo de responsabilidad compartida, los clientes que quieran tratar información clasificada en la Región AWS Europa (España) deben dirigirse al CCN y a la ONS para acreditar sus propios sistemas, apoyándose en la acreditación de AWS.

Cómo empezar

Los clientes de seguridad nacional y defensa pueden apoyarse en AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) para diseñar una arquitectura cloud para sus cargas de trabajo sensibles. La documentación de la acreditación está disponible para los clientes elegibles a través de AWS Artifact. Los clientes también pueden trabajar con sus equipos de cuenta de AWS para entender cómo se aplican a sus casos de uso la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted y TSE-SE.

Para más información sobre el cumplimiento de AWS en España, consulte la página de cumplimiento ENS de AWS y la página de Programas de cumplimiento de AWS.

Para más detalles, consulte la página web de AWS sobre NATO Restricted y Difusión Limitada para la Región AWS Europa (España)

In this article

A bot tested an AWS key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published it

Attackers used up about $60 in prepaid OpenAI and Anthropic credit

If you accidentally publish a key, revoke it and check your account for unexpected usage and charges

Eight seconds is barely enough time to notice a mistake, let alone fix it.

But researchers at Stony Brook University found that it was enough time for a bot to test a cloud access key they’d deliberately left inside a publicly available software package. The fastest observed use came just 7.86 seconds after publication.

You don’t need a company cloud account to have a key worth stealing. If you’ve created an API key for an AI service and used it in an app or script, someone who gets hold of it can run up charges on your account. OpenAI warns that they could also use up your quote and interrupt your service.

To see who was collecting those secrets, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis set up honeypots, or decoys that let researchers monitor what happens when someone takes the bait. Over four months, they published 300 honeypot images across eight public registries. The bait included working access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each key was tied to monitoring, so any use would show up in the provider’s logs.

The researchers didn’t advertise the images anywhere, but they were still downloaded tens of thousands of times.

Most of the early activity looked like bots checking whether the keys worked. Nearly every bot that tested an AWS key began with GetCallerIdentity, essentially a “who am I?” request that tells an attacker whether a key is live. About half the IP addresses researchers saw scanning for AWS keys stopped after that initial check. Only around 6% went on to sustained use of account resources.

A key that passes that check can still be sold on or used later. In the AI-service tests, the OpenAI keys sat quiet for weeks before someone used one to burn through the remaining balance in under 24 hours. The researchers offered an explanation:

“We speculate that the wait phase reflects validated keys being resold and held idle until a buyer eventually uses them.”

The researchers loaded about $60 in total onto their OpenAI and Anthropic accounts, and attackers used up all of it.

How to stay safe

The researchers published honeypot container images on Docker Hub and seven other registries, then shared their findings with Docker. According to the paper, Docker acknowledged the disclosure, and its security team was reviewing the findings.

The number of probing bots and their speed is something developers should worry about. If you use cloud or AI services, a few precautions can help keep your keys safe:

Keep secrets out of what you share. Don’t put keys in code, public repositories, or container images.

Scan before you publish. A bot can find an exposed key within seconds, so a check after publication is too late. The researchers also recommend that registries scan images as they’re uploaded.

Limit what each key can do. In the second round of tests, every OpenAI and Anthropic key that attackers used to burn through credits had unrestricted permissions. No restricted key was used that way. The scanners appear to check permissions first, so a narrowly scoped key gives them less to work with. A narrowly scoped key can only perform specific actions or access particular resources.

Prefer short-lived credentials. AWS recommends using temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys wherever possible.

Set spending limits and alerts. Check whether your provider’s budget setting just sends an alert or sets a hard limit on what you can spend.

If you’ve already published a key, treat it as compromised, even if it was public for only a minute. Revoke it and replace it. Then review account activity and charges.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
Context: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an...
Full Text: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes. It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine. “What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.” Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one. Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET. 'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking' OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work. “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.” That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing. The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t). After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works. The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems. “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.” 'No blocklist would have helped' In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit. It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then. The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.” While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein. “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.” Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds. “Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

Title: Iran-Aligned Volant Manticore Uses IPFS-Based KuboShell Backdoor in Espionage Campaigns
Context: The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in...
Full Text:
A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia.

A Windows backdoor, KuboShell, uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network.

"On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained.

"KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token."

Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server.

It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process -

PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory

PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor

JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands

It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown.

"We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said.

The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe."

"Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention."

"If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

Title: New Inception Extortion Brand Tied to SSO Vishing Campaign
Context: ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters
Full Text:
Okta and ReversingLabs have linked a new data-extortion brand called Inception to a voice phishing campaign that targeted single sign-on (SSO) credentials and used stolen access to take data.

Okta Threat Intelligence researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels and ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons detailed the activity in separate reports published November 23.

Okta's report focused on the operators behind the campaign, while ReversingLabs' analysis mapped the infrastructure that tied it to Inception.

A Likely Rebrand After ShinyHunters Arrests

Okta tracked the operators as O-UNC-053, a cluster at work since March 2026. It had previously associated the group with the ShinyHunters data leak site, where companies it had gone after were listed from March to September.

Okta said it did not know precisely how the two were connected, though the link "may have involved an agreement" between the cluster and the site's operators.

After two people allegedly tied to ShinyHunters were arrested in September, the gang's leak site went offline, and Okta saw no O-UNC-053 targets published on any leak site until Inception appeared on November 16. Okta found that targets appearing on Inception had been preceded by O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.

Okta said the cluster had "very likely changed their brand affiliation" but could not determine with high confidence whether O-UNC-053 operated the Inception data leak site itself or partnered with another extortion group.

The company was also unable to validate whether the published data was authentic. ReversingLabs counted seven claimed victims by November 21, which it treated as unverified claims.

Read more on ShinyHunters: Net Closes Around ShinyHunters with Another FBI Arrest

How the Vishing Campaign Works

The attacks relied on vishing, with callers posing as support staff and pressuring employees to reset passwords through fake sign-in pages. The campaign captured usernames and passwords before seeking additional multifactor authentication (MFA) factors, including one-time codes or push approvals.

ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters. It confirmed the phishing kit itself on 21 domains and attributed 41 more to the operation at a high confidence level and four at a medium level. Most mimicked Okta sign-in pages, though the kit adapted to other identity providers.

Okta noted that the kit could not get past phishing-resistant authentication. The two companies' advice included passkeys or FIDO2 security keys, checks on a caller's identity before help desks reset passwords or MFA and limiting sensitive applications to managed devices.

ReversingLabs also advised checking DNS, proxy and identity logs going back to October 21 for signs of the campaign.

Title: How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data
Signal blocks AI assistants from snooping on your encrypted messages
Context: Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to...
Full Text:
Signal, the privacy-focused encrypted messaging app, has started blocking Apple and Google's AI assistants from snooping on users' private conversations.

Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to their calendar. They may be happy for Onscreen Awareness for Apple's Siri and Google's Gemini Intelligence to answer questions and do tasks for them.

But it's far from welcome when the screen shows an encrypted conversation that was supposed to be private.

Once a message has been captured, it could end up in a locally-stored database or uploaded to a remote server - potentially putting everyone in the chat at risk.

Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post that unless proper safeguards were in place, putting AI agents into operating systems was "an existential threat to privacy at the application layer."

If you are running iOS 27 on your iPhone, Signal now blocks screenshots inside the app - which means Siri cannot read message content from the screen. A new setting called "Block Siri AI" allows users to toggle the feature on or off.

Meanwhile, on Android, Signal attempts to look where it can for an AI assistant trying to read the screen and when it spots one, automatically turns on its existing "Screen security" setting.

There are repercussions, of course, for anyone on iOS who wants to sometimes take screenshots of their own conversations, perhaps for innocent reasons. You can switch the protection off, but - as Signal warns - doing that might expose your chats to AI agents.

Furthermore, Signal admits that its efforts do not prevent every method an AI agent might use to try to read messages being sent via the app.

There is also no protection yet for Mac users, because Signal says it cannot reliably block the taking of screenshots on macOS. For that reason, the best advice if you are using the Signal desktop app on your Mac is to add it to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri.

And, of course, you need to bear in mind that there are also third-party AI agents, such as Meta's Muse, which can access sensitive data through accessibility permissions that users are encouraged to grant during setup.

Signal has called on Microsoft, Apple, and Google to to give developers an easy, well-documented way to opt their apps out of sharing data with AI agents, and to publish better technical details of how their AI features access and process data.

It is worth bearing in mind that this issue is not unique to Signal - any app that handles sensitive information faces the same problem. The difference is that Signal is publicly trying to do something about it.

As Whittaker says, "Signal is the canary in the coal mine."

Title: Impact of AI on CVEs : PROTECTION STRATEGIES
Context: By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed...
Full Text:
For enterprise software development operations, AI now handles work that was once too hard or too costly to justify, from reverse engineering and debugging to building fuzzing harnesses. Recent high profile security incidents shows how far this goes:

AI agents escaping ChatGPT sandboxes through zero-day logic flaws

Claude models breaking out of test environments while surfacing critical zero-days.

Independent researchers using LLMs to find dozens of vulnerabilities in heavily audited codebases.

Higher Volume and Lower Quality CVEs

In the first blog of this series, we explained how AI is a multiplier for security research experts, resulting in faster bug discovery and PoC development, which leaves more time for deep architectural analysis. For novices, however, it means the ability to create a large volume of low-quality CVEs that increase response time and amplify triage noise.

Published CVEs are accelerating sharply reaching 75,000 in just the first nine months of 2026

Perhaps a more serious consequence of vulnerability research with AI is “democratization” of nation state capabilities. It used to take the resources of a nation state to launch sophisticated hacks such as 0-click smartphone attacks and unauthenticated RCEs (Remote Code Execution) on enterprise servers. Using AI, these and other attacks can be launched by smaller groups such as ransomware gangs and even individual malicious actors.

Real World Evidence

This year alone, we have had more than 10+ Linux LPE (Local Privilege Escalation) vulnerabilities and have also seen multiple RCEs in popular open-source packages that power the internet, such as PHP, Chrome and Redis.

Confirmed in-the-wild exploits across major open-source projects from 2023 to October 2026

The trajectory is clear: CISOs and security teams should prepare themselves for disclosure of high severity vulnerabilities in well-known industry components by professional and amateur security researchers on a monthly basis.

Example: JFrog’s Zero-Click Chain

Exploiting a malformed image tile to achieve zero-click remote code execution

To demonstrate how AI compresses weeks of advanced exploit development into a matter of hours, our research team built a full zero-click attack chain targeting everyday desktop software. By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed image file into complete root-level system takeover without a single click from the user.

Libheif – Malicious images as an infection vector

The danger of parser vulnerabilities are well documented, , especially those that parse untrusted input sent from an attacker without user interaction. Vulnerabilities like these have been used extensively by nation-states and PSOAs (private-sector offensive actors), as well as cybercriminals, to deploy malware on systems with minimal, and in some cases, no human interaction whatsoever.

CVE-2026-47178 – Heap out-of-bounds write to popping calc

Feeling inspired by how nation-state-grade spyware infects devices, often using format parsing as the initial access vector, we started researching libheif, which is a library implementing the parsing of the HEIF image format.

Exploit flow from a malformed image tile to heap corruption and control-flow hijack

CVE-2026-47178 is a heap out-of-bounds write in the UNCI decoder in libheif that allows an attacker to overwrite virtual function pointers on the heap, thus leading to remote code execution. Leveraging AI, we discovered the vulnerability within 2 hours, as opposed to the weeks of research it would take a professional using conventional methods.

It took us another 5 hours to turn it into a reliable exploit against Debian’s File Explorer, without user interaction.

Researching & Confirming our Findings

The research environment was quite straightforward: We compiled heif-dec, the library-bundled C++ binary for parsing HEIF images using libheif with AddressSanitizer, and instructed the AI to find a heap out-of-bounds write using static analysis only and confirm its hypothesis dynamically via a crash under ASAN.

AddressSanitizer crash report confirming a heap-buffer-overflow during image decoding

The ASAN essentially acts as a truth indicator (oracle). This result tells us immediately that the LLM did not hallucinate its finding, and the finding is an actionable, real vulnerability.

We may now proceed to developing the actual exploit:

Debugger output showing a crash due to an overwritten vtable pointer from a virtual function call

Through specific heap manipulation, a technique known as heap feng shui, we successfully overwrote a virtual function pointer, a C++ object data structure, granting us direct control over the instruction pointer and completing another critical milestone. The classic convention is to set the instruction pointer to 0x41414141, to demonstrate instruction pointer control.

The final stage is to turn our control flow hijack into code execution. By default the stack is non executable, so we must utilize gadgets, or useful pieces of code that already exist in the executable’s memory space, for our needs.

Since our target was the gnome file explorer, nautilus, we decided to take a look as to how it decodes these heif images, and noticed that it uses a binary called `libheif-thumbnailer`, a binary that’s similar to libheif-dec, which uses the libheif library, alongside other libraries.

The library that’s particularly important this time is libdav1d, which is another codec. The library provided a useful gadget, akin to a one_gadget, that allows us to run `system()` with our own string specified in the `rdi` register, which is just perfect.

Now, we can run any code that we want, but not as root, and that’s the next stage.

DirtyClone – Elevating Linux LPE privileges

Now that we have remote code execution, we can begin elevating our privileges. We previously disclosed an LPE in the Linux kernel as a result of an incomplete patch of the dirtyfrag vulnerability. We won’t go in depth into the details of how the exploit works, but you can more info our previous blog post.

Exploit chain turning a corrupted vtable pointer into arbitrary code execution

The following is a summary of the attack scenario:

An attacker, using a delivery mechanism such as a messaging app (different delivery mechanism than what we outlined here), or even just downloading the file unwittingly and just navigating to the directory where the file is stored via file manager, will cause remote code execution as root.

JFrog Advanced Security’s Contextual Analysis goes beyond version matching. It examines source code, binaries, configurations, and dependency paths to decide whether the vulnerable conditions are actually present, and only then reports a CVE as Applicable.

Title: Address AI Agent Risks or Face Action, FCA Warns Financial Firms
Context: The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action
Full Text:
The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said that AI agents are being widely deployed in the financial services sector to improve productivity and convenience to customers.

“But these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data,” the regulator noted.

Banks now using these AI agents to initiate transactions, move money and make investment decisions.

Without appropriate safeguards in place, such as strict access controls, agents have been observed taking dangerous actions such as gaining access to sensitive systems and data, even in pursuit of legitimate aims.

The FCA guidance, published on November 24, said that senior managers responsible for AI models deployed in a specific area of the business need to take “reasonable steps” to understand the risks arising from AI. This includes providing effective oversight and ensuring governance controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks.

Regulated financial organizations should consider any liabilities from accepting agent instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent.

They should also help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

Responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with senior managers and the organization as a whole, whether the firm deploys agentic AI themselves or relies on a third-party provider, the FCA emphasized.

Read now: Bank of England, FCA and Treasury Raise Alarm Over Frontier AI

“We expect you to demonstrate that you understand the systems you use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations,” the authority wrote.

“We will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements,” it continued.

Failure to adhere to existing regulatory requirements, including data protection laws, will see the FCA use its powers to sanction non-compliant organizations. These powers include imposing financial penalties, prohibiting individuals from carrying out regulated activities, public censure and prosecution.

The FCA added that it welcomes early engagement from those deploying agentic AI in their products and systems, and that it offers support services including testing whether these tools meet regulatory requirements.

Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication.

The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir").

"A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today.

The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam, XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw.

Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5).

The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5).

The issues have been addressed in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300

VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890.

While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

Title: The Microsoft Outage Brought a Surge of Phishing Email
Context: 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend)
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R, Jeewan Singh Jalal

When a service you rely on goes down, you look for answers, and attackers know it. After the Microsoft outage on Nov. 12, KnowBe4 Threat Lab observed a sharp rise in outage-related email.

Read on for what we found, what the lures looked like, and how to protect your organization.

Key Findings

The surge peaked on the second day of the outage. On Nov. 13, outage-related phishing emails reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to Nov. 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend).

The lures were built to look like Microsoft. The lures we reviewed used a held-messages notice, a fake security check, an Exchange service notice, and a Teams notification.

One lure cited Microsoft's real incident number. A correct incident number does not make an email genuine.

The goal appears to be sign-in access. All four emails appear designed to steal sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

What Happened in the Microsoft Outage?

On Thursday, Nov. 12, a global outage hit the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services. According to Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report for incident MO1550821, dated Nov. 15, the incident ran from Nov. 12, 2026 to Nov. 13, 2026. It lasted nearly 24 hours and reached users around the world. Microsoft listed 14 affected services, including Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Copilot.

Exchange Online took the biggest hit. Most users could not reach their mailboxes, and email delivery was delayed for many. Microsoft said the outage came from a chain of events, not a single failure:

A hidden defect. A software fix deployed to the gateway servers in July contained a flaw that caused servers to stop responding under certain loads. It ran for more than three months without problems.

More load, less capacity. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams traffic moved to the gateway that also supports Exchange Online. At the same time, nearly 14% of server capacity was out of service for an unrelated reason.

A cascade. Servers that failed pushed traffic onto fewer healthy servers, which then failed too. At its lowest point, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint could move away from the gateway and partly recovered sooner. Exchange Online could not, so email stayed disrupted. Recovery took longer because servers that returned to service were overwhelmed again by waiting traffic. Microsoft also extended the email delivery window so delayed messages were not returned as undeliverable. The report is preliminary, and a final report will follow.

How Big Was the Surge in Outage-Themed Phishing Emails?

Phishing activity followed the outage. The peak came on the second day, Nov. 13, when outage-related email reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports.

What Did the Outage Lures Look Like?

We reviewed sender and subject patterns across all matched emails, and the message body of four examples. The first two use the subject "Outage -" plus a random string. The other two use different subjects.

Lure

What it says

What it wants

Held messages

Copies a Microsoft notice. Cites Microsoft's real incident number for the Nov. 12 outage, lists the affected services, and says four messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours.

A click on "Restore Messages."

Fake security check

Claims to be from a support desk and says "1 security issue found on your account."

A click on "Take Action," the only button in the message.

Exchange service notice

Styled as Microsoft Support, with the subject "Action Required: Microsoft Exchange Service Interruption" and a date. Refers to "our recent server outage" and asks you to update your email to avoid further disruption.

A click on "Update Email Now," pushed by a red "ACTION REQUIRED NOW!" banner.

Teams notification

Looks like a Microsoft Planner task notification assigning you a document to review. The subject is "Due To Microsoft Error Early- Access Doc" plus a code. It presents itself as a workaround for the Microsoft error, with an access code to "enter when prompted" that expires in 30 minutes.

A click on "Open in browser" or "Open in Teams," then entering the code.

This lure cites Microsoft's real incident number and warns that held messages will be deleted within 24 hours. The deadline and the "Restore Messages" button are meant to push a quick click.

This lure states that it comes from a "support desk" rather than Microsoft and claims "1 security issue found on your account." It has a single button, "Take Action," so there is only one place to click.

The Exchange notice has odd wording, such as "We've detect a refresh issue," which is a sign it is not genuine.

This lure imitates a Planner task notification and offers a "workaround" for the Microsoft error.

Why Do These Lures Work?

They match what people expect during an outage.

The failure was real. Mail delivery did fail, so a warning about held messages sounds plausible.

A security check feels natural. Users are already checking their accounts.

A Teams notice sounds like a sensible workaround. Email is down, so another route-in seems reasonable.

All four emails appear designed to steal your sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

How Can You Stay Vigilant?

Outages make people more willing to click. Build these habits before the next one:

Go to the source. Check Microsoft's official service status page or your IT team's usual channel. Do not rely on a link in an email. A real incident number can appear in a fake notice, so a correct number does not prove an email is genuine.

Treat sign-in prompts and deadlines with care. A request to "restore messages" or log in to "restore access" is more believable when services are failing. Never enter a sign-in code from an email or a Teams notice unless you started that sign-in yourself. Open the service directly instead.

Verify new contact details. Confirm any change in contact details sent during an outage with a contact you already know.

Look for odd subjects and wording. Random strings, typos, urgent red warnings, and unfamiliar senders are all signs to pause.

Question workarounds. Be wary of any message that offers another way in while Microsoft is down, such as a task, a document, or a Teams link. Confirm it with your IT team.

Report, don't click. If an email looks wrong, use your report button instead of clicking. Your security team can then spot the attack early and act on it.

Security teams should also watch for newly seen domains that send large volumes in a short time.

How Does KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security Help?

You cannot stop an outage. You can limit what attackers gain from one.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security), and PhishER Plus (incident response).

In this event, Defend detected outage-themed phishing emails as threats. PhishER helps your team act on what users report: it classifies reported messages, gives reporters instant feedback, and lets you remediate threats across every inbox with one click.

Training closes the gap. Security Awareness Training and Real-Time Coaching help your users spot urgent, outage-themed lures before they click.

Be Ready Before the Next Outage

Outages end. The habits you build for them endure. Start by asking your team one question today: where would you check first if email went down?

Title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap
Context: Attackers have already found a way around it
Full Text:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

In this article

Microsoft plans to bring eight Windows security checks together in 2027

Windows baseline protection will flag missing safeguards and let you turn some on with one click

Apps could use the result to warn you, limit features, or block access

Microsoft announced plans to introduce Windows baseline protection, a feature that brings eight existing safeguards together into a single, verifiable security status.

With the feature expected to become generally available in 2027, Microsoft wants to make a familiar Windows security problem less confusing. Your PC has a collection of built-in protections, but working out which ones are enabled and what to do when they aren’t can take some digging.

Windows baseline protection will show you what’s missing and help you fix it. It will also give software developers a simpler way to check whether your computer meets their requirements and decide whether to let an app run at all.

On the positive side, that could make security easier to manage. But it could also mean more encounters with software that says your PC isn’t secure enough to use it.

The protections already exist in Windows. What’s new is the way Windows evaluates them together and shares the result. For people using personal or unmanaged PCs, the most immediately useful change may be the explanation that comes with the result.

Microsoft says the new baseline protection page in Windows Settings will show which protections are missing.

Preview of Windows baseline protection in Settings (image courtesy of Microsoft)

Where possible, a single button will enable the missing protections and restart the computer. If you need to change your PC’s firmware settings, for example to enable Secure Boot or the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Windows will provide guidance.

The first version checks these eight requirements:

Security processor: Dedicated hardware, such as a TPM, that helps protect sensitive information.

Secure Boot: Protection against malicious software loading during startup.

Virtualization-based security: Hardware-assisted isolation that helps protect critical processes.

Memory integrity: Protection against malicious code running in protected parts of Windows.

Signed drivers only: A requirement that drivers have digital signatures.

Windows-certified drivers: A requirement that drivers meet Windows hardware signing requirements.

Kernel debugger protection: Restrictions that help prevent debugging tools from bypassing Windows security protections.

Vulnerable driver protection: Protection against known vulnerable drivers that could weaken the system’s security.

An application that wants to check a computer’s security configuration can use Windows’ baseline protection signal instead of maintaining its own collection of checks.

The intended uses are straightforward. An exam service might want to verify a student’s device before a test. A game might check protections relevant to anti-cheat measures. An organization might require a device to meet its security requirements before granting access.

Main takeaways

Windows baseline protection brings existing safeguards together into a common, hardware-backed security assessment and helps users enable any missing protections. That could make Windows security less confusing, but it also gives software vendors a simpler way to warn users, restrict features, or deny access when a computer falls short.

The developer decides what happens next. Will they require the entire baseline, or only the protections their application actually needs?

Windows baseline protection and security software such as Malwarebytes address different parts of the problem. Microsoft’s checks establish whether a set of underlying Windows safeguards is enabled. Malwarebytes Premium Plus adds protection against threats such as malware, ransomware, exploits, and malicious websites, along with browser protection and a VPN. Neither replaces the other: Installing security software does not switch on a missing Windows safeguard, and passing Microsoft’s checklist is not a guarantee that your PC is free of malware.

The feature is still in preview, and Microsoft says feedback will shape it before general availability.

A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

What to patch

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

Title: Introducing CORNERSTONE: delivering external services for the NCSC
Context: We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and...
Full Text:
The NCSC's existing services have developed strong standards, trusted market relationships and significant reach. But as demand grows, we need to consider how these services can be delivered in ways that are scalable, sustainable, and responsive to the UK’s changing needs.

As a result, the NCSC is exploring how it can modernise the way its external services are designed, delivered and developed. We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and make better use of the capabilities that exist across the cyber security industry.

CORNERSTONE is a multi-year project to develop a more scalable relationship between the NCSC and industry, with each focusing on where it can add most value. Our ambition for CORNERSTONE is not simply to outsource services currently run by the NCSC; we want to make our services more impactful, accessible and adaptable. This will allow the NCSC to focus on those areas where it brings unique insight as the national technical authority for cyber security.

Title: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks
Context: We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response
Full Text:
The NCSC believes the adoption of AI-enabled cyber can close the gap between attackers and defenders. We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response. However, it will take time for defensive AI-driven programmes to mature, so organisations can’t sit back and wait for agentic defence to protect them. AI-enabled cyber defence is not the sole answer to agentic attacks; the foundations of cyber security and basic cyber hygiene remain the priority.

As we stated in the NCSC’s 2026 ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ Annual Review, AI does not make established cyber security controls obsolete. In fact building strong foundations has never mattered more. AI is making weaknesses easier to find and faster to exploit; a forgotten key or an unprotected API which might once have gone unnoticed for years can be found in minutes.

Nearly everything the NCSC has seen can be prevented by implementing cyber security best practice, the application of modern cyber security approaches like zero trust, and by the diligent application of technical controls in line with your organisation's technologies and processes. For organisations seeking a structured approach:

zero trust principles can help protect against agentic attacks; explicitly verify identity, ensure least privilege everywhere, and deploy controls as if attackers are already inside your network

the Cyber Assessment Framework helps organisations responsible for essential services or critical functions assess and improve their cyber resilience

the NCSC’s Cyber Essentials sets out the minimum technical controls for organisations, as recommended by the government

Although they may not always be applied in the right place, the controls that mitigate the threat from agentic offensive frameworks will already be familiar to many organisations. Today's frameworks may be replaced by quieter, more capable ones, and tools will change. But the cyber security fundamentals won't.

This is your chance to get ahead of the threat. Consider how your organisation would answer the questions above, and make sure your answers hold up against an attacker that never needs a break and never gets tired of asking.

Kris B, Incident Handler, Incident Management

Ellen T, Lead Data Scientist, Vulnerability Management Team

David Chismon, CTO for Architecture

Title: OpenAI and Cisco Release Open-Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
Context: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install...
Full Text:
OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install permanent patches.

In a November 23 announcement, OpenAI said that Shirudo could guard live systems without forcing a restart.

Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, commented, "Finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow."

How the Shields Work

Shirudo is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which allows vetted mini-programs run inside the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system.

Each shield was designed to target only the one operation an exploit needed, leaving normal requests untouched, and operators could trial a proposed protection before approving it. OpenAI said shutting off a risky function entirely could cause an outage, because the same function could serve both attackers and legitimate users.

Shields carried a cryptographic signature that was verified before it could load. A Trusted Platform Module (TPM), a hardware security chip, kept a log of every protection added or removed, giving teams evidence of what had been active on a system.

Isovalent, a Cisco-owned company, described Shirudo as a rewrite of Tetragon, the open-source eBPF security platform it released in 2022. It said Tetragon already powered Live Protect, which Cisco uses to mitigate flaws in its own products.

Read more on Linux flaws: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public

Java4Shell Test and Early Limits

In a single controlled test, a shield written by OpenAI's Codex inserted validation into Java's Base64 decoding routine.

Attached to an Elasticsearch instance that was already running, it stopped a Java4Shell exploit attempt while the application stayed online. Isovalent said the mitigation "appears to be effective" and would protect affected applications until OpenJDK was patched.

The result came from a test designed and run by the project builders rather than an independent evaluation.

Isovalent engineer John Fastabend said at a Linux kernel summit in 2026 that his team often came across vulnerabilities with no suitable point in the kernel where a shield could attach, LWN reported.

Shirudo's GitHub repository described the project as pre-release, with production use requiring a Linux kernel carrying Shirudo's kernel patches and a TPM 2.0 chip.

OpenAI said it hoped eventually to release shields that had already been tested at the same time flaws were disclosed. It added that the two companies were designing Shirudo so AI agents could investigate flaws, write shields and check that they worked and called automatically generated least-privilege policies a longer-term aim.

Title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
