Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised.

Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer.

The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.”

The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added.

Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added.

The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment.

Norway tells customers to assume exposure

In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management.

“Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian.

It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway.

“Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.”

In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors.

Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20, the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised.

NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation.

“When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment.

Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw.

Urgent need to rotate credentials

Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added.

In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog, Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management.

The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies.

Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM.

“Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report.

NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets.

The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said.

Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough.

“If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post.

His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

Title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
Context: " The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22
Full Text: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

In this article

Researchers traced stolen prompts to three AI hosting providers

Some stolen prompts were marked “zero data retention”

Keep sensitive data out of prompts and check which providers your AI routing service can send them to

Attackers have been reading queries sent indirectly to online AI services. They’ve scoured these queries (also known as “prompts”) for sensitive data, in some cases trying out stolen access keys within hours.

Not everyone works directly with the likes of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. Plenty of people use other AI services, including hosting companies that run open-source AI models.

There are also third-party services that accept your prompts and then send them on to the most appropriate AI services. These services, known as routers, give you access to different models. Perhaps you prefer one for designing something for your 3D printer and another for coding. On some marketplaces, the router sends your AI prompt to whichever provider offers the lowest price for the model you want. The advantage to you is that you only have to deal with one company but get access to lots of different AI services.

Many of these hosting providers and routing services will tell you that they don’t retain any of your data. In reality, things are far less secure than you might think. Security company Dragos tested several AI services from July to November, sending them nearly 2 million AI prompts in total.

Those prompts were littered with “canary tokens“—unique URLs and login credentials that wouldn’t be found anywhere else on the internet. If someone visited a URL or tried to use a credential, the researchers could trace it back to the prompt it came from. That’s exactly what happened.

Dragos Chief Research Officer HD Moore found “widespread failures to protect customer data” as prompts given to these routing services cropped up in different places online.

According to the Dragos blog, at least three hosting providers were robbed of their prompts, and none of them knew about it until the security company tipped them off. In the largest breach, attackers stole around 200 access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon’s cloud service. The keys belonged to the researchers, who had tied them to empty AWS accounts.

Dragos highlights three ways that canary tokens get leaked. In the first, attackers compromised the hosting provider that was running the AI service. These tokens were sometimes stolen even when the service provider rejected the prompt that contained them, the researchers added. That meant the attacker was stealing the keys at the initial access point, rather than delving into the internals of the AI service.

Even if a service did its best not to retain prompt data, that’s not much comfort if the prompts are stolen before it can discard them. Moore said:

“…some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR [zero data retention]. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.”

The second technique saw attackers accessing prompts from routing services by advertising AI models at very low prices. That would cause the router to send them customer prompts. The attackers could then just turn on logging and see the prompts as they came through.

The problem here is that while prompts are encrypted in transit, they’re decrypted at every hop in the chain. Those hops are the different routing services, along with the hosting companies that run their services. Every time someone else sees your prompt, it’s another opportunity for it to be compromised.

Sometimes, the AI services that run the models extract secrets from the prompts that they are sent. One Chinese AI lab opened secret URLs from over half of the prompts that the researchers sent to its models. That included roughly two-thirds of requests marked “no data collection” or ZDR.

The lab also opened links from prompts sent to US hosting providers that were reselling its AI services. Someone who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the US could still have their prompt sent overseas.

Dragos didn’t name the Chinese lab in its blog post. But an email to customers from AI routing company OpenRouter published on X on November 21 said that unique test URLs sent to Chinese AI model provider MiniMax had been harvested.

On November 24, MiniMax acknowledged its security software had logged and opened URLs from prompts forwarded by OpenRouter and other providers. MiniMax said the software didn’t retain full conversations, and it has since disabled the process for the affected traffic and deleted the logged URLs.

OpenRouter said the research found no sign of a breach of its own systems. It removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility, some as a precaution.

What you can do

What does all this mean to you as an AI user? If you’re talking directly to services like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT, our usual advice applies. Be careful about what you tell them, especially if you’re pasting in something that contains passwords or personal information.

However, if you’re a company or an AI enthusiast using routing services or resellers for a better deal, or dealing with a hosting provider running an open-weight model, Dragos has some specific advice for you:

Host your own AI. Running your own AI locally keeps prompts on your own hardware, although a powerful model can require expensive equipment.

Go directly to the model provider. Going directly to the model provider means fewer companies handle your prompts. Check its privacy policy to see how it handles your data.

Choose who gets your prompts. If you’re going to use an AI routing service, hand-pick the providers you’ll let it send your prompts to.

Filter your secrets. Some providers can automatically filter out recognizable credentials, such as access keys, if you turn that setting on.

Use canary tokens yourself. Putting a unique test link or decoy credential into a prompt can alert you if someone uses it later.

Your name, address, and phone number may already be for sale.

Data brokers collect and sell your personal details to anyone willing to pay. Malwarebytes Personal Data Remover finds them and gets your information removed, then keeps watch so it stays that way.

Title: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents
Context: However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account...
Full Text:
More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

“Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security company UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more important than ever to attackers.

The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.

The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

Full Text:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

Subscription keys

Tokens used to call direct management APIs

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

Title: LaLiga Says Football Fans’ Personal Data Stolen
Context: The data theft was stopped and the attacker blocked on November 16, with no other LaLiga systems impacted, the statement said
Full Text:
Spain’s top professional football league has revealed a data breach which resulted in the compromise of fans’ personally identifiable information (PII).

LaLiga said in a brief statement on November 23 that the incident impacted an unnamed fan services platform between November 14 and 16.

A cybercriminal gained unauthorized access and exfiltrated PII belonging to users who had registered with digital services provided by LaLiga and some clubs, it noted.

The data theft was stopped and the attacker blocked on November 16, with no other LaLiga systems impacted, the statement said. System monitoring has been stepped up and the incident reported to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and the National Police's Central Cybercrime Unit.

Read more on football-related cyber threats: Hackers Steal Transfer Fees, Cripple Football Stadiums

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO EMEA at Huntress, argued that the sports sector in general has historically underinvested in cybersecurity relative to the value of what it holds.

“The Premier League introduced mandatory security standards this season specifically because the gap between the data sports organizations hold and the protection around it has become untenable,” he added. “LaLiga's breach reinforces that the problem isn't confined to English football. It's a sector-wide reckoning that European football's governing bodies need to treat with the same urgency the Premier League is now applying.”

Fans should be on the alert for potential follow-on scams using stolen personal data, Patel warned.

“Fraudsters use breach data to personalize their approaches,” he said. “A message that correctly references your team, your account, or your location feels more legitimate than a generic scam. That personalization is a warning sign, not a reassurance.”

Commenting on the data breach, Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA noted that the incident highlights a fundamental challenge for the global digital economy and society.

“An organization’s cybersecurity is increasingly dependent on the resilience of the entire ecosystem in which it operates,” he said. “Investing in internal security is essential, but it is no longer sufficient. Organizations must extend their cybersecurity governance to shared platforms and third-party providers, establish coordinated incident response protocols and invest in professionals with the skills to anticipate emerging threats.”

LaLiga oversees Spain's two professional football divisions, representing 42 clubs. Beyond organizing competitions, it manages media rights, international expansion and technological initiatives across Spanish professional football.

In recent years, LaLiga has invested heavily in anti-piracy and digital protection technologies. Earlier in 2026, LaLiga partnered with Fastly to deploy AI-based systems for identifying and disrupting illegal sports streams which it estimated costs its clubs between $700-$800m (€600-€700m) each year.

Title: Researchers Find a New AI Attack Path: Agent Instructions
Context: It found that, while malicious code is still a major threat, tool poisoning and prompt injection are more prevalent in some ecosystems, making agent instructions a new attack path
Full Text:
Threat actors are finding new ways to hijack and manipulate AI agents into doing their bidding which don’t require malicious code, Ox Security has warned.

The security vendor analyzed 542,207 open source software components between July and October 2026 to compile its Plug and Pray report.

It found that, while malicious code is still a major threat, tool poisoning and prompt injection are more prevalent in some ecosystems, making agent instructions a new attack path.

“Companies are giving AI agents access to critical systems while relying on trust signals built for a different era,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO of Ox Security. “Our research shows that the problem isn’t just what a tool can do. It’s who controls it, what code it actually runs, and what instructions it can give an AI agent. We need a new model for software trust.”

Read more on agentic threats: MCP Is Creating Major Governance Gaps, Researchers Warn

The researchers tracked suspicious components across four ecosystems: npm, PyPI, MCP servers, and agent skills.

They found that prompt injection and tool poisoning appeared in 22% of flagged MCP servers, while install- or import-time execution appeared in 16%.

In agent skills the gap was even wider: 26% and 0%. Additionally, over two-fifths (44%) contained instructions directing agents to send data out.

“The agent already has the permissions it needs. Attackers just have to convince it to use them,” said Moshe Siman Tov Bustan, research lead at Ox Security.

Three Questions for AI Agents

The report warned that traditional security approaches are ill-designed to spot such trickery. Teams have always made decisions on software based on who published it, what code it runs, and whether the code has been altered.

Yet in this new world, Ox Security found a source owner for only 70% of MCP servers (versus 93% of npm packages).

Furthermore, 67% ran on publisher-controlled infrastructure, which made it impossible to independently verify the deployed code. And 82% were malicious in their first observed version, meaning there was no clean version to compare against.

Organizations deploying AI agents must therefore go beyond checking whether dependencies contain vulnerable or malicious code, the report argued.

It suggested three questions security teams should find the answers to as part of their assessment:

Who controls the tools our agents connect to? Who is the publisher and where does the tool come from?

Can we verify the code those tools run? Does it match the publisher’s claims?

Will we know when that code changes? Can you see changes to a tool that runs on someone else’s infrastructure?

Title: WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without Login
Context: Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8
Full Text:
A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation.

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon.

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.

Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.

Update to a fixed release.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

Title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
Context: 20, 2026 ThreatDefence, VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 Zero-Day: Patching and Hunting The Cyber Sec Guru, How ARMORY CASTLE Used a vCenter Zero-Day to Reach ESXi Rescana, VMware...
Full Text:
CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it.

Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks.

Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch.

What Is CVE-2026-123890

Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009, which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately.

The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, the most powerful account in a vSphere environment.

From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb, the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM.

Two things make it easy to get wrong:

It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw.

There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change.

How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials

Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside.

ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials

Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764.

Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger.

Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key.

Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA.

Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again.

Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance.

Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off.

A few details that trip people up:

Patched in July doesn't mean patched now. Every vCenter below the builds in the table needs this update, including systems that already have the CVE-2026-59309 fix.

vCenter 7.0 is the hard case. vSphere 7.0 reached the end of general support on Oct. 2, 2025, so there's no public fix. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ also says to presume versions 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. If you're on any of these, restricting network access to port 2012 is your main protection until you can upgrade or obtain a fix.

ESXi isn't in the advisory. The flaw is in vCenter. ESXi hosts still matter for the cleanup, because the attackers used vCenter to reach them.

Don't run the GitHub "proof of concept." A repository that appeared on Nov. 20 claiming exploit code describes the wrong advisory and fixed versions. As of Nov. 21, Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module titled as an authentication bypass to root, so expect working public exploit code soon, if it isn't out already.

Why patching isn't enough

The patch fixes the login flaw. It does nothing about what an attacker took while the flaw was open, and in this case the stolen items are exactly the kind that keep working:

The token-signing key. Anyone holding vCenter's SAML signing key can mint valid administrator logins until that certificate is replaced. A patched vCenter will accept them.

New accounts. The attackers created an SSO administrator named sps- followed by random characters in vsphere.local. BONESAW can also add a machine account and grant Global Administrator rights on the vCenter root folder.

Appliance secrets. vCenter's master encryption key and PostgreSQL password were copied over SSH.

Host access. An SSH key was added to the ESXi root account.

Active Directory. A copy of NTDS.dit plus the SYSTEM hive is enough to recover the password hashes of every account in the domain, offline.

The exposure window also runs further back than most patch plans assume. Exploitation started in early September, more than 10 weeks before the fix. If any system that could reach your vCenter's management ports was compromised in that time, treat vCenter as possibly compromised too until you've checked.

After the patch: what to hunt for

Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise.

On the network

Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers.

Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080.

Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports.

Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66.

On vCenter

SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group.

A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after.

SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files.

On ESXi hosts

ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain.

New entries in root's authorized_keys.

Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py.

On internal Linux appliances

The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file.

/usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes.

Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env.

GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report.

After the patch: what to rotate and reset

If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task.

Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts.

Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went.

Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail.

Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local.

Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys.

Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit.

Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you.

Harden the vCenter control plane

This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries.

Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic.

Enforce rules below the application. Mandiant recommends its VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool, which applies default-deny iptables rules at the operating-system level, filters outbound traffic and forwards blocked connections and shell commands to a SIEM. By Mandiant's analysis, those rules would have blocked the exploit on port 2012, the forged logins on 443, the SSH pivot and the Slack command channel. Test any such rules under change control before production.

Close the visibility gaps. The attackers chose Linux appliances with no EDR as their staging ground. Inventory every appliance that can reach vCenter or ESXi, and get logs off them if you can't run an agent. Manage vSphere only from privileged access workstations, as set out in Mandiant's vSphere defender's guide.

Frequently asked questions

What is CVE-2026-123890?

CVE-2026-123890 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter Server. An attacker with network access to vCenter's TCP port 2012 can obtain an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local without a password. Broadcom fixed it on Nov. 19, 2026, in VMSA-2026-0009.

Is CVE-2026-123890 being exploited?

Yes. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 20, 2026, with a Nov. 23 remediation deadline for federal agencies.

Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890?

vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix; extended-support customers must go through Broadcom. There is no workaround.

I installed the July fix for CVE-2026-59309. Am I protected?

No. CVE-2026-123890 is a separate flaw, and Mandiant observed it being exploited against a vCenter already patched for CVE-2026-59309. You need the November builds.

Is there a public exploit for CVE-2026-123890?

As of Nov. 21, 2026, the attackers' tool hadn't been released, and a GitHub repository claiming a proof of concept was fake. Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module, so working public exploit code is expected soon.

Is CVE-2026-123890 a VM escape? Do I need to patch ESXi?

No on both counts. The flaw is in vCenter, and ESXi isn't listed in the advisory. But an attacker who controls vCenter can reach every ESXi host it manages, so check your hosts during cleanup.

Know which flaws are being used before the advisory lands

CVE-2026-123890 was exploited for more than 10 weeks before it was disclosed, and it was reached through a second zero-day in a remote-support appliance. Defenders can't patch what hasn't been disclosed, but they can know which of their exposed systems sit in an attacker's path and act within hours when exploitation becomes public.

Title: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
Context: The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software
Full Text:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.

"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.

The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.

The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.

Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.

The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.

To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.

"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said. "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."

Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.

Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.

"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

This involves the following steps -

An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures.

Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit.

The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry.

The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety.

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.

OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.

"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."

"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative."

Title: Hackers Exploit N-able MailAssure Flaw While AI Agents Exploit MONAI Label Zero-Day
Context: 8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory,...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The critical vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.

CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored.

"N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity."

CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement.

The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China.

"In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step."

Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server.

"In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root."

Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network.

The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft -

AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization.

AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain.

AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access.

In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework.

"The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection."

According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform).

In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts.

"In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC."

Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses.

"Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said.

"The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit."

Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the latest fixes for the two flaws by November 26, 2026.

Title: The Next Cyberattack Won’t Wait. Are You Ready?
Context: On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability
Full Text:
One day into the November Microsoft outage, Cofense Intelligence saw phishing emails posing as service notifications. The outage was real. The emails were designed to steal sign-in credentials. We published our findings on November 16. On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability. Security teams should act on the patch guidance and keep email defenses running while they address it.

Read our November 16 Flash Alert · Read CISA’s November 17 alert

One campaign can look like many

The FBI has warned that criminals use generative AI to make scams more convincing and easier to scale. In polymorphic phishing, different versions of the same campaign can land in different inboxes. AI can help attackers produce more of those variants. Even modern filters can miss a message that’s been designed to evade AI algorithms.

For a security team, the work starts when the first report comes in. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes.

Why AI alone isn’t enough

AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. But AI struggles with threats that don’t match previous patterns, and new lures are exactly what attackers are producing. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others.

In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows Threat Actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns.

Find the campaign and remove it

Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign.

See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages

What organizations can do now

Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. Start by checking who can remove a confirmed phish from multiple inboxes and how your team will coordinate if email is down.

Have Cyber Security solutions that are able to be flexible in the everchanging landscape of cybercrime and AI. You should have human resources working in tandem with supervised AI to ensure that you aren't left waiting for AI security models to catch up.

Map out alternative communication strategies for when you lose access to email or messaging platforms.

Have and verify backups for all important company data.

Ensure your internal Phishing Training programs are properly training your employees based on real life threats and targets weaknesses in your user base.

Document clear lines of communication. Employees should know who to contact when verifying a request or transaction. They should also know which backup channels to use if they suspect the original source has been compromised.

Don’t rely on a single layer of defense. No filter catches everything and attackers design campaigns to bypass them. Pair your automated security tools with detection and response to ensure that someone is finding what is slipping through.

Treat legitimate remote access tools with the utmost scrutiny. Attackers often abuse legitimate remote monitoring and remote management (RMM) tools, such as ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, because those tools blend in with normal IT activity. Block any RMM or remote access software your organization doesn't officially use and closely monitor the ones you do.

Patch with vetted updates. Apply tested patches for every known vulnerability. Prioritize anything actively exploited or facing the internet, like VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances.

Shrink your attack surface. Review and remove old or unused accounts, services, appliances, and applications. Anything you don't need is just one more way in.

Flag external email clearly. Use clear banners to warn users when a message comes from outside the organization. That simple visual cue helps users spot business email compromise (BEC) and impersonation attempts.

Title: Automation You Can Explain: Why AI-Driven Phishing Defense Needs Human Oversight
Context: Phishing attacks are increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors exploiting trusted platforms, legitimate services, and evolving techniques to bypass traditional security...
Full Text:
AI is transforming cybersecurity, enabling organizations to detect, analyze, and respond to threats faster than ever before. But as organizations increasingly rely on AI to make critical security decisions, an important question emerges: Who is ultimately accountable when AI takes action?

In its September 2026 report, Reduce AI Risk by Making Human “Guardians” Your Last Line of Defense, Gartner® examines the growing need for meaningful human oversight as AI becomes more deeply embedded in enterprise decision-making. Download the complete report here.

Gartner emphasizes that “real human oversight of AI outputs — not just ticking a compliance box or rubber-stamping decisions — is non-negotiable.”

This distinction is particularly important in phishing defense, where automated decisions can have immediate consequences for an organization's security and business operations.

At Cofense, we believe AI should empower security teams, not replace their judgment. The future of phishing defense isn't about choosing between human expertise and automation. It's about combining both to deliver faster, more accurate, and more accountable security outcomes.

Who Is Accountable When AI Acts Inside Your Inbox?

Phishing attacks are increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors exploiting trusted platforms, legitimate services, and evolving techniques to bypass traditional security controls. For security teams facing a constant influx of suspicious emails, AI-driven automation is essential to identifying and containing threats at scale.

But what happens when an automated system makes the wrong decision?

Consider an AI-powered security platform that identifies a suspicious email campaign and automatically quarantines messages across an organization. When the detection is accurate, the platform can prevent a potential compromise in seconds. But an incorrect classification could disrupt legitimate business communications, while a missed threat could expose employees to credential theft, malware, or business email compromise (BEC).

These scenarios and more, demonstrate why automation must be accompanied by clear accountability.

Gartner warns that “AI-driven workflows increase enterprise productivity but introduce significant risk, including biases, compliance gaps, and accountability voids.” As systems become more autonomous, organizations must be able to trace, explain, and challenge the decisions they make.

For phishing defense, we view that to mean knowing who is responsible for automated actions, understanding why a threat was flagged, and maintaining the ability to intervene when necessary.

AI can accelerate decision-making, but accountability must remain with the people responsible for protecting the organization.

Why Is Rubber-Stamping AI Not Real Oversight?

Only including a human in an automated workflow does not necessarily mean meaningful oversight is taking place.

If analysts are simply asked to approve AI-generated recommendations without understanding the reasoning behind them, their involvement becomes a formality rather than an effective security control.

Gartner addresses this challenge by calling for organizations to move from a traditional “human-in-the-loop” approach toward a “human-in-the-lead” model.

Under this model, human “decision stewards” take an active role in governing AI-driven decisions, with the authority to monitor, challenge, and override decisions when necessary. They recommend tailoring this oversight to the level of risk, applying stronger human controls to high-impact decisions while allowing lower-risk processes to operate with lighter supervision.

This approach is especially relevant to phishing defense.

Security analysts cannot manually investigate every suspicious email at the speed and scale required to combat modern attacks. AI can handle repetitive tasks, identify malicious patterns, and accelerate response times, while human expertise provides essential judgment when decisions become more complex.

The goal isn't to introduce unnecessary friction into every automated process. It's to ensure security professionals have the visibility and authority to intervene when it matters most.

Effective human oversight isn't about slowing AI down. It's about making automation more trustworthy.

What Does Real Human Oversight Look Like in Phishing Defense?

For organizations adopting AI-driven phishing defense, meaningful oversight should be embedded directly into the technology and its workflows.

Three capabilities are essential:

Human Authority Over Automated Actions Experts emphasize that decision stewards must have the authority to stop, pause, or question AI-driven decisions rather than simply approve them. In phishing defense, this means giving security teams control over how automation operates, including the ability to configure workflows, establish approval requirements, and intervene when necessary.

Explainable AI Decisions We see that Gartner highlights the importance of forensic accountability, including the ability to trace and explain AI-driven actions. For security teams, explainability means understanding why an email was classified as malicious and what indicators contributed to that detection. This context allows analysts to validate findings, investigate potential errors, and make informed response decisions rather than accepting AI-generated classifications at face value.

Complete Audit Trails According to Gartner, “Traceability makes enterprise governance transparent and defensible in the face of increasing regulatory demands.” Comprehensive audit trails document automated decisions, human interventions, and response actions, giving security teams the evidence needed to investigate incidents, evaluate performance, and demonstrate accountability to leadership and auditors. Together, these capabilities create a foundation for AI-driven phishing defense that balances operational efficiency with transparency and human control.

Why Does Human Oversight Matter Most in Regulated Industries?

For highly regulated industries such as financial services and healthcare, the consequences of poorly governed AI decisions can extend beyond operational disruption to regulatory exposure and reputational damage.

Organizations must be able to demonstrate that automated systems operate within established policies, maintain appropriate controls, and provide sufficient documentation for internal and regulatory review.

Yet many organizations are still developing the governance practices necessary to meet these expectations.

Gartner reports that only one in five organizations have highly effective AI governance practices and rank projects based specifically on an assessed AI risk-to-value ratio. Security leaders must also consider whether their technology supports transparent decision-making, documented response actions, and appropriate human intervention.

Data governance is another critical consideration, particularly when security platforms process sensitive email content. Organizations need to understand where their data is stored, how it is processed, and whether automated workflows align with their compliance requirements.

Responsible AI adoption requires more than proving that automation works. Organizations must also be able to explain how it works and demonstrate that appropriate safeguards are in place.

Can we understand why AI flagged a particular threat? Does the platform provide sufficient context to explain its detections, allowing analysts to validate findings and investigate potential errors?

Can we demonstrate accountability for every automated decision?

Does the platform maintain comprehensive audit trails documenting detections, response actions, and human involvement?

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of GNU Inetutils. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
