Title: Orgs that leak data 'prioritize corporate interests over customers' says Have I Been Pwned’s Troy Hunt
Context: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond...
Full Text: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all. Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.” Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.” Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms. Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.” Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.” Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed. If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter. Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.” Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach. Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless. Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways: Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it; Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site; Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm. Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.” The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text. The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well. “Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.” Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.” Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “absolutely nails it!” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

Title: Know the identity behind the role: Authorize and audit with trusted identity propagation
Context: Until now, TIP was available only for users who access AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center
Full Text:
Today, AWS is making it easier to grant access and audit activity based on the user or workload (a non-human caller, such as an application, service, or an automated workflow) behind an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role. Trusted identity propagation (TIP) carries the identity of the user or workload with each AWS request, so you can grant permissions to that user or workload and trace its actions in AWS CloudTrail. Until now, TIP was available only for users who access AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center. We’ve extended TIP to IAM federation and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, making it work for users and workloads that federate directly into IAM roles or use X.509 certificates to obtain AWS credentials. We’ve also made TIP simpler to use with IAM Identity Center.

This post explains how TIP works and what’s new with this launch. It then shows two examples of how TIP improves auditability and access control based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. The post ends with how to get started depending on your preferred federation path into AWS.

How trusted identity propagation works

Customers have told us they want to control access to AWS resources and audit activity based on the user or workload behind an IAM role. Today, access control decisions apply to the role, and CloudTrail attributes each action to the role session. To give two users or workloads different access, you either create a separate role or share one role and write policies that check session attributes. Separate roles lead to role proliferation. Session attributes carry across role sessions only when you grant additional permissions, and the session doesn’t record who set each attribute.

TIP addresses this gap by attaching identity context from a trusted source, such as your identity provider (IdP), to the role session at the time of credential issuance. This identity context identifies the user or workload behind a request and can include optional claims for the session, such as a risk score or a continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) workflow name. Trusted sources include external SAML or OIDC IdPs configured for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and X.509 certificates configured for IAM Roles Anywhere.

After AWS attaches identity context to a role session, the context can’t be changed for the lifetime of the session. This approach gives IAM policies and audit records a stable reference to the user or workload behind each request. The context also carries forward to supported downstream requests. When a TIP session (a role session that carries identity context) assumes another role, AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) carries the context into the new role session. Similarly, when an AWS service makes a downstream request on your behalf, the request uses forward access sessions (FAS), and the FAS credentials carry the identity context from your session.

Note: TIP context propagates to a new role session only when the target role is in the account where the identity provider is configured, or if the target role is in another account in the same AWS organization. To learn how account and organization boundaries determine TIP context propagation, see Understand where TIP context propagates in the IAM User Guide.

Figure 1 shows how this flow works end-to-end. A user or workload obtains AWS credentials through one of three paths. With IAM federation, the source is a SAML assertion or OIDC token for a user or workload. With IAM Identity Center, the source is the username that IAM Identity Center receives from your identity source. With IAM Roles Anywhere, the source is an X.509 certificate for a user or workload. AWS validates the source and attaches identity context to the role session. That context stays with the session’s requests, whether the session calls an AWS service directly, assumes another role, or causes an AWS service to make downstream requests through FAS. IAM policies then evaluate the identity context to authorize requests, as the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy example later in this post shows, and AWS CloudTrail records it, as the AWS Lambda example shows. With IAM outbound identity federation, the session can also request a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries identity context to an external service.

Figure 1: How TIP carries identity information into authorization and audit workflows

AWS represents the identity context carried in a TIP session through three groups of context keys. The following table summarizes their purpose and points to the corresponding documentation. For details about what these context keys contain and when they appear in a TIP session, see TIP context keys in IAM policies.

Context keys

Purpose

aws:OriginIdentity/*

Identifies the user or workload that started the request and the source that issued its identity.

aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/*

Carries optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name. Available only for IAM federation.

aws:IdentityCenterInstanceArn and aws:IdentityStoreArn

Identifies the IAM Identity Center instance and identity store behind a session. If you use IAM Identity Center permission sets or IAM account access manager, you can use these keys in IAM policy conditions. For example, you can allow access only to workforce users from a specific instance.

Table 1: TIP context key categories and what they represent.

aws:OriginIdentity/* is the common namespace for identity information from IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. Across all three paths, aws:OriginIdentity/Subject identifies the user or workload that started the request, aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType indicates whether the request was started by a user or workload, and aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer identifies the source that issued the identity. For IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, aws:OriginIdentity/FederatedProviderArn also contains the Amazon Resource Name ARN) of the IAM IdP or IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchor that authenticated the identity.

IAM policies can evaluate TIP context keys when those keys are present in the request. CloudTrail records identity context in the userIdentity element of events. The userIdentity.onBehalfOf section records the user or workload identity from aws:OriginIdentity context keys, and the userIdentity.transactionContext section records IdP claims from aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider context keys. For field definitions and examples see Logging TIP activity with AWS CloudTrail.

Key benefits of trusted identity propagation

TIP gives you the following benefits for authorizing and auditing access based on the user or workload behind an IAM role.

Audit by identity, not only by role – CloudTrail records the user or workload behind each request.

Authorize based on who’s asking – IAM policies can grant or restrict access based on the user or workload, or on optional claims from your IdP, such as a risk score. This gives you precise access control for each session.

Rely on identity you can trust – AWS attaches identity context from a trusted source when it issues credentials. That context can’t be changed for the life of the session, and it carries forward when the session assumes another role or an AWS service makes requests on your behalf.

Use one model across federation paths – IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere share the same core aws:OriginIdentity context keys, so you write policies and review CloudTrail consistently across more than 250 supported AWS services. Across supported workflows, identity context propagates without adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies.

What’s new with this launch

This launch extends TIP to IAM federation and IAM Roles Anywhere, and simplifies TIP in IAM Identity Center. You can also share identity context with services outside AWS through IAM outbound identity federation.

AWS IAM Identity Center – TIP already allows AWS applications integrated with IAM Identity Center, such as AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 Access Grants, to audit user activity and control access based on the user’s identity. When you enable the simplified experience, Identity Center adds a username, an identifier from your identity source, alongside the system-generated identity store user ID. This identity information is carried consistently across all access paths, including application access, account access through IAM Identity Center permission sets, and IAM account access manager. With this launch, you can now use the propagated username, mapped to the aws:OriginIdentity/Subject context key, in IAM policy conditions and view it in CloudTrail events. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation.

IAM federation – For users and workloads that use direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles, you choose the SAML assertion field or OIDC token claim that identifies the user or workload, and TIP attaches it to the role session. You can also map optional SAML attributes or OIDC claims, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name, into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM IdPs, and you can turn it on for existing providers. For more information, see TIP for IAM Federation.

IAM Roles Anywhere – For users and workloads outside AWS that use X.509 certificates with IAM Roles Anywhere, TIP attaches the identity from the certificate to the role session. After IAM Roles Anywhere validates the certificate against the configured trust anchor, AWS sets aws:OriginIdentity/Subject to the certificate’s Subject common name by default, or to its URI Subject Alternative Name. TIP is turned on by default for new IAM Roles Anywhere profiles, and you can turn it on for existing profiles. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere.

IAM outbound identity federation – A TIP session can now use the AWS STS GetWebIdentityToken API operation to request a signed JSON Web Toke that includes TIP session identity context for an external service. The external service validates the token and determines how to use the information. For details, see Federating AWS identities to external services.

Use identity context for auditability and access control

The following examples demonstrate two core benefits of TIP: auditability—tracing actions back to the user or workload—and access control based on that identity. In the first example, AnyCompany uses identity context logged in CloudTrail to identify the GitHub Actions workflow run that deployed new code to a production AWS Lambda function. In the second, AnyCompany uses an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket policy that grants read access only to low-risk sessions initiated from a specific IdP.

Trace a Lambda deployment to its GitHub Actions run

This example shows how TIP improves auditability: identity context in CloudTrail identifies the workload, and the specific workflow run, behind an action taken with a shared role. AnyCompany stores the backend code for its payment-processing application in the anycompany/payments-api GitHub repository. A code change merged into the repository’s main branch triggers the GitHub Actions workflow defined in .github/workflows/deploy.yml. The workflow uses GitHub OIDC federation to assume a shared CICDDeployRole role, then calls the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation to deploy the new code to the production payments-api-prod function. CloudTrail records this operation as an UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2 management event.

Before TIP, the CloudTrail event shows that the CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions role session updated payments-api-prod. It doesn’t identify the GitHub repository, workflow file, or workflow run that performed the update. Investigators must match the event timestamp with GitHub records to find the responsible workflow run.

Figure 2: How TIP enables attribution of a production Lambda code update to the GitHub Actions run that performed it

AnyCompany enables TIP on its GitHub OIDC IdP. It maps the GitHub OIDC token subject to aws:OriginIdentity/Subject, configures aws:OriginIdentity/SubjectType as workload, and maps the repository, workflow_ref, and run_id claims into aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys. The resulting role session identifies the workload and carries the information needed to trace the deployment to its GitHub Actions run.

With TIP, the CloudTrail management event for the Lambda UpdateFunctionCode API operation on payments-api-prod now contains the workload and workflow information:

{ "eventSource": "lambda.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "UpdateFunctionCode20150331v2", "recipientAccountId": "111122223333", "requestParameters": { "functionName": "payments-api-prod" }, "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/CICDDeployRole/GitHubActions", "onBehalfOf": { "federatedProviderArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com", "subject": "repo:anycompany/payments-api:environment:production", "subjectType": "workload", "issuer": "token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }, "transactionContext": { "IdentityProvider": { "repository": "anycompany/payments-api", "workflow_ref": "anycompany/payments-api/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@refs/heads/main", "run_id": "19283746550" } } } }

An investigator can now see that GitHub Actions run 19283746550 from the anycompany/payments-api repository updated the production payments-api-prod function through the deploy.yml workflow. The shared role, its trust policy, and its permissions remain unchanged. TIP adds workload and workflow attribution to the existing deployment model.

Authorize access based on session risk

This example shows how TIP supports access control: an Amazon S3 bucket policy uses a runtime risk signal from an IdP to decide, per session, whether a user of a shared role can read sensitive data. AnyCompany’s workforce users federate to AWS through an OIDC IdP and use a shared DataAccessRole to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. AnyCompany configures its IdP to evaluate each authentication and add a numeric risk score, from 0 to 100, to the OIDC token as a custom claim. AnyCompany enables TIP on the IAM OIDC IdP and maps the riskScore claim to the aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore context key. During federation, AWS validates the token and attaches the mapped riskScore value to the role session. AWS derives aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer from the iss (issuer) claim in the OIDC token.

Before TIP, a bucket policy that grants access to DataAccessRole gives every user who assumes the role the same access, regardless of how risky their authentication was. With TIP, an S3 bucket policy can evaluate both the IdP that issued the token and the risk score carried in the session. The following policy grants read access only when the expected IdP (issuer) issued the identity, and the current session has a risk score of 30 or lower. The issuer condition prevents a riskScore value from another IdP from satisfying the policy.

Figure 3: How an S3 bucket policy uses trusted identity context to make a per-session access decision

Note: This policy example is for the IAM federation access path. Mapping SAML attributes or OIDC claims to optional aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/* context keys is available only for IAM federation.

Amazon S3 bucket policy using trusted runtime context

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowLowRiskSensitiveDataRead", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DataAccessRole" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/restricted/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:OriginIdentity/Issuer": "idp.example.com" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "aws:TransactionContext/IdentityProvider/riskScore": "30" } } } ] }

The policy has two conditions: the identity must come from idp.example.com, and the session’s risk score must be 30 or lower. A low-risk session from idp.example.com satisfies both conditions. A session with a risk score above 30, a missing risk score, or a different issuer doesn’t receive access from this policy. The risk score remains fixed for the lifetime of the role session, so choose a session duration appropriate for the sensitivity of the access.

Additional considerations

Missing TIP context keys. A TIP context key is missing when the session carries no identity context or the request goes to an AWS service that doesn’t support TIP. To prevent an Allow statement from granting access when a required key is missing, use operators without IfExists, such as StringEquals or NumericLessThanEquals, as the preceding bucket policy does. Avoid operators such as StringEqualsIfExists in an Allow statement because they evaluate to true when the key is missing. In a Deny statement, add IfExists when the Deny should also apply if the key is missing. Such a Deny also applies to requests sent to AWS services that don’t support TIP, so confirm service support before adding TIP conditions. For more information, see Condition operators.

TIP conditions with cached AWS KMS data keys. Some AWS services, such as Amazon SQS, reuse cached AWS KMS data keys across requests from different sessions of the same IAM role, because the cache key is based on the role and does not include TIP context. When an AWS service reuses a cached data key, it does not send a new authorization request to AWS KMS, so AWS KMS does not evaluate the later session’s TIP context. If you use TIP context to control access to encrypted data, enforce the TIP conditions in the policy for the encrypted resource, such as an Amazon S3 bucket policy, rather than relying only on the AWS KMS key policy. For more information, see AWS KMS guidance for cached data keys.

Choose your TIP approach and get started

Your first step to getting started with TIP depends on how your users and workloads obtain AWS credentials. Use the following table to find the TIP option for your use case and get started.

Use case

TIP option

How to start

Centrally managed workforce access

IAM Identity Center

All IAM Identity Center instances can upgrade to the simplified experience for TIP. Before you upgrade, review the considerations for the simplified experience. For more information, see Simplified experience for trusted identity propagation.

Direct SAML or OIDC federation into IAM roles

IAM federation

New IAM IdPs have TIP turned on by default. For an existing IdP, turn on TIP on that provider, then map the claim that identifies the user or workload, and any optional claims your policies need, to TIP context keys. For more information see TIP for IAM Federation.

X.509-based access for users and workloads outside AWS

IAM Roles Anywhere

New profiles have TIP turned on by default. For an existing profile, enable TIP on the profile. For details, see Trusted identity propagation with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

With this launch, TIP carries the identity of the user or workload from a trusted identity source into the role session for IAM federation, IAM Identity Center, and IAM Roles Anywhere. You can grant access based on the user or workload making the request and use CloudTrail to trace actions across more than 250 supported AWS services back to that identity. This gives you a consistent authorization and audit model across federation paths, without creating a separate role for every identity or adding the sts:SetContext permission to role trust policies.

To get started, find your federation path in the preceding table and follow the steps in the How to start column.

Title: Scanning from Subnet 109.160.32.0/24, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
Context: The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open
Full Text:
This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing.

Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors.

A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command (uname -s -v -n -r -m) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs.

The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login.

Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL (230+) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below).

This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [7][8][9][10] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting.

Shodan Open Ports This is a random list of IPs checked against Shodan that list the same open ports. The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open. If the SSH service is listening, it is using 2 different version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS.

Title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
Context: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch...
Full Text: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

Title: Turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps
Context: The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows
Full Text:
Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.

When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.

Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

Artifacts started out as a work output you’d share, like a chart or a webpage. People now use them as tools for everyday work, like a meeting prep page that regularly pulls from their calendar and email, or a tracker for the orders that need to ship that day.

If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention.

What installed apps can do

Installed apps can send notifications or add items to your menu bar or system tray. You choose permissions for each app, and Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization.

People at Anthropic have used these to make:

Linnet (opens in new tab), a full layered image editor

Phosphor (opens in new tab), a file manager that looks made for a movie set

Sift (opens in new tab), which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized

Tern (opens in new tab), a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain

Vitals (opens in new tab), a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance

You can see more demo apps made by one of our engineers here (opens in new tab).

Permissions

There are three levels of permissions:

Default: Installed apps can only do what they’d be able to do in a browser.

App permissions: Apps can ask to use common features that Claude can tightly control, like creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, or sending notifications.

Full computer access: Apps can ask to run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time.

Your permission only covers the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even your own edits. If part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking you again.

You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization. Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust.

Getting started

Describe your app to Claude, try it as an artifact, and then click "Install as app." You don’t have to package or sign it, and it uses your Claude account, so there’s no API key or separate login.

Install as app is rolling out in beta on all plans. HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments can’t use it. It’s on by default for Team, with full access off. On Enterprise, it’s off until an owner turns it on. You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app. Some artifacts can’t be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

Update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact you use every day, and choose "Install as app" from the Share menu.

Title: What makes a great ChatGPT app
Context: Select capabilities, don’t port your product A common first thought is to list all of your product’s features and ask, “How do we bring these into ChatGPT
Full Text:
At DevDay we introduced ChatGPT Apps — a new way to bring your product directly into ChatGPT conversations. This post builds on that launch with practical guidance for developers, PMs, and designers on how to choose the right use case and design an app that’s actually useful once it’s live. We’ll focus on how to translate your product’s strengths into clear, well-scoped capabilities the model can apply across many different conversations and user intents. If you’re looking for the original technical workflow, you can jump straight into the Apps SDK quickstart and developer docs.

We’ll cover:

What a ChatGPT app really is (and isn’t)

The three ways an app can genuinely add value

How to design for conversation and discovery

How to know whether your app is actually helping

Concrete examples and suggestions for screenshots

What a ChatGPT app actually is

When teams build their first ChatGPT app, the starting point is often:

“We already have a product. Let’s bring it into ChatGPT.”

This often starts with taking an existing web or mobile experience — screens, menus, flows — and trying to reshape it for chat. It’s a reasonable instinct; for years, “software” has meant pages, navigation, and UI scaffolding.

However, building apps for ChatGPT is a different environment. Users aren’t “opening” your app and starting on the home page. They’re having a conversation about something and the model can decide when to bring an app into that conversation. They’re entering at a point in time. In that world, the best apps look surprisingly small from the outside. They don’t try to recreate the entire product. Instead, they allow users to access a few specific powers while using the app in ChatGPT: the concrete things your product does best that the model can reuse in any conversation.

Outside of ChatGPT, your app is often the destination. Users:

Tap your icon

Enter your environment

Learn your navigation and UI patterns

Most product decisions flow from that assumption: “We own the screen.” You can invest heavily in layout, onboarding, and information architecture because users are committing to your space.

Inside ChatGPT, your app plays a different role:

It’s a capability the model can call - for both context and visual engagement.

It shows up inside an ongoing conversation.

It’s one of several tools the model may orchestrate.

That means the “unit of value” is less your overall experience and more the specific things you can help the model and user accomplish at the right moment.

A practical definition:

A ChatGPT app is a set of well defined tools that can perform tasks, trigger interactions, or access data.

This has a few implications:

You don’t need to port every feature.

You don’t need a full navigation hierarchy.

You do need a clear, compact API: a handful of operations that are easy to invoke and easy to build on.

You can think of it this way: your ChatGPT app is a toolkit the model reaches for when the user runs into a specific type of problem. The more precisely that toolkit is defined, the easier it is to use in the flow of conversation.

Once you see your app as “capabilities the model can orchestrate,” rather than “a mini version of our product,” design decisions get clearer. You start asking “What can we help with here?” instead of “Where should the user go next?”

The three ways to add real value

A simple filter for any app idea:

Know: Does it let the user work with new context or data they couldn’t see otherwise in ChatGPT?

Do: Does the app take real actions on the user’s behalf?

Show: Does the app present information in a clearer, more actionable UI than plain text?

This applies to “serious” productivity apps and to “just for fun” apps like games. A game might not help someone ship a report faster, but it still does something the base model can’t do well on its own: maintain stateful game logic, track progress, enforce rules, or render interesting views of the game world. The value is delight and engagement, but the underlying pattern is the same.

1) New things to know

Your app makes new context available within a ChatGPT conversation:

Live prices, availability, inventory

Internal metrics, logs, analytics

Specialized, subscription-gated, or niche datasets

User-specific data (accounts, history, preferences, entitlements)

Sensor data, live video streams

In practice, this often means bridging into systems where data is correct, current, and permissioned. The app becomes the “eyes and ears” of the model in your domain, and can answer questions with more authority.

2) New things to do

Your app takes actions on the user’s behalf:

Create or update records in internal tools

Send messages, tickets, approvals, notifications

Schedule, book, order, or configure things

Trigger workflows (deploy, escalate, sync data)

Play interactive games (apply rules, advance turns, track state)

Take actions in the physical world (IoT, robotics control, etc.)

Here, the app is less a source of truth and more a pair of hands. It takes the user’s intent and turns it into concrete changes in the systems your team already lives in—or, in the case of games, concrete changes in the game state that make the experience feel consistent and fair. This is where your app shifts to an agent in a meaningful way.

3) Better ways to show

An app can present information in a GUI in a ChatGPT conversation, that makes the information more digestible or more actionable:

Shortlists, comparisons, rankings

Tables, timelines, charts

Role-specific or decision-specific summaries

Visual or structured views of game state (boards, inventories, scores)

This is especially valuable when users are making choices or trade-offs. Apps can give the model a language for structure: widgets that have columns, rows, scores, and visuals that match how people actually decide—or, in games, how they understand “where they are” in the world.

If an app doesn’t clearly move the needle on at least one of know/do/show, it tends to feel like it’s not adding value beyond what users can already do in ChatGPT. Users may not complain explicitly, but it’s a missed opportunity to provide more meaningful value to the user, whether the app is meant for work or play.

Here you can see an example of an experience enhanced by an app:

An example answer from ChatGPT

This answer is helpful, however, the user may want to use an app with additional capabilities to directly browse real properties without changing context or leaving the conversation.

Answer with the Zillow app

With the Zillow app, the user has the additional ability to search live property listings, filter by criteria, and view rich property details — all without leaving the chat.

Fullscreen mode for enriched discovery

The value here is you still get rich context from the model, and also an enriched app experience that can dynamically interact with your intent. Want to ask it for homes in a specific region? With the Zillow app, the model invokes the tool on the Zillow MCP server and re-renders the UI layer.

Select capabilities, don’t port your product

A common first thought is to list all of your product’s features and ask, “How do we bring these into ChatGPT?”

On paper, that sounds thorough. In practice, it usually produces a large, fuzzy surface area that’s hard for the model to navigate and hard for users to understand. If you struggle to summarize what the app does in one sentence, the model too will have a harder time understanding it.

A more effective path:

List the core jobs-to-be-done - Identify the specific tasks or outcomes users are trying to accomplish that your product helps make possible. These are the reasons your product exists in the first place. Starting here keeps you anchored in user outcomes instead of feature checklists. Examples:

Help someone choose a home.

Empower ideas into polished presentations.

Translate intent into a delightful discovery experience.

Turn raw data into a clear, shareable report.

For each job, ask:

“Without an app, what can’t the user do within a ChatGPT conversation?”

Common answers:

Access live or private data.

Take real actions in our systems.

Get the structured or visual output users need.

This is where your unique value starts to show up. You’re no longer thinking “What can we technically expose?” but “Where are we uniquely helpful?”

Turn those gaps into a handful of clearly named operations. For example:

search_properties – return a structured list of candidate homes.

explain_metric_change – fetch relevant data and summarize likely drivers.

generate_campaign_variants – create multiple ad variants with metadata.

create_support_ticket – open a ticket and return a summary + link.

These operations are:

Concrete enough for the model to choose confidently

Simple enough to mix with other steps in a conversation

Directly tied to value, not to your entire product map

Another way to think about this: if someone on your team asked, “What are the three things we absolutely need this app to do well?” those should map almost one-to-one to your product’s capabilities.

For example, the Canva app in ChatGPT can generate an entire presentation draft and the user can enter full screen mode that matches user expectations for navigating a slide deck, but deeper slide-by-slide editing still happens in the full Canva editor.

Design for conversation and discovery

In your MCP server, you can define the description that provides the model with context when to invoke your tool, and specifically which tool calls, to perform a specific task. This helps map user intent to your tools actions.

a) Vague intent

Help me figure out where to live.

A good app response will:

Use any relevant context already in the thread.

Ask one or two clarifying questions at most, if needed.

Produce something concrete quickly — for example, a few example cities with short explanations.

The user should feel like progress has started, not like they’ve been dropped into a multi-step onboarding flow. If they have to answer five questions before seeing anything useful, many will simply stop.

Let’s take a look at how that is handled in the Canva app:

Building a full scale presentation requires context. The Canva app asks for follow up questions to get the user to synthesize what they’re looking to build.

b) Specific intent

Find 3-bedroom homes in Seattle under $1.2M near well-rated elementary schools.

Here, the app shouldn’t ask the user to repeat themselves. It should:

Parse the query.

Call the right capabilities.

Return a focused set of results with useful structure.

You can still offer refinements (“Do you care more about commute or school rating?”), but they should feel like optional tuning, not required setup.

Canva example:

When the user’s intent becomes clear and asks to generate a presentation, the model knows exactly when to call Canva and what capability to invoke.

As seen below, the tool shares a few options and also probes deeper if the user wants additional refinements:

c) No brand awareness

You can’t assume the user knows who you are.

Your first meaningful response should:

Explain your app’s role in one line (“I pull live listings and school ratings so you can compare options.”)

Deliver useful output right away.

Offer a clear next step (“Ask me to narrow by commute, neighborhood, or budget.”)

Think of it as a cold start problem: you’re introducing what you are, why you’re helpful, and how to use you — all inside one or two messages.

Build for the model as well as the user

You’re designing for two audiences:

The human in the chat

The model runtime that decides when and how to call your app

Most teams are comfortable thinking about the first. The second is newer. But if the model can’t understand what your app does or how to use it, your human-facing experience won’t get many chances to run.

There’s a third dimension that matters just as much: what user data flows through your app when the model calls it. Good app design isn’t just about clear capabilities, it’s about being disciplined in what you ask for and how you use it.

Clear, descriptive actions and parameters: Make it obvious when your app is relevant and how to call it. Use straightforward names (search_jobs, get_rate_quote, create_ticket) and spell out which params are required vs. optional and how to format them. Ambiguity is a tax on routing.

Privacy by design: Only require fields you truly need. Avoid “blob” params that scoop up extra context. Prefer minimal, structured inputs and do not use instructions like “just send the whole conversation.”

Predictable, structured outputs: Keep schemas stable; include IDs and clear field names. Pair a brief summary (“Three options that match your budget and commute time”) with a machine-friendly list ([{id, address, price, commute_minutes, school_rating, url}, …]). This lets the model talk naturally while keeping precise handles on data.

Be intentional about what you do not return: Skip sensitive internals “just in case.” Keep tokens/secrets out of user-visible paths. Redact or aggregate when full fidelity isn’t necessary.

Be explicit about what you collect and why: Ask for the minimum to do the job. When you need something sensitive (e.g., account access), say why in one sentence. Design actions and schemas so it’s obvious what’s being sent where.

Design for an ecosystem, not a walled garden

In a real ChatGPT session, your app is rarely the only one in play. The model might call on multiple apps in the same conversation.

From the user’s perspective, it’s one flow. From your perspective, it’s a reminder that you’re part of an ecosystem, not a sealed product.

A few practical consequences:

Keep actions small and focused

search_candidates, score_candidates, send_outreach

rather than a single run_full_recruiting_pipeline.

Make outputs easy to pass along

Stable IDs, clear field names, consistent structures.

Avoid hiding important information only in free-form text.

Avoid long, tunnel-like flows

Do your part of the job and hand control back to the conversation.

Let the model decide which tool should handle the next step.

If other apps (or future versions of your own app) can easily build on your outputs, you’ve set yourself up to benefit from improvements elsewhere in the ecosystem instead of competing with them.

A quick checklist

A short checklist you can run before or after building:

1. New powers

Does your app clearly know, do, or show new things?

Would users in your target scenarios notice if it stopped working?

2. Focused surface

Have you picked a small set of capabilities instead of cloning your entire product?

Are those capabilities named and scoped in ways that map cleanly to real jobs-to-be-done?

3. First interaction

Does your app handle both vague and specific prompts gracefully?

Can a new user understand your role from the first meaningful response?

Do they see value on the first turn?

4. Model-friendliness

Are actions and parameters clear and unambiguous?

Are outputs structured and consistent enough to chain and reuse?

5. Evaluation

Do you have a small, thoughtful test set with positive, negative, and edge cases?

Do you have some notion of the win rate of the app-provided answer vs. the ChatGPT answer without the app?

6. Ecosystem fit

Can other apps and the user reasonably build on your output?

Are you comfortable being one link in a multi-app chain, rather than the whole journey?

You don’t need to be perfect in every dimension to ship. But if you can answer “yes” to most of these, you’re not just putting your product inside ChatGPT, you’re giving ChatGPT real leverage in your domain — and that’s where these apps start to feel indispensable.

Title: Production monitoring with Codex

Full Text:
When an alert sounds in the middle of the night, an on-call engineer usually scrambles to their computer and starts manually searching through various sources, trying to find out what went wrong. They’ll dig through logs, metrics, and code to compare to various hypotheses: was it the recent deployment that caused the issue? A traffic spike? Dependency failure?

As Codex deployment engineers, we routinely see engineering teams struggle with slow investigations or delayed alerts due to a manual or spotty production monitoring system. Oftentimes the root cause is unclear without an exhaustive search, where the engineer on-call must manually compare what they see across multiple platforms to validate or rule out a broad range of hypothesis.

Codex can come in to help the on-call engineer right when the alert happens, sorting through all the different sources of information for them. Once it is embedded within your existing production monitoring systems, it can investigate with the tools your team already uses to triage the issue and identify its root cause.

In this demo, we walk through investigations using Grafana, Kubernetes, and Codex Security.

Incorporating Codex

Let’s go back to that alert and explore how we can integrate Codex in the process. At a high level, it’s helpful to think about what information you would give an SRE onboarding onto your production monitoring system.

1 Evidence

Trigger

Alert, incident, or operator request

2 Evidence

Collect evidence

Logs, traces, metrics, and runtime state

3 Reasoning

Correlate context

Code, deployments, configuration, and incident history

4 Reasoning

Form hypotheses

Evidence-backed causes and discriminating tests

5 Action and approval

Propose a bounded action

Specific, reversible, and linked to evidence

6 Action and approval

Human approval

A named approver authorizes the action.

If approved, apply the change.

7 Verification and learning

Verify recovery

Check trusted, agreed recovery signals.

If recovered, document the outcome.

8 Verification and learning

Document outcome

Findings, decision, result, and follow-ups

Denied: revise proposal

Not recovered: investigate

Give it the right access

The first step is to ensure that Codex has access to the relevant context needed to make a judgment, including traces, runtime state, or deployment history, and that your instructions to the agent are clear about what and where those sources are. Keeping in mind the principles of progressive disclosure, the access to these sources should typically be read-only, and it’s better to start with a smaller scope and broaden access once there’s a need for more information. To best facilitate this, you can create service accounts in those systems to maintain granular control over the resources Codex can access.

Observability platform Detects alerts and stores evidence

Codex execution environment Connects evidence, code, and tools

Model inference layer Provides OpenAI models

Proposing a fix

With this context, Codex can collate all the information across these sources to form hypotheses about the root cause. Here, the instructions should require evidence and citations for every judgment it makes, so that the reviewer will be able to easily understand the rationale behind the decisions. You can also test out having multiple agents, such as an executor agent responsible for root cause analysis (RCA) and a reviewer agent for challenging the executor’s hypotheses.

Note: If you’re interested in learning more about single vs. multi-agent setups, check out the Codex subagents guide.

The next step is to have Codex propose a bounded solution. To make sure it is evidence-based, it should draw on its RCA and the citations it used to back up its hypotheses. Ideally, the solution should also be supplemented with a rollback plan as a precautionary measure. These proposed fixes can come in the form of a report or a PR.

Reviewing and verifying recovery

As part of a human-in-the-loop workflow, a human approver should be the gatekeeper and authorize the solution. Once the change is applied, Codex can work in tandem with the human to verify recovery signals across the same sources that it was granted access to at the start of this process.

Once the incident is resolved, Codex can also assist with the postmortem and documenting the outcome.

Creating a repeatable workflow

Take this workflow through representative scenarios, such as past incidents. Each time should act like a rehearsal, an opportunity to iron out the friction points and feed the lessons learned back into improving the instructions for the next time.

Once this process has been battle-tested a few times, it’s time to take a closer look at how to make this a repeatable workflow. Turning runbooks into skills is our recommended approach to codifying this otherwise tribal knowledge.

Use what you learned in the rehearsals to refine the workflow.

Identify the context Codex needs. List the connectors Codex used to investigate the incident. Try the same incident with fewer sources and note where Codex needs more evidence to reach a conclusion.

Revise the instructions. Find the step where someone had to correct Codex. Update that step to point to the right source or supply the missing context, then run the rehearsal again.

Compare agent setups. Run the same incident with one agent, then add a reviewer. Compare how long each setup takes to identify the root cause and mitigate the incident, and how often someone has to correct it.

Once the process has been largely standardized, capture it in a Codex skill or plugin to make it reusable across different team members. The next time an alert goes off at 3 a.m., Codex can be the first one to wake up.
