Title: US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise
Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
Context: Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it
Full Text: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.” Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle. To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6. “The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added. “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.” Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update. Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. ®

Title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
Context: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any...
Full Text: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

Title: Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access
Context: One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-...
Full Text:
The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.

The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.

First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.

One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.

"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."

The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."

One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.

It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.

The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.

Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -

Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.

Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.

What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.

"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.

"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

Title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
Context: Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government...
Full Text: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

Title: Protect identity data with point-in-time recovery in Amazon Cognito
Context: The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed
Full Text:
Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, microservices, and AI agents in minutes. Many of you rely on it for some of the most critical data you operate: the identities and attributes your applications use to authenticate and authorize every request. Recently, we launched point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Amazon Cognito user pools, which lets you restore a user pool to an earlier point in time if an accidental deletion, a faulty migration, or an erroneous bulk operation changes data you need. It’s turned on automatically for user pools on the eligible feature plans.

Before this launch, protecting user pool data meant building your own solution, such as exporting user attributes and group data on a schedule. That approach was time-consuming to build and operate, versioning the exports to find a clean point in time was another challenge, and reconstructing a pool from them was complicated. Users also got new sub identifiers as part of the restore process, which might break any downstream reference to the originals. Passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys might not be recovered, so every affected user had to reset.

In this post, we show you how to recover a user pool after an erroneous bulk operation, using the preview to review changes before you approve them.

How PITR works

On eligible user pools (see Prerequisites), Amazon Cognito now tracks changes so you can recover the pool to any point within the recovery window. The length of that window depends on your user pool feature plan. The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed.

One behavior to understand is what happens to passwords during a recovery. A recovery restores passwords for users it recreates. A user who still exists and changed their password after the target time keeps the same password. The recovery doesn’t revert password changes, so users who legitimately changed their credentials don’t lose them.

A recovery is preview-based and has three steps:

Initiate a recovery to a target point in time (InitiatePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito pauses write operations to the user pool and generates a preview for your review before any changes are applied. Read operations and sign-in continue to work normally. The call returns a RestoreId.

Review the recovery preview (DescribePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito reports how many users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys the recovery would create, update, or delete to return the pool to its state at the target time.

Approve or cancel. If the preview looks right, you approve the recovery with StartPointInTimeRecovery, and Amazon Cognito restores the pool to its state at the target time. If it doesn’t look right, you cancel it with CancelPointInTimeRecovery; no changes are applied, and write operations resume.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

An AWS account with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus feature plan. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. The examples use a pool named anycompany-prod-user-pool in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1).

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with permissions for the Amazon Cognito user pools PITR operations.

Before you run a recovery, keep these limits in mind:

You can run one recovery at a time per user pool, and one successful recovery per 24 hours per pool.

The target time must be at least 15 minutes in the past and no earlier than the pool’s creation time.

Recovery is initiated from the pool’s primary Region and can’t start while a multi-Region replication (MRR) operation, such as replica creation or deletion, is in progress on the pool.

Recovering a user pool after an unintentional change

AnyCompany runs its user sign-in on an Amazon Cognito user pool, anycompany-prod-user-pool.

At 15:45 PDT, an operator runs a bulk change that’s supposed to set an attribute on a subset of users. A defect in the script instead deletes and modifies users. By 15:54 PDT, support receives cases of failed sign-ins and the operator halts the script. The team needs the pool as it was at 15:39 PDT. They decide to use PITR and preview the recovery before approving it.

Step 1: Start the recovery

The team initiates a recovery with a target time of 15:39 PDT by running the command in the preceding example. Figure 1 shows the same step in the console, where the team enters the target time and starts the recovery. The response includes a RestoreId that identifies this recovery throughout the workflow, along with a RestoreStatus and the RestoreTimestamp that you targeted.

aws cognito-idp initiate-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-timestamp 2026-10-28T22:39:00Z

Figure 1: Initiating a recovery to a target point in time

Step 2: Review the recovery preview

DescribePointInTimeRecovery returns the Restoration for this RestoreId, including a RestorePreview that summarizes how many entities will be affected if the pool is returned to the target time. The team reviews the preview and confirms the number of affected users matches the scope.

aws cognito-idp describe-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a69b8c1e-9866-441d-EXAMPLE11111

In this case, the preview reports 16 users to create and 5 users to update, as the following sample response shows. Figure 2 shows the same preview in the console, with the create, update, and delete counts for users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys. These numbers match the scope of the bulk operation, so the team continues. If the preview had shown unexpected changes, the team could cancel the recovery with no changes applied.

{ "Restoration": { "RestoreId": "a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111", "RestorePreview": [ { "Entity": "Users", "CreateCount": 16, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 5 }, { "Entity": "Groups", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "User MFAs", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "Passkeys", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 } ], "RestoreStatus": "PREVIEW_GENERATED", "RestoreTimestamp": 1793227140, "TriggerTimestamp": 1793228700 } }

Figure 2: Reviewing the recovery preview before applying

Step 3: Approve the recovery

If the preview is correct, the team approves the recovery with the command in the following example, and Amazon Cognito restores anycompany-prod-user-pool to its 15:39 PDT state. Figure 3 shows the approval step in the console, and Figure 4 shows the confirmation that appears after the recovery starts. Writes to the user pool resume automatically after the recovery completes or is canceled.

aws cognito-idp start-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Figure 3: Approving the recovery

Figure 4: Recovery confirmation

aws cognito-idp cancel-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Your application integration doesn’t change

Because PITR rolls back the data in your existing user pool rather than creating a new one, your application integration doesn’t need any changes. A recovery restores user data and leaves your user pool configuration in place, so configuration changes you made after the recovery point are preserved. For example, a custom attribute you added to the schema, an AWS Lambda trigger you updated, or a password policy you tightened stays as it is. The user pool ID also stays the same, and so do your app client IDs and secrets, managed login and domain, identity provider and SAML/OIDC configurations, and the provider Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) that services such as Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer use to validate tokens. Recreated users keep the same sub identifiers, so downstream references to them keep working.

How PITR complements multi-Region replication

Multi-Region replication and PITR address different failure modes. Multi-Region replication keeps a synchronized replica of your user pool in another Region, so if the primary Region is impaired, you can fail over traffic to a replica Region with minimal downtime. PITR helps with data problems, such as erroneous bulk operations that corrupt your user pool’s state. You roll back to any point within your recovery window without changing your application integration.

Security considerations

A recovery changes the identity data that every sign-in and authorization decision depends on, so treat recovery permissions like any other high-impact administrative access.

Separate who initiates a recovery from who approves it. Because initiating and approving are separate API actions, you can assign them to different AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Give an operator the permission InitiatePointInTimeRecovery, and give an approver the permission StartPointInTimeRecovery. Both permissions need DescribePointInTimeRecovery and ListPointInTimeRecoveries to review the preview, and CancelPointInTimeRecovery to stop a recovery. IAM keeps the two permissions on separate roles, but it doesn’t stop one person from assuming both. Assign the roles to different people or teams, and grant the approver role only for the duration of an approved change.

Treat initiating a recovery as sensitive. Initiating a recovery pauses write operations on the user pool until the recovery is approved or canceled. If no action is taken within 24 hours, the preview automatically cancels and write operations are resumed. While writes are paused, users can’t sign up, reset their passwords, or update their profiles. A user pool also allows only one successful recovery per 24 hours, so an unauthorized recovery uses up a recovery you might need for a real incident.

Review restored users after a recovery. A recovery recreates users who were deleted after the target time, including users you removed on purpose, such as employees who have left or compromised accounts. After a recovery completes, check the recreated users against your incident timeline. Disable any that should stay removed and revoke their sessions with AdminUserGlobalSignOut.

Monitor recovery activity. Amazon Cognito records PITR API calls in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that notifies your security team whenever InitiatePointInTimeRecovery or StartPointInTimeRecovery is called, so that no recovery goes unnoticed.

Pricing

PITR is included at no additional charge in eligible feature plans with a recovery window of up to 1 day on the Essentials feature plan and up to 14 days on the Plus feature plan.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to recover an Amazon Cognito user pool after an erroneous bulk operation with PITR, from reviewing the changes in a preview to approving the recovery. PITR provides protection for your users’ identities, with no custom export-and-restore pipeline to build or operate. Because the recovery happens in place on the same user pool, your application integration keeps working unchanged. PITR is already enabled for eligible user pools. Before you need it, separate the initiate and approve permissions, add an alert on recovery calls, and practice the preview workflow on a test pool.

Title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: VMware 0-Day, Java4Shell, NGINX2Root, Ruby2Shell, and a Whole Lot of Shell Trouble
Context: ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been...
Full Text:
A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.

This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.

The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week.

⚡ Threat of the Week

Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.

Attackers now weaponize AI to launch personalized phishing attacks faster than employees can react. Fight AI with AI, using realistic simulations to train employees to spot and stop threats. Stop phishing before it becomes a breach.

🔔 Top News

Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks.

Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue.

New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.

GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser).

📰 Around the Cyber World

Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers.

A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India.

The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs.

Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries.

Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.

Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism.

Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed.

Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027.

Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days."

Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both."

Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025.

Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences."

At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service."

Conclusion

The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done.

That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

Title: Signal Moves to Block  iOS and Android AI Agents From Reading Chats
Context: Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini...
Full Text:
Signal has moved to stop AI agents built into iOS and Android from capturing users' chats, warning that it could not control anything they collected.

Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini on Android and Apple's Siri AI, "an existential threat to Signal."

Protections Vary by Platform

On Android, it said Screen security, an existing setting, would switch on automatically when Signal spotted an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Signal explained that because there are multiple versions of Android beyond Google, for many vendors, there is no reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Signal said it chose detection over blocking all screenshots, which would have impacted the user experiance.

Users could turn the protection off, though Signal warned this could leave their messages, and their contacts', open to AI agents. Blocking screenshots also does not stop agents from reading data already stored on a device, Signal said.

On iOS 27, Signal said it was preventing screenshots and showed a setting called "Block Siri AI."

However, on macOS 27, Signal said it had no dependable way to stop screenshots and that Apple's screen-protection options covered only streaming and copy-protected media. It advised users to add Signal to the Siri Excluded Apps list.

In 2025, Signal began blocking screenshots by default on Windows 11 to keep out Microsoft Recall, which takes screenshots every few seconds and stores their text in a searchable database that Signal said could keep even disappearing messages indefinitely.

Signal Presses Platform Makers for an Opt-Out

Title: US Lawmakers Propose CISA Board to Review Major Cyber Incidents
Context: It would also set out criteria for selecting incidents for review, require a majority vote to launch investigations and provide for regular congressional oversight
Full Text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) could soon be empowered with new authority to investigate and review major cyber incidents affecting national security.

Representatives Morgan Luttrell (R-TX) and Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced a new bill on November 18 that seeks to establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board (NCAI Board) within CISA.

This new board would examine significant cyber incidents affecting US organizations, identify root causes and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future.

The proposed bill, provisionally called the Reviewing Origins, Outcomes, and Threats from Cyber and Artificial Intelligence to Understand Security Events Act (ROOT CAUSE Act), specifies that the NCAI Board would have no regulatory or enforcement authority, and its reviews would not assign civil or criminal liability.

The legislation would establish governance rules covering board membership, conflicts of interest, access to information and the protection of sensitive material. It would also set out criteria for selecting incidents for review, require a majority vote to launch investigations and provide for regular congressional oversight.

Commenting on the legislation introduced through House Homeland Security Republicans, Rep. Luttrell described cyber as “the next phase in the evolution of warfare.”

“As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in this space, it is more critical than ever that we take action,” he added.

Read more: New UK Cyber Monitoring Centre Introduces 'Richter Scale' for Cyber-Attacks

Republican Congressmen Introduce Three Additional AI and Cybersecurity Bills

The proposed ROOT CAUSE Act was among four new bills proposed by Republican representatives of the US Committee on Homeland Security on November 18.

The Improving Nonhuman-Agent Security, Identification, Governance, Handling and Traceability Act (AI INSIGHT Act) would establish a framework for securing AI agents operating on US federal networks, requiring agencies to identify, monitor and control their access to systems and data.

Meanwhile, the Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act (BRIDGE AI Act) would create a CISA pilot program to recruit AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, academia and research institutions to strengthen the agency's technical capabilities.

Finally, the Sector Engagement for Cybersecurity through Unified Responsibility and Expertise in Information Technology Act (SECURE IT Act) would formally designate the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Information Technology Sector, reinforcing its role in coordinating efforts with industry to protect critical technology infrastructure.

Title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions
Context: A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code
Full Text:
A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1.

"Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

"Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled."

According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation.

The parser options include -

length

lengthInBytes

key

tag

offset, and

the alias passed to namely()

"Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead."

CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.

"[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

Hackers reportedly breached the FBI’s national crime database

The database held more than 19.3 million records in 2025. How many, if any, were exposed is unknown

If someone calls demanding payment over a warrant, hang up and call the agency directly

The FBI is investigating a reported breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database police use to check for outstanding warrants, identify stolen vehicles, and look up missing-person records.

CNN first reported the breach on November 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation. It is unclear when it happened or how the attackers got in. A law enforcement source confirmed the hack to ABC News. The FBI hasn’t publicly confirmed the incident.

NCIC is a computerized database that local, state, and federal agencies can all use. It holds records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. Police officers use it during traffic stops, investigations, and background checks.

The system held more than 19.3 million records in fiscal year 2025. It’s still unclear whether anyone stole data. The database includes the following types of records:

Wanted-person and warrant records

Missing-person records

Criminal history data

Protection orders

Records of stolen vehicles, firearms, and other property

NCIC is one of the databases the FBI checks during firearm background checks. The reports do not say that attackers breached the background-check system itself or that gun buyers’ information was exposed.

If someone stole NCIC data, people who could be affected include those with past arrests, people with protection orders, missing people and their families, and victims of crime. Possible risks include the following:

Exposure of sensitive records. Criminals could use criminal history or details from protection orders for harassment, extortion, or doxxing.

Targeted scams. Scammers could pose as police officers and use details from a real warrant to make a demand for payment sound convincing.

Data enrichment. Records from other sources could be linked to the data in this database, providing attackers with more details to make their messaging believable.

This is the second reported intrusion involving FBI systems in about two months. FBI employees whose information was exposed in the September breach face risks including phishing and identity theft. CNN reported that some felt left in the dark about whether they were affected.

How to stay safe

If you feel your data might be involved, here are some steps you can take while we learn more about the breach:

Be wary of unsolicited calls, emails, or messages from police or the FBI. Law enforcement won’t demand gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers.

Be wary of breach notification emails and texts. Don’t click links. Go to official sites directly.

Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication on your accounts. Passkeys are even better where they’re offered as an option.

Check your own online exposure with a tool like Malwarebytes’ Digital Footprint scan, and keep your devices updated.

Once more information or an official confirmation becomes available, we’ll keep you posted.

If your data was involved in a breach, read our guide for more advice: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

Title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
Context: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers
Full Text:
Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host.

"On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said.

The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine.

The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames.

In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload.

What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder.

It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation.

The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed.

Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online.

"Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said.

"As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026."

Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.

"An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs."

"A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

Title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
Context: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations
Full Text: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied. NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched. Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

Title: N-able Discloses Critical Mail Assure Vulnerability Found During Breach Investigation
Context: N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for...
Full Text:
N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers.

The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in.

The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered.

"An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says.

The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution.

N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline.

Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated.

It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords.

The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented.

The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws.

For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support.

The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install.

SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943.

What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

Title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
Context: One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive
Full Text:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.

Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.

When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.

Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.

The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.

The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.

The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.

The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

Title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
Context: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data...
Full Text: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®
