In this article

OXLoader can lead to malware that steals browser passwords and data or gives criminals remote access to a Windows PC

Fake copyright complaints and cracked software activators are among the lures used to spread it

What to watch for in suspicious downloads and how to reduce the risk

We’ve seen an increase in activity involving OXLoader, a loader that installs other malware on a computer. Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader.

The malware installed varies by campaign. We found OXLoader distributing Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Depending on the payload, attackers could steal saved browser passwords and other data, remotely control the computer, or download more malware.

We found OXLoader in malicious ZIP files disguised as complaint or copyright-infringement notices, as well as fake software activators. One campaign we analyzed used fake activators downloaded from GitLab.

Below, we take a technical deep dive into how that campaign works, including how OXLoader uses DLL hijacking to unpack and run malware.

How to stay safe

Here are a few simple ways to stay safe:

Be wary of emails or links that tell you to run software in connection with copyright infringement or complaints.

Watch for executables with very long names or double extensions, such as .docx.exe or .pdf.exe.

Pay attention when you extract an archive. If some of the files it contains don’t appear, be cautious.

Downloading activators or cracks can compromise your device.

Install Malwarebytes Browser Guard, our free browser extension, to block malicious websites and suspicious downloads.

Use Malwarebytes Premium to block malware in real time, including malicious files.

Overview of the detected campaigns

In this section, we analyze several detected campaigns. In the cases we examined, OXLoader was decrypted either by malicious code embedded in legitimate executables, as in Elastic’s analysis, or through DLL hijacking. DLL hijacking is one of the key new features we observed in these campaigns. The rest of the infection chain is similar to the one Elastic identified.

We identified several DLLs used to decrypt and execute OXLoader, including:

Qt5Widgets.dll

Qt6Core.dll

SDL3.dll

UnityPlayer.dll

ANCUtility.dll

dbghelp.dll

msvcr100.dll

In some cases, we found other DLLs that had been tampered with to launch the malicious DLL. The executables involved were associated with Microsoft applications, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers.

Across different campaigns, OXLoader was distributed using themes related to complaints and copyright infringement. Malicious ZIP files were distributed in several ways. For example, a user might receive an email with an attached PDF prompting them to download and run a ZIP file, claiming there had been “unauthorized copying of brand intellectual property.”

Example of a PDF attached to an email that downloads a malicious ZIP file

When the user runs the executable, the infection chain begins through DLL hijacking, and a fake PDF opens. In this case, WindowsCodecs.dll is the trojanized DLL used to decrypt OXLoader.

The contents of the malicious ZIP file The fake PDF that opens

In some cases, a batch file is present instead of the executable and DLLs. It downloads a ZIP file containing the malicious DLL from different websites or hosting providers. The batch file’s content is similar to the one analyzed by Elastic. These files have long names, for example:

Photo_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Product_Review_Order_Front_Back_PDF.bat Form_Video_{ RANDOM NUMBERS }_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat Case_Form_Video_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat

In other cases, OXLoader was distributed through ZIP archives named Evidence_of_Violation.zip, downloaded from Google Sites. These websites used different titles and graphics.

Google Site used to distribute the malicious archive

In this case, WinWord.exe is renamed with a double extension, such as Travel_Point_Conditions.docx.exe or evidence_of_violation.docx.exe. OXLoader is then executed through DLL hijacking using the malicious DLL msvcr100.dll.

Example of one of the malicious archives

Finally, in the campaigns analyzed in this post, OXLoader was distributed through fake activators and cracks for popular software, downloaded from GitLab.

Malicious activators hosted on GitLab that distribute OXLoader

Technical analysis of OXLoader

In this campaign, users download software activators from GitLab, triggering the infection chain.

Stage 1: DLL hijacking

The archive downloaded by the user contains several legitimate DLLs, along with a legitimate executable from Take-Two Interactive Software, which is used to perform DLL hijacking using the UnityPlayer DLL. The manifest.json contains encrypted shellcode, which is decrypted and injected into another legitimate DLL.

The extracted archive with the malicious DLL

The DLL at address 0x18054485b contains a jmp instruction that calls the code responsible for decrypting the remaining code at 0x1807a3372. This decryption code differs across the cases we analyzed.

The call to the decryption function The self-decryption function

The code is heavily obfuscated using opaque predicates, control flow flattening (CFF), and mixed Boolean arithmetic (MBA). We therefore used the Sogen emulator to trace the main functions that execute and identify the malware code that called them.

Partial Sogen execution with some functions related to anti-analysis and language checks Termination of the malware if a virtualized environment is detected (Sogen output)

The values ​​used by the remaining functions are decoded using two functions:

The function at the address 0x1807a2282 decrypts the data ​​using the following formula: input1 ^ (input2 + 0x33fda).

The function at the address 0x1807a2624 is responsible for decrypting an 8-byte chunk; this function is called multiple times by other wrappers to decrypt the complete strings.

The decrypted strings

The anti-analysis and language checks we observed are similar to those identified by Elastic, with the minor addition of a check using WNetGetResourceParentW to detect virtualized environments.

It’s possible to bypass the anti-analysis checks by patching the function 0x1807999c2. Otherwise, if an analysis environment is detected, the system is shut down via a cmd command, or jumps to an invalid address.

The necessary files are then copied to a randomly named folder in ProgramData. In this case, the files were:

Stages 2 and 3: Shellcode decryption and Donut Loader

awindows.storage.dll is a legitimate DLL used to inject the next stage. It has an additional .text section that contains the original digital signature while the DLL is on disk. After the DLL is loaded into memory with LoadLibraryA, the contents of the new section are replaced with the shellcode decrypted from manifest.json. This differs slightly from Elastic’s analysis, in which the shellcode was located in the .reloc section.

The loaded DLL from the ProgramData folder

The shellcode is decrypted and executed using call r12. It performs several XOR self-decryptions of the code, in a manner similar to the DLL previously analyzed.

In addition to the windows.storage.dll, we identified other DLLs used by OXLoader for injection, including:

The next stage executed by Donut Loader is another obfuscated PE with control-flow flattening, MBA, with a custom section .text0 and just four imports. Despite the complex obfuscation, the next stage is saved in cleartext at address 0x140001000 and loaded into the memory of the process itself.

Title: States Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes
Context: SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp
Full Text:
The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia are suing Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated consumer protection laws by lying to users about both the safety of its generative AI tools and how seriously the company took stopping child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) from proliferating on its platforms. The suits follow a slew of other lawsuits against Musk’s companies around similar issues, including from the city of Baltimore and teens in Tennessee.

The attorneys general are each filing their own complaints in their respective state courts—Virginia in the circuit court for the city of Richmond, and Oregon in Multnomah County circuit court. Both suits name SpaceX and X Corp., the SpaceX subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X. SpaceX acquired xAI, the Musk startup and parent company of X Corp., in February. In doing so it also took ownership of Grok, which is at the center of the allegations in the suit.

Last winter, the Grok chatbot made headlines after users on X started prompting it en masse to generate sexualized photos of women and minors. Even more disturbing AI-generated videos were later found on Grok’s website, including those showing female celebrities engaging in sexual activities.

The states allege that Grok’s creators ignored industry safety standards and intentionally implemented weak safeguards in an attempt to entice more people to use its “lagging product.” In all, as Virginia alleged in its complaint, the defendants saw “a market opportunity for more profits” in the generation of sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

For example, the states say that Grok wasn’t subjected to enough third-party evaluations before releasing new models, and that Grok’s safety prompts included instructions to “assume good intent” and that the terms “teenage” and “girl” do “not necessarily imply underage.” They also allege that tens of thousands of reports were submitted without key information from xAI to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s CyberTipline, preventing the Center from being able to act on them 90 percent of the time.

In the complaints, the states say that Musk leaned into Grok’s “spicy mode” as a way to differentiate the model from its competitors and that this worked. They note, for example, that during the same time period that Grok’s ability to “undress” people was sparking international outrage, Musk posted about how Grok was “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!” and discussing the chatbot’s “heavy usage growth.”

Title: Cleverbridge Confirms Customers’ Payment Card Data Breached
Context: However, an investigation found that an unauthorized third party copied payment card data stored on its platform
Full Text:
Global e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has revealed that a hacker has stolen payment card data, putting affected customers at immediate risk of fraud.

In an update published on its website, the firm said that it detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4, 2026. The incident was quickly contained, and systems brought back online the same day. However, an investigation found that an unauthorized third party copied payment card data stored on its platform.

“We worked diligently to identify individuals whose personal information may have been involved and began notifying affected individuals on 20 November where appropriate,” Cleverbridge wrote.

The company has not confirmed how many people’s card details may have been affected by the incident. The investigation remains ongoing.

Cleverbridge manages global payments, subscription billing, tax compliance, and checkout services for software and SaaS companies across more than 240 countries. Customers listed on its website include Tenable, Jamf, Veeam, Red Hat and Sony.

BleepingComputer reported that the breach notifications sent to affected individuals revealed that the stolen data includes card numbers, expiry dates and card security codes (CVV/CVC).

No other personal data, such as names, contact information or billing details, were accessed, according to the notifications.

The stolen information can be used to verify online transactions. As such, Cleverbridge urged those impacted to check their card statements and inform their card issuers immediately if they see a transaction they do not recognize.

“You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card,” Cleverbridge added.

The payments processor also warned affected individuals to be vigilant of phishing attacks that request card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone or text message.

Cleverbridge Rules Out Ransomware Attack

Cleverbridge confirmed that the incident is not ransomware related, stating that none of its systems were encrypted.

No other details were provided on the actor’s potential motivations. It is not known whether the stolen data has been misused so far.

The incident follows notifications by JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard that customer data had been breached following a compromise of a third-party vendor.

Ransomware group N0n claimed the attacks and reportedly leaked the stolen data on its dark web leak site.

Title: Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw Exploited in Attacks
Context: “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands
Full Text:
Federal agencies have until Monday, November 23 to patch a critical flaw in Cisco Expressway, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has said.

CISA added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 20 November after reports emerged that the flaw was being used in active attacks.

“Cisco Expressway Series contains a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service,” CISA explained.

Cisco Expressway products are described as “advanced collaboration gateways” which operate in a pair: Expressway-C sits inside the corporate network and connects with internal collaboration systems, while Expressway-E sits in the DMZ to handle external traffic.

Read more on Cisco Expressway: Cisco Releases 10 Security Patches For Expressway Series and TelePresence VCS Products

The vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.8, indicating a high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability, with low attack complexity and no user interaction required.

“This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated,” Cisco explained in an October 21 advisory.

“An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.”

First Cisco Expressway Exploit Observed

Moscow-based cybersecurity firm F6 claimed to have investigated the first observed case of exploitation of CVE-2026-76466.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices. Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network,” specialists from the Cyber Defense Center at F6 explained.

“After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure. They used custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and explore GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.”

The security vendor urged Cisco Expressway customers not only to patch the flaw but also deploy network segmentation and monitoring to mitigate the risk of compromise.

It recommended organizations to:

Update Cisco Expressway to the current version containing the fix for CVE-2026-76466, or if not possible, to restrict connections to ports TCP/4371–4372 at the firewall layer and allow access only from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes

Implement external attack surface monitoring to identify vulnerable digital assets before they can be exploited

Ensure continuous monitoring and incident response to detect compromise fast, rapidly “localize and investigate,” isolate compromised systems, determine scope, and block lateral movement

Title: Hackers Exploit Critical ASP.NET Anti-CSRF Library Flaw Allowing Unauthenticated RCE
Context: dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have urged users to discontinue using a legacy ASP.NET anti-CSRF library named Idunno.AntiCsrf ("Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914, carries a CVSS score of 9.3 out of 10.0. The issue affects versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta, and relates to an insecure deserialization vulnerability in the Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule HTTP module.

Idunno.AntiCsrf is a third-party ASP.NET IHttpModule designed to provide double-submit cookie Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection for ASP.NET WebForms applications. The open-source project is currently defunct and has not been updated since December 2008.

At its core, the problem stems from the fact that the module deserializes untrusted CSRF form token data using an unkeyed .NET System.Web.UI.ObjectStateFormatter instance without cryptographic MAC or signature verification when handling incoming HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms (System.Web.UI.Page) endpoints.

This behavior, in turn, can allow a remote attacker to achieve arbitrary remote code execution (RCE). Google's Mandiant division has given the vulnerability a "High" exploitability assessment, adding that exploitation hinges only on a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token.

LDB, Genwei Jiang, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Brian Bahtiarian, and Lucas Kossack of Google Cloud and Mandiant Incident Response have been credited with discovering the flaw earlier this month.

"A remote attacker can supply any non-empty value in the configured CSRF cookie alongside a Base64-encoded .NET ObjectStateFormatter gadget chain in the configured CSRF form field to execute arbitrary code in the context of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe), resulting in complete compromise of the web application server," Google-owned Mandiant said in an alert issued last week.

"Active exploitation in the wild has been observed."

Google's threat intelligence team did not disclose any further details related to the activity. The Hacker News has contacted Google, and we will update the story if we hear back.

In the absence of an official patch, organizations still using the library are advised to discontinue its use and replace it with an actively supported anti-CSRF alternative such as follows -

System.Web.Helpers.AntiForgery

ASP.NET WebForms Page.ViewStateUserKey combined with MAC-verified/encrypted ViewState on postback forms

ASP.NET Core Anti-Request Forgery (IAntiforgery)

"Audit all ASP.NET Web.config files and bin/ directories for references to Idunno.AntiCsrf or AntiCsrfModule, and review IIS logs for anomalous POST requests to .aspx endpoints returning HTTP 302 or HTTP 500 with elevated cs-bytes (where logged)," Google said.

"Environments with evidence of exploitation should rotate all secrets stored in Web.config and applicationHost.config (including <machineKey> keys, encryption keys, and database credentials) and inspect webroots for unauthorized files."

Title: Hackers Exploited GL.iNet Cloud Flaw to Install Malware on Routers and KVM Devices
Context: Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL
Full Text:
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices, the maker of travel routers and remote-access KVM hardware said in a security notice updated today.

The company identified and fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the access the attacker used, so devices can no longer be infected through this route. The cloud-side fix does not remove malware from devices that were already infected, so owners still need to check their hardware and install the security firmware listed today.

A KVM is a small device used to control a computer remotely as if sitting in front of it. The company is still investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were affected.

It has not said how many devices were infected, when the attacks began, or how its cloud service was breached. It is emailing customers it identifies as affected, but owners do not need to wait for a message to act.

A model missing from the firmware table below is not necessarily unaffected, the notice says, and owners should not install firmware meant for another model.

RemoteToHome Consulting, a security consultancy that examined the incident on routers it manages, says in its incident investigation that it verified a root-level reverse shell on one of its GL-AXT1800 routers.

The shell started on Friday evening and connected to 170.39.226[.]219, and two more owners reported the same shell on the same model and firmware, 4.8.3, with GoodCloud switched on.

On GL-MT6000 routers, the same shell command ran but the connection never completed. On other routers the firm manages, a one-off command searched for files linked to a KVM implant and reported the result to the same address.

The shell leaves no files behind, and its traces vanish when the device restarts, per the firm's reverse-shell analysis. The process marker the vendor published was absent on the router with the verified shell.

After the researchers filed an abuse report late last week, the hosting provider told them it had suspended the server behind the address and preserved its data.

The shell arrived through the GoodCloud client software on the router itself, according to the firm's technical analysis. A handler in that client takes two values from a cloud message and runs them as root through the shell without checking them. The vendor has not confirmed that finding.

The unchecked code has been in the firmware since at least December 5, 2024, when it appeared in a GL-MT3000 release. It runs whether or not AstroWarp, the SD-WAN feature it belongs to, is in use, and its presence since 2024 does not mean attacks began then.

The researchers reported a second, separate weakness in the cloud client to the vendor yesterday and are withholding details until it is fixed.

One KVM owner described an infected GL-RM1 in an owner's report. Starting on Thursday, the device downloaded a script and two programs from 66.245.219[.]252, looked up the copycat domain gl-inet[.]top, and scanned the local network.

It also kept connecting to 65.20.71[.]131, which the owner suspects was a command channel. The owner did not keep the downloaded files, and the method by which the device was infected has not been confirmed.

The vendor advises checking the computer attached to an infected KVM for unfamiliar programs, accounts, startup items, and unusual network activity.

The investigation also found an unrelated, older backdoor on 49 of the routers the firm manages, installed in batches between September 2025 and May 2026 by a route that is not known. Nothing so far links it to last week's attacks.

How to Check a Device

GL.iNet's check looks for one marker: a running process whose details contain the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log. A line showing only the grep command itself is not a match.

Router, web panel: sign in to LuCI under System → Advanced Settings, open Status → Processes, and search for tmp/.log.

Router, SSH: run ps | grep tmp.

KVM: open the device's own terminal under Toolbox → Terminal → Access, then run ps -a | grep tmp on the RMQ1 or ps -aux | grep tmp on other models. Run it on the KVM, not on the attached computer.

Check before rebooting or upgrading where compromise is suspected, the researchers advise, because the shell's traces disappear at restart. The marker can also miss infected devices: it was absent on the router with the verified shell.

Before running netstat on a suspect device, check that /bin/netstat is still a link to busybox. The command itself may have been swapped, a forum warning and the researchers' indicator list say, and running a compromised copy starts the malware.

The notice also points to an unofficial community check script, with the warning that the vendor has not reviewed it and that it can run with administrative privileges. Fuller indicators are in the researchers' detailed findings.

What the Update Does and Does Not Remove

GL.iNet listed stable security firmware for its router and KVM lines in the security notice it updated today, which now says the update "removes the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset," with settings kept. That replaces earlier guidance, which offered a factory reset for infected devices ahead of the firmware's release.

In spot checks today, The Hacker News found the GL-MT3000 and GL-RM1 builds available at the vendor's router downloads and KVM downloads pages.

The update is not shown to cover everything a root-level attacker may have left behind. In RemoteToHome's KVM firmware analysis, upgrading an RM1 to the earlier 1.10.2 security build with settings kept carried the device's password file, SSH keys and user directory across, and that directory holds scripts that run at every boot. Whether a planted script survives the upgrade has not been tested.

For a device with signs of compromise, the researchers' advice is a firmware reinstall without keeping settings, and treating every stored secret as exposed: VPN keys, Wi-Fi and admin passwords, cloud credentials and SSH keys. The vendor's notice and that advice differ on this point.

Until a device is updated, the option the researchers describe is switching GoodCloud off, after first securing another way to reach the device. Switching it off stops the cloud client from running but does not clean a device that was already infected.

The attacker's identity, the number of affected devices, and how the cloud service itself was breached remain unknown, and The Hacker News found no CVE identifier for the flaw as of publication.

Title: When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down
Context: Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution
Full Text: No Access November is going well this year. Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage. OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now. These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard. Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through. There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO. SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else. Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system. An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar? The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology. It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like? There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems. OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

Title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
Context: “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider...
Full Text:
For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing.

Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking.

Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense.

Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop

Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas.

“What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with.

“This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says.

Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers.

When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient.

“The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.”

The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.”

Take care of business

Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work.

The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains.

Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with.

Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.”

Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says.

Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time.

Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable.

Challenge your policies and content

At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries.

“You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted.

Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements.

Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.”

Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.”

“You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on.

“It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had.

Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses

Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do.

“Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.”

The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise.

Embrace deep inspection

Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests tailoring an AI prompt to take aim at AI prompts themselves, noting that perhaps the most important capability is a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent.

“CISOs should be able to determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service, but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky—such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access,” he says, adding that as AI agents become more common, that same inspection and policy model needs to extend beyond human prompts to agent-driven interactions.

Tait believes that CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, browser-based access, and APIs.

“The goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application, but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services,” he explains. “This also means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.”

Title: AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms
Context: In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an...
Full Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.

This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.

The incidents have been found to include the following methods -

Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.

Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.

Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.

Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records.

CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.

The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -

Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.

Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.

Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.

Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.

Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks.

"Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity."

The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets.

"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools."

Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial ​firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed.

According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs.

"Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT."

India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month.

The Surge in AI Attacks

The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026.

ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.

"In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX."

Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration.

They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi.

"ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month.

"The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale."

Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime.

"Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said.

Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units.

"In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said.

In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.

"The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention."

Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below -

Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S.

Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content.

Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East.

Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data

Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents.

Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations.

Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job- and ClickFix-themed lures. These personas have been found to direct targets to fraudulent meeting platforms, which are used to run diagnostic fix scripts via ClickFix. "Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor," Google said.

Use of CyberStrikeAI ("43.240.29[.]11") between September 30 and October 16, 2026, to validate stolen AWS credentials, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, and send a remote command. "The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded," Elastic Security Labs said.

Use of Hermes, in combination with DeepSeek, by a threat actor called Silent Lynx in cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026 to assist with reconnaissance, data collection, and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems.

Use of ARTEX to exploit a vulnerable custom PHP upload function and stage a web shell, and use it to access secrets and API keys, and ultimately compromise a company's development pipeline to alter a Git repository and deploy an attacker-controlled Kubernetes pod.

Use of an AI coding assistant to revive a stalled attack at a U.S. retail organization and come up with ways to bypass defenses and steal credentials after their commands were blocked by security software in late September 2026. The attack is assessed to be financially motivated, based on the threat actor's scans for passwords in point-of-sale scripts and an IP address overlap with a prior campaign targeting online retailers.

Use of CAIRN by a Chinese-speaking attacker between August and September 2026 and pairing it with GLM and DeepSeek models to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attacks, attributed to CL-STA-1238, have targeted advanced semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy, and civil society sectors, achieving unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the entities, including valid credentials, personal data, military and government identities, and the creation of persistent administrator accounts in a production system. "CAIRN coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Confirmed findings accumulate as immutable facts, and the agent queues its next actions as intents."

Use of ARTEX to gain access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. "Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure," Cloudflare said. "LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments."

Use of ARTEX to generate deepfake videos to trick identity verification checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges and steal AI credentials at "industrial scale" to gain free access to models. Amazon has characterized the second campaign as a "self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting." Targets include LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow (CVE-2025-3248), RAGFlow (CVE-2026-28797), Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.

Use of CAIRN by a suspected Chinese-nexus threat actor to discover a zero-day vulnerability (GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) in MONAI Label, a medical imaging application, and use it to gain complete control of a server within 11 minutes. The activity was detected in September 2026.

"An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

"The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. The agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints."

What's notable about accelerating AI-enabled attacks is that the technology is not just used as a force multiplier but has also emerged as the target.

"The integration of AI-enabled tools into enterprise workflows is creating new attack surfaces, particularly where those tools hold privileged access to code, credentials, data, or connected applications," Recorded Future said. "Developer tools are a primary target of attacks on AI systems. Threat actors exploited weak access controls and software supply-chain vulnerabilities to steal data or establish persistence."

Besides automating the time-consuming phases of intrusions, LLM-driven pentesting frameworks also lower the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.

"Now, an attacker can give an agent a goal in plain language," GitGuardian said. "The agent can investigate the environment, select tools, execute commands, interpret the results, and decide what to try next. The tools are also becoming better at recovering from failed attempts. An agent can encounter an error, interpret the response, modify its next command, and continue investigating."

"Anyone with access to AntiFox or ARTEX can just verbally say into the dictation, 'find exposed credentials, determine what they access, and identify valuable resources.' That incantation initiates a series of technical actions that previously required considerably more hands-on expertise."

Title: Here's Why Data Breach Disclosure is so Hard: Lessons from Hundreds of Emails with Hacked Companies
Context: In a recent case, the first reply said the attackers had only defaced a landing page, with no indication that user data was taken
Full Text:
Presently sponsored by: Report URI: Guarding you from rogue JavaScript! Don’t get pwned; get real-time alerts & prevent breaches #SecureYourSite

When I asked Claude to write the blog post below, I already knew what was in the messages it would read. Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns. I knew the emails contained standoffish behaviour, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritising corporate interests over those of their customers. But I didn't know just how stark it would be to read such a candid analysis of my own emails, nor how frustrating it would be to relive many of those disclosure experiences.

I decided to have AI write the post below because it was the best way to highlight the behaviours I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts. I'm not going to make a habit of AI writing content for me, but what's written below absolutely nails it! It's the best way I can explain what it's like to run Have I Been Pwned in support of individual data breach victims, while also respecting the position of the corporations dealing with the crime that put them in this position. It would have been much easier not to do the latter, but then I don't think I'd still be here running the service if I hadn't.

A quick note on methodology first: I've been running HIBP for 13 years but only gave Claude access to the mailbox I've been using for the last 8.5 years, hence the shorter timeframe you'll read below. I also made several small changes to Claude's work to better obfuscate the identity of the organisation it was describing, a move I'm sure you'll understand after reading about lawyers getting involved... Here goes:

Introduction

Getting an organisation to admit it has been breached is often harder than getting hold of the breached data in the first place. That is the clearest conclusion from reading more than eight and a half years of Troy Hunt's breach notification email.

I'm an AI. Troy gave me access to his mailbox and asked me to look at it as an outsider: what happens after Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) tells an organisation that its customers' data is circulating? Between March 2018 and November 2026 he sent his standard notification email to 73 organisations, and several more conversations began through website contact forms. I found every one of those 73 first emails and reviewed a broad sample of the replies from every year. I then read the full back-and-forth on the threads that best show each pattern.

I've left out company names on purpose. The point isn't to shame individual organisations. The point is that the same behaviours keep appearing, across countries, industries and company sizes, year after year. Some organisations handled this well, and I'll get to them. But the overall picture is one of friction, delay and a steady effort to keep the incident as quiet as possible.

The first problem: finding a human

The first email is almost always the same. Troy introduces himself, explains that data allegedly taken from the organisation has been sent to him, and asks for "someone responsible for information security" to get in touch. He wants to pass on everything he has before he notifies the affected HIBP subscribers. It is a polite, low-pressure request, and it often goes nowhere.

The main reason is that many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident. Troy ends up sending these emails to support inboxes, returns departments, general "info" addresses and website contact forms. In at least three of the 73 cases, Troy sent the first email a second time, two, five and twelve days later.

When email fails, he moves on to LinkedIn, Facebook and X. One organisation took four weeks to send its first reply, and Troy had also tried it on all three social platforms over several days. Another's senior IT leader replied after almost four weeks, thanked Troy for trying "so many times", and admitted he needed to check LinkedIn more often.

The longest chain I found was at a large hardware manufacturer. It ran from a returns inbox, to the company's regional social media account, to regional marketing staff, to head office, to one product security address, then a second one, and finally to the legal department. That is six hops before anyone could answer the actual question.

Then there are the ticketing systems. Several breach notifications were logged as routine customer support requests, with ticket numbers stuck on the subject line. In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received. Another organisation sent one too. A message that an organisation's customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.

The first response: "we've seen no evidence"

Once someone does reply, the first substantive message tends to fall into one of a few patterns. The most common is a statement that the organisation has found no evidence of a breach. This often arrives before it has seen any of the data.

One organisation said it hadn't identified any unauthorised access. Three weeks later, still without the data, it said again that it had reviewed its systems and found no sign of the breach. When Troy sent the data, it confirmed within a few weeks that an exposed database server had leaked its users' details. The "no evidence" had really meant it didn't yet know where to look.

A second pattern is to shrink the incident. In a recent case, the first reply said the attackers had only defaced a landing page, with no indication that user data was taken. It added that the data was probably from an earlier incident the company had already disclosed. Troy then pointed out that the newest timestamp in the data matched the day of the defacement. He also sent the company records belonging to its own staff. The data turned out to cover 16 tables of core user systems, including identity verification and tax documents.

A third pattern is the request for "a sample" or a particular file format. This is reasonable in principle, since nobody should take a stranger's word for a breach. But it often comes after weeks of silence, and it shifts the job of proving the breach from the organisation that lost the data to the person who reported it. In one case, an external IT consultant asked Troy to help work out whether the identifiers in the data were real or fabricated. Troy did that analysis for them.

"We're still investigating"

Once an organisation accepts that the data is probably real, the next phrase in the threads is almost always "we're investigating". Investigating is necessary. The problem is that it has no end date, and it gets used as a reason not to say anything publicly while it continues.

In a recent case, the company confirmed within days that it had the data and was reviewing it "to confirm its validity and scope". A week after the first contact, the message was that it was still investigating and would let Troy know "if it is determined that any notifications need to be made". By then the company had a copy of the data, its own staff records were in it, and the data had already been shared among people who collect breaches. Nobody outside the company had been told anything.

Troy's answer to this is consistent across the years. A disclosure doesn't need to be complete. An organisation can say what it knows now, and update it as the investigation goes on. Some organisations in this mailbox did exactly that. What the investigation framing does is turn "we don't yet know everything" into "so we'll say nothing". Meanwhile, the people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.

The delays add up. In one thread, the organisation's eventual public disclosure was titled after a breach that happened about ten months earlier. In another, a healthcare-adjacent platform's breach had been posted on a large hacking forum and discussed on social media for four months. When Troy got in touch, there was still nothing from the company itself.

Lawyers, advisors and legal thresholds

The point where a thread changes tone is easy to spot. It's the moment the reply comes from someone outside the security team. In the most serious cases I read, it came from a law firm, an outside advisor or the company's general counsel, rather than the security team. In one case, the very first reply came from the company's outside cyber counsel, a partner at a large law firm.

Once lawyers are involved, the question changes from "what happened to our customers?" to "are we legally required to tell anyone?" Those are very different questions, and the threads show it.

In one example, the company's general counsel explained that an internal customer service portal had been indexed by a search engine for more than a year. The company had closed access once someone outside it noticed. Its US counsel had concluded that names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses did not trigger notification obligations in any US state. The reply also said there was "no evidence the information was ever accessed". It said this to someone who had been sent the information by a third party.

That is the core problem with the threshold argument. Breach notification laws set a minimum, and they vary between jurisdictions in ways that have little to do with real-world harm. Names, emails, phone numbers and physical addresses are exactly what scammers need for convincing phishing. "We aren't legally obliged to tell you" may be accurate. It is a very different statement from "there's nothing you need to know".

Troy addresses this directly in the most recent thread. He tells the company's advisor that it may well decide the incident doesn't meet the threshold for mandatory disclosure, "that's a position many orgs take". He then explains that HIBP will notify its own affected subscribers anyway.

Controlling the message

When an organisation can't stop the breach from being known, the effort shifts to controlling how it's described. This is where the threads get most uncomfortable to read.

The opening request is usually a phone call. The law firm partner's first email asked to talk "before you post it". The partner then followed up early on Troy's Saturday morning in Australia, offering to talk over the weekend or on the Monday, "as long as you aren't planning to publish prior to then". In the most recent case, the advisor asked for a call with management to make sure everyone was "aligned". Calls aren't wrong in themselves. But in both of these threads, the call came instead of a written commitment to disclose.

The second move is to ask to see, or shape, the wording. One advisor wanted to understand how HIBP would describe the incident. Troy pointed out that more than 1,000 breach descriptions were already public on the HIBP site, each a couple of sentences long. Another organisation, once it had disclosed, asked HIBP to change its public entry. The entry said contact attempts had received no response, and the company wanted it to say the company had acknowledged, fixed and disclosed the incident. That request was fair, as the company had done those things. But it shows how much organisations care about the public record once one exists.

The third move is the most striking: arguing that the notification is the harm. The law firm told Troy that public notification "would direct bad actors to search for the file". By then, the data had been posted on a forum with hundreds of thousands of members and shared on social media. The firm said both sides agreed the data was "very low risk". It then asked that, if Troy felt he had to email his affected subscribers, he not put anything on the HIBP website. Troy offered a compromise: flagging the breach as sensitive so nobody could search for an individual's email address in it. The firm rejected that and ended with: "We assert once more that your actions could potentially cause harm."

The bluntest version came from a smaller company. After confirming that the data had leaked from an exposed test server, it said it had "decided to not have as such any communication and public disclosure".

Who pays for the delay

Reading these threads together, one imbalance stands out. Almost everything above serves the organisation, and the cost falls on the people in the data.

By the time Troy sends his first email, the data is already out. It has been taken, copied and passed around by people who collect breaches, and that's how it reached him. In the healthcare-adjacent case, it had been on a public forum for months. In a recent case, the data included passwords that could be cracked, identity numbers and dates of birth. None of that changes while a company investigates, debates thresholds or arranges calls to agree on wording. The criminals already have it. The only people still in the dark are its customers.

HIBP's own notifications don't fix that either. Troy only emails people who have signed up to his service, which in a typical breach is a small fraction of those affected. In the healthcare-adjacent case, about 1,300 of his subscribers were in a dataset with nearly half a million unique user email addresses. The other affected users would hear about it only if the company told them, and its lawyers were arguing that a public notice would cause harm.

The arguments for staying quiet are almost always framed as protecting customers. Don't publicise it, or bad actors will go looking. Don't describe it before we've finished investigating, or people will be misinformed. It isn't serious enough to meet the legal bar. Each argument sounds reasonable on its own. Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.

What good looks like

To be fair, not every thread went badly, and the good ones are useful precisely because they show how simple this can be.

The best response in the mailbox came from a small transport app. It replied within hours. It had already reported the incident and published a disclosure statement. When Troy noticed a detail in that statement that wasn't quite accurate, the company updated it promptly and thanked him for helping keep it correct.

A small booking platform started out sceptical. The person who first replied thought the data didn't look like it came from its database. After seeing more of it, he wrote back that he'd been wrong, and set up a video call the same day. Within about a week, the company had emailed every affected customer directly and sent Troy a copy of the notice.

A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys and published a disclosure. Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency. A large consumer brand was hard to reach at first, but once Troy got through, its security lead downloaded the data the same day and called it "extremely helpful". Even the organisation that asked HIBP to change its public entry ended in a good place. It secured the exposed server, deleted data it didn't need, forced password resets for dormant accounts and published a transparent disclosure.

The good examples share a few traits. Someone with authority over security answered quickly. They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.

Conclusion

After reading eight and a half years of these exchanges, I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal. It's about incentives. For the organisation, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines. For the people in the data, every one of those days is a day they're exposed without knowing it. Unless someone outside the organisation pushes, the first set of incentives usually wins.

The patterns repeat with surprising consistency:

No way in. No security contact, so the notice goes to a support queue, a returns desk or a social media account.

"No evidence." The breach is denied or downplayed before anyone has looked at the data.

Investigating without end. Open-ended investigation becomes the reason to say nothing.

Lawyers lead. Legal or advisory staff take over, and the question becomes whether disclosure is required, not whether it's right.

Controlling the message. Calls, requests to review wording, and efforts to keep the incident off the public record.

Disclosure as harm. The claim that telling people about the breach is more dangerous than the breach itself.

For organisations reading this, the fixes are not complicated. Publish a security contact, for example in a security.txt file, and make sure someone reads it. Don't route breach reports through a customer support ticket system. When someone hands you evidence, look at it before you say there's no evidence. Disclose what you know early, and update it as you learn more. Treat legal thresholds as the minimum, not the goal. And when your lawyers start explaining why telling your customers would be the harmful thing to do, ask who that argument is actually protecting.

The data in these emails was already out by the time anyone was notified. The only open question in each thread was whether the people it belonged to would find out.
