Full Text:
Over 27 years ago, CVE-1999-0001 was reserved as the first vulnerability in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database. Since then, this catalog has grown quickly, especially in recent years with the advent of AI-assisted security research. In this post, we introduce Mitigeddon, a new public website that security practitioners and leaders can use to stay on top of the latest impactful vulnerabilities, and better estimate the risk that specific exposures cause to the industry.

The number of CVEs keeps growing faster than real risk

In 2026 so far, well over 100k CVEs have been published. For comparison, this number was 50k in 2025 and 40k in 2024.

However, not all CVEs are created equal. Most CVEs don't appear widely in real-world environments, and only a tiny fraction are exploitable. Of 34k CVEs applicable to software applications, 38% are present in the sample of environments Datadog monitors, 12% are exploitable, and only 0.8% are known to be exploited in the wild according to VulnCheck and CISA. These numbers are similar for CVEs applicable to OS packages and container images: of 113k CVEs, 56% are present in environments, 10% are exploitable, and 0.6% are exploited in the wild.

This evolution means that to keep up, practitioners increasingly need to cut through the noise.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild get weaponized faster

To understand how fast attackers move once a vulnerability is disclosed, we measured the time between a vulnerability's release date and when it was added to the CISA or VulnCheck Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs. In 2026 so far, 17% of vulnerabilities reported as exploited in the wild were exploited on the same day the vulnerability was released, and another 20% within a week. The median time from disclosure to exploitation was 33 days, down from 60 days in 2025 and 163 days in 2024 (these numbers exclude KEV entries released prior to the vulnerability itself, which are indicative of zero-day exploitation rather than weaponization of a freshly released vulnerability).

Mitigeddon: a new project to browse impactful vulnerabilities and visualize their industry impact

Today, we're proud to release Mitigeddon, a website that aggregates data from osv.dev, CISA KEV, VulnCheck KEV, and aggregated Datadog telemetry data from a sample of thousands of real-world applications.

Mitigeddon allows you to:

Quickly identify impactful vulnerabilities that are relevant to cloud environments

Visualize a timeline for each vulnerability, including when it was released, when an exploit was made publicly available, and when threat intelligence sources such as CISA or VulnCheck flagged it as exploited in the wild

Estimate the prevalence of a vulnerability in the industry

Moving forward, we'll also embed live Mitigeddon data in our posts covering Emerging Vulnerabilities. Below is an example of what this looks like for the Java4Shell vulnerability.

We'd love to hear from you

If you have any comments, feedback, or data that you feel we should add to Mitigeddon, shoot us an email at securitylabs@datadoghq.com!

Title: Building security review into your SDLC with Codex Security
Context: Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available
Full Text:
As AI accelerates the SDLC, it’s putting pressure on security workflows. Security teams need to prevent insecure code from being committed in the first place, but manual security reviews for PRs can’t scale at the same pace that agents are producing and revising code.

Application security programs have followed the pace of human development: a design review before implementation, a manual pass on the riskiest pull requests, and periodic work to triage vulnerability backlogs. To keep up, we must now deploy agentic security workflows that match the speed of agentic SDLC.

This post presents four principles for agentic security workflows, then shares how to build and run those workflows through Codex Security and our CLI.

Four principles for agentic security workflows

Expanding security review capacity requires a clear basis for evaluating changes and a clear way for teams to assess the results. We recommend four principles for integrating security agents into development:

Give agents system-specific context

Agents need to understand the application’s assets, trust boundaries, and security requirements to evaluate a change. Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available. Regularly reviewing these artifacts and keeping them current gives agents a reliable foundation for their investigations.

Integrate review into development

Security feedback should reach developers while changes are still in progress. Connect reviews to local work, pull requests, and CI workflows, with clear triggers for when they should run. This makes security review a consistent part of the development process.

Set review scope and reporting thresholds deliberately

Review scope should reflect the change and the components it could affect. A diff scan, a component assessment, and a full repository scan serve different purposes. Reporting thresholds should also reflect risk, giving sensitive areas such as authentication and billing appropriate attention.

Make findings inspectable

Reviewers need enough information to evaluate a finding and determine what action to take. Reports should explain the relevant code locations, reasoning, severity, confidence, and remediation guidance. They should also identify what was reviewed, excluded, or deferred so teams can understand the investigation’s limits.

Seeding context for security reviews

Differences among threat models, AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md, and knowledge bases

AGENTS.md keeps shared engineering instructions that establish consistent expectations. SECURITY.md tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported. A threat model describes the security reality of the system. They overlap, but the threat model is usually one part of the broader policy.

For example, a threat model would include details about assets, entry points, attacker-controlled inputs, trust boundaries, authentication assumptions, privileged operations, and risky components. Commit it as a separate file, docs/security/threat-model.md, so Codex Security can reference it during pull request reviews and security scans.

<!-- docs/security/threat-model.md --> # Threat Model The public API accepts untrusted JSON and file uploads. Requests cross from the internet-facing API into internal billing and identity services. Attackers are unauthenticated users or compromised tenant accounts. Protect tenant data, billing mutations, and service credentials.

The SECURITY.md file tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported.

<!-- SECURITY.md --> # Security Policy ## Security Invariants - Every billing mutation must be authorized for the active tenant. - Uploaded content must be parsed within explicit size and resource limits. - Service credentials must never be returned to clients. ## Reportable Findings Report realistic violations of tenant isolation, authentication bypass, unsafe parsing, secret exposure, or unauthorized billing mutations. ## Severity Context Cross-tenant access is Critical. Single-tenant unauthorized mutation is High. ## Out of Scope Development-only tools that cannot be included in production builds.

Finally, a knowledge base supplies supporting documents to particular scans. This can include architecture documents, policies, additional threat models, or operational context that the CLI scanner should consider. Here’s an example of a Markdown architecture document you can pass to the CLI when running a security scan against a codebase.

<!-- docs/security/payment-service-context.md --> # Payment Service Security Context ## Purpose The payment service creates charges, issues refunds, and stores references to payment-provider customers. It does not store full card numbers or CVVs. ## Deployment and Exposure - `POST /api/payments` is internet-facing through the API gateway. - `POST /internal/refunds` is reachable only from the support service. - Background workers consume messages from the `payment-events` queue. - The service runs with access to the payment-provider API and billing database. ## Authentication and Authorization - Public endpoints use JWTs issued by the identity service. - The API gateway validates signatures, issuer, and expiration. - This service remains responsible for tenant authorization. - Internal requests use workload identity; network location alone is not trusted. - Refunds above £1,000 require a previously recorded approval. ## Trust Boundaries 1. Internet client → API gateway 2. API gateway → payment service 3. Payment service → payment provider 4. Payment service → billing database 5. Message producers → `payment-events` consumer Inputs crossing any of these boundaries must be treated as untrusted unless the receiving component performs the documented validation. ## Sensitive Assets and Operations - Payment-provider API credentials - Customer-to-provider identifier mappings - Charge creation - Refund issuance - Webhook signature secrets - Tenant billing history ## Important Data Flows ### Creating a charge 1. The API receives an authenticated request containing an order identifier. 2. The service retrieves the order using both tenant ID and order ID. 3. The service calculates the amount from server-side order data. 4. The service creates the provider charge with an idempotency key. 5. The resulting provider identifier is stored in the billing database. Client-supplied amounts must never be passed directly to the provider. ### Processing a webhook 1. The raw request body is retained. 2. The provider signature is verified over the raw bytes. 3. The event timestamp must be within five minutes. 4. Duplicate event IDs are ignored. 5. State changes occur only after all validation succeeds. ## Relevant Code - `src/http/payments.ts`: public payment endpoints - `src/http/refunds.ts`: refund endpoints - `src/webhooks/provider.ts`: webhook validation - `src/workers/payment-events.ts`: asynchronous event processing - `src/auth/tenant.ts`: tenant authorization - `src/provider/client.ts`: provider API wrapper ## Security Assumptions - The identity service is trusted to authenticate users, but not to authorize access to payment records. - Queue publishers may be compromised; consumers must validate message content. - API-gateway authentication does not replace service-level tenant checks. - Provider webhook payloads are attacker-controlled until signature validation completes. ## Known Limitations - Legacy refunds created before 2025 do not have idempotency keys. - Webhook replay protection is local to one region. - The development payment-provider emulator does not validate signatures.

It can be supplied to the scan using the following command:

npx @openai/codex-security scan . \ --knowledge-base docs/security/payment-service-context.md

Putting it all together, a useful arrangement could look like the following:

SECURITY.md docs/security/ ├── threat-model.md ├── architecture.md ├── payment-service-context.md ├── authentication.md └── deployment-boundaries.md

Seeding a threat model

Committing a threat model is a core component of informing how Codex should conduct security reviews. You can initialize a threat model by invoking the threat model skill within Codex and committing it.

Generate a Threat Model of this repository that covers entry points and untrusted inputs, sensitive data paths, and privileged actions.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

You can invoke the threat model skill through Codex by simply typing $threat-model. Once a threat model has been created, commit it to the repository under /docs/security and then link to the threat model within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. If a threat model is not specified, Codex will regenerate the threat model for every security review.

When generating a threat model, pay particular attention to assumptions that the code alone can’t establish, such as compensating controls and responsibilities shared with other services.

Want an even better example? Look at the trust model for Backstage, an open-source framework for building an internal developer portal. A generated model might treat its authentication and catalog plugins as isolated because they run on separate hosts. However, Backstage’s threat model explains that this separation does not establish a security boundary if the catalog plugin can still access the authentication plugin’s database.

Correcting the model allows a review to inspect deployment configuration and access grants to determine whether another plugin can read or modify authentication data. This turns an architectural assumption into a requirement. Changes to database access, shared caches, or plugin placement should trigger another review of that boundary.

Lastly, don’t forget to revisit the threat model when entry points, trust boundaries, or privileged operations change. Those are useful triggers for keeping the review context aligned with the application.

Seeding a SECURITY.md

You can use the $define-security-policy skill to generate a seeded security policy within the repository.

Define Security Policy for the Northstar Bank API. Here are key policies that should be included: Authentication and Authorization: - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

A strong security policy should include thorough details about how the application operates. Here’s an example of what to ask Codex to include in SECURITY.md:

<!-- SECURITY.md --> ### Authentication and Authorization - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover. - Authentication secrets and tokens must never appear in logs, URLs, analytics, or error responses. - Authorization must occur before every read, mutation, transaction, export, or administrative action. - Possession of a valid account or resource identifier never proves authorization. - Customer, account, and tenant isolation must hold across list, detail, search, bulk, export, and indirect-reference endpoints. - Server-side authorization must not rely on client-supplied roles, ownership fields, prices, balances, or approval state. - Administrative and service-to-service permissions must use least privilege. - Failures allowing cross-customer access are reportable even when only one endpoint is affected. ### Transaction and ledger integrity - Transactions must be authorized against the authenticated customer and eligible source account. - Amounts, currencies, destinations, fees, limits, and approval state must be validated server-side. - Transaction requests must be protected against replay, duplication, race conditions, and idempotency-key confusion. - Balance checks and ledger updates must be atomic. - Posted ledger entries must be immutable or corrected through auditable compensating entries. - High-risk transactions must enforce applicable limits, step-up authentication, approval, or fraud controls. - No failure path may produce an ambiguous transaction state without reconciliation. ### Data protection - Sensitive data must be encrypted in transit and at rest using approved controls. - Secret material must come from an approved secret-management system rather than source code or ordinary configuration files. - Logs, traces, metrics, support tooling, and security artifacts must exclude credentials and minimize personal and financial data. - Data exports and backups must receive equivalent authorization and protection to primary data. - Error responses must not expose internals, sensitive records, credentials, or authorization details. - Retention and deletion behavior must follow the system’s approved data-governance requirements. ### Input and output handling - Treat headers, paths, query parameters, bodies, uploaded files, webhook payloads, third-party responses, and stored customer content as untrusted. - Apply schema, type, range, length, and format validation before security-sensitive use. - Database access must use parameterized queries. - Outbound requests must restrict destinations, protocols, redirects, DNS behavior, and response sizes. - Parsers, uploads, decompression, and serialization must be bounded against resource exhaustion. - Customer-controlled content must be safely encoded for its output context.

Let’s take a look at Apache Superset, an open-source business intelligence web application, as an example. The application connects to databases and lets users explore data, run SQL in SQL Lab, and build and share charts and dashboards. The security policy within their open-source repo establishes detailed context concerning roles and capabilities, as well as how async execution and realtime notifications operate. For example, the policy defines:

Asynchronous execution paths do not create a separate data-access capability. A background task is a continuation of an already-authorized action, such as reading chart data or executing SQL through SQL Lab. The initiating route, command, or scheduler must enforce the same route-level and object-level checks the synchronous path would enforce before it creates the task, and the worker must execute under the initiating principal’s effective identity when row-level security, impersonation, embedded guest-token scope, or similar controls affect the result.

This makes vulnerability reporting more precise because it defines what must remain true as execution moves from a request into a background worker. A reviewer can trace the initiating user, the requested resource, the authorization checks before task creation, and the identity used during execution. As a result, reports from both security researchers and agents can test the policy requirement, the code paths that could violate it, the attacker’s starting permissions, and the resulting unauthorized capability.

Codex Security

Once context is established, you should choose a review workflow that works with your team’s existing development process. Local review gives a developer feedback before a PR is opened. Automatic PR review provides a consistent team checkpoint. The CLI supports workflows that need explicit targets, saved artifacts, or custom CI integration.

You can also use multiple workflows. However, you should start with one workflow, inspect its results on a change the team understands, and then expand once the review is producing evidence people can use.

Codex Security Review in GitHub Cloud

The fastest way to automate security reviews in GitHub Cloud is through the Security Review feature within ChatGPT. This is available through the same product surface as Codex Code Reviews available within your organization at https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/settings/code-review.

Codex Security Review goes deeper than Code Review on security-specific risks by analyzing the pull request diff, supporting repository context, and configured threat models or security guidance.

Difference between Code Review and Security Review

Code Review is a broad engineering review that assesses code quality. For example, Code Review asks: “Could this change break the product or introduce a serious engineering problem?” It reviews issues such as incorrect control flow, data corruption or loss, compatibility regressions, or incorrect API behavior. The intended users for Code Review are software developers within the organization.

Codex Security is a specialized, deeper assessment of security risks in the same PR changes. Security Review is for both software developers responsible for remediating vulnerabilities, as well as application security engineers responsible for securing CI/CD pipelines and source code. It assesses issues such as authentication and authorization bypasses, cross-tenant access, injection and unsafe parsing, or sensitive data exposure.

Configuring security reviews

There are two options for configuring security reviews. The auto-review reporting determines which findings Codex posts to the PR when Security Review runs automatically. It is defaulted to High, so only High and Critical findings are posted.

The option for manual review controls which findings Codex posts after someone explicitly requests a Security Review. It is defaulted to Medium, so Medium, High, and Critical findings are posted.

When configured, posted vulnerabilities will surface within the PR.

It’s best to choose automatic reporting thresholds around what the team is prepared to investigate consistently. For a targeted investigation, use the manual review settings to surface the additional detail relevant to that question.

Setting path overrides

Path-based reporting overrides the minimum severity published to the GitHub PR. Given that a repository’s risk is rarely uniform, this feature can tailor the risk threshold for more critical paths, such as:

Lowering the threshold for authentication, authorization, payments, cryptography, CI workflows, or infrastructure.

Keeping a higher threshold for lower-risk or especially noisy areas.

You can modify the path overrides within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. In this example below, we have established that src/** should have auto reviews for low vulnerabilities or higher. Changes to GitHub workflows or dependencies will enforce reporting for medium vulnerabilities.

A practical starting point is to identify the application’s sensitive operations and map them to paths with their owners. For the payment service example at the beginning of this post, that includes tenant authorization and billing mutations. I would review those paths with the team that owns them and choose a reporting threshold that reflects the consequence of a missed issue.

Going back to our Apache Superset example, I would keep a High repository-wide reporting threshold, but lower it for these paths:

Repository-relative path prefix

Minimum severity to report

Why it deserves additional attention

superset/security/

Low

Path contains code for central authorization, guest tokens, password recovery, and session invalidation

superset/row_level_security/

Low

Path controls the policies determining which data rows users can access

superset/sqllab/ and superset/commands/sql_lab/

Medium

Path focuses on SQL execution, query authorization, result retrieval, and exports

superset/embedded/

Medium

Path focuses on boundaries for dashboards embedded in other applications

If these settings were applied, then Codex Security Review would only report High vulnerabilities for all paths except those stated above. In those paths, Low and Medium would be reported given the additional sensitivity of the code.

Codex Security Review in Codex Desktop

For a more interactive experience reviewing PRs or uncommitted changes, you can also execute reviews through the security tab within Codex.

Alternatively, you can prompt Codex within the repository project of Codex by invoking the skill.

Please run a Security Diff Scan on the changes in the current branch.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

This workflow is most useful when the implementation is still fresh in your mind and you can investigate a finding immediately. If the review points to an authorization assumption, you can inspect the caller and the affected operation before the change moves into a separate review queue.

Codex Security Review in the CLI

Reviewing uncommitted local work

You can use the CLI to review uncommitted local work with seeded context about the repository and security policies.

Run the examples in the same shell from your Git checkout. They assume your security policy is in SECURITY.md and your supporting documents are in docs/security/. The setup creates a temporary directory for scan results.

northstar_repo="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" northstar_kb="$northstar_repo/docs/security" northstar_results="$(mktemp -d)"

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --working-tree \ --base HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/working-tree"

This reviews staged and unstaged changes relative to HEAD.

Before starting, be sure to confirm that the working tree contains the change you intend to assess. Unrelated edits broaden the investigation and can make it harder to connect the findings to the question that prompted the review.

Reviewing PRs or branch commits

Another option is to review a PR or branch for security issues. Check out the branch to review and fetch its target branch. This example uses origin/main.

northstar_pr_base="$(git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base origin/main HEAD)" npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$northstar_pr_base" \ --head HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/branch"

Note that a diff scan evaluates the proposed changes and does not scan the entire repository. Once complete, the output directory will contain the following files:

report.md: readable review

scan-manifest.json: confirms the exact base, head, target, and artifacts

findings.json: presents the severity, confidence, locations, and remediation

coverage.json: identifies the reviewed surfaces, exclusions, deferred work, and completeness

Scanning monorepos

In a monorepo, a change to a shared library can affect multiple services. Codex should receive enough context to review those interactions, while CI determines which components and checks are required.

Repository context

Keep shared engineering instructions in AGENTS.md and security expectations in SECURITY.md. A typical repository could look like this:

monorepo/ ├── AGENTS.md ├── SECURITY.md ├── docs/security/ │ ├── architecture.md │ └── threat-model.md ├── packages/auth/ └── services/ ├── billing/ └── reporting/

Use existing ownership and build metadata to connect each component to its dependencies, consumers, and tests. For example, a change to packages/auth may require reviewing both services even when their files are unchanged. This scope mapping is maintained by your organization; it is not automatically configured by adding Codex.

Component assessment

Large repositories may not always require scanning the entire codebase for each PR. One option is to use a path scan when a monorepo contains separate services or packages. Repeat --path to assess a shared library and its consumers together.

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --path packages/auth \ --path services/billing \ --path services/reporting \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/paths"

This scans only the selected paths rather than the entire repository.

PR and diff scanning

For a PR, use its exact base and head commit hashes from authenticated GitHub metadata. Both revisions and their history must be available in the checkout. The following example reuses the variables above and saves the diff results separately:

BASE_SHA="<full PR base commit SHA>" HEAD_SHA="<full PR head commit SHA>" BASE_REVISION="$( git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base "$BASE_SHA" "$HEAD_SHA" )" || exit npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$BASE_REVISION" \ --head "$HEAD_SHA" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --auth chatgpt \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/pr"

A diff scan focuses on the proposed changes. If a shared-library change requires broader consumer review, also run the component assessment against a clean checkout of that PR’s head revision. Keep the results distinct: --diff and --path are separate scan modes and cannot be combined.

Scanning alerts from GitHub

You can also assess code scanning alerts from the default branch using the Codex Security CLI.

northstar_github_repository="example/northstar" northstar_github_alerts="$northstar_results/github-alerts.json" # Import all open alerts as complete JSON. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Or import a selected subset. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --github-alert 12 \ --github-alert 18 \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Run from the corresponding local repository; imported contents are data. cd "$northstar_repo" npx @openai/codex-security validate "$northstar_github_alerts"

GitHub Actions workflows

Instead of enforcing security reviews through Codex, it is also possible to create custom workflows that run the Codex Security CLI. We’ve packaged this workflow to easily be used as a GitHub Action.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-repository.yml name: Codex Security review on: workflow_dispatch: schedule: - cron: "23 7 * * 1" # Mondays at 07:23 UTC permissions: contents: read jobs: security: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 with: persist-credentials: false - uses: openai/codex-security@3f61e5150981a5087c32e4395bbaa8ce5ce0c3e3 # action-v0.3.0 with: model: gpt-5.6-sol effort: high env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }}

These workflows can also be applied to other source code management tools like GitLab, BitBucket, or Jenkins. Take a look at our documentation page to learn more: Run Codex Security in CI.

Managing supply chain risk in CI/CD

You can also leverage the Codex Security CLI to assess dependencies in the codebase, such as when a new dependency is introduced or a version is bumped.

This is extremely useful in preventing vulnerable packages from presenting supply chain risk – you can achieve this by deploying the Codex Security CLI as commands within custom workflows.

Validating Dependabot alerts

Codex Security provides a skill for validating existing third-party vulnerabilities, including Dependabot, for reachability and exploitability. You can invoke the skill directly in the UI or through the CLI.

Use Triage Finding to import and triage Dependabot vulnerabilities against this repository.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

Codex will triage each of the Dependabot alerts and subsequently present a ledger of each presented risk with a reason why the alert was validated or not.

Looking at Apache Superset again, we can take its documentation toolchain to identify a security advisory related to it (such as webpack-dev-server advisory).

Using Codex, we can trace the dependency through Docusaurus, check the resolved version, and follow the development, build, and deployment paths to establish where the affected functionality could run. The reviewed lockfile selected version 5.2.6, which the advisory identifies as patched.

Codex’s analysis therefore supported a specific conclusion: the advisory did not affect the version selected by that documentation revision. Before closing a corresponding Dependabot alert, we would reconcile its reported version and revision with this evidence and verify the installed dependency.

Running scans when package versions change

It is also possible to run security scans against the latest version of a dependency when the version is changed.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-dependency.yml name: Codex Security dependency scan on: pull_request: paths: - package.json - package-lock.json permissions: contents: read jobs: scan: name: Scan dependency changes if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 timeout-minutes: 45 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - name: Set up Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7 with: node-version: "26" - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@5fda3b95a4ea91299a34e894583c3862153e4b97 # v7 with: python-version: "3.14" - name: Install Codex Security run: | set -euo pipefail npm install \ --prefix "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security" \ --ignore-scripts \ --no-audit \ --no-fund \ @openai/codex-security - name: Verify Codex Security env: CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security run: | set -euo pipefail test -x "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" --version - name: Check out the pull request uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} fetch-depth: 0 persist-credentials: false - name: Install project dependencies run: | set -euo pipefail npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund - name: Run full repository scan env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }} CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-state SCAN_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results run: | set -euo pipefail "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" scan . \ --auth api-key \ --output-dir "$SCAN_DIR" \ --fail-on-severity high \ --json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security.json" - name: Preserve scan results if: always() uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7 with: name: codex-security-dependency-results path: | ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security.json if-no-files-found: warn retention-days: 7

Wrapping up

As agents contribute more code, security teams must carve the right scaffolding for agentic systems to reason across the codebase for application security reviews and enforce gates when insecure code could be committed.

Start with a few critical repositories, commit your threat models and security policies, then review the pull requests to assess how accurately agents are reasoning against enterprise context and the codebase. When you begin to feel confident in the quality of the results, begin to expand into a broader number of repositories or pipelines as you expand agentic security coverage in the SDLC.

Title: A brief history of syslog timestamps, (Sun, Nov 22nd)
Context: Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2...
Full Text:
BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023.

As any of my FOR577 students will tell you, I'm a fan of ISO-8601 (ok, RFC 3339, too, see below). They'll probably also tell you I'm a firm believer in UTC||GTFO especially on servers (also true, and I've made stickers to prove it). I was also asked recently why the syslog timestamps in newer Ubuntu and Debian systems changed to ISO-8601 (well, probably actually RFC 3339, but I won't got down that rabbithole in this handler's diary) timestamps from the historical Mmm dd hh:mm:ss format we've known since the 1980s. I had noticed the same, a few years ago, but never really paid attention to it. Given the question from a student, I decided to do a little research on the subject and this diary is the result.

To back up some, the syslog protocol and syslogd were originally the creation of Eric Allman in 1983 because he needed a way to debug sendmail[1]. They became part of BSD 4.2 that same year. BSD 4.2 also happened to be my introduction to Unix in 1983. Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2 major branches of Unix at the time. System V adopted the protocol and routing interfaces but built the daemon on top of System V internals.

The first effort to develop the protocol into an actual standard was an IETF draft in Oct 2000 that evolved into RFC 3164[2] in 2001, by which time the protocol was actually already 18 years old. This is the syslog message format we've all come to know so well over the years. Meanwhile, around 2005, rsyslogd added the option of outputing RFC 3339 timestamps. In 2009, RFC 3164 was superceded by RFC 5424[3] which defined the timestamp to be of the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss]Z or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss](+/-)hh:mm. Despite the new RFC, the default setting even for rsyslogd in most Linux distros continued to be to write messages to the log files in the older format (referred to as the BSD format, as specified in the title of RFC 3164), by setting a directive in /etc/rsyslog.conf (the RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat directive).

That brings us to 2023, with the release of Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 23.04 (not a LTS release) both distros stopped installing rsyslogd by default and defaulted to the systemd journal for logging and removed the directive from the default config file for those who did install it.. Many system administrators continue to install rsyslogd because they had infrastructure in place for forwarding syslog to central log servers and/or SIEMs. These are the folks most likely to have noticed the format change. Meanwhile, Fedora and Alma (and presumably the rest of the RedHat family) have left the directive in place when the package is installed.

From a Ubuntu 24.04 system:

From a Fedora 44 system:

Meanwhile you can get either one with journalctl by setting the output format to either short (BSD format) or short-iso-precise (ISO format).

Also, note that rsyslogd is not the only option for a syslog server. I've been using syslog-ng as the syslog server on my home log collector since about 2000. In syslog-ng, the new 'ISO' timestamps can be enabled by setting the following two options in syslog-ng.conf: ts-format(iso) and frac-digits(6). Since I have just been upgrading my central log server for years, I haven't done a fresh install lately, so I'm not sure if that is the default. I had to explicitly add it to my config.

References:

1. The History of Centralized Logging

2. RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol

3. RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol

Title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
Context: The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had...
Full Text:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.

Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.

In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.

OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.

The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.

The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.

Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.

Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.

What the Providers Have Disclosed

An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.

Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.

A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.

At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.

The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.

Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.

Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.

The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.

What Users Should Do

The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.

Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.

Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.

A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

Title: Perplexity and Intelligence
Context: I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are...
Full Text: Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
Context: The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out
Full Text:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.

Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.

Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.

Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.

GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

Title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
Context: They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root
Full Text:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.

Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.

Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.

Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.

If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

Title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge
Context: The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026)

CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025)

CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026)

Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884.

The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

Today we are joined by Prince Chaddha, ProjectDiscovery researcher, discussing how abliterated models can get you pwned. ProjectDiscovery researchers demonstrated that modified open-source AI models can contain hidden backdoors that remain undetected by standard benchmarks and security evaluations.

By poisoning a small amount of training data, they created a model that behaved normally until a specific trigger phrase prompted it to execute malicious commands and exfiltrate credentials, with the attack costing less than $50 to build. The researchers warn that compromised models could be distributed through trusted repositories and recommend sandboxing AI agents, restricting network and command access, monitoring tool activity, and verifying model provenance before deploying modified weights.

Title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
Context: The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers
Full Text:
PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

The threat actor gets in through the web application.

Reads the configuration file;

Dumps the customer database;

Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

Is session upload progress on?

Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?

Does php-cgi face the internet?

Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

Title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
Context: But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers
Full Text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
