Title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
Context: 6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month
Full Text: On Thursday, PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month. For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep. In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings. Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults. Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.” No cookies for impostors In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline. Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit. For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote. Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before. Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote. Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link. Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry. The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well. The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight. Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs. Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies. PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range. Another tricky day for PHP devs For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles. As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. “In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote. Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®

Title: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials
Context: When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it
Full Text:
When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own set of credentials that keep the caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity but carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both.

You can call GetScopedCredentials with the temporary security credentials you already use, such as those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function. In each call, you pass a scope down policy, a shorter session duration, or both. A scope down policy is an inline policy that describes the maximum permissions for the new credentials. The resulting permissions are the intersection of your session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy, so they can only be reduced. Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further.

GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. Because it scopes down permissions on the credentials you already have, you can build it into agent frameworks, services that issue credentials to other components, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and your own applications. You can also call it again with scoped-down credentials, so an orchestrating agent can give each sub-agent narrower access than its own.

In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it.

Example use cases

You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section.

Limit what AI agents can do

When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it.

Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box.

Scope down permissions based on runtime context

Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request.

Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all.

How to call GetScopedCredentials

This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials", "Resource": "*" }] }

To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

Step 1: Define a scope down policy

Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches.

Option A: Write the policy yourself If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*" }] }

Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials.

To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction. This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "NotAction": [ "iam:*", "organizations:*", "account:*", "sts:AssumeRole*", "s3:DeleteBucket", "ec2:TerminateInstances", "rds:DeleteDBInstance", "dynamodb:DeleteTable" ], "Resource": "*" }] }

Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot.

We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table.

import json import logging import os import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb") table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"] def _response(status_code, message): return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})} def handler(event, context): try: request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}") report_id = request["reportId"] except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError): return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId") if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id: return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string") try: dynamodb.put_item( TableName=table_name, Item={ "reportId": {"S": report_id}, "status": {"S": "READY"}, }, ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)", ) return _response(200, "Report status saved") except ClientError as error: code = error.response["Error"]["Code"] if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException": return _response(409, "Report status already exists") logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code) return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status")

Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t.

iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \ --region us-west-2 \ --account 123456789012 \ --service-hints dynamodb \ --max-policy-size 2048 \ --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \ --pretty

IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy.

{ "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "kms:Decrypt" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": [ "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com" ] } } } ] }

IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access.

However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json. If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy.

Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials

Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration.

aws sts get-scoped-credentials \ --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --scoped-session-description report-status-job \ --region us-west-2

The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents.

{ "Credentials": { "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY, "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "SessionInfo": { "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane" }, "SessionTokenUtilization": 17, "SessionTokenSize": 724, "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1 }

Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys.

The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration.

Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example.

{ "eventVersion": "1.11", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "principalId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:janee", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "accessKeyId": "ASIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE", ... }, "eventTime": "2026-10-12T02:55:00Z", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "GetScopedCredentials", "awsRegion": "us-west-2", ... "requestParameters": { "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Action\":\"s3:GetObject\",\"Resource\":\"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*\"}]}", "scopedSessionDescription": "report-status-job", "durationSeconds": 300 }, "responseElements": { "credentials": { "accessKeyId": "ASIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "sessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "sessionInfo": { "scopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane" }, "sessionTokenUtilization": 17, "sessionTokenSize": 724, "scopedPoliciesCount": 1 }, "readOnly": false, ... }

The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId, which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session.

Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again

You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action.

Managing access to GetScopedCredentials

You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn, aws:PrincipalTag, and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where.

Availability and request quota

GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference.

Conclusion

GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs.

For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference. To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account. Now go build!

Title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
Context: In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS...
Full Text: Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses. On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information. Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand. Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers. “We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.” Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program. According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said. It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker. Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text, and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. “This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.” Customer data has left the building The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published. All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.” Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

Full Text:
TL;DR

PHP disclosed three additional critical vulnerabilities, separate from the PHP2Shell issues covered in our October analysis.

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36, as appropriate for your branch; check with your vendor for package availability or backported fixes.

Inventory PHP deployments and confirm each has an owner and a patch path. For background on the earlier PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, read our October analysis.

PHP2Shell reminded us that PHP powers a vast range of websites, applications, and products, often running behind the scenes in places organizations may not immediately think to look. With three new advisories now drawing attention to PHP’s internals, security teams face a familiar challenge: understanding where the runtime is deployed, how it is configured, and who can move quickly when a fix is available.

New Flaws Impact Memory Safety and Session Handling Issues in PHP

PHP’s three critical advisories point to different failure points in the runtime, from memory cleanup to session parsing. Their impact depends on the PHP version and, in some cases, how the application is configured.

Vulnerability

Description

Fixed Version / Remediation

Backtrace use-after-free (CVE-2026-129474)

When PHP records an error’s history, it can mistakenly refer to memory that has already been cleared while handling certain method calls. Under specific conditions in PHP 8.5, an attacker may be able to exploit this to run code as the PHP process.

Upgrade to PHP 8.5.13

Timezone-cache use-after-free (CVE-2026-129496)

A startup warning can leave PHP pointing to timezone data that is no longer in use. If another warning occurs during an early request, PHP may crash or mishandle memory; in some conditions, that could let an attacker run code as the PHP process.

Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13

Session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560)

PHP can save session data in one format and later read it as another. If upload-progress tracking is enabled and the application has the right code available, an attacker may be able to turn that mismatch into code execution.

Disable upload progress (workaround) or upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, or 8.5.13.

Memory-safety flaws are especially consequential in a language runtime because they can let an attacker influence how a process handles data or control flow. Here, the affected paths include backtrace generation and timezone-cache handling, which are operations that may sit outside the application code teams typically review. Under the right conditions, the outcome can range from a worker crash to code execution with the PHP worker’s privileges.

Session handling carries a different risk: the same stored data can be interpreted differently by different readers. If one component writes session data using one format and another reads it using a different format, attacker-controlled content may be treated as serialized objects. Teams should check for upload-progress settings, shared session stores, and applications or processes that use different serializers.

Finding PHP is Only Half the Job

The fixes are available, but applying them across an organization can take more than updating a public-facing server. PHP may also run in internal services, containers, test environments, appliances, and products maintained by another vendor

Start with an inventory, then track each deployment through to a verified fix:

Find every PHP runtime. Include internet-facing and internal services, containers, test environments, appliances, and products that bundle PHP.

Identify the owner and patch path. Note who maintains each deployment and whether it comes from PHP, an operating system distributor, hosting provider, or product vendor.

Confirm the fix for its branch. Apply the appropriate patched release or a vendor backport, and verify that the update reached each deployment.

Review session settings. Where session upload progress is enabled, use the advisory’s workaround while arranging the upgrade.

A patch plan is only complete when teams can confirm that affected deployments have been updated or mitigated, including less visible systems and bundled runtimes. For more on the inventory and ownership challenge, see our October analysis of PHP2Shell.

Title: n0n extortion gang leaks data of JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard customers
Context: In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and...
Full Text:
Data belonging to customers of three of the biggest companies in global finance has been leaked online, after hackers breached third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard.

The finance companies have all acknowledged that security incidents have occurred at unnamed third--party companies, after the n0n extortion gang named all three on its dark web leak site earlier this week.

In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses" there had been "no disruption" to its services.

Mastercard also said that its payment network had not been affected, and that cardholders could continue to use their cards.

According to Visa, the breach occurred at an unnamed third-party provider based in Asia Pacific.

n0n claims to have stolen "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions" related to JPMorgan Chase. All three of the corporations were given 48 hours to negotiate with the extortion gang, but none of them paid. So, n0n published data on its website exposing the details of thousands of customers.

News of the security breach impacted the share prices of all three companies, after a jittery week of high-profile technology outages in the United States.

According to Reuters, the leaked JPMorgan Chase data included more than 16,000 customer email addresses, and what appeared to be the email addresses of some 124 employees of the bank. Some of the customer information included phone numbers, and post codes.

Clearly scammers and fraudsters could exploit information like that in a variety of ways, including by contacting members of the public claiming to be employees of their bank.

Meanwhile, according to a Cybernews report, the leaked Visa data includes details of over 6000 premium card holders who are signed up to Asia-Pacific dining programmes, including names, phone numbers, the messaging apps they use, and restaurant booking details.

n0n is believed to be a Russia-based extortion gang, and despite only having been operating for a couple of months has already managed to claim the scalps of approximately 200 corporate victims.

Security researchers say n0n has typically broken into organisations using valid login credentials, harvested by info-stealing malware or obtained by credential-stuffing VPNs and poorly secured remote desktop (RDP) services, before using legitimate admin tools to gather data. It is not yet known how the vendors in this case were compromised.

Of course, financial institutions are very experienced at securing their own infrastructure. Where they appear to have fallen down on this occasion is through the use of third-party marketing agencies or loyalty scheme operators who have been less diligent in securing their systems.

You are only as safe as the weakest link in the chain. And customers don't really care whose server it was that leaked their data, when they entrusted it to your care in the first place.

The advice for concerned Chase, Visa or Mastercard customers is simple: be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls claiming to come from your bank. It would not be a surprise at all if scammers exploit the breach by mentioning it to customers, and offering compensation, or inviting members of the public to "verify" their account.

If you are unsure, contact your bank directly using its published number.

WhatsApp Patches 3 Security Flaws, Including Android Bug Suspected of Use in Scams
Context: When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign
Full Text:
Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871, has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4.

The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said.

The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue.

When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added.

WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful.

Also addressed by the company are two other flaws -

CVE-2026-102769 - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted.

CVE-2026-44908 - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70.

Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message.

It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key.

"Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation."

WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

Title: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
Context: Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability...
Full Text:
Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory.

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report.

What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

Indicators of compromise

The following addresses appear in records dated September 8 to 10, 2026. 142[.]4.98.145 142[.]4.107.34

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

Title: Report: Attackers Are Increasingly Using AI Attack Frameworks
Context: ” Threat actors are also integrating AI into commodity cybercrime platforms to help unskilled crooks launch sophisticated attacks
Full Text:
Threat actors are expanding their use of multi-agent AI attack frameworks, according to researchers at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG).

The researchers have observed attackers abusing open-source pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, which can fully automate large portions of attacks.

“Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally,” GTIG says. “Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions.

Current attacks using these tools are noisy and fairly easy to detect, but GTIG believes this will change in the near future.

“Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity,” the researchers write. “Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.”

Threat actors are also integrating AI into commodity cybercrime platforms to help unskilled crooks launch sophisticated attacks.

“The Jieyou phishing service, an active Chinese-language PhaaS platform first observed in March 2026, is primarily used by cybercriminals to deploy and manage highly convincing phishing campaigns, with a particular focus on e-commerce fraud,” GTIG says. “The service introduced an LLM chatbot assistant in its June 2026 backend update. This chatbot allows threat actors to easily configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands, significantly lowering the technical barrier for deploying campaigns....The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier. Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly.”

Title: Bazuka Android Malware Uses Fake Screen Overlays to Hide Credential Theft and Device Control
Context: " ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan.

"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping."

One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background.

Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API.

One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities -

Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures

Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process

This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store.

One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed -

A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager

A downloader that directly downloads the main payload

It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them.

"Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]."

The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically.

"Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging."

"When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon."

Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely.

Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels -

Control, which is used to issue commands

Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams

Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft -

call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands

clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones

contacts, to collect contact information

device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands

file_manager, to access the file system

input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input

location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi

media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio

oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart

optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays

preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment

proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy

push, to create and manage local Android notifications

screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services

self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client

session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays

smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device

system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures

tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards

toast, to display text messages on the device's screen

twofa, to capture one-time verification codes

uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application

ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator

The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian.

"ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application."

"Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest."

ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data

Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate LLM. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data.

"What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said.

Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers.

Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure.

An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features -

Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device

Abuse accessibility services for full remote control

Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments

Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively

Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications

Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password

"The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said.

"To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off."

Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations.

"By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

Title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
Context: The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed...
Full Text: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim. "As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said. The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders." Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy. "It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience." Smart specs can't shake the hate When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees. "Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time. Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces. Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time. Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas. On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning. With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general. A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children. There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy. A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament. The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

Title: Two Incidents, One Lesson in Trust
Context: But dig a little deeper and you’ll notice that criminals didn’t get in through brute force or exploiting a zero-day vulnerability
Full Text:
Optimizely unfortunately suffered two incidents in nine months, so clearly they must be doing something wrong and the answer to that is to buy a bigger firewall.

But is that really the answer?

One incident started with a phone call. The other started with a flaw in a signup form and ended with malicious code served to visitors of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, and HSBC. On the surface they have nothing in common. But dig a little deeper and you’ll notice that criminals didn’t get in through brute force or exploiting a zero-day vulnerability. They exploited trust. And when trust is the attack surface, your workforce is both the target and a critical line of defense.

February: It's Good to Talk (To the Wrong Person)

On February 11, a threat actor got in touch with Optimizely to say they already had access to its systems. They weren't bluffing. According to the company's own breach notification, the way in was a "sophisticated voice-phishing attack." Someone picked up a phone, and the person on the other end said the right things.

Optimizely says the attacker couldn't escalate privileges, install software or plant backdoors, and what left the building was basic business contact information. SecurityWeek reported that the systems touched included internal business platforms such as Zendesk and Salesforce. Although Optimizely didn't name the group, the tactics seemed consistent with that of ShinyHunters.

While it’s easy to downplay that it’s “just” contact data, it’s valuable information that can be used to craft even more convincing phishing emails or phone calls. A breach of business contacts isn't the end of an attack. It can often be the reconnaissance phase of the next one, aimed at somebody else.

November: The Script Everybody Trusted

On November 16, Scott Helme and the team at Report URI spotted malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. Optimizely told BleepingComputer the attacker had abused a flaw in its account signup flow, which let them insert code into customers' Project JavaScript.

The payloads included card skimmers, crypto wallet address swappers, and routing that pushed iPhone users towards an exploit kit.

Not one of those 178 organizations was breached in the traditional sense. Their own systems were fine. They had simply trusted a vendor's script.

To be clear, there's no public evidence that the February and November incidents are connected. One was social engineering, the other a software flaw. But that’s kind of the point. They are two very different routes to one destination.

The Inbox Is Not the Only Door

For years, security awareness was quietly treated as a synonym for "don't click the dodgy link in the email."

Email is still the most popular avenue, but look at where the attacks this year on Optimizely actually came from. A phone call, a helpdesk and CRM platform, and a trusted third-party script running in a browser. Not one of those is an inbox.

That's the reality for most organizations now. Work happens across email, Teams, Slack, Zoom, SMS, voice calls, shared documents, and a long tail of SaaS tools, each with its own notifications, its own login prompts, and its own sense of "this is internal, so it's safe." And that’s before you factor in the increasing number of AI agents.

Vishing groups ring the helpdesk pretending to be an employee. They message staff on Teams pretending to be IT. They follow up an email with a phone call to make it feel real. The more channels we use, the more places trust can be borrowed.

This is why collaboration security matters. Protecting all channels across wherever people talk. They need to have the same defenses to protect them against social engineering whether it comes through an email, a chat message, or a voice note.

Why Training Matters More Than Ever

The February breach is the obvious case of a convincing voice and a person who wanted to be helpful. While you want your helpdesk to be helpful, you need to equip them with the skill to pause when a call, a message or a request seems a bit odd and verify it through a trusted channel.

The recent November breach initially appears like a purely technical problem. Which is partly true. Consider what happens next when customers of 178 organizations now have reason to be worried about their card details. Criminals know that a worried person makes for an easier target. Expect "your account may have been affected, please verify your details" emails, texts and calls, because every high-profile incident is followed by a wave of opportunistic phishing riding on its coattails. Stolen business contact data, like the kind taken in February, makes those follow-ups more targeted and more believable.

Therefore training has to change shape. Annual click-through modules about suspicious emails won't be enough when the threat is an authoritative and polite voice claiming to be from IT, or a Teams message from a "colleague" asking you to approve an MFA prompt. Simulations need to reflect the channels people actually use. Coaching needs to happen at the moment, not once a year. The goal isn't to turn everyone into a security expert. It's to build a culture where checking is normal and nobody feels silly for saying "I'll call you back on the number I've got."

But training isn't a magic bullet either. People will make mistakes, or overlook issues, especially when the attack arrives on a platform they believe is safe. That's why the human layer and the technical layer have to work together to catch what they can across every channel, and trained people who catch what slips through, with each one feeding the other.

What Security Leaders Can Do This Week

Train for all your channels, not just the inbox. Run vishing simulations, especially for helpdesk and support teams who are paid to be helpful and are therefore prime targets.

Make call-back verification a habit. Any request to reset credentials, approve MFA, or move money gets verified through a known number or channel, never the one the request came in on.

Extend protection to collaboration tools. Treat Teams, Slack, and other platforms as attack surfaces, with the same scrutiny you give email.

Brace for the follow-up phish. After any big public incident, warn staff and customers that scam messages exploiting it are likely, and tell them how you will and won't contact them.

Know your third parties. Inventory the scripts and SaaS platforms you trust, monitor what they do, and rotate credentials and tokens when a vendor has an incident.

Make reporting easy and blame-free. The colleague who says "I think I just spoke to a scammer" within five minutes should be celebrated as a win, never shamed for making a mistake.

Trust Is the New Perimeter

Optimizely isn't unique, it's simply a well-known name. The lesson is that trust is now the thing attackers exploit, whether it's trust in a voice on the phone, a message in Teams or a script on a web page.

That's why at KnowBe4 we think about securing the whole workforce. Attack Simulation & Training builds the instincts people need across every channel, Email & Collaboration Security protects email and the platforms where work really happens, and Agent Security looks after the AI agents that increasingly sit alongside your staff. Each layer makes the others stronger.

None of it replaces a person who stops, thinks and says "hang on a minute."

Title: JPMorgan Confirms Customer Data Breach Following Third-Party Compromise
Context: JPMorgan has confirmed a data breach following a cyber-attack on third party vendors used by the financial institution
Full Text:
JPMorgan has confirmed a data breach following a cyber-attack on third party vendors used by the financial institution.

The investment banking giant, part of the JPMorganChase group, revealed on X on November 19, at 13.29 GMT, that it believes attackers accessed certain marketing data held by the impacted vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.

“There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” JPMorgan wrote.

The firm added that the incident is not related to a service disruption on November 16, which it said was caused by a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems.

Chase, which is the consumer and retail banking arm of JPMorganChase, issued the same statement on its X account on November 19.

N0n Ransomware Claims Attacks on JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard

The notification came after the ransomware group N0n listed the financial institutions JPMorganChase, Visa and Mastercard on its data leak site.

Reuters reported that Visa and Mastercard confirmed they had experienced data breaches as a result of a third-party compromise. Visa said that no payment data has been impacted while a Mastercard spokesperson revealed that the breach affected non-payments information from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.

None of the compromised third-party vendors have been named, so it is unknown at the time of writing if the incidents are related.

Following JPMorgan’s data breach notification on November 19, N0n reportedly released data relating to customers of the three banks, stating that they had each missed a 48-hour deadline to pay its extortion demand.

Title: Report: Threat Actors Are Refining Their Use of AI Tools
Context: In addition to integrating AI into their attacks, threat actors are also taking advantage of the growing popularity of AI tools to launch social engineering attacks
Full Text:
Recorded Future warns that threat actors continue to use AI to accelerate their attacks, making traditional techniques such as phishing, supply-chain compromise, and extortion more effective. Both state-sponsored threat actors and criminal gangs are using these tools, with at least one attack operating almost entirely without human intervention. While fully autonomous attacks are still rare, the researchers expect this to change as AI tools improve.

“As agentic techniques mature and diffuse across the threat landscape, autonomous and orchestrated campaigns are likely to become more frequent, alongside a growing underground market for illicit access to commercial models and rising ‘noise’ from low-level automated intrusions that complicate the detection of serious threats,” the researchers write.

In addition to integrating AI into their attacks, threat actors are also taking advantage of the growing popularity of AI tools to launch social engineering attacks.

“Attackers are spoofing the landing pages of popular AI developer tools, standing up fake utility pages, and impersonating products such as OpenClaw with fraudulent wallet pages designed to steal crypto assets,” the researchers write. “These attacks increased significantly after March 2026, demonstrating that threat actors are taking advantage of the increased interest in AI to deliver malware. AI-related lures have been used in the ‘ClickFix’ campaign, which delivers malicious pop-up messages on compromised sites, as well as in search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning techniques that target users searching for AI-related websites. The prevalence of these campaigns demonstrates the long-established trend of opportunistic cybercriminals taking advantage of hype or fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) around a newsworthy subject.”
