Title: Ransomware Recovery Takes 20 Days for the Typical Victim, Report Finds
Context: The report also showed a gap between diagnosis and full recovery: while 68% of forensics findings arriving within two days after the attack is detected, only 32% of victims...
Full Text:
Ransomware recovery takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims need more than six weeks.

In a new report published on November 19, Rubrik’s Zero Labs examined the ransomware landscape in 2026, drawing on a combination of internal telemetry, 16,953 publicly reported incidents from January to October 2026 and real-world recovery cases.

According to Rubrik's findings, ransomware recovery takes a median of 20 days, from the start of the recovery process to case closure and full restoration.

The report also showed a gap between diagnosis and full recovery: while 68% of forensics findings arriving within two days after the attack is detected, only 32% of victims observed by Rubrik had completed full recovery within two weeks.

Furthermore, 28% of ransomware victims took longer than six weeks to return to business as usual.

Additionally, the report found that ransomware attackers are increasingly targeting the systems organizations rely on to recover.

Rubrik detected activity from 21% of the ransomware groups identified in its research within its customers' backup environments. These groups were responsible for 62% of all publicly reported ransomware attacks, and at least 7% of ransomware recovery cases involved attackers attempting to log into the victim's backup management console.

Eight Ransomware Groups Drive Half of Attacks

As has been reported several times in the past, the Rubrik report confirmed that modern ransomware is increasingly about stealing data, not just locking systems. Out of the 16,953 incidents used for the report, the researchers analyzed 2931 that specifically described how victims were extorted.

They found that 67% of them involved data theft, while only 45% explicitly involved encryption. A smaller subset of victims (13%) reported both stolen and encrypted data.

According to the report, the ransomware landscape continues to be fairly concentrated in 2026.

While the researchers identified 100 active ransomware groups, eight groups accounted for approximately half of attributed incidents. Among those eight groups, the top three (Qilin, INC Ransom and The Gentlemen) together accounted for 30%.

The leading group itself, Qilin, is reportedly responsible for 15% of observed incidents.

Title: Europe’s 2027 Cyber Compliance Year: What’s Fixed, What’s Moving, and What One Incident Looks Like Under Four Laws
Context: DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review
Full Text:
On Dec. 11, 2027, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, and every new connected product placed on the European market will need security built in and a CE mark to prove it. That is the date most 2027 planning decks lead with. It is also the only big date of the year that is truly fixed.

Around it, almost everything else is in motion. NIS2 is being amended while three member states still haven't passed it. DORA's first round of threat-led penetration testing (simulated attacks on live systems) is underway, and the list of tech providers it supervises directly is due for review. The UK's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is weeks or months from becoming law, with its duties phased in after that.

So the useful question for 2027 isn't "what's due when?" It's "which of these dates can I build on, which might move, and which depend on things that aren't ready yet?" This 2027 cyber compliance guide sorts all four regimes that way. It then follows a single cyber incident through all four laws at once, because that is where the overlap actually hurts.

The four laws in brief

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) regulates products: hardware and software with digital elements sold in the EU. Manufacturers must design them securely, handle vulnerabilities for a set support period and report actively exploited flaws.

NIS2 regulates organizations: "essential" and "important" entities in 18 sectors, from energy and health to managed IT services. It requires risk-management measures, incident reporting and accountability for senior management. As a directive, it works through national laws.

DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, regulates the financial sector's ICT resilience. It has applied since January 2025, and for banks, insurers and other financial entities it takes precedence over NIS2. It also lets EU financial supervisors oversee critical tech providers directly.

The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill updates the UK's 2018 NIS Regulations. It brings managed service providers, data centres and designated critical suppliers into scope for the first time and tightens incident reporting. It doesn't apply in the EU, and the EU laws don't apply in the UK, but a UK company selling products or services into the EU can face all four.

What's fixed: the dates you can build on

These are in force or set in law, and nothing on the legislative calendar is likely to move them.

CRA reporting is already live. Since Sept. 11, 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting their products: an early warning within 24 hours and a fuller notification within 72, submitted through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The European Commission is explicit that this covers products already on the market, not just new ones. If your 2027 plan still lists CRA reporting as a future task, it's a year late.

The CRA applies in full on Dec. 11, 2027. From that date, the essential security requirements, technical documentation, software bill of materials (SBOM) and CE marking apply to products placed on the EU market. Products already on sale before then are caught by these requirements only if they are substantially modified afterwards. Open-source software stewards also pick up reporting duties on the same day.

DORA's first testing cycle closes in January 2028. Financial entities designated as significant must run threat-led penetration testing at least every three years. DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025, so the first cycle runs out in January 2028, and 2027 is when most of those tests will happen. Each one involves live production systems and often the entity's critical tech suppliers.

NIS2 is live in 24 member states. Where a national law is in force, the obligations already apply: registration, risk-management measures, 24-hour early warnings for significant incidents and management accountability. 2027 isn't a NIS2 start date for most of the EU. It's the second year of supervision.

Talk to Cyble about 2027 Cyber Compliance readiness and see how exploitation intelligence fits into your CRA and NIS2 reporting process.

What's moving: rules being rewritten while you comply

NIS2 is being amended before it's finished. France, Ireland and Spain still had no national NIS2 law in force in November 2026, and the Commission referred late countries to the EU Court of Justice in July. France's National Assembly passed its bill at first reading on Nov. 17, 2026; it still needs a joint committee of both chambers.

Meanwhile, the Commission's January 2026 amending proposal would add a small mid-cap category that moves many companies from "essential" to "important," standardize ransomware reporting data and let a cyber posture certificate count as proof of compliance. The Commission is aiming for political agreement in early 2027, and member states would then have a year to transpose the changes. Plan against today's national law; budget for a second update in 2028.

The Cybersecurity Act is being replaced. The same package proposes a new Cybersecurity Act (often called CSA2) that would let the EU name third countries that pose a cyber risk and restrict high-risk suppliers of key ICT assets used by NIS2 entities. If adopted in the form proposed, that becomes a supply-chain question for every NIS2 organization.

Incident reporting may get a single front door. The Digital Omnibus simplification package proposes one entry point for reporting incidents under several EU laws. The Council's Oct. 21, 2026 position favors a national single entry point in each country plus an EU information point run by ENISA. It's still a proposal, so the separate channels remain the ones that count in 2027.

DORA's supervised-provider list is due for review. EU financial supervisors designated 19 critical ICT third-party providers, including AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud, in November 2025, and are expected to reassess the list during 2027 using 2026 data. A provider that lands on it gets direct EU oversight; its financial-sector customers get new contract and exit-planning questions.

The UK Bill is close but not yet law. The House of Lords finished with the Bill on Nov. 2, 2026, and it went back to the Commons over two amendments peers had made. Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties then arrive through secondary legislation, and a House of Lords Library briefing says commencement may run through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the Information Commission (the renamed ICO).

What depends on infrastructure that may be late

The CRA's Dec. 11, 2027 date is fixed. What isn't fixed is whether the machinery for meeting it will be ready.

Harmonised standards. Most manufacturers would prefer to show compliance by applying harmonised European standards, which give a legal presumption of conformity. As of late August 2026, no CRA harmonised standard had been cited in the EU's Official Journal for any product category, and the cross-product standard covering all the essential requirements isn't due until 2027.

Notified bodies. Products in the CRA's "important class II" and "critical" categories need a third-party assessment from a notified body. So do "important class I" products, such as password managers, VPNs, browsers and smart home devices, unless the manufacturer fully applies a harmonised standard or certification scheme. The rules for designating these bodies have applied since June 11, 2026, but none had been designated by late June, and the target of having enough of them by Dec. 11, 2026 is a best-efforts goal.

Put those together and the practical deadline for many manufacturers is earlier than December 2027. If a class I product can't rely on a published standard, it may need a notified body, and assessment slots are likely to fill up well ahead of the deadline. The safe assumption is that standards arrive late and assessors are scarce: start the technical file and risk assessment now, and book an assessor as soon as one is designated for your product category.

One incident, four clocks

Comparison tables make these laws look like separate tracks. They stop being separate the moment something goes wrong. Here is a single, hypothetical incident and every reporting clock it starts.

The setup. A UK-headquartered managed service provider runs IT for European customers, including a bank in the EU. It also sells its own remote-management agent, the software installed on every customer machine it looks after. At hour zero, it discovers that attackers used an unknown flaw in that agent to push ransomware across several client networks, including the bank's.

Clock 1: DORA, for the bank. The bank must decide whether this is a "major" ICT incident. If it is, the initial notification to its financial supervisor is due within four hours of that decision and no later than 24 hours after the bank became aware. An intermediate report follows within 72 hours of the initial one, and a final report within a month after the last intermediate report. The bank can't write any of them without facts from the provider, which is why DORA requires ICT contracts to include help during incidents.

Clock 2: NIS2, for the provider. Managed service providers are in scope of NIS2. A provider based outside the EU that serves EU customers must name a representative in a member state and answers to that country's authority. For a significant incident, NIS2 requires an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within a month.

Clock 3: the CRA, for the provider as a manufacturer. The flaw is in a product the provider sells, and it's being actively exploited. Under the CRA, that means an early warning within 24 hours, a vulnerability notification within 72 hours and a final report within 14 days of a fix being available, all through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. The provider must also tell affected users.

Clock 4: the UK Bill, once commenced. As a medium or large managed service provider, the company would also owe the UK regulator an initial notification within 24 hours and a full report within 72. If personal data was exposed, GDPR's 72-hour breach notification makes it five clocks.

One hypothetical incident: reporting deadlines under DORA, NIS2, the CRA and the UK Bill

Three lessons fall out of the timeline. First, the earliest deadline belongs to the customer, not the company that was breached: the bank's four-hour clock depends on information from the provider, so provider contracts need a customer notification commitment measured in hours, not days. Second, each law uses a different trigger, whether "major," "significant" or "actively exploited," so the same event can be reportable under one law and not yet under another. Third, the facts are the same in every report. Keep one incident record and map it to each format, rather than writing four reports from scratch at 3 a.m.

Reality check: what enforcement actually looks like

Search for NIS2 or DORA fines and you'll find confident lists of six-figure penalties. Most can't be traced to a regulator. Here is what can, alongside claims that keep circulating.

Claim

Status

What the record shows

Austria's FMA fined Western Union International Bank €42,000 under DORA (July 14, 2026)

Verified

Repeatedly late incident reports under DORA's reporting rules

Romania's DNSC fined a public body 50,000 lei, about €10,000, under NIS2 (Sept. 29, 2026)

Verified

Missing the deadline to notify the authority that it was in scope

Germany's BSI fined a cloud provider €850,000 under NIS2 (February 2026)

Not traceable

Widely repeated; independent trackers found no published NIS2 fine as of July 2026

"Most CRA obligations apply from September 2027"

Wrong

Reporting applied from Sept. 11, 2026; everything else from Dec. 11, 2027

"DORA's compliance deadline is in 2026"

Wrong

DORA has applied since Jan. 17, 2025

Two lessons. The first verified fines are about process, not breaches: a late report and a late registration. Supervisors are starting with the obligations that are easiest to prove, so registration deadlines and reporting clocks are where 2027 risk is most concrete. And the ceilings, up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover for essential entities under NIS2, are a long way from any penalty actually imposed so far. Use the ceilings to size the risk, not to predict the bill.

A 2027 plan in six moves

Map exposure by entity and by product. NIS2, DORA and the UK Bill attach to what your organization is. The CRA attaches to what it sells. A UK software company with EU banking customers can be inside all four. List every legal entity and every product, then the regimes each one triggers.

Build one reporting matrix and rehearse it. For each regime, record the trigger, the deadline, the recipient and the format. Then run the four-clock scenario above as a tabletop exercise and time how long it takes to decide whether an incident is "major," "significant" or "actively exploited."

Rewrite supplier contracts around hours. Your customers' clocks may start before yours. Agree customer notification times in hours, make sure financial-sector contracts carry DORA's required incident-assistance terms, and require component suppliers to tell you about exploited vulnerabilities fast enough for your own CRA reporting.

Run the CRA as two projects. Reporting is live and operational. Product compliance is a December 2027 engineering project: risk assessments, technical files, SBOMs, support periods and, for some products, a notified body. Don't let the second wait on the first.

Build to today's law and watch the drafts. Comply with the national NIS2 law in force now, and track the amendments, CSA2's supplier restrictions, DORA's provider review and the UK's commencement regulations without engineering to drafts that may change.

Get registrations right. The first verified NIS2 fine was for a missed registration notice. Check NIS2 registration in every country where you operate, and if you're a UK managed service provider, have your registration ready for the three-month window after commencement.

The question that starts the CRA clock

One phrase in the CRA deserves more attention than it gets: "actively exploited." A vulnerability in your product isn't reportable just because it exists. The 24-hour clock starts when you know it's being used in attacks. That knowledge rarely comes from inside your own engineering team. It comes from exploitation seen in the wild, chatter on criminal forums, proof-of-concept code and attacks on other organizations running the same component.

That makes threat intelligence a compliance input, not just a security one. Cyble tracks vulnerability exploitation, dark web activity and attacker infrastructure across the open, deep and dark web, which is the evidence a manufacturer needs to know when its clock has started and to show regulators why it reported when it did.

Frequently asked questions

What cyber compliance deadlines fall in 2027?

The main fixed date is Dec. 11, 2027, when the EU Cyber Resilience Act applies in full, including essential security requirements, SBOMs and CE marking for products placed on the EU market. DORA's first three-year cycle of threat-led penetration testing also runs through 2027 and ends in January 2028. NIS2 amendments and the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill's commencement are expected but not yet fixed.

Do UK companies have to comply with the CRA, NIS2 and DORA?

Yes, if they sell into the EU. The CRA applies to any product with digital elements placed on the EU market, wherever the manufacturer is based. NIS2 can apply to UK providers serving EU customers, which must appoint an EU representative. DORA applies to EU financial entities and reaches UK tech providers through contracts and, for critical providers, direct oversight.

When will the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill take effect?

Royal Assent is expected between late 2026 and spring 2027. Most duties will then be brought in by secondary legislation, possibly in phases through 2028. Medium and large managed service providers will have three months from commencement to register with the regulator.

Does DORA replace NIS2 for banks?

For financial entities, DORA is the sector-specific law and takes precedence over NIS2 on ICT risk management, incident reporting, testing and third-party risk. A bank reports major ICT incidents under DORA's timelines, not NIS2's.

Has anyone been fined under NIS2 or DORA?

Yes, but the verified fines are small. Austria's financial regulator fined a bank €42,000 under DORA in July 2026 for late incident reports, and Romania's cybersecurity directorate fined a public body about €10,000 under NIS2 in September 2026 for a late registration notice.

In this article

The Threat Disruption Center brings investigators and companies together to disrupt criminal networks targeting Americans

It aims to help warn victims sooner, interrupt payments, and take down scam infrastructure

If you’ve been scammed, report it promptly to the FBI’s IC3; don’t wait for the center

When someone realizes they have been scammed, the obvious question is: Can I get my money back?

A new US initiative aims to improve the chances of intervening before stolen money disappears—and, perhaps more importantly, before victims send more money.

The Threat Disruption Center will connect investigators with participating companies to help pause payments, freeze funds, take down malicious domains, and ban accounts scammers use to approach victims. TRM Labs is providing the investigative technology behind the effort.

TRM Labs is an existing blockchain intelligence company that helps financial institutions, crypto businesses, and government agencies detect and investigate crypto-related financial crime and fraud. It has been selected as the center’s primary private-sector partner.

The Threat Disruption Center sits within the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center, which is co-led by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. It will serve as a shared technology and collaboration resource for a task force that includes more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners.

The reason

The practical aim is to help investigators sort through victim reports, connect related activity, and identify opportunities to intervene. TRM’s CEO told Bloomberg that the company is looking at how artificial intelligence (AI) can help triage reports in near real time and highlight cases where quick action could return funds to victims.

Scammers depend on legitimate services to reach people and move their money: social networks, website hosts, banks, payment providers, and cryptocurrency platforms. Those dependencies also create opportunities to interrupt them.

The center is intended to provide a standing channel through which investigators and participating companies can share intelligence in near real time. Depending on the circumstances, a company could then:

Pause a victim’s payment

Freeze stolen funds

Take down a malicious domain

Ban a social media account used to approach victims

The intended beneficiaries are anyone targeted by scams, cybercrime, and sextortion, not just people who own cryptocurrency. For consumers, the most valuable intervention may be the payment they never make.

Cryptocurrency investment scams often unfold over time. A scammer builds trust, introduces an apparently profitable investment opportunity, and encourages the victim to keep adding money. The FBI says some victims identified through its existing Operation Level Up initiative were preparing to sell their homes, liquidate retirement savings, or take out substantial loans. Reaching someone before that next transfer can prevent an already serious loss from becoming much worse.

What it’s not

Tracing money, freezing it, seizing it, and returning it to a victim are different stages. The announcements describe interventions intended to preserve funds while investigations and legal proceedings continue.

It should not be mistaken for a new public-facing recovery service, and it does not guarantee that victims will get their money back. The announced route for reporting a scam remains the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, or IC3.

Do not wait for a new initiative to reach you. The FBI recommends:

Stop sending money immediately. Do not pay additional “taxes,” “verification charges,” or withdrawal fees demanded by a suspicious investment platform.

Report the scam promptly at ic3.gov. Rapid reporting can support recovery efforts and help investigators connect related complaints.

Be wary of anyone offering to recover your money for a fee. Recovery services can themselves be scams.

Verify unexpected contact from law enforcement independently. The FBI warns that criminals impersonate agents and legitimate anti-fraud operations. Contact your local FBI field office to verify an approach rather than relying on an email’s appearance.

In this article

A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers

The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed

Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing

Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks.

On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters:

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line.

Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program.

Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole.

What information was exposed?

The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified.

The companies have disclosed the following:

JPMorgan Chase: Marketing data held by vendors, potentially including some customer names and email addresses.

Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected.

Mastercard: A limited number of email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. Mastercard described this as non-payment information.

The n0n leak site lists JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard and claims their data was published after the ransom deadline passed on November 16.

Screenshot of n0n leak site, November 20, 2026

Researchers at Cybernews reported additional details from the leaked datasets:

JPMorgan: Roughly 16,000 customer email addresses, some phone numbers, identifiers described as account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses.

Visa: A dataset involving more than 6,000 premium customers, with fields including names, email addresses, phone numbers, messaging-app information, and booking details such as dates and addresses.

Mastercard: Data posted by n0n includes marketing information related to customers in North America, the Middle East, and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses, according to Reuters.

How to protect your accounts

If you’re concerned your information may be involved, these steps can help protect your accounts and identity:

Verify messages independently. Open your bank’s official app, use a website address you already know, or call the number on your card or statement. Do not use a link or phone number supplied by someone claiming to be investigating the breach.

Never read out a login or payment-verification code to an unexpected caller. Those codes can be the missing piece that allows a criminal to access your account. Enter them only when completing an action you initiated through the genuine service.

Do not transfer money to “protect” it. A caller who tells you to move your savings into a “safe account” is trying to steal them. Hang up and contact your bank independently.

Verify any offer of breach support before enrolling. JPMorgan says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.

Consider a credit freeze as a separate identity-protection measure.

Title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
Context: The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2
Full Text:
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.

If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration.

Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

Title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
Context: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument...
Full Text: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now." The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026. The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users. The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals. A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data. "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies." Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

Title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability

CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Mail Bombing Attacks Fuel IT Helpdesk Impersonation Scams
Context: FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter...
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are conducting large-scale “mail bombing attacks”, followed by IT helpdesk impersonation in order to compromise user accounts.

Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) are tracking the campaign, which involves inboxes being deliberately flooded with emails.

In an update on the campaign, published by FIRE on November 19, the researchers noted that mail bombing does not require access to a target mailbox. Rather a target’s inbox is flooded with subscriptions after an attacker has submitted a target email address to newsletter, registration and other signup forms across unrelated websites.

This email flood can interrupt activities like customer service and routine correspondence, as well as obscuring account alerts, payment notifications and other messages that may require attention.

FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter subscription boxes.

Mailchimp and its transactional service, Mandrill, were the most frequently observed delivery services, followed by Amazon SES and SendGrid.

“In the attacks observed so far by the FIRE team, the average email delivery of a mail bombing attack is at a peak of 10k messages per active campaign, around 1k emails per day,” Fortra said.

FIRE said it has also detected phishing attempts during these mail-bombing waves, which are harder to detect among the wave of otherwise legitimate emails.

The mail bombing campaign has been followed by vishing calls in which contact is made by the threat actor through Teams.

“In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality, attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both,” the researchers explained.

Fortra said that these mail bombing campaigns can be difficult to detect because individual subscription emails can appear entirely normal and may not contain malicious links.

Meanwhile, allowlist exceptions can make containment harder when they cover delivery platforms carrying the flood.

Security Teams Advised to Monitor Email Volumes

Fortra recommended that security teams monitor email volume per recipient against the normal baseline. Investigate bursts involving many unrelated senders, subscription wording and mailing-list headers.

Security teams should also confirm the scope and duration directly with the email delivery provider.

During FIRE’s investigation, Mailchimp advised that senders could request temporary subscription blocking for a specified recipient. Mailchimp also documents a separate automatic control that restricts an address from joining additional audiences for 24 hours after rapid repeated signups.

Fortra did not attribute the campaign to a particular group.

Title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
Context: Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2
Full Text: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

Title: Catching Ransomware: Introducing encrypts-files and Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486
Context: Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the...
Full Text:
When we search for ransomware samples during an investigation or detection test, we usually want to answer a direct question: Did this file actually encrypt user documents when executed?

Modern ransomware families implement file encryption in many different ways. While commodity builders may call standard operating system cryptographic APIs, contemporary Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) payloads written in Rust, Go, C++, or .NET frequently embed statically linked AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA, or custom intermittent encryption routines that never touch OS crypto libraries. At the same time, benign installers, browsers, and updaters legitimately use cryptography and write thousands of temporary files during normal execution.

This week, we rolled out three updates across VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence to identify malware that encrypts user files:

New encrypts-files Tag Across Windows and macOS Sandboxes: A cipher-agnostic behavioral trait (behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) and file-level search tag (tag:encrypts-files) emitted across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only when dynamic analysis confirms real encryption of user documents.

Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486 Gating in CAPE Sandbox: Previously, generic CAPE file-churn signatures mapped high-volume file deletes, overwrites, or moves directly to T1486. Newly scanned CAPE reports now require verified user-file encryption before emitting those T1486 mappings, cutting CAPE-only daily T1486 hits from 1,039/day (78.5% with 0 AV detections) to 0 on benign files and reducing false positives across platform-wide T1486 volume by 97.6% (from 7,238 to 171 files per day).

Real-Time VirusTotal Livehunt Support: Real-time YARA-X matching on sandbox reports via vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Figure 1: High-level overview of how CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage verify user-document encryption before emitting tag:encrypts-files and gating CAPE T1486.

How Cipher-Agnostic File-Encryption Verification Works

Across CAPE Sandbox (Windows), Zenbox (Windows), and macOS Mirage (Apple Silicon), each sandbox environment contains realistic user documents across standard user profile directories.

During and after detonation, our sandboxes apply three verification gates before emitting encrypts-files (and before CAPE emits generic T1486 mappings):

Content Destruction and Entropy Verification (Cipher-Agnostic): Rather than hooking OS cryptographic APIs, each sandbox inspects modified user-file content on disk using format-aware verification tailored to its platform. Depending on the file type and sandbox, checks evaluate destroyed file structures, elevated entropy, or non-text byte patterns alongside corroborating ransomware behaviors without relying on a single fixed entropy threshold. Because verification evaluates the resulting files on disk, it catches AES, ChaCha20, intermittent encryption, and XOR ciphers alike.

Coordinated Ransomware Extension Renames: Many ransomware families read original user documents, write encrypted copies under a uniform new extension (for example, .k404, .lkd, .INC, .BLWZ, or .heartbreaker), and delete the originals. Our sandboxes correlate reads, writes, moves, and unlinks across user directories to confirm coordinated encryption renames across user documents.

Benign File-Churn Exclusion Guards: Self-extracting archives, software installers, compilers, browser caches, and logs are explicitly excluded when they only generate routine temporary or application files rather than encrypting user documents. Similarly, dropping a README.txt file or calling crypto APIs alone never triggers encrypts-files without corroborated document encryption.

Real-World Ransomware Caught in Action

Across 328,257 newly submitted unique files (405,469 total files including rescans) analyzed in CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage since November 17, tag:encrypts-files matched 55 files and surfaced in-the-wild and validation payloads across Windows executables, Python scripts, DLLs, compressed archives (ZIP and RAR), and a rescanned Apple Silicon macOS binary with zero benign software false positives across all 55 manually reviewed matches (alongside 0 benign false positives across 9,976 random CAPE reports and 400 macOS Mirage runs in pre-rollout backtesting). Below are three examples you can inspect on VirusTotal.

1. Catching Zero- and Low-Detection In-the-Wild Lockers: The .k404 Campaign and lkd.exe

Static signatures often lag behind script-based or freshly compiled lockers. In an active .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17-18, Python locker fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354 (system_update.pyw) was flagged by 0 out of 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis, while companion PE binary 3dd45ab8e2f9c1af773a75221d792fb78870764419170e9c9c5941160364c700 (K404T_Fidye.exe) had 10 / 75 detections and separate Windows locker a8c2402ef3ae115300f5428712ccb0b5461f4a2f14b5bfdfbe08d5ad86bd3087 (lkd.exe) had 3 / 75 at the time of analysis.

Figure 2: VirusTotal Behavior report for undetected Python locker system_update.pyw (fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354, 0 / 59 AV on GUI at capture), showing encrypts-files, T1486, and Desktop user files encrypted with the .k404 extension.

When detonated in Zenbox, system_update.pyw runs under pythonw.exe from AppData\Roaming\WindowsSystemUpdate\, self-deletes, and rewrites Desktop user files into .k404 ciphertext, while K404T_Fidye.exe and lkd.exe encrypt user documents in CAPE Sandbox using .k404 and .lkd extensions alongside k404t.txt and read_me_restore.txt ransom notes. In CAPE Sandbox, verified encryption sets both tag:encrypts-files and T1486. Note that Zenbox, macOS Mirage, and third-party sandboxes (such as Dr.Web vxCube or VMRay) keep their own rule-level T1486 mappings, so a file can carry T1486 from another sandbox rule without tag:encrypts-files.

2. Enterprise RaaS & High-Speed Windows Encryptors: INC Ransom and BlackWizardLock

Modern Windows ransomware families optimize encryption speed using asynchronous I/O and multi-threaded directory queues. In sample d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 (INC Ransom), CAPE Sandbox captures the payload binding user files to Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), rewriting user documents into .INC files, and dropping INC-README.txt across directories.

Figure 3: INC Ransom (d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645) Behavior report showing T1486 user-file encryption and user documents rewritten with the .INC extension.

Similarly, sample 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e (BlackWizardLock) executes unpacked payload code from dynamically allocated memory, stages temporary .~BLWZ.tmp files, overwrites user documents with .BLWZ extensions (such as bitaddress.pdf.BLWZ and cover-letter-uidev.docx.BLWZ), and presents a full-screen Russian extortion lock screen that directs victims to @seedware on Telegram and threatens to destroy the Master Boot Record (MBR) after five wrong key attempts.

Figure 4: BlackWizardLock (98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e) Behavior report showing encrypts-files, T1486 impact, and user documents encrypted into .BLWZ files.

3. Native Apple Silicon macOS Ransomware: Heartbreaker (Historical macOS Sample Rescanned in macOS Mirage, 16 / 75 AV at Analysis)

While native macOS ransomware is rare in the wild compared to Windows, re-analyzing historical macOS samples validates Apple Silicon coverage. Sample 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 (first submitted in May 2025 and rescanned in macOS Mirage) is a self-signed 64-bit ARM64 Mach-O binary detected by 16 out of 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

Figure 5: Native macOS Heartbreaker ransomware (6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18) Behavior report in macOS Mirage showing encrypts-files, T1486, and user files in Downloads encrypted to .heartbreaker.

When detonated on bare-metal Apple Silicon in macOS Mirage, the binary installs a persistent LaunchAgent (/Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist), drops /Users/admin/Desktop/README.txt, and encrypts user documents in /Users/admin/Downloads/ into Invoice_INV-2026-0842.pdf.heartbreaker and Vendor_Payment_Schedule.xlsx.heartbreaker. This triggers both ENCRYPTS_FILES and T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact).

What This Signal Does Not Catch

tag:encrypts-files is a high-precision confirmation signal, not an exhaustive recall filter. A missing tag does not mean a sample is benign or lacks ransomware logic. Automated sandbox runs will not emit the tag in several common scenarios:

Samples that require command-line arguments or passwords: Affiliates often guard execution with a runtime flag (such as LockBit 3.0 builds that require -pass <key> to decrypt their payload).

Sandbox evasion, user-interaction gates, or long sleeps: Samples that exit on VM checks (DETECT_DEBUG_ENVIRONMENT), stall past the analysis window (LONG_SLEEPS), or wait for specific locales or clicks never reach their encryption loop.

Unreachable command-and-control key servers: Families that fetch an encryption key from an offline C2 server before touching local files abort prior to file modification.

DLLs with custom exported entry points: Standard rundll32 detonation executes DllMain, which misses DLL lockers that require calling a specific named or ordinal export with structured arguments.

Network-share-only targets or executable file infectors: Samples configured to encrypt only SMB shares, niche database extensions absent from the VM, or parasitic .exe infectors (such as Virlock and Neshta) do not encrypt user documents on the local profile.

Safe ransomware simulators and analysis timeouts: Tools that only encrypt their own newly created test files rather than user documents, as well as samples that time out before reaching their encryption loop, do not trigger the tag.

Practical Security Use Cases & VirusTotal Intelligence Queries

Security teams can use tag:encrypts-files (or behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) immediately across VirusTotal Intelligence Search and the v3 REST API to streamline four common workflows:

Building Clean Ransomware Validation Corpora for EDR and Storage Defense: Endpoint protection engineers, NAS/SAN storage security teams, and purple teams need fresh samples guaranteed to perform real disk-level file encryption when testing ransomware rollback and anomaly-detection sensors. Filter directly on samples verified to encrypt user documents across operating systems and architectures:

All confirmed file-encrypting samples: entity:file tag:encrypts-files

64-bit Windows PE encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:peexe tag:64bits

Archive, script, and non-PE file encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files NOT type:peexe

macOS Mach-O encryptors (low in-the-wild volume): entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:macho (note: 20 of the first 55 tagged files match NOT type:peexe, mostly ZIP/RAR archives plus .pyw scripts and DLLs)

Uncovering Evasive or Newly Emerged Ransomware Families: Combine dynamic encryption proof with low static antivirus detection thresholds to catch novel packers, custom Go or Rust lockers, or targeted affiliate builds before broad signature coverage arrives:

Low-detection file encryptors (< 10 AV detections): entity:file tag:encrypts-files p:10-

Rapid SOC Triage and Impact Prioritization: During incident response, seeing behaviour_tags:crypto on a suspicious binary only tells an analyst that cryptography libraries were linked or called. Seeing encrypts-files paired with T1486 confirms destructive file-encryption capability immediately, enabling faster containment and backup isolation decisions.

Confidential Detonation in Private Scanning: When triaging sensitive incident samples that cannot be uploaded to the public corpus, you can detonate them in Private Scanning to run the same CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage checks inside an isolated tenant.

Real-Time Hunting with VirusTotal Livehunt and YARA-X

Beyond retrospective search, you can receive real-time IOC Stream notifications whenever newly submitted or sandbox-analyzed files exhibit verified document encryption by pairing VirusTotal Livehunt with the vt YARA-X module.

1. Core Livehunt Rule: Verified ENCRYPTS_FILES Trait

The rule below matches any file whose sandbox behavior emits vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES. Because CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only emit this trait after verifying user-document encryption, ANDing T1486 adds no extra precision:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Ransomware_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Detects files verified to encrypt user documents in sandbox execution (ENCRYPTS_FILES trait)" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

2. Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting

To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the 0/75 system_update.pyw script and 3/75 lkd.exe binary above), add a vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious threshold:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Evasive_Ransomware_LowAV_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Alerts on low-detection files (< 10 AV engines) verified to encrypt user documents in sandboxes" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious < 10 and for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

Two practical tips when authoring Livehunt behavioral rules:

Prefer vt.behaviour.traits over vt.metadata.tags for immediate behavioral matching: Livehunt evaluates dynamic rules as soon as sandbox reports finish (vt.behaviour.traits), so checking vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES matches directly on the normalized sandbox report without waiting for downstream file-tag indexing.

When (if ever) to query T1486 in Livehunt: Do not AND T1486 onto ENCRYPTS_FILES rules, because vt.behaviour.mitre_attack_techniques aggregates across every sandbox (including broader Zenbox and third-party mappings) and adds no precision over the trait. Only add a case-insensitive technique.id iequals "T1486" check in separate rules when you want broader T1486 hits from third-party sandboxes that do not emit ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Try It Out and Share Your Feedback

tag:encrypts-files (across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage) and stricter T1486 gating (in CAPE Sandbox) are live in production for newly scanned and re-analyzed files:

Where the tag appears: Check the top file header badges or Behavior > Behavior Tags (attributes.tags and behaviour_traits in the v3 API).

Where triggering file paths are recorded: Inspect Signatures and File system actions > Files written in the Behavior tab (or signature_matches[].match_data in /api/v3/files/{sha256}/behaviours) to see the specific affected file paths.

Click Reanalyze in the VirusTotal web UI to queue dynamic runs on eligible sandboxes that have not yet analyzed that hash (POST /api/v3/files/{id}/analyse in the API refreshes static AV only unless the file is re-uploaded or detonated in Private Scanning).

Title: Suspected North Korea-Aligned Group Hides C2 on Solana Blockchain
Context: A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts
Full Text:
A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts. Cisco Talos said the group used the Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), an infostealer and a cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker.

Cisco Talos detailed the activity in research published November 18. It tracks the group as UAT-12643 and assessed with low confidence that it was a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT).

Talos based its assessment partly on earlier use of Overlord by UNK_DeadDrop, a cluster it described as likely North Korean, and on a Solana C2 technique previously linked to North Korea's Lazarus Group. It noted that other actors had used both.

How Overlord RAT Stays Hidden

The operators stored encrypted C2 addresses, which tell infected machines where to get instructions, in memos attached to transactions from a Solana wallet they controlled. The Go-based Overlord RAT checked that wallet for updates, so the operators could switch servers without redeploying the malware.

Overlord also resisted removal. Trying to terminate it crashed Windows with a Blue Screen of Death, and it planted itself in the Windows Recovery Environment, the part of Windows used to repair or reset a PC, which Talos said ensured "the implant survives a full system reset."

Talos identified 35 commands. Beyond surveillance, including keylogging, screenshots and webcam and audio capture, they covered file and process control, script execution, movement through internal networks and in-memory plugin delivery.

Read more on blockchain C2: Six npm Packages Read C2 Addresses From Ethereum Wallet

Targets Include Gamers and Cryptocurrency Holders

Talos said the lures and payloads pointed to three groups of targets: cryptocurrency holders, people with gaming accounts and users of internet phone software. Lures included a fake financial statement, a tampered Viber installer and files named after an internet phone app.

The actor also used Good Game, a publicly available Python infostealer that collected browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets and gaming-related information. Talos said the campaign actor was not its developer. The stealer searched files for keywords in English, French, Spanish and Portuguese, which Talos said pointed to possible victims in Europe.

The toolset also included a clipboard hijacker that swapped copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses for ones the attackers controlled. Talos did not see how the malicious files reached victims and gave no victim count.

An operational security mistake also left the actor's file server publicly reachable, Talos said, giving researchers a view of its toolset and C2 settings.

Title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
Context: Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers
Full Text:
Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

“I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added.

These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems.

Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility.

The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail. Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis, told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards.

“We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.”

The math at stake

Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics:

Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers)

Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc.

“What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO.

Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science.

“The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.”

2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece

Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance.

“A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained.

AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978).

“The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added.

Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.”

Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen.

The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis.

Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’

Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis.

Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded.

Q-Day and LLMs

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography.

“We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.”

Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use.

“We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”
