Title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
Context: Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4
Full Text: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

Title: TfL Warns 265,000 Photocard Customers May Have Had Personal Data Exposed
Context: Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or...
Full Text:
Transport for London (TfL) has been impacted by a cyber incident, which may have exposed the personal data of around 265,000 photocard customers.

On November 16, unauthorized actors sent emails to Oyster Photocard customers from TfL’s system. TfL said these emails were “generated as a result of the compromise.”

The emails asked customers to create an account, despite them already having a photocard account.

In a statement shared with Infosecurity, Shashi Verma, TfL’s director of technology strategy & revenue, said the organization immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated.

"While we acted swiftly, we now believe that around 265,000 photocard customers may have had their account details compromised as part of this incident,” he warned.

Oyster photocards are personalized smartcards which can be used by eligible customers for free or discounted travel across public transport in London.

Customers whose account details were potentially compromised include children with Zip Oyster cards, whose ages range from 5-18. However, Verma said he does not believe the names or date of births of any children with a Zip Oyster card have been compromised.

Other customer accounts that may have been affected are those who have 18+ Student Oyster cards, 18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocards, 60+ London Oyster photocards, Apprentice Oyster photocards and Veterans Oyster photocard.

TfL’s current assessment is that no passwords, bank or payment card details or customer journey information were accessed in the breach.

Verma added that TfL, which manages most of London’s public transport network, has now contained the incident.

“Due to the speed with which this incident was identified and addressed, we believe that the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced,” he said.

“We are continuing to investigate what has happened but have already contacted affected customers to make them aware of this,” Verma continued.

The body has informed the UK’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), of the incident.

TfL Customers Urged to Change Passwords

While there is currently no evidence that the affected data has been misused, TfL said it will be asking all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer. It also advises customers to change their password on any other online service using the same information.

Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or text messages impersonating TfL.

“Account holders should be particularly cautious of unexpected communications, avoid clicking suspicious links and always verify messages through TfL's official website or customer service channels,” Akhtar said.

The TfL photocard website remains offline at the time of writing and displays the following message: “We are currently investigating an issue where photocard customers have received emails asking them to create an account, when they already have a Photocard account. We have temporarily taken the TfL Photocard portal down while this is being investigated and apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.”

Current Oyster photocard customers can continue to travel as normal, while any customer who need to renew their photocard or query any journey history can still do so by contacting TfL’s Customer Services.

Verma said TfL hopes to restore the affected website services “as quickly as possible.”

TfL was previously impacted by a cyber-attack in September 2024, resulting in customer data being breached. This included Oyster refund data, encompassing bank account numbers and sort codes for around 5000 customers.

Two individuals, Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five years and six months in prison after being convicted of offenses relating to the attack in July 2026, which the judge said was motivated in part by “selfish bravado” rather than purely financial gain.

Title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
Context: The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them...
Full Text: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related. Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

Title: A Fifth of UK Employees Share Passwords with AI
Context: It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one...
Full Text:
Large numbers of UK employees are sharing sensitive information with unmanaged AI tools and allowing them to take actions on their accounts without considering the security risks, Dashlane has warned.

The credential security specialist polled 1000 UK workers and 250 IT execs as part of a wider survey group of 3800 across the UK, US and France to create its latest report, Misplaced Trust: Inside the Workplace’s New AI Security Blind Spot.

It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one activity without seeking permission first, including accessing emails, company files and customer information.

Read more on AI risks: NCSC Publishes Guidance on Securing Agentic AI Use

Dashlane unearthed a high propensity among UK workers to use shadow AI without thinking about the repercussions for their employer.

It found that:

37% would be willing to lend their login credentials to a new AI tool after one week

15% have granted an AI tool access to a file, system or account they subsequently discovered it should not have accessed, with 45% claiming the access remains active

23% have copied sensitive information into AI that they would not normally share with a colleague, website or other work system

21% have failed to check where information would be stored or sent

Just a quarter (25%) say they always consider security risks when using an AI agent at work

“Our latest data shows an emerging ‘AI Colleague Effect’ where employees are overextending trust to AI systems, sharing credentials and granting access to AI agents, sometimes without fully understanding what those tools can do with the permissions they've been given,” explained Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“That creates significant challenges for security teams trying to detect misuse or investigate incidents.”

Security Leaders Are Over-Confident

Sharing sensitive information with LLMs/agents or allowing agents access to internal corporate systems represent a significant compliance and security risk.

Information may end up on third-party servers which could be compromised, and it may be used to train models and regurgitated in responses to other users. Agents are a possible target for hijacking by threat actors.

In fact, 72% of IT and security executives Dashlane polled said their organization has experienced a security incident involving an AI agent’s credentials or access in the past 12 months.

Yet the vast majority (92%) also claimed they were confident that they know about every AI agent operating within their organization, the report found. That contradicts the claims from a quarter (25%) of employees who said they use AI tools their employer does not know about.

Business demands for adoption are weighing heavily on the minds of security leaders.

More than two-thirds (68%) of UK IT security executives claimed to feel caught between pressure to deploy AI quickly and the need to keep the organization secure.

"The challenge for security leaders is that the pace of change presented by AI and the potential consequences of misuse is unlike any other technology before it,” concluded Frenet.

“The principles that make up the foundation of a good security program for securing human identities – just-in-time provisioning, least privilege, good credential hygiene and authentication – have to be applied to our new AI colleagues as well."

Title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
Context: "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained
Full Text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

Scattered Spider used phishing texts and SIM swaps to steal $11.6 million in cryptocurrency

Tyler Robert Buchanan’s six-year sentence doesn’t mean the wider group has disappeared

A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds.

Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million

Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing, to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems.

The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes.

SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims.

Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years.

The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges.

Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider?

Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said.

There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life.

Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers.

We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025.

How to protect your number from SIM swapping

Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts:

Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM.

Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. These options aren’t tied to your phone number in the same way.

Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t initiate. Attackers may flood you with requests in the hope that you’ll approve one.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Title: Rakuten Securities Breach Could Impact 15 Million Customers
Context: The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its...
Full Text:
One of Japan’s leading online brokerages has revealed a major breach of customer account data which could impact nearly 16 million people.

Tokyo-headquartered Rakuten Securities allows retail investors to trade stocks, bonds, foreign exchange and other financial instruments.

The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its systems the day before.

“As a result of our investigation, we confirmed that on Wednesday, November 11 some information managed within our test environment system may have been leaked to an external party,” it said. “We are continuing our investigation into the cause and detailed circumstances of the unauthorized access.”

Read more on Japanese breaches: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs

The securities giant said that branch/customer code, login ID, name, date of birth, address, phone number, email address, employer, withdrawal account details, annual income, asset information, and last login date for around 4.47 million accounts had been compromised.

An even larger group of 11.25 million accounts had just their Rakuten Securities branch/customer code and login IDs taken, it added.

The firm confirmed passwords, PINs and other information have not been taken and there’s no sign of unauthorized access to customer accounts.

Security experts questioned why production data was allowed to be used in a test environment.

“This isn’t some advanced security concept or something that requires sophisticated technology to address. It’s one of the most fundamental rules of protecting sensitive information, and yet we continue to see organizations make these mistakes,” argued Black Hills Information Security owner John Strand.ㅤ

“The proper way to do this is to have separate development, testing, and staging environments, each with clearly defined security controls.”

Rakuten Urges Passkey Adoption

Rakuten Securities warned customers of follow-on phishing attempts, presumably trying to trick individuals into handing over their logins.

It said over 90% of customers currently log in using phishing-resistant passkeys, and urged the remainder to switch to mitigate the risk of account takeover.

Last year, regulator the Financial Services Agency (FSA) warned of a sharp increase in account hijacking at Japanese securities companies, with hackers making illegal trades of over 304 billion yen ($2bn).

It claimed the hackers were attempting to manipulate the market by boosting the value of small-cap stocks that they own, in order to sell them at a bigger profit.

Rakuten Securities’ woes come at the end of a bad year for Japanese companies, which have been hit by a string of data breaches and extortion attacks.

They include Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (8 million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million).

In October, GMO, a virtual desktop company popular with foreign-exchange traders told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by ransomware actors.

Title: Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
Context: That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms
Full Text:
We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work.

For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level.

But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach.

The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done.

Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, risk ratings and remediation backlogs.

What they frequently lack is the organizational machinery to translate that knowledge into effective, sustained remedial action.

And that is not primarily a technology problem.

The uncomfortable reality behind remediation backlogs

Consider what happens when a large enterprise identifies a critical vulnerability.

The security team assesses its severity and potential impact. It raises a ticket, assigns a priority, identifies an owner and requests remediation.

On paper, the process looks straightforward.

In practice, that is often where the real problems begin.

The infrastructure team may be managing ageing systems with complex dependencies. The development team may have committed to a demanding release schedule. Production operations may be unwilling to accept additional downtime. Business stakeholders may resist disruption to revenue-generating services.

Some systems may have very limited maintenance windows. Others may require extensive regression testing before deploying patches. Legacy applications may depend on components that cannot easily be upgraded.

And ownership itself may be disputed.

Security teams frequently have the responsibility to identify and report vulnerabilities but lack the authority to enforce remediation. Technology teams control the systems but may have competing priorities and insufficient resources.

The result is familiar: escalating tickets, repeated exceptions, missed deadlines, unresolved disputes and growing remediation backlogs.

None of these problems can be solved simply by producing a better vulnerability score.

Prioritization is necessary, but it is not the answer

The industry has increasingly recognized that organizations cannot remediate everything.

That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms.

These capabilities have genuine value: There is an obvious difference between a vulnerability that is actively exploited on an internet-facing critical system and one that exists on an isolated, low-value asset.

But prioritization is only the beginning of a management process. It is not its outcome: A perfectly prioritized remediation backlog remains a backlog.

In many organizations, the difficulty is not deciding which vulnerabilities matter most. It is securing agreement on who will fix them, when the work will take place and who has the authority to resolve conflicts or accept the risk.

These are matters of governance, accountability and business priorities.

The cybersecurity industry remains disproportionately focused on the what, when the real challenge lies in the how and the who.

AI is about to make the problem considerably worse

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability discovery.

AI-assisted tools can analyse code, identify weaknesses and accelerate vulnerability research on a scale and at a speed that would previously have required substantial human effort.

According to Google Threat Intelligence Group, monthly vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August 2026, while observed exploitation also increased significantly. AI is contributing to that acceleration, although changes in disclosure practices also influence the figures.

The consequences for large organizations could be significant.

We are moving towards a world where the identification of vulnerabilities becomes increasingly automated, increasingly inexpensive and potentially continuous.

But what happens when the volume of identified vulnerabilities increases dramatically while the organization’s capacity to remediate them remains essentially unchanged?

The answer is predictable: Larger backlogs. More pressure on technology teams. More exceptions. More disputes over priorities. And potentially greater exposure, despite unprecedented visibility into technical weaknesses.

The Cloud Security Alliance has already highlighted this growing disconnect between accelerated vulnerability discovery and the capacity of organizations to absorb and remediate findings.

AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery while remediation remains trapped in organizational structures designed for another era.

That is the real emerging challenge.

AI cannot negotiate a production maintenance window

Of course, AI can also contribute to remediation.

It can establish proofs of concept, generate and test fixes, propose configuration changes, analyse dependencies and automate certain deployment activities.

These are important developments, and organizations should embrace them where appropriate.

But their practical impact must not be overstated.

AI cannot independently decide that a critical production system should be taken offline during a peak business period. It cannot assume accountability for disrupting customer services or resolve competing priorities between a business unit, an infrastructure team and the security function.

It cannot simply override legacy dependencies, contractual obligations or regulatory constraints.

Even where AI can technically generate a suitable fix, somebody still needs to validate it, approve its deployment, ensure that the fix has not broken something else and verify that remediation has been successful.

Some of those steps can be automated. Others require judgement, authority and organizational coordination.

The more powerful AI becomes, the more visible those remaining management bottlenecks will be.

And this is where the traditional cybersecurity approach is increasingly inadequate.

Vulnerability management needs an operating model, not another dashboard

What large organizations need is not simply better vulnerability management technology.

They need a remediation operating model that establishes clear accountability across security, development, infrastructure, operations and business management.

That model should address several fundamental questions.

Who owns the remediation of vulnerabilities affecting shared platforms or complex applications? Who allocates the necessary resources? Who can authorize emergency changes? Who resolves disagreements when remediation conflicts with business priorities?

How are maintenance windows negotiated and secured? How are persistent exceptions challenged? Who accepts the residual business risk when remediation cannot be completed within the expected timeframe?

And, crucially, who is responsible for ensuring that agreed actions happen?

These responsibilities cannot be left to informal relationships between technical teams or to the persistence of individual security managers.

They need to be embedded in management processes, supported by executive authority and reinforced through meaningful performance measures.

Security should provide risk intelligence, challenge and assurance. Technology teams should own the delivery of remediation within their environments. Business management should participate in decisions where operational disruption or investment trade-offs are unavoidable.

The CISO’s role is to help establish and oversee that machinery, not to become the organization’s chief ticket chaser.

Measuring remediation effectiveness, not just reporting activity

There is also a fundamental problem with how vulnerability management performance is measured.

Too many organizations remain focused on the number of vulnerabilities identified, severity distributions, compliance with remediation deadlines and the volume of outstanding findings.

Those indicators have their place, but they can encourage an administrative approach to vulnerability management: Closing tickets becomes a proxy for reducing risk.

What matters is whether material exposures are being eliminated within acceptable timeframes and whether the organization can demonstrate that remediation has worked.

Management should pay particular attention to recurring remediation failures, ageing high-risk exposures, operational bottlenecks, the effectiveness of exception handling and the time required to implement verified fixes.

The distinction between a vulnerability being reported as resolved and genuinely being remediated is essential.

AI can help generate more accurate and timely evidence. But it cannot substitute for accountability over the results.

Auditability and regulatory obligations add another critical dimension to this challenge.

Regulators increasingly expect organizations not only to identify and assess vulnerabilities, but also to demonstrate that appropriate remedial actions have been taken within reasonable timeframes.

This requires clear ownership, documented decisions, traceable exceptions periodically reviewed and reliable evidence that remediation has been completed.

As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and potentially automates parts of the remediation process, maintaining an auditable chain of accountability becomes even more important.

Ultimately, compliance cannot rest on the ability to identify problems: It needs to rest on the ability to demonstrate that they have been effectively addressed.

The real opportunity for AI is to transform execution

This is where I believe the cybersecurity industry should concentrate its attention.

Rather than simply applying AI to discover more vulnerabilities and refine their prioritization or their treatment, vendors and practitioners should focus on how AI can accelerate the entire remediation lifecycle.

That means understanding dependencies, identifying suitable deployment opportunities, preparing changes, automating testing, coordinating workflows, validating results and providing management with reliable evidence of progress across the whole cycle.

In highly automated environments, AI agents may eventually execute substantial portions of that process under clearly defined controls.

But the objective should not be automation for its own sake: It should be to reduce the friction between identifying a problem and resolving it.

And that requires technology to be designed around a functioning governance model, rather than expecting governance to emerge from the technology.

The technology will change. The management problem will not.

I have argued for years that cybersecurity is fundamentally a leadership and management challenge supported by technology.

Vulnerability management provides perhaps one of the clearest demonstrations of that principle.

The same structural problems that prevented organizations from patching critical systems fifteen years ago remain visible today: fragmented responsibilities, competing priorities, operational constraints, weak governance and insufficient management follow-through.

AI will not make those problems disappear.

On the contrary, by accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the time available to respond, it is exposing them more brutally than ever.

The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated vulnerability discovery capabilities.

They will be those that have built the governance, accountability and operational discipline required to translate technical intelligence into effective remedial action.

The future of vulnerability management will not be determined by how quickly we can find what is wrong. It will be determined by how effectively organizations can get things fixed.

And that has always been a management problem.

Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP UpdateFirmware requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device.

Additional Details

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
Context: Conclusion Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code
Full Text:
[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.

While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]

A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]

A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them.

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.

Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].

AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with <sensor-ip>, and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].

The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.

A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.

A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.

Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.

Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.

Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. And that type of sleeper agent is exactly what this is like, because it could be triggered by a set of tokens, which is basically a set of words. It could be triggered based on time of day, or it could be both. But the thing that's so surprising about this, and they've named it Lazarus, not in the sense of the North Korean group that's called Lazarus, is because you can have these types of sleeper agent activities buried deep in a model. And here's what's particularly interesting: this was discovered and documented by AI. So Microsoft not only proved that this could happen, but they also prescribed some things that could be done to prevent it. So my advice for this would be you should be using open source, open weight models. But don't go by the number of downloads and assume that that means it's safe, because some of the models that have been backdoored in the past have thousands or even 100,000 downloads. So you can't just assume because it's popular that therefore it means it's safe. There are mechanisms that you can use to check these. Shockingly, it's AI that you use to basically verify these, but it's an extra step. And for the tinkerers, the people that are using agentic AI, et cetera, the stakes are higher because if you're using something like Hermes Agent or GrokBot or Claude, you may give it full access to your computer. Here's my full access to my entire hard drive, et cetera, and suddenly the stakes change. And the next thing you know, your cryptocurrency wallet is just as empty as mine.

GRAHAM CLULEY

I mean, that is when it gets really scary though, isn't it? Is when it's agentic AI, which is gonna go wrong rather than the chatbot going wrong and telling you something daft. You don't have to tell me if you're not comfortable doing so, Ray, but do you let an AI actually do things on your computer?

RAY REDACTED

100%. Absolutely.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Oh my goodness, Ray.

RAY REDACTED

There are ways you can use agentic AI and be safe. For example, I run armies in a container. I use Docker, right? It doesn't have access to read/write activities. If you want to give it financial accounts, there are ways you can do read-only so that it can't write and it doesn't have any credentials, et cetera. But here's the problem, Graham. The problem is 99% of the people that are using these agents are not doing that. They're defaulting to give it full access to absolutely everything. And by the way, in the case of Muse, this is Facebook. So you do have to ask yourself, would you give Facebook copies of the keys to your house and your car and your children's Social Security numbers? Right? Because millions of people are doing that.

GRAHAM CLULEY

They've already got that. Why do they need it again?

RAY REDACTED

But so yes, with agentic, it changes the stakes, so to speak. But in theory, running local models and giving that agentic ability, if it's properly segmented, if it's got separate VLANs, et cetera, it can be the safest way to do this because you're not transmitting that to the cloud. Microsoft's put a little bit of a wrinkle in it because now they're saying just because it's a local open source, open weight model doesn't mean you can assume that it's safe. And I think we're going to see a lot more of these types of attacks. Primarily because if you think about the story you just told about FaceStealer, that was probably several hundred hours of work for that threat actor.

Title: Prompting GPT-Live for languages and regional accents
Context: Start with the right voice First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices
Full Text:
Even if a voice agent speaks Spanish, it can still sound off for the audience you’re building for. It might use an accent from a different region, choose wording that feels too formal, or read a price in a way a local speaker wouldn’t expect.

While the default options for GPT-Live can go a long way, there are additional considerations when building voice applications for audiences across languages and regions. Let’s look at voice selection and session instructions to get better results, using regional varieties such as Indian English, Spanish from Spain, and Emirati Arabic.

Start with the right voice

First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices. Some may already have a language or regional influence close to what you need: for example, Bossa and Tempo have a Brazilian Portuguese influence, while Nira is a Hindi voice. Test them with your own conversations before designing something new, as the built-in voices have high naturalness out of the box.

Use lowercase API names when selecting a built-in voice (for example, nira). The voice options guide has the complete current catalog.

If you need a more specific regional sound, you can use prompt-to-voice to generate a synthetic voice from a text description. Describe the region as precisely as you can, along with the pitch, pace, and vocal character you want. When generating a voice, you can use the script_hint field to add representative speech in the target language, and for a bilingual voice, include both languages in the sample text and describe the desired sound in each. Use original adult voices, and don’t impersonate real people. See the responsible-use guidance.

Eligible customers can also create a custom voice from a recording of a consenting speaker. Check the supported models and accents before choosing a recording-based voice. Before uploading, obtain the speaker’s express consent and secure the rights needed to use the recordings and the resulting voice in your application. The consent recording and reference sample must come from the same speaker. For any generated voice, make clear to listeners that they are hearing AI-generated speech.

Voice creation is ineligible for Zero Data Retention. See the data controls guide for the settings that apply to GPT-Live sessions.

Example: Hindi-influenced English with Nira

For an English-speaking agent serving users in India, set session.audio.output.voice to "nira" when creating the session, then add this prompt to the session instructions:

You are in a natural, clean English voice conversation. Speak fluent English in your natural Hindi-influenced Indian English accent. Keep that familiar rhythm throughout.

Example: Spanish from central and northern Spain

Suppose you’re building a shopping assistant for customers in Spain. Rather than asking for a generic Spanish accent, open the voice Playground and try this description in its prompt-to-voice workflow:

An original adult feminine voice, clear and lightly bright, with a medium pitch and gentle warmth. Speak Spanish with a natural standard Peninsular Castilian accent of central/northern Spain, with native Spanish vowels, consonants, stress, and sentence melody. Naturally distinguish s from z and c before e or i, without exaggeration. Use a moderately lively conversational pace, natural pauses, and varied intonation.

Pair it with a Spanish script_hint that gives the voice some ordinary connected speech to work with:

Hola, ¿qué tal? Estoy aquí para ayudarte. Podemos revisar las opciones con calma y elegir la que mejor encaje contigo. ¿Prefieres empezar por los colores o por las tallas? Esta chaqueta azul combina bien con unos zapatos cómodos. Acércate a la ventana para ver el color con luz natural.

This targets a particular variety of Spanish; the distinction described in the prompt isn’t universal across Spain or the Spanish-speaking world. With this prompt, you can generate a few candidates, keep the saved voice you prefer, and test it on a fresh sentence that wasn’t in the creation script until you’re satisfied.

Example: Emirati Arabic from Dubai

Arabic is another case where naming the language alone leaves a lot unspecified. For a conversational Dubai voice, an Arabic voice-design description might be:

صوت رجالي خيالي أصلي لرجل بالغ، بلهجة أهل دبي الإماراتية الحضرية المعاصرة. نطق الحروف وحركة الكلام وإيقاعه محليّان ومتناسقان، وتبقى الكلمات واضحة داخل الكلام اليومي المتصل. طبقة متوسطة تميل للانخفاض، ورنين دافي وصافي. يتكلم على مهله، والجملة تمشي كفكرة وحدة بنبر متنوع حسب المعنى.

The description asks for an original adult masculine voice with a contemporary urban Dubai accent, warm resonance, a slightly lower pitch, and connected, relaxed speech. Use a conversational Arabic script_hint as well:

هيه، شفت رسالتك. أنا هني صوب الحديقة، لا، أقصد صوب المواقف عند الباب الثاني. زين؟ المكان أهدى من اللي كنا فيه أمس. خذ راحتك، أنا توني واصل وما عندي شي مستعيل عليه. تبانا نتمشى شوي ولا نقعد؟ عادي، اللي يريحك.

In general, keep the voice design focused on sound. Managing details like whether the agent should answer an Egyptian caller in Emirati Arabic, switch into English, or confirm an order belongs in the session instructions, which we’ll cover later on.

Test the voice on what your application will actually say

But having a solid voice is only the starting point. Once you have a voice, you can build a small listening set with fresh sentences, realistic conversations, and the words or values your application handles most often to stress-test your voice.

A few edge cases are particularly useful to test:

Pronunciation in context: Include names, place names, product names, and specialized vocabulary. For Japanese, for example, give the agent a reading such as 承る（うけたまわる） and test it in a full support sentence. Or if your agent is pronouncing Lakshmi with a “my” ending instead of the intended “mee,” you can include guidance in the session instructions: लक्ष्मी — अंत में ‘क्ष्मी’, ‘क्ष्माई’ नहीं. For tonal languages, listen to important words in several sentence contexts.

Regional number conventions: The Indian system of numeration uses lakh and crore. One lakh is 1,00,000 (100,000), and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (10,000,000). For an English-speaking agent serving India, test whether ₹1,25,000 is spoken as “one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees” when that’s the intended convention.

Identifiers and corrections: Have a caller spell a fictional booking code, pause, and correct one character. Check that the agent waits for the correction and reads back the final code accurately. Test email addresses and other alphanumeric inputs your product accepts.

Mixed-language speech: Try an Arabic sentence containing an English product name and a price, then switch languages for the next turn. Check the spoken amount, currency, and product name separately from the accent.

For dates, amounts, and identifiers, validate what your application actually sends to the backend as well as what the caller hears. In many regions, 04/05 could mean two different dates, so it may be worth asking for clarification and reading the month back by name.

Prompt the agent for the conversation

Once you’ve chosen a voice, select it when creating the GPT-Live session. For a saved generated voice, set session.audio.output.voice.id to the returned voice ID. Put the agent’s role, language policy, delivery, and conversation behavior in instructions, and reinforce the original voice description there.

For a single-language application, write the instructions and examples in the language you want the agent to speak. Here’s a starting point for the Spanish shopping assistant:

Eres un asistente de compras. Habla en español de España, con acento castellano del centro y norte de la península, un ritmo conversacional y una entonación natural. Usa un tono cercano y respetuoso, sin sonar como un anuncio. Responde en español salvo que el cliente pida cambiar de idioma. Haz una pregunta cada vez. Si un nombre o una talla no están claros, pide que los repita. No confirmes precios, disponibilidad ni cambios en un pedido hasta que el sistema los haya verificado.

For a multilingual application, decide what should trigger a language switch and whether the underlying regional speaking style should remain fixed. Those are separate choices. For an Emirati Arabic and English assistant, first extend the earlier voice description with English delivery guidance, such as “In English, speak naturally with a light Emirati influence while keeping the same warmth and lower pitch.” Include representative English speech alongside the Arabic in script_hint, such as “I can check the available sizes for you,” before generating the bilingual voice. Then use a session policy like this:

Answer in the language of the caller's latest clear utterance. Switch between Arabic and English when the caller clearly switches. A short “OK,” number, name, or English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not by itself change the conversation language. When speaking Arabic, use conversational urban Emirati Arabic from Dubai, even when the caller speaks another Arabic variety. Prefer natural local wording where appropriate: شو for “what,” الحين for “now,” وين for “where,” and مب for negation. Keep the dialect coherent without exaggeration. In English, keep the same speaker identity. Use these as phrasing examples, not fixed answers: - Clarification: «تقصد العلبة الصغيرة ولا الكبيرة؟ وكم وحدة تبا؟» - Unclear name: «الاسم مب واضح عندي، ممكن تعيده أو تتهجّاه لي؟» Say amounts in the current conversation language and preserve their exact value and currency. Only confirm a lookup, price, or completed action when the backend supports that statement.

This example deliberately keeps the assistant’s Arabic dialect fixed while allowing English language switches. If your product should accommodate a caller’s requested dialect instead, write and test that policy explicitly. While voice descriptions and session prompts can steer an accent, they don’t guarantee that every reply will retain it, so test switches in both directions, including after a session reconnects.

Give examples of the register you want

Language and accent also leave the level of formality open. In Hindi, a courteous support agent might use आप and respectful verb forms. You can make that preference concrete in the session prompt:

ग्राहक से "आप" कहकर बात करें। सम्मानजनक भाषा और क्रिया रूपों का उपयोग करें। "हाँ, बताओ" की जगह "जी, बताइए" कहें। "तुम कैसे हो?" की जगह "आप कैसे हैं?" कहें।

The examples distinguish a casual “yes, tell me” from a more courteous equivalent. That gives the model a clearer target than simply asking it to sound professional. Use phrases a local support representative would actually say, and test them in context rather than translating an English script word for word.

For more on pronunciation cues, personality, greetings, and interruption behavior, see the GPT-Live prompting guide. The voice agent evaluation guide covers how to turn your listening cases into a repeatable evaluation as you change voices, prompts, or models.

Title: AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
Context: Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can...
Full Text:
Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities.

Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root.

In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix.

The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components.

The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7, Wiz, Xint, and Ikotas Labs, while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir, Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.”

Exploitation is likely

No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable.

Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic.

Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default.

Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers.“Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.”

Patch and check what you’re actually running

Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support.

Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http. Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up.For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d.Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted.

“The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”

Title: Another critical PHP security release has dropped
Context: The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical
Full Text: Apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” including at least one rated "critical." These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation said is very unlikely in real-world applications. Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here. The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites. While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers. The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®

Title: Outage or attack? Don’t let social media fill in the gaps
Context: AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible
Full Text:
Your banking app won’t load. Someone posts that an airline is having computer problems. Then you see a screenshot showing trouble at a cloud provider.

By the time you’ve scrolled through a few more posts, someone is telling you to withdraw cash and prepare for a nationwide blackout.

That is quite a journey from an error message.

Recent technology disruptions have provided plenty of material for this kind of speculation. As CNN describes, real outages have become mixed up with exaggerated reports, unrelated events, and conspiracy theories about what might happen next. A routine emergency alert test was even folded into the narrative.

The outages are real and so is the inconvenience. The problem with reporting on computer failures is how quickly “the system is down” becomes “the system is under attack.”

Non-malicious causes include faulty software updates, configuration mistakes, equipment failures, power interruptions, and damaged cables. Cyberattacks can also disrupt services by overwhelming them with traffic or using ransomware to make systems unusable. From the outside, both can have you staring at much the same unhelpful error message.

There has been a lot of this recently. So much so that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio felt the need to dismiss widespread concerns that the recent tech outages in the past week are connected.

What actually went down

During an outage, users want immediate answers, but investigators need time to establish what’s gone wrong. In that information vacuum, speculation thrives.

Let’s have a look at some recent events:

European refrigeration attacks disrupted cooling systems at some businesses. Separately, monitoring systems at three French blood-storage sites were affected, but staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised.

Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a latent software defect in networking gateways. Several organizations lost a full day of work.

The FAA nationwide ground stop in the US due to a telecommunications failure that disrupted some air traffic control communications. The ground stop led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays are ongoing.

JPMorgan Chase and knock-on banking problems were caused by a software bug in an on-premises hardware system that slowed transaction processing. The issue delayed transactions; no lasting damage has been reported.

Optimizely Web Experimentation supply-chain attack served malicious code on 178 popular websites. The issue was fixed rapidly, but visitors may have been exposed to malicious code that infected their devices.

There is an important distinction between outages caused by bugs and those caused by attacks, but the cause alone doesn’t tell us how disruptive an incident will be.

A technical failure can cause enormous problems without an attacker being involved. And an attack can cause harm without producing a spectacular outage.

We should judge the cause and the consequences separately and not assume that the most visible disruption must be the most sinister.

How social media amplifies the alarm

These things happen all the time, and sometimes the impact is bigger than at other times. That’s not a reason to panic or assume they’re all part of a big conspiracy. The recent claims that the US was about to face a 90-day blackout are a good example.

Combined with social media algorithms, these incidents can quickly pull people who show an interest in these incidents into a vortex of bad news, making it feel as if the end of the world is just around the corner. A feed full of outages is not evidence of an approaching “bugalypse.” Before accepting that explanation, ask what connects the incidents beyond the fact that they appeared in your feed.

The 90-day blackout claim shows how quickly genuine events can be turned into evidence for a much bigger story. Social media users turned a routine US emergency alert test into a prediction of a 90-day blackout. Some posts pointed to the Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop as evidence that the disaster was already unfolding. Others misrepresented military contingency planning as advance knowledge of an imminent crisis.

In reality, the alert was a scheduled test, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) explicitly said there were “no blackouts, no secret emergencies.” The test went ahead without the predicted catastrophe. That is the problem: Genuine disruptions were being used to support a much larger claim for which there was no evidence.

Where AI fits in

AI is helping both software vendors and attackers find more bugs. That can mean larger updates from Microsoft, Google, and others, covering more vulnerabilities at a faster pace. AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible.

Reports of misaligned AI agents can make it harder to see how AI can work both ways. That’s because the balance in cybersecurity isn’t where we want it to be yet. But in other fields, AI is helping scientists and researchers make large strides.

For an example of AI doing something genuinely useful, look at protein research. Determining a protein’s three-dimensional structure experimentally can take years. AlphaFold can often generate a useful prediction in minutes or hours, and its freely accessible database contains predictions for more than 200 million protein structures. Those models still need expert scrutiny and, where necessary, experimental validation. But they give researchers a starting point at a speed and scale that laboratory work alone could not match.

What to do

You can take cybersecurity seriously without treating every error message as a warning of impending disaster.

An outage deserves an explanation. An attack deserves investigation. Neither benefits from speculation presented as fact. Companies need to explain what they know, what they’re still investigating, and what customers should do. Those of us reporting on these incidents have a responsibility to make those distinctions clear and not connect the dots before we know whether there is a connection.

As readers, we can pause before sharing the next alarming prediction. Does it offer evidence, or just a collection of things that happened around the same time? Is there something useful we should do, or is someone simply giving us another reason to keep scrolling?

Keep your software updated. Protect your devices. Have a backup plan for services you depend on. But don’t let someone else’s take on things fill the gaps in what is known.
