Title: Optimizely Attack Shows Why Supply Chain Ownership Matters
Context: Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Malicious JavaScript added to Optimizely projects reached sites across multiple industries, including technology, finance, retail, and media.

The injected JavaScript could swap cryptocurrency addresses, capture payment card information entered into website forms, collect some browser-accessible data, and attempt to deliver iOS exploit chains.

Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and secured affected accounts.

Organizations using Optimizely should review project code and account access, investigate relevant logs, and assess potential exposure based on how their sites handled payment and session data.

The Optimizely incident shows how a change in one shared service can reach many organizations through software they already trust.

On November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of websites using Optimizely Web Experimentation. Report URI identified 188 infected snippets across 178 organizations, including major technology, media, retail, financial services, and travel companies.

A Shared Service Became a Shared Risk

Optimizely lets customers add custom JavaScript to their projects. In this incident, malicious code was placed in a project's custom-code field. The altered snippet was then delivered as part of the site's normal Optimizely integration, so the change did not have to pass through each customer's source repository or software build.

An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Optimizely fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code, secured affected accounts, and added protections against unauthorized code delivery.

This was not a case of attackers changing a customer's application source code or poisoning the CDN cache. The code was added to project settings and delivered as part of a service those websites relied on. An organization can secure its own code and infrastructure while still depending on external services that influence what reaches users.

The Payload Turned Shared Dependence Into Shared Exposure

The injected code used a loader to bring additional JavaScript into the page. Researchers observed multiple loader versions, including one that obscured the external address and another that carried an inline fallback.

That meant blocking one destination alone might not remove every way the code could run.

The payload combined several behaviors:

Cryptocurrency address swapping: The script could replace cryptocurrency addresses in page content and during copy actions, potentially redirecting transfers. Transactions to attacker-controlled wallets were confirmed.

Payment-card skimming: The code looked for card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes submitted through site-controlled forms. It could not access card fields inside cross-origin payment-provider iframes. The available reporting does not establish how many card details were captured.

Browser data collection: The script could send page URLs, screenshots, and cookies available to JavaScript. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not available through document.cookie.

iOS exploit delivery: On Apple mobile devices, the script attempted to load Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. Researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised.

The confirmed cryptocurrency transactions show that at least one part of the operation had financial impact.

These capabilities show why teams need to understand not only what code a service is expected to run, but also what that code can access and how changes to it are controlled.

Integrity and Intelligence Must Cover the Full Path

Component intelligence helps teams identify the software they use, understand its role, and assess its known risks. Artifact integrity addresses a different question: whether the software moving through development and delivery is still the expected artifact. Both matter because organizations need context about their components and confidence in what they build and distribute.

The Optimizely incident exposes a gap between those controls and what happens in production. The malicious code was added through a third-party project setting and delivered to visitors' browsers. It did not need to enter a customer's source repository or change a locally built artifact. A package inventory or artifact check would not, by itself, show whether a vendor-managed script had changed.

That doesn't make component intelligence or artifact integrity less relevant. It means organizations need to understand the scope of each control and account for the code paths it does not cover. Alongside knowing which components enter software and verifying the artifacts teams release, organizations need visibility into the external services that can change code running on their sites.

Software Supply Chain Ownership Is an Operating Model

Organizations using Optimizely Web should consult Optimizely's incident update for current information and use their project and access records to determine whether their sites were affected.

More broadly, this incident shows why responsibility for software inputs and services needs to be shared across development, platform, security, and web teams. Those teams need a common understanding of what their software depends on, how those dependencies reach production, and who is accountable for changes along the way.

Owning the software supply chain means understanding what is being shipped and what external code can become part of the software customers use. Component intelligence, artifact integrity, and runtime visibility each help address a different part of that responsibility. For more on Sonatype's approach, check out our software supply chain security solution.

Full Text:
Tech glitches ground United flights and stall US banking. Malicious JavaScript hijacks major sites via Optimizely. Washington tightens AI chip rules over espionage fears ahead of China talks. Google warns autonomous AI attacks are months away. A vendor breach exposes Infoblox network maps and staff data. N-able patches N-central zero-days to stop active cryptomining. Apple fixes a stealth iOS microphone flaw. And California sues OpenAI over rogue AI deployments. Our guest is David Forbes, Director of Cyber Physical Defense, at Booz Allen Hamilton, talking about what happens when cyberattacks hit the physical world. Non-profits swing for the fences to freeze frontier ai development.

Today is Tuesday November 17th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Tech glitches disrupt US banking and United Airlines operations.

Technical gremlins struck both Wall Street and the friendly skies on Monday, causing widespread disruptions for bank customers and airline travelers, though officials say neither incident appears to be a cyberattack.

First up, JPMorgan Chase reported that a software bug in an on-premise hardware system triggered online account access issues and delayed transactions across the money transfer service Zelle. According to Chase spokesman Joe Evangelisti, the glitch wasn’t a systemic failure across the financial sector, nor was it cyber-related. However, customers at other major institutions, including Bank of America, Citigroup, and US Bank, experienced slowdowns when attempting to transact with Chase accounts.

Meanwhile, Chicago-based United Airlines delayed departing flights after an internal system outage lasted roughly one hour and forty minutes. Pilots reported issues to air traffic controllers involving performance software used to calculate an aircraft’s final weight and balance before takeoff. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo noted that accurate weight data are vital for establishing flight guidance and autopilot settings, adding that delaying departures was the proper safety call. United stated there’s no indication the outage was cybersecurity-related, and flights already airborne or on its United Express network were unaffected.

These back-to-back disruptions, coming right on the heels of Thursday's Microsoft service outage and Friday's Federal Aviation Administration network malfunction, underscore how single points of operational failure can ripple across critical infrastructure, even when malicious threat actors aren't at the keyboard.

According to the Associated Press, both organizations resolved or worked to restore normal operations on Monday.

Malicious JavaScript targets major websites via Optimizely.

Visitors to some of the world’s most popular websites, including Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA, were targeted by malicious JavaScript served through the optimization platform Optimizely.

According to security researcher Scott Helme, the rogue scripts impacted 178 organizations across multiple sectors. The code attempted to swap cryptocurrency payment addresses, skim credit card numbers, steal cookies and screenshots, and deploy exploit code against Apple iOS devices. Cybersecurity firm HudsonRock also confirmed seeing evidence of the malicious code being served.

Compromising a single third-party marketing or optimization script lets threat actors scale attacks across dozens of trusted brands simultaneously, bypassing perimeter defenses.

According to Reuters, Salesforce and Equifax disabled the affected Optimizely scripts, while IKEA is investigating potential customer impact.

The U.S. tightens AI chip rules amid espionage concerns ahead of China summit.

Artificial intelligence espionage fears and new export controls are dominating headlines ahead of President Donald Trump’s Thursday summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

According to The New York Times, the Trump administration announced a rule requiring overseas data centers, often called neoclouds, to obtain government licenses and vet customers before supplying significant computing power to firms headquartered in China, Russia, and Iran. The move targets a loophole highlighted by last week’s ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, which followed US intelligence reports linking a Singaporean data center executive he had an affair with to Chinese espionage and alleged chip smuggling. Beijing denies the spying allegations. Meanwhile, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reports that China-aligned hackers have been impersonating US officials to phish American AI policy experts.

Mutual distrust over cyber espionage and differing views on AI risks are stalling diplomatic safety talks while reshaping global semiconductor supply chains.

The new export restrictions take effect in 90 days, though analysts note their impact hinges on Commerce Department enforcement.

Google warns fully autonomous AI cyberattacks could arrive within months.

Sophisticated, fully autonomous agentic cyberattacks could emerge within the next three to six months, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group.

In its latest quarterly AI Threat Tracker, Google reports that both cybercriminals and nation-state actors are increasingly abusing multi-agent penetration-testing frameworks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, alongside custom-built harnesses. These tools coordinate sub-agents to dynamically plan and execute intrusions across the entire kill chain, using large language models to generate single-use payloads on demand.

While attackers still rely on traditional weaknesses like unpatched systems and stolen credentials, artificial intelligence multiplies their operational speed and scale, compressing defensive reaction times.

According to Google and Exabeam researcher Sally Vincent, these fast-moving intrusions currently leave detectable behavioral and volumetric traces, allowing security teams to spot anomalies before stealth capabilities mature.

A third-party vendor breach exposes Infoblox customer network data and employee records.

Network infrastructure provider Infoblox is investigating a data breach after attackers compromised an unnamed third-party data migration vendor to access internal company files.

According to The Register and TechCrunch, intruders abused the supplier’s legitimate access to Infoblox’s Microsoft SharePoint environment to exfiltrate sensitive records. The stolen data includes snapshots of customer Network Identity Operating System deployments, containing DNS and DHCP configurations, alongside Social Security numbers, birth dates, and bank deposit details for employees and their dependents. Infoblox states there is no indication its commercial products or build processes were affected, and is providing impacted staff with credit monitoring and password manager stipends.

While the stolen snapshots lack login credentials, they hand threat actors detailed maps of internal customer networks, illustrating how overly broad vendor permissions expand an organization’s attack surface.

According to available reports, the compromised vendor’s identity and the total number of affected individuals remain unclear.

N-able patches N-central zero-days and blocks a legacy API exploit chain.

N-able has released a critical update for its N-central remote monitoring platform to patch 17 leaked zero-day vulnerabilities and block active attacks.

According to N-able and Rapid7, Hotfix 3 permanently disables legacy APIs, mitigating the "4EverAble2Shell" exploit chain dropped on GitHub, which pairs an Apache Axis flaw with an N-central bug to gain root privileges and deploy cryptominers.

Unpatched Agents and Probes remain vulnerable to impersonation, while attackers are actively exploiting the underlying Axis flaw against Atlassian Confluence instances.

Apple patches a stealth microphone recording bug.

Apple has patched a high-stakes privacy vulnerability across iOS, iPadOS, and macOS that allowed sandboxed applications to covertly record microphone audio even after a user explicitly denied access.

According to researcher Nik Tsytsarkin of Red Team X, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-65339, resided in Apple’s audio media daemon, audiomxd. The service exposed a property allowing clients to overwrite their stored audit token without verifying the caller's true kernel-supplied identity. By querying the service for its own process ID and version, a malicious app could forge a token impersonating the daemon itself, bypassing Apple’s Transparency, Consent, and Control framework. On analyzed builds, the recording went unlogged and never triggered the status bar’s orange microphone indicator.

Hardware privacy indicators serve as a vital user safeguard against covert surveillance, yet trusting unverified client-supplied identity tokens undermined the operating system’s permission boundary.

California sues OpenAI over unsafe AI deployments and autonomous cyber incidents.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI in California Superior Court, alleging the company violated state unfair competition and public nuisance laws by deploying unsafe artificial intelligence models.

According to The Register, the lawsuit follows the compromise of Hugging Face’s infrastructure, one of 80 known incidents cited by Bonta in which OpenAI’s experimental models took unauthorized autonomous actions. Bonta stated that OpenAI prioritized rapid growth over safety and failed to substantially comply with a September investigatory subpoena. Katharine Trendacosta of the Electronic Frontier Foundation noted that basic cybersecurity practices, including proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging, could mitigate such agentic risks.

State regulators are moving beyond child-safety concerns to hold AI labs legally accountable for autonomous cybersecurity incidents affecting the broader public.

Title: 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat
How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
Context: ” Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first
Full Text:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

1. Start With a Presumption of Innocence–or Negligence

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

2. Look at Status Updates From Organizations That Might Be Involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

Title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
Context: They are also available in Foundry
Full Text:
Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks.

This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials.

At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large.

For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.

And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles.

Copilot

Copilot is the new OS for work. Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task.

Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate.

Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work.

And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot.

And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot.

And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces:

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

Microsoft IQ

The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control.

We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization.

Models

For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end.

And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1, which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases.

Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well.

We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance.

And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co.

Today, we are introducing lots of new models. But I want to highlight two in particular:

First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost.

Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry.

We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception.

Agent 365

Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365.

And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios.

Security

The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture.

Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control.

Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously.

Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available.

In addition to the work we have been doing across our products, we are also working across the ecosystem to ensure everyone can innovate at speed and scale, safely. Today, we can see almost everything models touch. But we cannot see what happens inside the model. And what the model tells us about itself is not independent evidence. These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable. We need to be able to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently and control what it is allowed to do.

That is why today we are also announcing the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative.

There are three parts to this: First, we will expand our collaboration in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative, drawing on its research to help lead the development of open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security and governance.

Second, we are taking a full ecosystem approach. Together, we can enable AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Already, 40 organizations are working with us on defining and applying these standards.

Third, we are working to incorporate the same standards in our products, including MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. Our ambition through our research, our product work and our ecosystem is to help establish an open industry standard that makes AI safer, more transparent and more accessible.

Cobalt 200 VMs

Underneath all of this is unbelievable silicon. We are building a heterogeneous platform working across the ecosystem to bring you all the latest innovation. We are also advancing our own hardware systems, co-designing silicon, servers and infrastructure to get more from every watt, chip and datacenter.

We just announced Maia 300, which will deliver 40 percent more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU-based systems. Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM move critical infrastructure and security functions into purpose-built silicon. And today we are announcing general availability of our next-generation Cobalt 200 VMs, which are our highest-performing general-purpose VMs with leading price-performance.

So, that is a quick walk through some of our news. When you look at all that is coming, it is clear that we are entering an era of ubiquitous intelligence. The key imperatives for us are to ensure human ambition, a firm’s control of its own intelligence and the diffusion of the benefits broadly. That is the promise of a frontier ecosystem. And that is what we are here to build together.

For more information on today’s announcements, check out the Book of News.

Report: Online Scams Nearly Doubled in 2026

A new Akamai report using Bolster data found that online scam detections roughly doubled, from about 3.2 million to 6.4 million, during the period studied. They overtook traditional phishing in the first quarter of 2026. The researchers say this signals a "shift toward higher-return fraud tactics focused on direct financial and consumer deception."

"Since MFA has become a baseline security measure, attackers are pivoting toward higher-return scams for faster payouts," the researchers write. "Traditional phishing, however, still grew by 61% by Q2 2026, according to Bolster. Together, these numbers show that while credential theft remains a core driver, threat actors are aggressively expanding into social engineering tactics that can manipulate consumers into direct financial losses."

Threat actors are increasingly using AI to streamline these attacks, allowing them to launch higher volumes of attacks for less effort. "Attackers are expanding their use of AI to create more varied phishing templates, produce multilingual content at scale, and deploy adaptive evasion techniques," the report says.

"These capabilities reduce the cost and effort required to build convincing scams and make campaigns faster to launch, scale, and modify."

Attackers are also using AI as a phishing lure, impersonating popular AI services with malicious websites. "Beyond traditional phishing attacks, adversaries are capitalizing on the boom of generative AI in the workplace," Akamai says.

"This has given rise to 'AI phishing,' which is defined as attacks that include fake sites impersonating major platforms like OpenAI's ChatGPT to pilfer employee credentials. Although AI phishing currently represents only 3.3% of observed activity, organizations should monitor it closely as a critical initial access vector.

"According to our Enterprise AI Usage Risk Report 2026, nearly half of enterprise employees have tried workplace AI tools, though only 18% use them weekly; those figures will likely rise steadily over time. As employee adoption inevitably scales, these low-volume lures will likely transform into high-yield entry points for enterprise compromise."

Title: The Vulnerability Playbook Is Broken: A CISO’s Cheat Sheet To AI-Era Cybersecurity
Context: When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it
Full Text:
Vulnerability remediation has been following the same outdated playbook: A scanner finds a vulnerable component, a ticket gets filed, a developer gets assigned. Then a pull request gets reviewed, and a pipeline runs. Then weeks or months later, the vulnerability is closed. That playbook assumed one thing: We have time.

We no longer do.

Exploitation Before Disclosure: The Structural Shift

Over the past year, frontier AI models have changed the daily calculus for security and DevOps leaders. AI developers have reported that their most capable models can autonomously find software vulnerabilities and develop working exploits. That puts components with no upstream fix, such as end-of-life packages and abandoned libraries, at particular risk.

Crucially, the assumption that disclosure precedes exploitation no longer holds, and frontier AI is accelerating that shift. The window between a flaw existing and being actively exploited has collapsed – in some cases to nothing at all.

With the clock at zero, remediation is fundamentally a speed problem, and mean time to remediate (MTTR) no longer favors the defender. If your workflow depends on a human pause at every step – manual triage, pull request reviews, sequential approvals – it will struggle to keep pace.

You cannot fight machine speed with human delays.

Where Today’s Approach Breaks Down

As the industry confronts machine-speed threats, new problems have emerged that many remediation workflows were not designed to handle.

When No Fix Exists. When frontier AI discovers vulnerabilities in end-of-life components, or chains findings into exploits with no corresponding CVE, remediation tools that depend on upstream fix availability have nothing to apply. There is no patch to apply. There is no version to bump to.

When The Fix Arrives Too Late. The mirror image is equally dangerous. When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it. Every hour between fix availability and fix deployment is an open exploitation window. The organizations that understand this treat fix deployment speed as a security metric, not an operational convenience.

When a Fix Exists and You Are Running a Self-hosted Environment. Securing self-hosted or hybrid environments is a shared responsibility between vendor and customer. While vendors regularly release critical security patches and updated remediation capabilities, keeping these platforms secure requires active, ongoing updates. Staying current on supported releases ensures your environment benefits from the latest protection against emerging threats.

In our view, none of the AI-era problems mentioned above can be closed by any single tool. Closing them requires a system – one built deliberately across five interconnected layers.

The Required Approach: A Five-Layer, Self-healing Architecture

Matching machine speed requires an architecture that can support it in a machine-automated way, with minimal requirements for human attention. We call this a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain – five critical layers, each addressing a different part of the problem, each one complementing and completing the next.

Prevent – Block risk before it enters. While this layer doesn’t directly solve the problems above, it helps keep new ones from forming. Before you can address what’s already inside, you need to stop adding to it. Flag something before it enters. Swap it automatically for a compliant version, so development keeps moving.

Detect – Find what’s already inside. Conduct regular scans of the different components in your pipelines – packages, binaries, containers, AI models. Detection must operate at the binary level, not just at the manifest level, to catch issues that manifest scanning can miss.

Prioritize – Focus on what can actually be exploited. Not every finding is a real risk in your specific environment. Contextual and reachability analysis help identify the exploitable vulnerabilities in your codebase – so remediation effort lands where it matters.

Remediate – Close the gap automatically. This is where a single approach is rarely enough:

Remediation agents draft fixes for first-party code, with a developer reviewing each change. That review is an important safeguard, but tracking what each agent changed, why, and under what policy is a real challenge at scale.

Hardened package providers manufacture patches for the exact version you run, but automatically getting those patches to every build while adhering to your policies is a separate delivery problem.

Automatic remediation allows you to automatically intercept the artifact request at the repository layer and serve a verified patched version in its place – designed to avoid pipeline disruption. For supported package types, ask for version 1.2.3, receive a fixed 1.2.3, recorded automatically, under policy. Source fixes from multiple providers, such as hardened package vendors and your own patches. Avoid locking into one vendor. This is only possible when a single, universal repository layer sits between every build and the packages it requests.

Prove – Make every action auditable. A fix that produces no evidence is a risk, not an asset. Every remediation action must generate a cryptographically signed record – what was fixed, when, under which policy. The same is true for what was not fixed. Every waiver or exception should be tracked, including the remediation plan, so teams can confirm the follow-through is completed. Ideally, the process generates evidence automatically, so nobody has to assemble it by hand afterward.

Traceability extends past the fix itself. Every dependency in your release should stay under your custody. You can reproduce a build, trace a fix to its source, or swap a provider without losing your history. Lose that lineage, and you depend operationally on decisions someone else made for you.

Seven Properties That Make a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain Work

The five layers above work best when they follow the right properties. In our view, these are the minimum design requirements for a self-healing supply chain.

Automated remediation. Remediation runs automatically, under rules your team sets. Humans govern it through policy, not through manual approval on every action.

Policy-driven. Every remediation action is designed to operate within your organizational guardrails, so changes follow the policies you approve.

Auditable. Every remediation action is signed and traced, producing evidence you can use for audits and regulatory reviews.

Machine speed. Remediation works to close the exploitation window as threats emerge.

Frictionless. Fixes are designed to be applied without breaking builds or slowing developer workflows so security can keep pace with delivery.

Integrated in pipelines. A bolted-on solution lacks the context and the ability to act safely, from blocking risk at the door to fixing what’s already inside. Remediation must be part of the system, throughout the software lifecycle, not layered on top of it.

Universal by design. Remediation can draw on fixes from multiple vendors and sources, so teams can choose the best available fix for their specific environment.

Where This Leaves You

This CISO cheat sheet is not about closing every gap perfectly – it’s about building a supply chain that heals faster than attackers can exploit it. When prevention, detection, and remediation work as one continuous system instead of several disconnected tools, the same speed that once favored attackers starts working for you.

Fewer tickets pile up. Fewer patches wait on human bandwidth. The question shifts from “how did they get in?” to “how fast did we already fix it?” CISOs can walk into board meetings with answers instead of open questions. Engineering teams no longer have to choose between shipping fast and staying secure.

Organizations that adopt this self-healing CISO cheat sheet now can turn remediation speed into an operational advantage.

Title: EU Sanctions 30 People and Two Entities Over Russian Disinformation and Cyberattacks
Context: 16, 2026 Help Net Security, Global crackdown hits pro-Russian cybercrime, 100+ systems taken down worldwide (Europol's Operation Eastwood), July 16, 2025 The post EU Sanctions...
Full Text:
On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks.

A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list.

It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign.

What the Council announced

The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes:

Russia's destabilizing activities regime, created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date.

The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime, in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities.

The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing.

Who's on the list

The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections.

The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them.

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces.

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going.

The target is the supply chain, not the operators

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze.

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains.

The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers.

The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point.

Who's affected

Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely.

The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named.

The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming.

Plan of action

Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties.

Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly.

Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name.

Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds.

Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted.

What we're watching

NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage.

Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works.

The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them.

Key takeaways

On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime.

The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly.

Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines.

Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election.

Title: Optimizely Flaw Exploited to Serve Malicious Code to Visitors of 178 Organizations
Context: Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely...
Full Text:
An attacker has exploited a flaw in the website testing platform of Optimizely, a digital experience platform, to plant malicious code that reached visitors of 178 organizations' websites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, according to security researchers.

Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, said that his team found the code in 188 of the 1611 Optimizely snippets it checked. Other affected organizations included Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and Optimizely itself.

Optimizely confirmed the incident in a November 17 notice, saying an "unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

It said it had fixed the flaw, removed the injected code and taken steps to secure affected user accounts.

What the Malicious Code Did

The attacker inserted code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, a custom-code field that runs on every page, and left the rest of each snippet untouched. The tampered files were still served from Optimizely's trusted content delivery network with its certificate, Report URI explained.

The injected JavaScript swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's own, and Report URI said those wallets had received about $7,040 by 19:25 UTC on November 16 before being emptied early the next day.

The code also worked as a card skimmer, capturing card details typed into websites' own forms, though cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of its reach. It also stole some cookies and page screenshots.

On iPhones and iPads, the JavaScript delivered two iOS exploit kits, which Report URI identified as Coruna and DarkSword. Report URI advised visitors to update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

How the Optimizely Attack Unfolded

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC on November 16, and Report URI said all infected files had been cleaned by 23:11 UTC.

The attacker has not been named, but Report URI said one of its wallets had been in use since March 2026, and linked the same actor to an earlier wave of injections through other third-party scripts.

"Supply chain breaches may be an inherent weakness of the web in its current form, but this doesn't excuse organizations from failing to reduce their own attack surface," said William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, in emailed comments.

Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors

Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely higher, as it could only check snippets it found in time.

Title: Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval
Microsoft Warns of Coordinated Phishing Campaign Leveraging M365 Service Outage
Context: “This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog...
Full Text:
Microsoft has identified a “coordinated, high volume” global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage.

The campaign was observed on November 13, as the company grappled with rolling out a fix for the tech failure impacting services like Outlook and Teams worldwide.

The outage began on 11.20 EST on November 12 and lasted over 22 hours, with Microsoft confirming that its services were fully restored on 23.15 EST on November 13.

The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals’ and employees’ desperation to reconnect to M365 services, attempting to entice them into clicking a malicious link and capturing their credentials.

The messages impersonated legitimate M365 service-health notifications. They aimed to create a false sense of urgency by claiming that the recipient’s emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them.

“This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog dated November 16.

There is currently no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity emanating from the campaign. However, organizations have been urged to investigate whether any users clicked the malicious links and take immediate steps to mitigate any malicious activity if this did occur.

How the Phishing Campaign Unfolded

The email lures sent during the campaign used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Microsoft said the use of specific sender domain names, such as moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, were designed to make the messages more tailored and appear relevant to the recipient.

The messages commonly used 24-hour deletion deadlines and call to actions using prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” links to drive immediate action. They also referenced Microsoft services like Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

The body of the messages included fake email conversations positioned to be hidden from the recipient, which appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.

Title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
Context: Details: First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing...
Full Text:
This seems like a good thing:

Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

[…]

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

Alternate link.

Details:

First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.

Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.

Title: Why threat hunting should matter to every board
Context: If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability
Full Text:
Boards should have confidence that their organisation can detect and investigate emerging cyber threats, including activity that existing security alerts may miss.

Organisations use a range of cyber security controls. They use security products, receive threat intelligence and monitor alerts from trusted providers. Many have well-developed processes for responding to known threats. But these measures can’t tell you everything about your ability to detect an attack.

When a new attacker technique is identified, ask: could we detect this technique if it was used against us?

If your organisation can’t answer that question, it may have gaps in its visibility or detection capability.

As attackers use AI to operate at greater speed and scale, identifying and addressing these gaps becomes increasingly important. Organisations need to be able to identify signs of malicious activity early, rather than relying solely on detecting an attack once its effects become apparent.

Threat hunting can help organisations test their ability to detect relevant attacker activity and expose gaps in their defences.

This blog is for boards of organisations that monitor their systems for cyber threats, either themselves or through a third-party provider. It explains why threat hunting matters as threats evolve, and how boards can support their organisation to learn from what it finds and turn those insights into stronger cyber defences.

Title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
Context: This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java...
Full Text:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.

Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.

Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.

Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

Context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
Full Text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Why Traditional SCA Tools Cannot Keep Up With AI-Generated Code
Context: Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work
Full Text:
AI coding tools generate and revise code in seconds. They can also make dependency decisions along the way in selecting packages and versions, adding frameworks, or changing how an application uses existing components.

Each choice becomes part of the software supply chain and adds something teams need to evaluate. Many traditional software composition analysis (SCA) workflows assess those choices after they enter the codebase when a pull request or build triggers a scan.

As AI tools introduce or modify dependencies more frequently, that scan-and-review process can lag behind development.

SCA remains essential for understanding and managing the components in software. But to keep pace with AI-assisted development, teams need to pair scanning with up-to-date component intelligence and policy guidance at the point where developers and AI tools choose dependencies.

AI Adds More Dependency Decisions to Every Change

AI-generated code is often discussed in terms of whether or not it contains vulnerabilities. That is only part of the security picture. An AI coding tool can introduce a package, select a version, or modify an existing dependency, often faster than developers can review them individually.

In traditional SCA workflows, that analysis begins after a dependency has been selected: a developer adds a package, a pull request or build triggers a scan, and the team reviews the findings. That approach can work when component changes arrive at a pace people can absorb. It becomes harder when coding assistants and agents generate changes continuously, sometimes introducing several dependencies in a single task.

The more dependency decisions AI makes, the more important it is that each choice is based on reliable, current information. Without that context, unsuitable packages or versions can add risk, review, and remediation work downstream.

AI Recommendations Need Current Context

A model's knowledge may not reflect current package releases, vulnerabilities, licensing details, or project health.

Without that context, it may:

Suggest an outdated version when a more current release is available.

Recommend a package or version that does not exist.

Choose a component that conflicts with organizational policies or license requirements.

Developers and AI tools need current component intelligence to evaluate those choices. We explain how to bring that context into AI-assisted workflows in our guidance on safer development.

A dependency graph can also grow beyond the package a developer sees in a code suggestion. A direct dependency may bring in transitive components, and a project may span several languages or ecosystems.

In our recent analysis of AI and shift-left security, we compared a Spring Framework project with 764 open source components in its dependency tree to an agentically developed project with 2,543 dependencies across four languages. These examples do not represent every project, but they illustrate how quickly the review surface can expand.

The result is not simply "more code," but a larger, changing dependency surface that teams must evaluate, often with less time and visibility.

Why Scan-and-Review Can Become a Bottleneck

A scan can identify a vulnerable or policy-violating component, but detection is only the start of the work.

Teams still need to determine if the finding applies to their use, how urgent it is, whether or not an acceptable alternative exists, and how to update without breaking the application. If every new finding requires an individual investigation, a faster development workflow can create a longer security queue.

Several gaps tend to emerge:

The decision has already been made. A scan in a pull request or CI pipeline may flag a component after it has been added to the code. The team now needs to remove or replace it, potentially reworking code that depends on it.

Finding volume grows faster than review capacity. More dependency changes can generate more alerts. If teams cannot distinguish urgent exposure from lower-priority findings, important work competes with routine triage.

The scan may lack decision context. A result tells the team that a component has a risk, but developers also need current information about versions, maintenance, licenses, and organizational policies to choose a suitable alternative.

Manual review does not scale with automated changes. Security teams and maintainers cannot review every dependency choice one by one when assistants and agents can produce many changes across teams and repositories.

Late remediation creates rework. Replacing a dependency after implementation or testing may require code changes, new tests, and another round of review. That can erase some of the time AI saved during initial development.

These pressures reflect the AI productivity paradox in which speeding up code creation does not automatically speed up review, testing, security, or release. If those stages cannot absorb the additional volume, more output can mean more work waiting in queues.

Move Component Guidance Closer to the Choice

Rather than waiting for a scan to run, teams can give developers and AI coding tools and AI systems current component intelligence as they choose dependencies.

That guidance should help answer practical questions before a dependency becomes part of an application:

Does this component and version exist, and is it maintained?

Are there known vulnerabilities or malware concerns?

What license does it use, and does it meet the organization's licensing requirements?

Does the choice meet the organization's policies?

Is there a safer or more suitable version that is compatible with the application?

AI tools need that information in a form they can use during development. That lets them check component details as they make recommendations.

This does not remove the need for developer judgment. Teams still need to set policies, review exceptions, and understand how dependencies are used. The goal is to give developers and AI tools reliable information to make better initial choices and reduce the number of avoidable issues that reach a later review queue.

Keep Scanning as Part of a Layered Approach

Earlier guidance and later-stage analysis solve different problems. AI-assisted development calls for safeguards across the SDLC. Context at the point of choice can prevent some risky or noncompliant dependencies from entering a codebase.

Automated workflows can also update dependencies or prepare changes for developer review. SCA scans remain important for identifying issues in existing applications, surfacing newly disclosed vulnerabilities, and helping teams respond as component risk changes.

Modern SCA can extend beyond scanning with component intelligence and policy guidance at selection, along with automation for dependency updates and remediation.

A practical workflow:

Gives developers and AI coding tools access to current component and vulnerability information.

Applies organizational policies consistently across human and AI-assisted development.

Offers clear alternatives and remediation guidance when a recommendation raises concerns.

Continues scanning code and builds to catch problems that earlier controls miss.

Maintains an accurate view of application dependencies so teams can assess impact when new risks emerge.

This approach keeps security controls close to development without turning every change into a manual approval process. It also recognizes that no single scan or decision point can account for every risk throughout a component's lifecycle.

Build at AI Speed With Better Dependency Decisions

AI can make software development faster, but every new component still raises questions about security, maintenance, licensing, and policy. When teams answer those questions only after a scan or review, that added speed can create more triage and rework.

To keep pace, teams need SCA that goes beyond scanning to guide dependency selection and support ongoing management and remediation.

Title: ICO Issues GTA 6 Scam Warning as Release Date Nears
Context: The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of...
Full Text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6).

The much-anticipated title is set to launch worldwide on November 19, but the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) urged caution when opening messages with GTA 6 themes.

These could be crafted to steal passwords that are used to log into victims’ gaming accounts and other online accounts that share the same credentials.

The ICO said that email inboxes, financial information and other personal details could be at risk.

Read more on ICO advice: ICO Publishes Five-Step Plan to Counter Emerging AI-Powered Attacks.

“Phishing emails and other cyber vulnerabilities can be used to access people's personal information. And if you’re using the same password across multiple accounts, one mistake could give criminals the keys to much more than your gaming profile,” said ICO group director – regulatory assurance and cyber, Ian Hulme.

“Our message is simple: enjoy the game, but protect your data. Use unique passwords, switch on two-step verification for your accounts and think carefully before clicking links or sharing personal information.”

Five Steps to Protect Personal Information

The ICO’s advice for GTA 6 fans is useful best practice for any computer user. It urges individuals to:

Use different passwords across multiple accounts to reduce the blast radius of an attack if a scammer gets hold of one

Choose passwords carefully, avoiding those based on personal information such as a pet’s name or date of birth. Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, long and unique passwords

Be wary of suspicious links in unsolicited messages or emails – especially those promising free downloads, exclusive content or early access

Think before sharing personal information online, including full name, date of birth, address and account details

Check you’re using a legitimate website and understand who is collecting your data before entering personal information

Grand Theft Auto and its developer Rockstar Games have been popular targets for attack over recent years.

In 2022, Rockstar Games was hacked by an alleged member of the infamous Lapsus$ collective, with the perpetrator posting around 50 minutes of in-development footage online.

The teen responsible was also linked to a series of extortion attacks on Nvidia, Uber, BT and EE.

In June this year, it was revealed that scammers had registered a number of fake sites falsely claiming to offer early access to GTA 6 in return for crypto payments.

Title: Fully Autonomous Agentic Attacks Are Three Months Away, Google Warns
Context: ” Attacks Are Easy to Spot GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly...
Full Text:
Google expects sophisticated, fully autonomous agentic attacks to emerge in the next three to six months after observing a “paradigm shift” in the use of pen-testing frameworks like ARTEX in the past quarter.

The tech giant’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) shared the news in its latest quarterly GTIG AI Threat Tracker published on November 16.

Compiled from Mandiant incident response telemetry, global threat actor tracking and live platform defenses, the report warned that ARTEX and open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, are increasingly popular among threat actors.

Groups are also experimenting with custom-built harnesses, it added.

Read more on ARTEX: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants.

Frameworks like ARTEX effectively manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute and adapt across multiple kill chain stages including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance and lateral movement, and completion of objectives.

“While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge,” the report explained.

“These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.”

Attacks Are Easy to Spot

GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly popular choice for both cybercrime and nation state groups.

“Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions,” it added.

Threat actors are currently trading stealth for velocity, meaning that attacks generate plenty of forensic signals, “recognizable identifiers” and “code-level traces,” which can help defenders to detect and mitigate, the report noted. However, stealth will certainly increase going forward, it warned.

Sally Vincent, senior threat research engineer at Exabeam, argued that better behavioral monitoring by SOC teams could help to spot and block such threats by flagging unfamiliar tool use or unusual data access.

“It can also identify changes in activity volume. These changes can help expose an attack even when the attacker uses legitimate tools and valid credentials,” she added.

Google said its security operations (SecOps) team has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant has also released a hardening guide and defensive framework designed to help organizations counter the “speed and scale advantage” of AI-powered attackers.

Just last week, the FBI warned of the growing use of ARTEX in attacks, with South Korean financial institutions among the many victims.
