Title: From AI ambition to business impact
Context: They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning
Full Text:
Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs?

That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries.

Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams.

More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning.

The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together.

What this looks like in practice

Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations.

3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations.

Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees.

Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing. Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service.

KT, one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions.

Saint-Gobain, the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab.

Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same:

Begin with the value, not the technology.

Redesign the process, not just the task.

Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams.

Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one, so scaling doesn’t stall.

This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time.

New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact.

We’re holding ourselves to the same standard

If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to.

The real measure of success

The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build.

Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours.

Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company.

Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world.

Title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
Context: “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information...
Full Text:
Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC, commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain.

In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale.

What the research found

Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters.

Measurement is the next test. Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms.

Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks.

Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy.

“Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC.

AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings

Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses.

Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability.

Where scale stalls

66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them.

The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design.

Inside the Frontier Firm

IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause.

What they do differently comes down to five behaviors:

They invest ahead of plan. 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend.

They deploy AI broadly, across most of the business, not just a few teams.

They put agents to work. 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows.

They govern so they can scale. 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters.

They build skills everywhere. 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters.

At Bristol Myers Squibb, the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time.

Four disciplines for scaling AI value

The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off.

I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER. “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.”

Unlock model choice

Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data.

Redesign workflows around agents

Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters.

Govern decisions and actions

Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do.

Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.”

Measure and optimize value

Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest.

Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start.

Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch.

Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite

IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall.

What this means for business

The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation.

First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day.

Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business.

Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI.

The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next.

Title: Weak Passwords Expose SQL Servers to Cryptominer and Gh0st RAT
Context: Attackers Scan and Brute-Force SQL Servers A brute-force tool then tried usernames including "sa" and "admin" against more than 2700 passwords on each host the scanner found
Full Text:
A campaign has been breaking into internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances with weak passwords to install a Monero cryptominer and a Gh0st remote access trojan (RAT).

FortiGuard Labs, Fortinet's research team, uncovered the campaign in early October 2026 and rated it high severity, according to new research published on November 12. The report did not say how many servers were compromised or who was behind the campaign.

The initial Go payload contained the open-source Naabu port scanner. It retrieved an IP range from its server, scanned it for TCP port 1433, the default SQL Server port, and recorded the hosts that responded, before requesting another range and starting again.

Attackers Scan and Brute-Force SQL Servers

A brute-force tool then tried usernames including "sa" and "admin" against more than 2700 passwords on each host the scanner found.

After a successful login, the malware ran Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands on the server. T-SQL is SQL Server's extension of the SQL database language, adding programming features to standard queries.

The commands enabled xp_cmdshell, which runs operating system commands, then downloaded or unpacked a loader. They also scheduled the loader to run daily and placed a copy in the Startup folder so it ran when the server booted.

The loader pulled additional malware from an FTP server and registered each compromised server with the attackers' backend. The data sent back included the public IP address, country, Windows edition, processor and memory details, Windows installation time, user name and host name.

Cryptominer and Gh0st RAT Hide on Servers

One payload was a Monero cryptominer based on XMRig that used the compromised server's processor. It was named to look like a Microsoft Edge update, as were two of the scheduled tasks the malware created, and reported to the attackers when mining began.

Read more on cryptomining: Cryptominer Abuses Linux PAM to Hide From SOC Analysts

The second payload was a Gh0st RAT variant named after a Windows system process. Its command-and-control (C2) server had shut down before Fortinet's analysis, so researchers examined its code without running it.

The RAT supported keylogging, data theft and over 30 control commands, with plugins providing screen capture and remote desktop. It could also clear event logs, check for 78 security products by process name and steal data from the QQ messaging app.

For persistence, it used a registry Run key, a Windows service and a scheduled task that ran every 30 minutes.

In effect, the search had no built-in end, continuing for as long as the attackers’ server kept handing out new address ranges.

Title: WhiteArmor gang claims responsibility for latest cyber attack on shipping giant Maersk
Context: In 2017, the company was hit by the NotPetya malware attack which forced the firm to reinstall more than 4000 servers and 45,000 workstations, and ended up costing it up to US...
Full Text:
Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that one of its systems was broken into by hackers who have stolen data.

In a statement published yesterday on its website, the company said that it had detected the unauthorised access to a "local legacy system". The Danish company has not said which system was hit, what data was taken, or when the security breach occurred.

The firm has, however, said that it has seen no sign that the breach involved other Maersk systems, or that shipments have been impacted. To date, Maersk says that it has not seen any evidence that any sensitive information has been breached.

Responsibility for the attack has been claimed by the WhiteArmor cybercrime group, which has listed Maersk on its dark web leak site. There it demanded a ransom equivalent to US $5 million be paid within 30 days, for the 100GB worth of data it claims to have stolen from a platform built by LF Logistics, a firm that Maersk acquired in 2022.

WhiteArmor is a relatively new cyber-extortion group, having emerged late last month, but it is already claiming more than a dozen victims on its leak site including Chinese electronics and home appliance manufacturer Hisense.

According to WhiteArmor, its data haul from Maersk includes nearly 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords, purchase orders, advance shipping notices, signed delivery receipts, and 27,842 mobile device records containing phone numbers, email addresses, and IMEI numbers.

While Maersk has not confirmed the veracity of the hackers' claims, it is advising customers and partners to treat unexpected messages about the security breach with caution, and to always verify with a trusted contact at the company before taking any action.

Regular readers of the Hot for Security blog will be well aware that this is not Maersk's first brush with cybercrime.

In 2017, the company was hit by the NotPetya malware attack which forced the firm to reinstall more than 4000 servers and 45,000 workstations, and ended up costing it up to US $300 million.

On this occasion the breach appears to have happened because of IT systems inherited from an acquisition. As such it serves as a salutary reminder that when you buy a company you also buy its IT systems, and any security problems which may lurk within them.

Title: Hacked Asian Telcos Used to Intercept Taiwanese Calls and Texts
Context: Enea, a firm providing software for telecommunications and cybersecurity, named the actor SilentAir in its November 11 research, which also covers Liminal Panda, a group that...
Full Text:
A newly identified state-level actor has used compromised mobile operators in Asia to intercept calls and texts, mainly targeting subscribers in Taiwan. Enea has watched it since early 2025.

Enea, a firm providing software for telecommunications and cybersecurity, named the actor SilentAir in its November 11 research, which also covers Liminal Panda, a group that has attacked mobile operators.

The company said it saw a possible but unproven connection between the two groups.

SilentAir Targets Taiwanese Subscribers

Enea is highly confident that SilentAir operated at state level. The actor launched Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) and Diameter attacks from hijacked equipment in operators across at least six Asian countries, hitting targets in a dozen more countries and territories.

The attacks came in waves, from a handful of subscribers to several thousand in a month, with quiet spells of months in between. Interception accounted for 18.30% of SilentAir's activity, against 2.07% for the surveillance companies behind most signaling attacks.

For some targets, two-factor authentication (2FA) codes arrived moments after interception began, which Enea said showed an aim of breaking into their other accounts. Most of its other activity was silent SMS, texts that never show on the phone, sent largely to Taiwanese users around midnight.

Enea linked SilentAir to China-nexus operations with low confidence, citing the Taiwan focus, the lack of Chinese targets, working hours matching China's time zone and lulls over Chinese holidays. Some targets were political and government VIPs.

Read more on telecom espionage: Singapore Takes Down Chinese Hackers Targeting Telco Networks

Liminal Panda Expands GTPDoor

Enea said its firewalls spotted and blocked GTPDoor and other Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators from early 2026, detecting several hundred attempted command-and-control (C2) exchanges.

GTPDoor, a Unix backdoor, hides its C2 traffic in the GPRS Tunneling Protocol (GTP), which carries roaming data.

Enea said it had seen at least five to 10 operators infected by Liminal Panda, directly or through strong indications, and believed the true figure might be several dozen, concentrated in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

It also found a new GTPDoor version that rode on GTP-U, the part of the protocol carrying user data. That traffic is far heavier and, according to Enea, less closely watched, and unlike the control side it carries over into 5G. Enea believed the new version mostly served as a fallback.

CrowdStrike linked Liminal Panda to China-nexus operations in November 2024, also with low confidence.

Enea said it helped customers clear out Liminal Panda and alerted operators hosting SilentAir sources. It said both groups had been set back for now, but warned the conditions remained for them, or others, to return.

Title: Apple’s HomeView Tries Face Authentication Without FaceID
Context: “This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post
Full Text:
Apple's HomeView, which debuts on Friday, is a smart home device—think of it as a an iPhone-Apple Watch hybrid sitting on your counter—that can be personalized for up to six people and connected to each of their iCloud accounts. Using ambient face and voice data, it is designed to seamlessly switch between users while maintaining each of their privacy. You can ask HomeView about your schedule for the day and what movie your friend recommended in a text, but you'll be stopped from asking about your roommate's travel plans or her texts from last night. The feature doesn't rely on one of Apple's battle-tested biometric locks, like FaceID or TouchID, though. Instead, it uses new “person recognition” technology built off of an Apple architecture for securing sensor data.

This is a key departure for Apple. On the one hand, the company has still been very careful to think about security and privacy comprehensively. Not only does HomeView check for your face and voice before accessing your data from iCloud, it is also designed like an Apple Watch to check that your iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network as the HomeView and has been recently unlocked (with FaceID or a PIN). On the other hand, expanding the architecture used to process biometric data and authenticate users creates more opportunities for mistakes and potential vulnerabilities. And when it comes to attempting to access users' Apple data, both law enforcement and exploit brokers consistently go to great lengths to attempt to break the company's on-device defenses.

FaceID is built for the use case where a person is staring at their device head-on from less than an arm's length away. It provides reliable security that’s difficult to defeat because it stores your biometric data on a special, physically isolated chip known as the Secure Enclave—first introduced in 2013 for the iPhone 5s. The architecture is so robust that Apple also relies on the Secure Enclave as the foundation of a device's entire encryption scheme. But Apple concluded that FaceID wasn't the best fit for the HomeView, because it needs to bounce quickly between users and relies on AI processing, which can't all be squeezed into the Secure Enclave.

As a result, HomeView uses Apple's recently announced Secure Exclave (note the “x”) to handle the video and audio data the device uses to evaluate who is in a room at a given time. Apple says it has actually been laying the groundwork for the Secure Exclave for a long time—early versions of the architecture were already in place for the iPhone 16 and 17 and MacBook Neo. Instead of being an entirely separately chip, the Secure Exclave is a dedicated, memory-protected space in recent Apple processors. It is in Apple's latest S11 chip for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, as well as the A20 Pro chip for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

Even though the Secure Exclave isn't based on the tried and true Secure Enclave technology, Apple argues that it is robust and expands the company's ability to secure a range of features, including improving the security of existing mechanisms. In a blog post on Thursday, the company even goes into some detail about how it used the mathematical technique known as formal verification to vet the “microkernel” designed for the Secure Exclave.

“This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as ‘Hey Siri’ detection,” the company writes in a blog post. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks.”

HomeView and the MacBook Neo also use the Secure Exclave to govern the indicator light that tells users when their camera or microphone is active. The goal is to isolate this process and the chain of command governing it to make it even more difficult for attackers to try to disable an indicator light when it should be on or stop it from coming on in the first place.

The HomeView's “person recognition” technology is simply not as comprehensive as FaceID, though, and it is possible that the technology is more susceptible to reconstructed 3D depth map attacks—and potentially voiceprint attacks—than FaceID.

Of course, you don't have to have a HomeView in your house. Or if you do, you can use it on guest mode or a less involved “personalized” mode that only incorporates things like your playlists for other users to access as well and doesn't access calendar or Messages data. But as Apple forges deeper into AI integration, HomeView's departure from FaceID provides insight into the scale of the changes Apple is planning.

Title: Lego Takes BrickLink Marketplace Offline After Detecting Unusual Activity
Context: In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to...
Full Text:
Lego Group has taken its BrickLink Marketplace offline after identifying “unusual activity” on the platform.

An update was posted on November 11 by the Danish toy firm which said, “Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.”

The company is currently investigating the activity and said it needs to “fully understand” what has happened before bringing the site back online.

“That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.”

It is not yet known how long the downtime is expected to last and when the service will be reinstated.

BrickLink is an online marketplace owned by Lego Group where independent third-party sellers can buy and sell individual Lego parts – like eBay for Lego. Lego Group acquired the online marketplace in 2019.

The Lego marketplace has previously found itself at the center of security issues. In 2022, Salt Labs investigated BrickLink and found API vulnerabilities that could have allowed an attacker to take over user accounts, leak personal data and gain access to internal production data. Lego resolved the issues after Salt Labs disclosed the issues to the toy firm.

In November 2023 BrickLink was taken offline for a number of days due to a suspected cybersecurity incident.

Professional Lego reviewer Jay Ong, who runs Jay’s Bricks Blog, covered the downtime and noted that users were prompted to update their passwords. However, in an email he received at the time of the incident, he was reassured that his BrickLink account had not been compromised.

Managing Software Supply Chains with Nexus Repository Insights
Context: But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job
Full Text:
Repositories give teams a managed source for build inputs. They proxy public registries, host internal components, and cache packages.

That work remains essential. But when more tools and teams contribute to a build, making software available is only part of the job.

A typical build may pull in open source packages, container images, internal libraries, build tools, and models. Those inputs can enter in several ways:

A developer selects a package or library.

A pipeline retrieves a component.

An AI agent adds a dependency while changing code.

A package manager resolves additional components required by another library.

Because many requests happen automatically, teams need to understand what is available through the repository path and manage the inputs that pass through it. A repository used as a common source can provide that operational inventory.

From Artifact Storage to Software Inventory

A repository inventory describes the artifacts available through a managed source: the formats and versions present, and the assets associated with them.

Sonatype Nexus Repository gives teams a shared view of components available through managed repositories.

That view can help answer questions such as:

Which packages, containers, models, and build artifacts are available through managed repositories?

Which versions are hosted or cached?

Do developers, pipelines, and agents have a common route to obtain software?

Can teams apply consistent policies and block known malicious packages before they are served?

Consider a routine library update. An engineer needs to know which versions are available through the team's standard source. When groups rely on separate proxies or caches, that information may be scattered. A shared repository gives teams a common place to check.

Know What the Repository Inventory Covers

A component appearing in Nexus Repository does not necessarily mean it is included in a deployed application. It means the component is managed or available through the repository. Build records or software bills of materials (SBOMs) identify what went into a specific application or release.

These views answer different but related questions. The repository inventory helps teams manage the shared supply path, and build records help them understand a particular application's inputs.

That distinction also gives teams a place to start an investigation. If a package is flagged, they can check whether it is managed or available through Nexus Repository, then consult build records to determine if a specific application included it.

Software Delivery Starts With What Teams Pull

Most applications depend on components their teams did not write. A developer might add a framework, then a package manager resolves its dependencies.

Each component can affect the application in different ways:

Compatibility: Dependencies may conflict or require specific versions.

Maintenance: Older or unsupported components create upgrade work.

Security: A malicious component requires investigation and response after it enters development.

When these issues surface after development begins, replacing a component can mean code changes, retesting, and release delays.

AI tools can add or update dependencies while changing code, increasing the pace of these choices. A faster request does not tell a team whether or not a component is compatible, maintained, or appropriate for the application. Teams need enough context to assess those choices before they create work downstream.

Make Centralized Access the Trusted Default

A shared repository gives teams a consistent place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs their workflows need. Developers and pipelines can use a managed route that supports their existing package managers and build tools, instead of relying on separate collections of external sources.

In day-to-day work, that shared route gives teams a common way to:

Retrieve components and resolve dependencies through the organization's configured source.

Manage the software supply chain used by multiple groups, rather than having each team create its own process.

Route AI agent dependency requests through the same access and intake controls used for other development activity.

Configure supported formats in a shared repository, giving new projects a starting point instead of another one-off source.

Centralizing access does not automatically cover packages downloaded directly from a public registry or through an unconfigured source. Teams need to route the requests they want managed through Nexus Repository. Then it can serve as a common point for understanding the inputs it handles and applying controls to them.

Block Known Malicious Packages Before They Reach the Build

Nexus Repository sits between upstream sources and the developers, pipelines, and agents requesting software. In the Pro+ and Enterprise editions, malicious package protection and configurable policies can block known malicious packages when requests pass through a protected repository path, before Nexus serves them downstream.

If a malicious package reaches a development environment, teams may need to remove it from the repository if it is still available, then:

Identify which developers, pipelines, or agents retrieved and used the package, and assess what systems or data may be affected.

Assess which systems or credentials it could access.

Determine whether builds or releases incorporated it, and assess downstream exposure.

Blocking the package at the repository can prevent that specific input from becoming part of a downstream investigation. Developers also do not have to identify every suspicious package name or track each campaign themselves. Protection applies where component requests already flow.

Repository protection does not address every dependency or application risk. A component can cause compatibility problems without being malicious, so teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. For dependency decisions and remediation, Sonatype Guide brings intelligence into developer and AI coding workflows to inform component choices and help automate dependency upgrades.

Within the broader Nexus One platform, Guide complements repository protection: developers and agents get support for choosing and updating dependencies, while Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise can block known malicious packages and packages flagged as suspicious, even before they are confirmed as malicious at the repository request point.

Make the Repository Part of Delivery Infrastructure

A reliable software supply chain depends on more than where artifacts are stored. Teams need a consistent way to find the components their workflows can use, manage the route those components take, and keep known malicious packages out.

Nexus Repository provides a shared source for the software inputs it manages. Its Pro+ and Enterprise editions add protection that can block known malicious packages at the point where components enter the managed path. Together, these capabilities give teams both a clearer view of available inputs and a way to stop a known threat before it reaches a build.

As developers and AI agents make more requests, that combination becomes more useful. Teams can make software available through a common route, apply consistent controls to incoming requests, and understand the limits of what the repository inventory shows.

Know what your teams can get through the repository. Make trusted access the default. Block known malicious packages before they become part of the work.

Title: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
Security Teams Must Shift from Patching to Mitigation in the AI Era
Context: This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026
Full Text:
Organizations “can’t patch their way out of AI” and should instead focus on mitigation post exploitation, according to Dick O’Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec.

Speaking at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11, he highlighted the rapid closure of the patch window in the past year due to attackers’ use of AI.

This includes AI tools to discover zero day flaws and the ability of frontier models to chain together low severity vulnerabilities together to find an exploit path in a way that humans would not be able to do.

The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard that tracks the collapse of the time-to-exploit (TTE) window from CVE disclosure to confirmed exploitation in the wild, has estimated that the average time to exploitation following public disclosure of a vulnerability fell from one week in 2025 to one day in 2026. The initiative estimates that in 2027, the average time will be a minute.

“Once you get to a minute, what can you do realistically? We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities,” O’Brien said.

This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026. O’Brien noted that the first reporting exploitation attempts occurred just 19 minutes after the bug was made public.

Amazon also reported that it detected an attempted exploitation attempt of PHP2Shell four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

Agentic AI Orchestration of Attacks

Post-initial access, O’Brien expects threat actors to move to an era of “end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks” in the next year, shifting away from using AI as an assistant for various tasks towards AI agents undertaking attacks independently.

This will make it significantly harder for defenders to detect and respond to threats in their organization’s environments.

There have been a few examples of this approach taking place so far. One of these was an attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026, where AI agents executed the post-compromise tasks independently, operating at machine speed.

According to an analysis by Symantec of the DIVD’s assessment report, it took 19 minutes for the attack to be detected, but 19 hours before the response began, and a further nine hours to contain the threat.

“This is what we’re dealing with. It’s an excess of 24 hours and you know you’re not going to be able to compete with something operating at machine speed,” O’Brien commented.

Adopt an Assume Exploit Mindset

In this landscape, organizations should assume exploitation is inevitable and prepare for machine-speed post-compromise activity, where attackers can move from initial access to impact in minutes rather than days.

“Stop measuring your mean time to patch and start measuring your mean time to mitigate. Assume an exploit is going to happen and the plan your preparedness for that,” O’Brien advised.

He set out a number of mitigation tasks security teams can immediately focus on:

Behavior blocking

Default-deny for what runs

Least privilege for every agent and token

Inspect data before it leaves the device

Bind every agent action to a named human

“These are all things you can start doing right now before you become aware of a vulnerability,” O’Brien added.

Longer-term, organizations must integrate detection and protection technologies on multiple different control points, which are able to identify behavioral anomalies of rogue or malicious AI agents.

Title: NCSC Launches Cyber Adversary Testing to Boost Resilience
Context: The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience
Full Text:
The UK’s leading cybersecurity agency has officially launched a new scheme designed to help providers of critical infrastructure to test and improve their cyber resilience.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) first trailed its Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme at the CYBERUK 2025 conference.

It enables participating organizations to choose from a list of vetted suppliers, who then craft realistic attack plans based on reconnaissance of the client’s IT infrastructure, exposure, and threat landscape.

“Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs),” the NCSC said.

Read more on cyber resilience: NCSC: Observability and Threat Hunting Must Improve

The CyAS scheme is designed to complement other NCSC initiatives including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA).

It’s hoped that larger organizations, CNI providers, and government bodies in particular use these frameworks to better understand their security posture and resilience.

“By enabling rigorous, realistic end-to-end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organizations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber-attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience,” said NCSC CTO, Ollie Whitehouse.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.”

Building Resilience for the Future

Andrew Costis, engineering manager of the Adversary Research Team at AttackIQ, welcomed the program's potential to help organizations test how well they can keep essential services running during an attack.

“Building each simulation around an organization’s actual exposure should uncover weaknesses that a generic assessment might miss. Looking back, that approach could have exposed gaps in detection or containment before an intrusion became a prolonged outage,” he said.

“The longer-term opportunity is turning those findings into an ongoing practice through adversarial exposure validation.”

Costis explained that teams must repeat attack behaviors after remediating a weakness to check that the fix has worked, and adapt their testing over time as environments change.

“An assured provider gives organisations confidence in the assessment’s quality,” he concluded. “Keeping those lessons current will determine how much resilience the scheme delivers.”

CyAS will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), so that the NCSC can test demand, refine its methodology, and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

Full Text:
Maersk has disclosed a data breach involving one of its IT systems after an extortion group claimed to have stolen 100GB of logistics-related data from the company.

The shipping and logistics giant said in a November 11 statement that it “identified unauthorized access and data extraction,” although it didn’t clarify when.

The incident affected one of its “local legacy systems from a previous acquisition,” it claimed.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI [electronic data interchange],” the statement continued.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.”

Read more on Maersk: Cybersecurity Lessons from Maersk’s Former CISO

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, explained that ownership of acquired systems often gets muddled during M&A activity, and pen tests should be carried out during due diligence to highlight any potential weaknesses.

“Acquired systems arrive with their own credentials, their own patch schedule, and connections into the parent network that were set up during integration and rarely revisited,” he added.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at Ridge Security, said that investigators must determine what the attackers accessed, how they gained entry, and whether the boundaries separating that legacy environment from other systems held.

“The lesson for organizations isn't simply to replace every legacy system,” he argued. “It's to know what you own, understand how inherited systems connect to the business, and continuously validate that the security controls protecting them work.”

WhiteArmor Ramps Up Attacks

A relatively new extortion group known as WhiteArmor claimed responsibility for the attack, according to screenshots of its leak site posted to X.

The group demanded $5m in Bitcoin, claiming it has 100GB of data linked to Maersk’s OCF/LF logistics platform, including driver records and plaintext passwords, staff accounts, delivery receipts, purchase orders, inventory rows, and mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEIs.

WhiteArmor is behind a string of extortion demands ranging from $140,000 to $20m over the past month, according to Nick Harris, CISO at cyber-insurance specialist Assured.

Citing publicly available information on the attacks, he noted that several were aimed at the logistics sector, with victims including J.B. Hunt, Ryder, and Echo Global Logistics.

“The group describes itself as focused on data-theft extortion, intending to expand into ransomware, and says its encryptor is nearly complete,” Harris said.

“The protections include cycling credentials, strong access controls, data loss alerts and validating third parties. If they aim to recruit insiders, treat security as “assumed compromise” and set controls and alerts accordingly.

Maersk hasn’t experienced a serious cyber incident since the NotPetya campaign in 2017, which it claimed at the time may have cost the firm as much as $300m.

Greater automation and analyst efficiency. High-confidence AI classifications trigger automated email processing, reducing manual triage and helping teams focus their expertise on complex, high-risk threats.

Title: Securing persistent agents like OpenClaw at OpenAI
Context: With traditional software, we have relied on configuration and code to be deterministic and for threats to come (mostly) from external attackers
Full Text:
When OpenClaw launched almost a year ago, it showed the world the capabilities of a persistent agent. Unlike regular codex sessions which involve a fixed goal and human steering, persistent agents run 24/7 with a broad scope and the ability to proactively take actions without user input.

While persistent agents are extremely capable, their real world deployment has been limited to date. These deployments present many novel challenges compared to traditional software. With traditional software, we have relied on configuration and code to be deterministic and for threats to come (mostly) from external attackers. Persistent agents can change their configuration and write arbitrary code to accomplish a goal. Attacks come from the inside when agents take misaligned actions.

At OpenAI, we currently have persistent agents deployed across the entire company, including hundreds of OpenClaw agents. This post covers some of the controls we’ve adopted to enable OpenClaw deployments at OpenAI.

Separate trusted and untrusted execution

In order to secure persistent agents, we needed to isolate trusted deterministic logic from un-trusted LLM execution. Trusted logic includes critical components like networking, identity, and sandboxing. This is traditional static code that, outside of software bugs, should behave as configured. Agents, the environment they execute in, and the code they write are considered untrusted. This is an environment where agents can dynamically generate code to accomplish a goal with no hard guarantees on behavior.

To support this in OpenClaw, we ended up implementing remote harness execution in the open source project. This enabled the OpenClaw Gateway to run in a separate container (and in our case, a separate cluster), from the agent harness.

By implementing the split, we could treat the gateway, the component that configured the agent, as trusted deterministic code and focus on sandboxing the agent workload as untrusted code.

Enforce hard security boundaries

Security boundaries for agent workloads are enforced through sandboxing, which limits the actions agents can take.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the following sandbox controls:

network: control what endpoints an agent can access - we used an organization-managed allowlist with explicit denials for restricted endpoints

workspace: control what files an agent can access - we only allowed writes to agent working directories

process: control what processes an agent can access - we relied on process isolation via codex linux sandbox

secrets: control what secrets an agent can access - we manage secrets through a credential broker so secrets are not visible to the agent

For our OpenClaw deployment, we used the built-in sandbox from the codex harness. The following are some of the settings we employed, divided between requirements.toml (restrict what options are available in codex configuration) and config.toml (actual codex configuration). Note that we also enabled some additional security controls - removing the ability to use danger-full-access mode and relying on cached web search which routes web searches through OpenAI’s own index for search queries.

requirements.toml

# Exclude unrestricted "danger-full-access" sandbox mode. allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"] # Permit cached hosted search, but not live hosted search. allowed_web_search_modes = ["cached"] # Require the managed network proxy. experimental_network.enabled = true # Prevent user-level configuration from expanding the domain allowlist. experimental_network.managed_allowed_domains_only = true # Allow only these destinations; replace with the workload's required hosts. experimental_network.allowed_domains = [ "github.com", "api.github.com", "codeload.github.com", ] # Explicitly block these destinations, including cloud metadata endpoints. experimental_network.denied_domains = [ "pastebin.com", "*.pastebin.com", "webhook.site", "metadata.google.internal", "169.254.169.254", ]

config.toml

# Select the permission profile defined below. default_permissions = "openclaw" # Use cached hosted search. web_search = "cached" [permissions.openclaw.filesystem] # Allow reads needed by the minimal runtime environment. ":minimal" = "read" # Allow reading and modifying the agent's workspace. "/home/dev-user/openclaw-workspaces" = "write" # Allow reading managed assets without modifying them. "/home/dev-user/read-only" = "read" # Prevent access to SSH credentials. "/home/dev-user/.ssh" = "deny" [permissions.openclaw.network] # Permit network access through the administrator-required proxy. enabled = true # Do not inherit an upstream proxy. allow_upstream_proxy = false # Keep the proxy's local/private-address guard enabled. allow_local_binding = false # Disable the SOCKS5 listener. enable_socks5 = false # Disable SOCKS5 UDP support. enable_socks5_udp = false # Do not permit proxy listeners on non-loopback addresses. dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy = false # Do not permit unrestricted Unix-socket access. dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false [shell_environment_policy] # Preserve default filtering of sensitive environment variables. ignore_default_excludes = false # Remove GitHub credentials from agent command environments. # This does not hide credentials stored in accessible files. exclude = [ "GH_TOKEN", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_BASIC_AUTH", "OPENCLAW_GITHUB_READONLY_BASIC_AUTH", ] [apps._default] # Disable apps unless individually enabled. enabled = false # Disable destructive app operations by default. destructive_enabled = false # Disable open-world app operations by default. open_world_enabled = false

Add model-based safeguards

All the controls we talked about so far are static in the sense that they rely on traditional deterministic code to prevent an agent from taking misaligned actions. As models get smarter, it’s critical that we also have defenses that scale with compute - aka other models.

With Auto-review, a second agent can monitor and approve the actions of a primary agent. Constantly requiring human review creates review fatigue where humans are trained to blindly accept all permission prompts. By using an LLM based reviewer as a filter, we reserve human attention for high value approvals. This is a feature that is natively supported in both OpenClaw and Codex.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we enforce auto review on all agent actions.

Split agent identity from user identity

When an agent takes an action, we need to be able to audit said action, give the agent access to resources, and distinguish whether that action was initiated by the agent or by the user. Agent identity gives us the means to do so. There are emerging specifications like WAG that give agents their own access to resources, and others like XAA that let agents act on behalf of the user through OAuth delegation. Note that agent identity is different from service accounts which provide separate API access for bots. The two should be used together - for example, your agent should act with its own agent identity and access third party services through service accounts which are linked to said identity.

For our OpenClaw deployment, each agent has a unique identity that is associated with a ChatGPT Service Account. This gives each agent its own inference credential separate from the user’s and allows teams to connect custom plugins to the agent. This also lets us audit agent actions and if needed, turn off inference.

Observe everything

Comprehensive observability lets operators understand the full lifecycle of agents - from how they were configured to what actions they took. With persistent agents, it’s critical that we have this coverage in order to trace and detect misaligned actions.

For our OpenClaw deployment, we log everything - every configuration change on the control plane and all turns from the agent. Because agent turns can contain sensitive information, these logs are locked down and only available to a select few individuals in the security team.

Closing thoughts

We are still at the beginning of the adoption curve when it comes to deploying persistent agents. The lack of established best practices makes it difficult to adopt agents in many enterprises today.

When we rolled out our internal pilot of OpenClaw at OpenAI, we witnessed a huge jump in both productivity and adoption, from both technical and non-technical teams across the company. We now have over 500 agents that run proactively in the background doing meaningful work - everything from automatically opening PRs in response to product feedback to continuously running data experiments on new features.

During OpenAI dev day, we announced OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE), an open source vendor neutral agent control plane. If you use OCE, you can launch an agent with many of the safeguards we talked about built-in when using the standard codex preset. Note the project is currently still in the pilot phase and that we plan to get to a 1.0 release by the end of the year.

We believe many of AI’s biggest gains in industry will come from persistent agents. By sharing what we’ve learned and building OCE in the open, we hope to make them safer for everyone to deploy.

Title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
Context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
Full Text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

Title: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
Context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
Full Text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.
